### AssertJ 3.27 — `actual()` Direct Access and New `CompletableFuture` Assertions

AssertJ 3.27.0 added `.actual()` on assertions to directly access the object under test, and introduced two new `CompletableFuture` assertion methods for async testing:

```java
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.time.Duration;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class AsyncOrderServiceTest {

    @Test
    void completesWithValueMatchingWithin() {
        CompletableFuture<String> future = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> "ORDER-123");

        // New in 3.27: isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin
        // — asserts completion within timeout AND that value matches predicate
        assertThat(future)
            .isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin(
                value -> value.startsWith("ORDER-"),
                Duration.ofSeconds(2)
            );
    }

    @Test
    void completesExceptionallyWithin() {
        CompletableFuture<String> failingFuture = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("payment failed"); });

        // New in 3.27: completesExceptionallyWithin
        // — asserts that the future completes with an exception within timeout
        assertThat(failingFuture)
            .completesExceptionallyWithin(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
            .withThrowableOfType(RuntimeException.class)
            .withMessage("payment failed");
    }

    @Test
    void accessActualValueDirectly() {
        var order = new Order("ORD-001", "PENDING");

        // New in 3.27: actual() — retrieves the subject to use in further assertions
        // without ending the AssertJ chain
        String rawStatus = assertThat(order)
            .satisfies(o -> assertThat(o.getId()).startsWith("ORD-"))
            .actual()   // returns the Order instance
            .getStatus();

        assertThat(rawStatus).isEqualTo("PENDING");
    }
}
```

---

### AssertJ 3.27 — `doesNotMatch(Predicate)` and Predicate Description Overloads

AssertJ 3.27 added `doesNotMatch(Predicate<T> predicate, String description)` and description overloads for `anyMatch` / `noneMatch` to produce readable failure messages.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class OrderValidationTest {

    @Test
    void noOrderHasFutureDeliveryDate() {
        List<Order> orders = loadTestOrders();

        // noneMatch with description — failure message reads:
        // "Expecting no element of actual to match '<has future date>'
        //  but found: [Order{id='ORD-003', deliveryDate=2028-01-01}]"
        assertThat(orders).noneMatch(
            o -> o.getDeliveryDate().isAfter(LocalDate.now()),
            "has future date"
        );
    }

    @Test
    void orderStatusIsNotExpired() {
        Order order = new Order("ORD-001", "ACTIVE");

        // doesNotMatch(Predicate, description) — replaces verbose isNotEqualTo chains
        // for predicate-based negation assertions
        assertThat(order)
            .doesNotMatch(
                o -> o.getStatus().equals("EXPIRED"),
                "order is expired"
            );
    }

    private List<Order> loadTestOrders() {
        return List.of(
            new Order("ORD-001", "ACTIVE"),
            new Order("ORD-002", "SHIPPED")
        );
    }
}
```

### AssertJ 3.27.7 — CVE-2026-24400 XXE Fix in `isXmlEqualTo`

AssertJ 3.27.7 fixed CVE-2026-24400: `isXmlEqualTo()` used a `DocumentBuilder` without disabling external entity (XXE) processing. Malicious XML input could trigger SSRF or local file reads during test execution when testing XML-processing code.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class XmlResponseTest {

    @Test
    void xmlResponseMatchesExpected() {
        String actual = """
            <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
            <order id="ORD-001">
              <status>SHIPPED</status>
            </order>
            """;

        String expected = """
            <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
            <order id="ORD-001"><status>SHIPPED</status></order>
            """;

        // Safe after AssertJ 3.27.7 — XXE processing is disabled in DocumentBuilder
        // Always use assertj >= 3.27.7 when asserting on XML from external sources
        assertThat(actual).isXmlEqualTo(expected);
    }
}
```

**[community] — AssertJ `isXmlEqualTo` before 3.27.7 is exploitable when test input includes attacker-controlled XML:** If tests load XML from external sources (API responses, files, databases) and pass it to `isXmlEqualTo`, an attacker who can influence those sources could embed `<!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>` and read arbitrary files from the CI runner filesystem. Upgrade to AssertJ 3.27.7+ immediately if tests receive XML from external systems — even in CI-only test code, the attack surface is real in shared build environments.

### Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 25 Additions [community]

**JUnit 6 requires Java 17 minimum — projects with mixed Java 11 modules must split test scope [community]** — JUnit 6 dropped Java 8/11 support entirely (Java 17 is the baseline). If your project has a multi-module Maven/Gradle build where some modules still target Java 11 (e.g., a shared API module), you cannot use JUnit 6 in those modules' test scope. Options: (1) bump all modules to Java 17+ (recommended), (2) stay on JUnit 5.13.x in legacy modules and use JUnit 6 only in new modules, (3) use the JUnit Platform Launcher programmatically from a Java 17 test harness that calls into Java 11 module code via reflection. Do not mix JUnit 5.x and 6.x JARs on the same classpath — the API packages overlap and cause `LinkageError`.

**Spring Boot 3.4 `@MockitoBean` and `@MockBean` produce different context cache keys — mixing them doubles test startup time [community]** — Spring Boot 3.4 introduced `@MockitoBean` as the successor to `@MockBean`, but both annotations are supported simultaneously. The context cache key includes the full set of mock definitions. A test class using `@MockitoBean(OrderService.class)` and another using `@MockBean(OrderService.class)` create separate cached contexts, even though the resulting bean configuration is identical. Grep the test codebase for both annotations and unify to `@MockitoBean` in one atomic commit to restore context sharing.

**Testcontainers 2.0 `ScriptSplitter` O(1) optimization only applies to ANSI SQL — PostgreSQL `$$` dollar-quoting still breaks [community]** — The Testcontainers 2.0 release notes highlight the ScriptSplitter optimization from O(n*m) to O(1). However, this optimization only applies to standard ANSI SQL tokenization. PostgreSQL dollar-quote stored procedures (`$$...$$`) are still parsed incorrectly. Any init scripts containing `CREATE FUNCTION` with `LANGUAGE plpgsql` and dollar-quoting will fail at container startup with a confusing syntax error. Workaround: use Flyway or Liquibase migrations (which have correct PostgreSQL dialect parsers) for container initialization instead of `withInitScript()`.

**AssertJ 3.27.0 `extracting(Function...)` return-type change was reverted in 3.27.3 for Kotlin 1.9 compatibility — you may be on a version with different behavior [community]** — The return type of `assertThat(list).extracting(Function...)` changed to propagate the common supertype in 3.27.0, broke Kotlin 1.9 projects, and was reverted in 3.27.3. Teams that pinned to exactly 3.27.0–3.27.2 will observe different type inference behavior from those on 3.27.3+. Verify AssertJ is at 3.27.3 or later before upgrading Kotlin to 2.x — the interaction between AssertJ's type propagation and Kotlin's type inference is version-sensitive.

**Mockito 5.22 UUID class corruption under JDK 25 was a silent data corruption bug, not a test failure [community]** — Mockito 5.22.0 fixed a `UUID.class` corruption issue that occurred when the inline mock maker rewrote `UUID` bytecode under JDK 25 EA. The corruption manifested as UUID strings producing incorrect `toString()` output (e.g., truncated hyphens) in assertions — tests comparing UUID string output could pass in JDK 21 but produce subtle false positives in JDK 25 EA builds. If you were running JDK 25 EA with Mockito < 5.22, audit any tests that asserted on UUID string representations and re-run the full suite on JDK 25 with 5.22+ to confirm correctness.

**Spring Boot 3.5 profile name validation breaks CI pipelines that use branch names as Spring profiles [community]** — Spring Boot 3.5 enforces that profile names may only contain letters, digits, dashes, and underscores. CI pipelines that dynamically activate profiles named after Git branches (e.g., `feature/PROJ-123-new-api`) will fail at application startup with `InvalidProfileNameException`. The slash in typical feature branch names is now rejected. Update CI pipeline scripts to sanitize branch names before passing them as profile names (e.g., replace `/` with `-` and strip any characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`).

### JUnit 6 — `CancellationToken` and Fail-Fast Test Execution

JUnit 6.0.0 introduced a `CancellationToken` mechanism and first-class `--fail-fast` support in `ConsoleLauncher`. The fail-fast mode cancels test execution after the first failed test, enabling faster feedback loops for long-running suites where early failures signal a broken build.

```java
import org.junit.platform.launcher.Launcher;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.LauncherExecutionRequest;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.LauncherDiscoveryRequest;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.LauncherFactory;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.LauncherDiscoveryRequestBuilder;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.CancellationToken;
import org.junit.platform.engine.discovery.DiscoverySelectors;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.listeners.SummaryGeneratingListener;

public class FailFastTestRunner {

    /**
     * Run tests and cancel execution the moment any test fails.
     * Useful for smoke-test suites where a single failure is actionable.
     */
    public static SummaryGeneratingListener.Summary runWithFailFast(Class<?>... testClasses) {
        LauncherDiscoveryRequest discovery = LauncherDiscoveryRequestBuilder.request()
            .selectors(DiscoverySelectors.selectClasses(testClasses))
            .build();

        // Create a cancellable token — share it with the listener
        CancellationToken token = CancellationToken.create();
        SummaryGeneratingListener listener = new SummaryGeneratingListener();

        try (Launcher launcher = LauncherFactory.create()) {
            launcher.execute(
                LauncherExecutionRequest.builder()
                    .launcherDiscoveryRequest(discovery)
                    .cancellationToken(token)
                    .build(),
                new FailFastListener(token, listener)  // cancels token on first failure
            );
        }

        return listener.getSummary();
    }
}

// Listener that cancels execution upon first failure
class FailFastListener implements org.junit.platform.launcher.TestExecutionListener {
    private final CancellationToken token;
    private final org.junit.platform.launcher.TestExecutionListener delegate;

    FailFastListener(CancellationToken token,
                     org.junit.platform.launcher.TestExecutionListener delegate) {
        this.token = token;
        this.delegate = delegate;
    }

    @Override
    public void executionFinished(
            org.junit.platform.launcher.TestIdentifier id,
            org.junit.platform.engine.TestExecutionResult result) {
        delegate.executionFinished(id, result);
        if (result.getStatus() == org.junit.platform.engine.TestExecutionResult.Status.FAILED) {
            token.cancel();  // stops remaining test execution
        }
    }
}
```

**When to use `--fail-fast` vs full suite [community]:** Use fail-fast in CI pre-merge pipelines where the goal is "is this branch broken?" rather than "what is the full defect list?" Fail-fast saves wall-clock time when tests are slow. Do NOT use fail-fast for nightly or weekly suite runs where you want full defect counts for trend reporting. In Maven use: `mvn test -Djunit.platform.launcher.interceptors.enabled=true`. For ConsoleLauncher add `--fail-fast`. **[official] — `CancellationToken.cancel()` is idempotent; calling it multiple times has no additional effect beyond the first cancellation.**

---

### JUnit 6 — JFR Integration Moved to `junit-platform-launcher`

JUnit 6 removed the standalone `junit-platform-jfr` module and integrated Java Flight Recorder support directly into `junit-platform-launcher`. This simplifies dependency management but requires a dependency update for projects that recorded test execution events.

```xml
<!-- BEFORE (JUnit 5): separate JFR module required -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-platform-jfr</artifactId>
    <version>1.11.x</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

<!-- AFTER (JUnit 6): JFR is built into launcher — no extra dep needed -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-platform-launcher</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

```java
// Enable JFR recording for a test suite via ConsoleLauncher arguments:
// java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=test-suite.jfr,duration=5m \
//      -jar junit-platform-console-standalone.jar --scan-classpath

// Or programmatically via launcher configuration — no extra imports needed:
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.LauncherConfig;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.LauncherFactory;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.Launcher;

class JfrTestSuiteRunner {
    Launcher buildLauncher() {
        return LauncherFactory.create(
            LauncherConfig.builder()
                .enableTestExecutionListenerAutoRegistration(true)
                // JFR listener auto-registers when JVM has an active recording
                .build()
        );
    }
    // Combine with -XX:StartFlightRecording to capture per-test events in .jfr file
    // JFR events: jdk.junit.TestStarted, jdk.junit.TestFinished, jdk.junit.TestSkipped
}
```

**[official] — JFR events recorded by JUnit 6 include test start/end, skipped events, and failed test details. These events integrate with JDK Mission Control for visual drill-down into slow or flaky tests.** **[community] — The removal of `junit-platform-jfr` causes `ClassNotFoundException: org.junit.platform.jfr.FlightRecordingListener` at test startup if the old artifact remains on the classpath alongside JUnit 6. Remove `junit-platform-jfr` from `pom.xml` or `build.gradle` when migrating to JUnit 6 — the `org.junit.platform.jfr` package now lives inside `junit-platform-launcher`.**

---

### Spring Boot 3.4 — `MockMvcTester` Fluent AssertJ API

Spring Boot 3.4 auto-configures `MockMvcTester` when AssertJ is on the classpath. `MockMvcTester` wraps `MockMvc` with a fluent AssertJ-style assertion API, eliminating the imperative `perform()` / `andExpect()` pattern and producing richer failure messages that include the response body.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import java.util.List;

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;          // AssertJ-based wrapper — auto-configured in 3.4+

    @MockitoBean
    ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void getProducts_returnsJsonArray() {
        given(productService.findAll())
            .willReturn(List.of(new Product(1L, "Widget"), new Product(2L, "Gadget")));

        // Fluent MockMvcTester API — no andExpect() chains needed
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/products"))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith("application/json")
            .bodyJson()
            .hasPathSatisfying("$[0].name", name -> assertThat(name).isEqualTo("Widget"))
            .hasPathSatisfying("$[1].id",   id   -> assertThat(id).isEqualTo(2));
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_returns404_whenNotFound() {
        given(productService.findById(99L)).willReturn(java.util.Optional.empty());

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/products/99"))
            .hasStatus(404)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.error").isEqualTo("Not found");
    }
}
```

**`MockMvcTester` vs classic `MockMvc` [community]:** The classic `MockMvc` API returns `ResultActions` with `andExpect(status().isOk())`. Failure messages say only "Status expected: 200 but was 404". `MockMvcTester` includes the full response body in the failure message, dramatically reducing debug time. **[community] — `MockMvcTester.bodyJson()` returns `null` for non-JSON responses — always assert `.hasContentTypeCompatibleWith("application/json")` before chaining `.bodyJson()`, or the chain produces a `NullPointerException` with an unhelpful stack trace.**

---

### Spring Boot 3.4 — `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase` Auto-Detects Container DataSources

Spring Boot 3.4 enhanced `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase` to automatically detect when the DataSource is provided by a Testcontainers `@ServiceConnection` bean, applying `replace=Replace.NONE` implicitly.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@DataJpaTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryPostgresTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    // BEFORE Spring Boot 3.4 — required explicit replace=Replace.NONE annotation:
    // @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
    //
    // Spring Boot 3.4+: @AutoConfigureTestDatabase detects @ServiceConnection
    // DataSource beans and applies Replace.NONE automatically.
    // Remove the manual annotation to avoid IDE warnings about redundant configuration.

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Test
    void savesOrderToPostgres() {
        Order order = new Order("customer-42", "PENDING");
        orderRepository.save(order);

        assertThat(orderRepository.findByCustomerId("customer-42"))
            .hasSize(1)
            .first()
            .extracting(Order::getStatus)
            .isEqualTo("PENDING");
    }

    @Test
    void findByStatus_returnsMatchingOrders() {
        orderRepository.saveAll(List.of(
            new Order("cust-1", "PENDING"),
            new Order("cust-2", "SHIPPED"),
            new Order("cust-3", "PENDING")
        ));

        assertThat(orderRepository.findByStatus("PENDING")).hasSize(2);
        assertThat(orderRepository.findByStatus("SHIPPED")).hasSize(1);
    }
}
```

**[official] — Before Spring Boot 3.4, every `@DataJpaTest` with Testcontainers required `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)` or the auto-configured H2 DataSource silently replaced the container DataSource.** Tests appeared to pass against H2 but used PostgreSQL-specific queries that failed in production. Spring Boot 3.4 eliminates this footgun automatically. **[community] — Teams that added `replace=NONE` as a workaround can now remove it — the annotation is harmless but redundant after 3.4.**

### Spring Boot 4.0 — `RestTestClient` for Reactive Controller Testing

Spring Boot 4.0 introduced `RestTestClient` in the `spring-boot-resttestclient` module, providing an auto-configured wrapper around `WebTestClient` for reactive (`WebFlux`) controller tests. It replaces the pattern of manually constructing a `WebTestClient` with base URL and codec configuration.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.reactive.WebFluxTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.reactive.server.RestTestClient;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import reactor.core.publisher.Flux;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

@WebFluxTest(InventoryController.class)
class InventoryControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    RestTestClient client;       // auto-configured by spring-boot-resttestclient

    @MockitoBean
    InventoryService inventoryService;

    @Test
    void getItems_streamsResponse() {
        given(inventoryService.streamAll())
            .willReturn(Flux.just(
                new Item("SKU-001", 10),
                new Item("SKU-002", 5)
            ));

        client.get().uri("/api/inventory")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBodyList(Item.class)
            .hasSize(2)
            .contains(new Item("SKU-001", 10));
    }

    @Test
    void getItem_returns404_whenMissing() {
        given(inventoryService.findBySku("UNKNOWN"))
            .willReturn(Mono.empty());

        client.get().uri("/api/inventory/UNKNOWN")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound();
    }
}
```

```xml
<!-- Add to pom.xml for Spring Boot 4.0+ reactive controller testing -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-resttestclient</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

**[official] — `RestTestClient` is auto-configured by `@WebFluxTest` and `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment=RANDOM_PORT)` in Spring Boot 4.0+. No manual `WebTestClient.bindToController()` setup is needed.** **[community] — Do not mix `RestTestClient` with the deprecated `@AutoConfigureWebTestClient` annotation in Spring Boot 4.0 projects — the two produce separate `WebClient` instances with different codec configurations. Use `RestTestClient` exclusively and remove `@AutoConfigureWebTestClient` from the test class.**

### Java Records as Test Fixtures — Wither Pattern

Java records are immutable, but tests frequently need slight variations of a canonical test object. The "wither" pattern provides `with*` methods that return a new record with one field changed, enabling terse test variants without repeating all constructor arguments.

```java
// Production record with wither methods for test ergonomics
public record Order(
    String id,
    String customerId,
    String status,
    java.math.BigDecimal total,
    java.time.Instant createdAt
) {
    // Wither methods — each returns a new instance with one field changed
    public Order withStatus(String newStatus) {
        return new Order(id, customerId, newStatus, total, createdAt);
    }
    public Order withTotal(java.math.BigDecimal newTotal) {
        return new Order(id, customerId, status, newTotal, createdAt);
    }
    public Order withCustomerId(String newCustomerId) {
        return new Order(id, newCustomerId, status, total, createdAt);
    }
}

// Test class using wither pattern — base fixture shared across test methods
class OrderServiceTest {

    private static final Order BASE_ORDER = new Order(
        "ORD-001", "CUST-42", "PENDING",
        new java.math.BigDecimal("99.99"),
        java.time.Instant.parse("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z")
    );

    @Test
    void cancelsOrder_whenStatusIsPending() {
        Order pending = BASE_ORDER.withStatus("PENDING");
        assertThat(orderService.cancel(pending).status()).isEqualTo("CANCELLED");
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsCancel_whenStatusIsShipped() {
        Order shipped = BASE_ORDER.withStatus("SHIPPED");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> orderService.cancel(shipped))
            .isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("Cannot cancel a SHIPPED order");
    }

    @Test
    void appliesDiscount_forHighValueOrders() {
        Order highValue = BASE_ORDER.withTotal(new java.math.BigDecimal("500.00"));
        assertThat(orderService.applyDiscount(highValue).total())
            .isLessThan(new java.math.BigDecimal("500.00"));
    }

    private final OrderService orderService = new OrderService();
}
```

**[community] — Why wither pattern beats builder pattern for records in tests:** Builders require re-specifying every field to create a variant. Wither methods require only the field being changed. For records with 5+ fields, wither methods reduce per-test-variant line count by 60–70%. **When NOT to use wither on production records:** If the record class is in a shared API module consumed by external teams, adding `with*` methods couples the API to test convenience. Instead, create a `OrderTestFixtures` companion class in `src/test/java` that provides the wither functionality without modifying the production record.

### Sealed Classes — Exhaustive Pattern Matching in Tests

Java 17+ sealed classes allow `switch` expressions verified by the compiler to cover all permitted subtypes. Tests should leverage this exhaustiveness check to catch missing branches when new subtypes are added to a sealed hierarchy.

```java
// Sealed type hierarchy — compiler enforces all subtypes are handled in switch
public sealed interface PaymentResult
    permits PaymentResult.Success, PaymentResult.Declined, PaymentResult.Error {

    record Success(String transactionId, java.math.BigDecimal amount) implements PaymentResult {}
    record Declined(String reason) implements PaymentResult {}
    record Error(String code, String message) implements PaymentResult {}
}

// Exhaustive switch test — adding a new subtype causes compile error, not silent test gap
class PaymentResultHandlerTest {

    private final PaymentResultHandler handler = new PaymentResultHandler();

    @Test void handlesSuccess() {
        var r = new PaymentResult.Success("TXN-001", new java.math.BigDecimal("50.00"));
        assertThat(handler.describe(r)).isEqualTo("Payment of 50.00 succeeded");
    }

    @Test void handlesDeclined() {
        var r = new PaymentResult.Declined("Insufficient funds");
        assertThat(handler.describe(r)).isEqualTo("Payment declined: Insufficient funds");
    }

    @Test void handlesError() {
        var r = new PaymentResult.Error("TIMEOUT", "Gateway timed out");
        assertThat(handler.describe(r)).isEqualTo("Payment error [TIMEOUT]: Gateway timed out");
    }

    static class PaymentResultHandler {
        public String describe(PaymentResult result) {
            // No default — compiler flags missing subtypes at compile time, not at runtime
            return switch (result) {
                case PaymentResult.Success(var txn, var amt) ->
                    "Payment of " + amt + " succeeded";
                case PaymentResult.Declined(var reason) ->
                    "Payment declined: " + reason;
                case PaymentResult.Error(var code, var msg) ->
                    "Payment error [" + code + "]: " + msg;
            };
        }
    }
}
```

**[community] — When NOT to use exhaustive switch in tests:** If the sealed hierarchy lives in a third-party library that may add new subtypes in patch releases, an exhaustive switch in your test code will fail to compile after the library upgrade. In those cases, add a `default -> fail("Unhandled subtype: " + result.getClass())` branch to catch new subtypes at test runtime rather than compile time. Use compile-time exhaustiveness only for hierarchies you own.

### JUnit 6.1 — `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` Annotations

JUnit 6.1 introduced `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` to pin the JVM-wide `Locale.getDefault()` and `TimeZone.getDefault()` for the duration of a test. This is thread-safe in parallel execution and replaces manual `Locale.setDefault()` + `@AfterEach` teardown patterns.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.util.Locale;

class CurrencyFormatterLocaleTest {

    @Test
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultLocale("de-DE")
    void formatsNumberWithGermanLocale() {
        // de-DE: thousands separator is ".", decimal separator is ","
        String formatted = NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.getDefault()).format(1234.56);
        assertThat(formatted).isEqualTo("1.234,56");
    }

    @Test
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultLocale("en-US")
    void formatsNumberWithUsLocale() {
        // en-US: thousands separator is ",", decimal separator is "."
        String formatted = NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.getDefault()).format(1234.56);
        assertThat(formatted).isEqualTo("1,234.56");
    }

    @Test
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultTimeZone("America/New_York")
    void schedulerUsesNewYorkTimezone() {
        java.util.Calendar cal = java.util.Calendar.getInstance();
        assertThat(cal.getTimeZone().getID()).isEqualTo("America/New_York");
    }

    @Test
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultLocale("fr-FR")
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultTimeZone("Europe/Paris")
    void combinedLocaleAndTimezone() {
        assertThat(Locale.getDefault().toLanguageTag()).isEqualTo("fr-FR");
        assertThat(java.util.TimeZone.getDefault().getID()).isEqualTo("Europe/Paris");
    }
}
```

**[community] — `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` live in `org.junit.jupiter.api.condition` — NOT in `org.junit.jupiter.api`. Many IDEs do not auto-import from the `condition` subpackage. If imported incorrectly, the annotation is silently ignored — `Locale.getDefault()` inside the test still returns the JVM default.** Verify by adding a quick assertion on `Locale.getDefault()` the first time you use the annotation. Also note: `@BeforeAll` methods run BEFORE the per-test locale is applied — move locale-sensitive initialization to `@BeforeEach` if it must run under the annotated locale.

### JUnit 6.1 — `@EmptySource` Extended to `Iterable` Subtypes

JUnit 6.1 extended `@EmptySource` to inject empty instances of `Iterable` subtypes beyond the standard `Collection` types, covering custom `Iterable<T>` implementations.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.EmptySource;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.NullAndEmptySource;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class BatchProcessorTest {

    private final BatchProcessor processor = new BatchProcessor();
    private final InputValidator validator = new InputValidator();

    // @NullAndEmptySource is shorthand for @NullSource + @EmptySource
    @ParameterizedTest
    @NullAndEmptySource
    void processOrders_handlesNullAndEmptyGracefully(List<Order> orders) {
        assertThat(processor.process(orders)).isEmpty();
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @EmptySource
    void validateItems_rejectsEmptySet(Set<String> items) {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> validator.validate(items))
            .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
            .hasMessage("Items must not be empty");
    }

    // JUnit 6.1+: @EmptySource also supports custom Iterable subtypes
    @ParameterizedTest
    @EmptySource
    void processIterable_handlesEmptyIterable(Iterable<String> tokens) {
        assertThat(processor.count(tokens)).isZero();
    }

    // Complete null / empty / blank coverage for string validation tests
    @ParameterizedTest
    @NullAndEmptySource
    @ValueSource(strings = {" ", "\t", "  "})
    void rejectsNullEmptyAndBlankInput(String input) {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> validator.validateName(input))
            .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }
}
```

**[community] — `@EmptySource` does NOT inject empty strings or empty primitives.** For empty string coverage, use `@ValueSource(strings = {"", " "})` or `@EmptySource` + `@ValueSource`. The typical null/empty/blank trifecta for string validation is: `@NullAndEmptySource` (covers null and `""`) plus `@ValueSource(strings = {" ", "\t"})` (covers whitespace-only strings). **[community] — `@EmptySource` for custom iterables requires JUnit 6.1+. On JUnit 5.x or 6.0.x, passing a custom `Iterable` parameter type to `@EmptySource` throws `ParameterResolutionException: No ParameterizedTestExtension supports...` because the empty value factory does not know how to instantiate the custom type.**

### Testcontainers — Kafka Container vs `EmbeddedKafkaBroker` Tradeoff

Spring Boot testing provides two approaches for Kafka consumer tests: `EmbeddedKafkaBroker` (in-process, no Docker, Spring-specific) and `KafkaContainer` via Testcontainers (real Docker broker, version-accurate). Spring Boot 3.4 added first-class `KafkaContainer` support via `@ServiceConnection`.

```java
// Option A: EmbeddedKafkaBroker — fast, no Docker required (~200ms startup)
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.kafka.test.context.EmbeddedKafka;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
@EmbeddedKafka(partitions = 1, topics = {"orders"})
class OrderConsumerEmbeddedTest {

    @Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, String> template;
    @Autowired OrderConsumer consumer;

    @Test
    void consumesOrderEvent() throws Exception {
        template.send("orders", "{\"id\":\"ORD-001\",\"status\":\"PLACED\"}");
        assertThat(consumer.getLatch().await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue();
        assertThat(consumer.getLastOrderId()).isEqualTo("ORD-001");
    }
}

// Option B: Real Kafka via Testcontainers 2.0+ (~10s startup, version-accurate)
// Note: Testcontainers 2.0 renamed class from containers.KafkaContainer
// to kafka.KafkaContainer in the testcontainers-kafka artifact
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderConsumerContainerTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    // Testcontainers 2.0+: org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer (NEW class name)
    // Testcontainers 1.x:  org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer (OLD, removed)
    static org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer kafka =
        new org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer("apache/kafka:3.7.0");

    @Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, String> template;
    @Autowired OrderConsumer consumer;

    @Test
    void consumesOrderEvent() throws Exception {
        template.send("orders", "{\"id\":\"ORD-001\",\"status\":\"PLACED\"}");
        assertThat(consumer.getLatch().await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**[community] — Decision matrix for Kafka testing:**
- Use `EmbeddedKafkaBroker` for unit/integration tests where Docker is unavailable, CI must be fast, and Kafka version fidelity does not matter.
- Use `KafkaContainer` when testing specific Kafka versions, compression codecs (Snappy/Zstd), consumer group rebalance behavior, or rack-awareness.
- **[community] — Testcontainers 2.0 renamed `org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer` to `org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer` and removed the old class. Projects upgrading from 1.x will get `ClassNotFoundException` at container startup — not at compilation — because Maven may resolve the 2.0 artifact yet the import still compiles via IDE caching of the old class.**

### ArchUnit — Custom `ArchCondition<T>` for Project-Specific Rules

ArchUnit's built-in rules cover common layered-architecture patterns, but project-specific rules require implementing `ArchCondition<T>` directly. Custom conditions integrate fully with the fluent rule DSL and produce readable violation messages.

```java
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.domain.JavaClass;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.ArchCondition;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.ConditionEvents;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.SimpleConditionEvent;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.ArchRule;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.AnalyzeClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.ArchTest;

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example")
class CustomArchitectureRulesTest {

    // Custom condition: @Service beans must have names ending in "Service"
    static final ArchCondition<JavaClass> HAVE_SERVICE_SUFFIX =
        new ArchCondition<JavaClass>("have name ending in 'Service'") {
            @Override
            public void check(JavaClass javaClass, ConditionEvents events) {
                boolean ok = javaClass.getSimpleName().endsWith("Service");
                events.add(new SimpleConditionEvent(
                    javaClass, ok,
                    javaClass.getName() + (ok ? " has" : " does NOT have") + " 'Service' suffix"
                ));
            }
        };

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule servicesShouldHaveServiceSuffix =
        ArchRuleDefinition.classes()
            .that().areAnnotatedWith(org.springframework.stereotype.Service.class)
            .should(HAVE_SERVICE_SUFFIX);

    // Rule: repository interfaces must not be injected directly into controllers
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule controllersShouldNotDependOnRepositories =
        ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..controller..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..repository..");

    // Rule: event listener beans must reside in the events package
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule eventListenersShouldBeInEventsPackage =
        ArchRuleDefinition.classes()
            .that().containAnyMethodsThat()
                .areAnnotatedWith(org.springframework.context.event.EventListener.class)
            .should().resideInAPackage("..events..");
}
```

**[community] — ArchUnit `@ArchTest` in abstract base classes requires `@AnalyzeClasses` on the CONCRETE test class, not just the base.** If only the abstract base carries `@AnalyzeClasses`, the JUnit Platform finds the methods but cannot analyze any classes — all rules pass trivially. No violations are reported. The failure is completely invisible. Always put `@AnalyzeClasses` on the concrete subclass or on a meta-annotation applied to it. **[community] — ArchUnit caches imported classes per unique `@AnalyzeClasses` configuration — two concrete classes with the same `packages` value share the import cache, making the second test class near-instant.**

---

### Virtual Thread Pinning Detection in Tests

Virtual threads can be pinned to their carrier thread by `synchronized` blocks or native frames, degrading throughput under high concurrency. Tests can detect pinning via the `jdk.tracePinnedThreads` system property or JFR events.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeAll;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class VirtualThreadPinningTest {

    @BeforeAll
    static void enablePinningLog() {
        // short: logs thread name without stack trace
        // full:  logs complete stack trace of pinning event
        System.setProperty("jdk.tracePinnedThreads", "short");
    }

    @Test
    void databaseService_doesNotPinVirtualThread() throws Exception {
        java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream capture = new java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream();
        java.io.PrintStream original = System.err;
        System.setErr(new java.io.PrintStream(capture));

        try (ExecutorService exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(20);
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                exec.submit(() -> {
                    try {
                        databaseService.findById(1L);
                    } finally {
                        done.countDown();
                    }
                });
            }
            assertThat(done.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue();
        } finally {
            System.setErr(original);
        }

        String pinnedOutput = capture.toString();
        assertThat(pinnedOutput)
            .as("Virtual thread pinning detected in DatabaseService — " +
                "review synchronized blocks and consider ReentrantLock")
            .doesNotContain("VirtualThread");
    }

    private final DatabaseService databaseService = new DatabaseService();
}
```

**[community] — `jdk.tracePinnedThreads` output format changed between JDK 21, 22, 23, and 24.** String-matching tests that check for "VirtualThread" will break on JDK upgrades. The stable, version-agnostic alternative is JFR-based detection: the `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` JFR event fires for every pinning occurrence and is queryable via `RecordingFile` without text parsing. **[community] — For production code that MUST use `synchronized` (e.g., legacy third-party libraries), the fix is to replace `synchronized` blocks with `ReentrantLock` in the wrapper layer you control, or to configure the virtual thread executor to use a larger carrier thread pool via `-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=N`.**

---

### Mockito — `thenAnswer` with Stateful `Answer<T>` for Complex Stub Sequences

`thenReturn(v1, v2, v3)` cycles through values sequentially, but a stateful `Answer<T>` enables richer behavior: returning values computed from arguments, simulating transient failures, or tracking invocation counts within the stub itself.

```java
import org.mockito.stubbing.Answer;
import org.mockito.invocation.InvocationOnMock;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class RetryClientTest {

    @Test
    void retryClient_succeedsOnThirdAttempt() throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(0);
        ExternalApiClient mockClient = mock(ExternalApiClient.class);

        // Stateful Answer: fail twice, succeed on third call
        when(mockClient.fetchData(anyString())).thenAnswer(inv -> {
            int attempt = calls.incrementAndGet();
            if (attempt < 3) {
                throw new java.io.IOException("Transient failure (attempt " + attempt + ")");
            }
            // Third attempt echoes the argument to verify correct input propagation
            return "data-for-" + inv.getArgument(0, String.class);
        });

        RetryClient client = new RetryClient(mockClient, 3);
        String result = client.fetchWithRetry("record-42");

        assertThat(result).isEqualTo("data-for-record-42");
        assertThat(calls.get()).isEqualTo(3);
        verify(mockClient, times(3)).fetchData("record-42");
    }

    @Test
    void formatter_echoesInputAsUppercase() {
        NameFormatter formatter = mock(NameFormatter.class);

        // Answer that transforms the argument — useful for identity/transformer stubs
        when(formatter.format(anyString()))
            .thenAnswer(inv -> inv.getArgument(0, String.class).toUpperCase());

        assertThat(formatter.format("alice")).isEqualTo("ALICE");
        assertThat(formatter.format("bob")).isEqualTo("BOB");
    }

    @Test
    void thenCallRealMethod_delegatesForSelectiveMethods() {
        CachingService spy = mock(CachingService.class);

        // thenCallRealMethod() — real method for some calls, stubs for others
        when(spy.cacheKey(anyString())).thenCallRealMethod();  // use real logic
        when(spy.fetchFromDb(anyString())).thenReturn("cached-value");    // stub the slow part

        assertThat(spy.cacheKey("user:42")).isEqualTo("CACHE:user:42");
    }
}
```

**[community] — Use `thenAnswer` when return value depends on argument, call count, or external state. Use `thenReturn(v1, v2, v3)` for simple sequential values. Use `thenCallRealMethod()` (shorthand for `thenAnswer(inv -> inv.callRealMethod())`) to create partial mocks without the overhead of a full `spy()`. Avoid `thenAnswer` for simple cases — it is harder to read and maintain than `thenReturn`.**

---

### Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 26 Additions [community]

**JUnit 6 `CancellationToken.cancel()` does not abort the currently executing test method — it prevents new tests from starting [community]** — When `cancel()` is called (e.g., by a fail-fast listener), the currently executing test method runs to completion, including its `@AfterEach` methods. Tests with side effects that write to shared infrastructure (databases, message queues, files) will still complete their side effects after cancellation. Never rely on cancellation as a cleanup mechanism — always implement `@AfterEach` cleanup unconditionally.

**Spring Boot `MockMvcTester.bodyJson()` silently returns `null` for non-JSON responses [community]** — If the controller returns `text/plain` or a 204 No Content, `bodyJson()` returns `null`. Chaining `.hasPathSatisfying(...)` on a null `bodyJson()` result throws `NullPointerException` with a stack trace pointing inside AssertJ, not at the assertion that failed. Always assert `.hasContentTypeCompatibleWith("application/json")` first, or use `.andExpect(content().contentTypeCompatibleWith(...))` from classic `MockMvc` for conditional content-type checks.

**`@DefaultLocale` in JUnit 6.1 is silently ignored if `@BeforeAll` runs locale-sensitive initialization before the annotation takes effect [community]** — The `@DefaultLocale` annotation applies to a single test method scope, not the entire class. If `@BeforeAll` creates localized resources (formatted date strings, `NumberFormat` instances) that are reused across tests, those resources are created with the JVM default locale, not the test's declared locale. Move locale-sensitive initialization into `@BeforeEach` or directly into each test method to ensure it executes within the annotated locale scope.

**Testcontainers 2.0 Kafka class rename causes `ClassNotFoundException` at runtime only — not at compile time — when Maven BOM versions conflict [community]** — `org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer` was removed in Testcontainers 2.0. If a Maven BOM pins `testcontainers-kafka` to 1.x and a child module upgrades `testcontainers` BOM to 2.0, the old class import may still compile via IDE class caching while the Maven-resolved JAR is 2.0 (which doesn't contain the old class). Run `mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.testcontainers:testcontainers-kafka` to verify the resolved version, and update all imports to `org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer` atomically with the BOM upgrade.

**ArchUnit `@ArchTest` rules in abstract base classes run zero checks if `@AnalyzeClasses` is only on the base [community]** — If an abstract base class carries `@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example")` and concrete subclasses do not, all rules pass trivially (zero classes analyzed). ArchUnit emits a warning log, but if CI does not check for warnings, this silently disables all architecture checks. The fix: always place `@AnalyzeClasses` on concrete test classes, or create a meta-annotation combining both that is applied to each concrete class.

**Virtual thread pinning detection via `jdk.tracePinnedThreads` string output is JDK-version-sensitive [community]** — JDK 21 prints "VirtualThread pinned for...", JDK 23 changed the message prefix, and JDK 24 further altered it. Tests that parse this output break silently on JDK upgrades — the test passes (no matching string found) but pinning still occurs. Prefer JFR-based detection (`jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` event) for stable, version-agnostic CI enforcement. Use text-based detection only as a quick local diagnostic, not as a CI gate.

## Cycle 27 — 2026-05-14

### JUnit 6 — `@ParameterizedClass` for Shared Parameterized State

`@ParameterizedClass` (available since JUnit 5.13, promoted in JUnit 6) allows an entire test class to receive parameters, eliminating the duplication of repeating source annotations on every parameterized test method inside a suite that shares setup.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedClass;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// One @CsvSource annotation drives ALL test methods in this class
@ParameterizedClass
@CsvSource({
    "USD, 100, 100.00",
    "EUR, 100, 100.00",
    "JPY, 100, 100"      // JPY has no decimal places
})
class CurrencyFormatterTest {

    private final String currencyCode;
    private final int amount;
    private final String expectedDisplay;
    private CurrencyFormatter formatter;

    CurrencyFormatterTest(String currencyCode, int amount, String expectedDisplay) {
        this.currencyCode = currencyCode;
        this.amount = amount;
        this.expectedDisplay = expectedDisplay;
    }

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        formatter = new CurrencyFormatter(currencyCode);
    }

    @Test
    void format_producesCorrectDisplay() {
        assertThat(formatter.format(amount)).isEqualTo(expectedDisplay);
    }

    @Test
    void format_roundTrip_parsesBack() {
        String formatted = formatter.format(amount);
        assertThat(formatter.parse(formatted)).isEqualTo(amount);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ParameterizedClass` reduces boilerplate when 3+ test methods share the same parameter set. Use it when you want to test a component across multiple configurations and each configuration needs full lifecycle setup. **Do not use it** when test methods need different parameter sets — use per-method `@ParameterizedTest` instead. `@ParameterizedClass` cannot be combined with `@Nested` test classes in the same test class definition.

**[official] — `@ParameterizedClass` was added in JUnit 5.13 and is a first-class citizen in JUnit 6. It uses the same `@MethodSource`, `@CsvSource`, `@EnumSource`, and `@ArgumentsSource` providers as `@ParameterizedTest`.**

### JUnit 6 — `CancellationToken` Consumption Patterns and Fail-Fast Behavior

JUnit 6's `--fail-fast` mode and the `CancellationToken` API enable fine-grained test execution control. Understanding the lifecycle of cancellation prevents subtle test suite state corruption.

```java
import org.junit.platform.launcher.TestExecutionListener;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.TestIdentifier;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.TestPlan;

/**
 * Custom fail-after-N listener that cancels execution after
 * a configurable number of test failures.
 * Usage: register with LauncherDiscoveryRequestBuilder.
 */
class FailAfterNListener implements TestExecutionListener {

    private final int maxFailures;
    private int failureCount = 0;
    // In JUnit 6, CancellationToken is obtained from LauncherSession
    private org.junit.platform.launcher.core.CancellationToken token;

    FailAfterNListener(int maxFailures) {
        this.maxFailures = maxFailures;
    }

    // Called once before any test runs — capture token here
    @Override
    public void testPlanExecutionStarted(TestPlan testPlan) {
        // Actual JUnit 6 API: token = launcherSession.getCancellationToken()
        // Shown conceptually; concrete usage depends on LauncherSession API
    }

    @Override
    public void executionFinished(
            TestIdentifier testIdentifier,
            org.junit.platform.engine.reporting.ReportEntry reportEntry) {
        // NOTE: executionFinished is called AFTER the test, including @AfterEach
        // cancel() stops NEW tests from being scheduled — it does not abort the current test
        if (failureCount >= maxFailures && token != null) {
            token.cancel();
        }
    }
}
```

**[official] — `CancellationToken.cancel()` does NOT interrupt the currently running test. It prevents new tests from being scheduled. `@AfterEach` and `@AfterAll` cleanup methods always execute even after cancellation is requested.**

**[community] — When integrating fail-fast with CI pipelines, prefer the ConsoleLauncher `--fail-fast` flag over a custom `CancellationToken` listener. Custom listeners introduce timing races when tests run in parallel and `cancel()` is called mid-fork. The built-in `--fail-fast` is thread-safe. A custom listener is only justified when you need threshold-based cancellation (fail after N failures, not just 1).**

### Spring Boot 3.4/4.0 — `@MockitoBean` Migration from `@MockBean` with Context Caching Impact

`@MockitoBean` (Spring Framework 6.2+) replaces `@MockBean` but has a critical behavioral difference regarding Spring context caching that can cause cache invalidation when mocked-bean sets are inconsistent across test classes.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// CORRECT: @MockitoBean on test class field
@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Autowired
    private OrderService orderService;

    @MockitoBean
    private PaymentGateway paymentGateway;

    @MockitoBean
    private InventoryService inventoryService;

    @Test
    void placeOrder_chargesPaymentAndDeductsInventory() {
        given(paymentGateway.charge("card-123", 99_00L))
            .willReturn(PaymentResult.success("txn-999"));
        given(inventoryService.reserve("SKU-001", 1))
            .willReturn(true);

        Order order = orderService.place(new OrderRequest("card-123", "SKU-001", 1));

        assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.CONFIRMED);
        assertThat(order.transactionId()).isEqualTo("txn-999");
    }
}

// WRONG: @MockitoBean is NOT supported on @Configuration classes.
// @MockBean (now deprecated) allowed this — @MockitoBean does NOT.
// Always place @MockitoBean on a test class field.
```

**Tradeoff:** `@MockitoBean` is the preferred replacement for `@MockBean` in Spring Boot 3.4+ and is required for Spring Boot 4.0. Unlike `@MockBean`, it uses Spring Framework's Bean Override mechanism and is not supported on `@Configuration` classes. Moving `@MockitoBean` off `@Configuration` onto test fields is a required migration step.

**[official] — Spring Boot 3.4 deprecated `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean`. Both are removed in Spring Boot 4.0. The replacement annotations are `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` from `org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito`.**

**[community] — Context cache miss rate increases when different test classes use `@MockitoBean` for different bean sets. Two test classes that mock different beans create different context configurations and cannot share a cached context. Consolidate shared mocked beans into a base test class or a shared `@TestConfiguration` imported by all affected test classes. A test suite fast with `@MockBean` can become 3-4x slower after migration if mocked-bean sets vary per class.**

---

### Spring Boot — `MockMvcTester` Fluent AssertJ Patterns vs Classic MockMvc

`MockMvcTester` (auto-configured in Spring Boot 3.4+ when AssertJ is on the classpath) provides a fluent AssertJ-based API with no static imports and automatic async result collection.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvcTester mvc;

    @MockitoBean
    private ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void getProduct_returnsProductJson() {
        given(productService.findById(42L))
            .willReturn(new Product(42L, "Gadget", 29_99));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/products/42"))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith("application/json")
            .bodyJson()
                .extractingPath("$.name").isEqualTo("Gadget");
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_notFound_returns404() {
        given(productService.findById(99L))
            .willThrow(new ProductNotFoundException(99L));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/products/99"))
            .hasStatus(404)
            .hasBodyTextContaining("Product not found");
    }

    @Test
    void createProduct_invalidBody_returns400WithValidationErrors() {
        assertThat(mvc.post()
                       .uri("/products")
                       .contentType("application/json")
                       .content("{}"))
            .hasStatus(400)
            .bodyJson()
                .extractingPath("$.errors").asArray().isNotEmpty();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `MockMvcTester` for new tests — it has cleaner failure messages, no static imports, and handles async results automatically. Migrate classic `MockMvc` tests incrementally — the two APIs can coexist in the same class. `MockMvcTester` is auto-configured only when AssertJ is on the classpath; if your project uses Hamcrest only, you must add AssertJ to the test scope.

**[community] — `MockMvcTester.bodyJson()` returns `null` (not an empty assertion) when the response content type is not JSON. Calling `.extractingPath(...)` on a null `bodyJson()` result throws `NullPointerException` inside AssertJ with a stack trace that does not point to the test method. Always assert `.hasContentTypeCompatibleWith("application/json")` before chaining `bodyJson()` calls.**

### Spring Boot Testcontainers — `@ServiceConnection` vs `@DynamicPropertySource`

`@ServiceConnection` (Spring Boot 3.1+) auto-configures application properties for known container types, eliminating the boilerplate of `@DynamicPropertySource`. Understanding when each approach is correct prevents subtle configuration drift.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class UserRepositoryIntegrationTest {

    // @ServiceConnection auto-configures spring.datasource.* from the PostgreSQL container
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    // For GenericContainer, provide the service name hint
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection(name = "redis")
    static GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);

    @Test
    void saveUser_persistsToDatabase() {
        // Spring Boot connects to the Testcontainers-managed postgres
        // No @DynamicPropertySource boilerplate needed
    }
}

// Use @DynamicPropertySource only when @ServiceConnection does not support the container type
// OR when you need to customize the registered property names:
class CustomContainerTest {

    @Container
    static GenericContainer<?> vault =
        new GenericContainer<>("vault:1.15").withExposedPorts(8200);

    @org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertySource
    static void vaultProperties(org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("spring.cloud.vault.uri",
              () -> "http://localhost:" + vault.getMappedPort(8200));
        r.add("spring.cloud.vault.token", () -> "root");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ServiceConnection` is less code and less error-prone for well-known containers (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Kafka, Redis, RabbitMQ, Elasticsearch). Use `@DynamicPropertySource` when the container type is not auto-supported, when you need custom property keys, or when you need to compute a value from multiple container ports.

**[official] — Spring Boot 3.4 expanded `@ServiceConnection` support to include Kafka, Redis, Redis Stack, Grafana LGTM, and Hazelcast containers.**

**[community] — `@DynamicPropertySource` injecting `DynamicPropertyRegistry` directly into `@Bean` methods is deprecated as of Spring Boot 3.4. Use a `@Bean` returning `DynamicPropertyRegistrar` functional interface instead. The old approach can cause lifecycle issues where the container has not yet started when the registry is consulted.**

### Java Records as Parameterized Test Argument Providers

Java records make natural value objects for `@MethodSource` parameterized tests, especially when each test case requires multiple logically-related inputs and an expected output.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class SlugifyTest {

    // Record acts as a named, self-documenting test case
    record SlugCase(String description, String input, String expected) {
        @Override public String toString() { return description; } // JUnit uses this in display names
    }

    static Stream<SlugCase> slugCases() {
        return Stream.of(
            new SlugCase("basic lowercase",        "Hello World",      "hello-world"),
            new SlugCase("multiple spaces",        "  foo   bar  ",    "foo-bar"),
            new SlugCase("special chars stripped", "C++ is fun!",      "c-is-fun"),
            new SlugCase("unicode normalized",     "Angstrom Cafe",    "angstrom-cafe"),
            new SlugCase("already slugified",      "already-slug",     "already-slug"),
            new SlugCase("empty string",           "",                  ""),
            new SlugCase("only special chars",     "!!!",               "")
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0}")
    @MethodSource("slugCases")
    void slugify_convertsCorrectly(SlugCase tc) {
        assertThat(Slugify.slugify(tc.input())).isEqualTo(tc.expected());
    }

    record ErrorCase(String description, String input, Class<? extends Exception> expectedException) {}

    static Stream<ErrorCase> errorCases() {
        return Stream.of(
            new ErrorCase("null input throws NPE", null, NullPointerException.class)
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0}")
    @MethodSource("errorCases")
    void slugify_throwsOnInvalidInput(ErrorCase tc) {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Slugify.slugify(tc.input()))
            .isInstanceOf(tc.expectedException());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Record-as-test-case is more readable than `Arguments.of(...)` tuples because fields are named and the `toString()` override produces meaningful JUnit display names. The downside is extra boilerplate for the record declaration; for simple 1- or 2-arg cases, `@CsvSource` is more concise. Use records when you have 3+ fields or when tests also need error-type assertions.

**[community] — Overriding `toString()` on the record to return the description field is the key trick for readable parameterized test display names. Without it, JUnit shows the full auto-generated record `toString()` including all field values, which is verbose and can truncate for long inputs. The `name = "{0}"` attribute on `@ParameterizedTest` picks up whatever `toString()` returns for the first argument.**

---

### AssertJ — `usingRecursiveComparison` for Deep Record and Graph Equality

AssertJ's `usingRecursiveComparison()` is the correct way to compare complex record hierarchies when you need to ignore specific fields (e.g., auto-generated IDs, timestamps) or when comparing across different types with matching field names.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class OrderMapperTest {

    record Address(String street, String city, String zip) {}
    record OrderItem(String sku, int quantity, long unitPriceMillis) {}
    record OrderSnapshot(Long id, String customerId, Address shippingAddress,
                         List<OrderItem> items, Instant createdAt) {}

    @Test
    void mapToDomain_ignoresIdAndTimestamp() {
        OrderDto dto = new OrderDto(
            "cust-99",
            new AddressDto("10 Elm St", "Springfield", "12345"),
            List.of(new OrderItemDto("SKU-A", 2, 999L))
        );

        OrderSnapshot result = OrderMapper.INSTANCE.toDomain(dto);

        assertThat(result)
            .usingRecursiveComparison()
            .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt")
            .isEqualTo(new OrderSnapshot(
                null, "cust-99",
                new Address("10 Elm St", "Springfield", "12345"),
                List.of(new OrderItem("SKU-A", 2, 999L)),
                null
            ));
    }

    @Test
    void mapToDomain_timestampIsRecent() {
        Instant before = Instant.now();
        OrderDto dto = new OrderDto("cust-1", null, List.of());
        OrderSnapshot result = OrderMapper.INSTANCE.toDomain(dto);
        Instant after = Instant.now();

        assertThat(result.createdAt()).isBetween(before, after);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `usingRecursiveComparison()` handles nested records, collections, and maps automatically without requiring `equals()` to be defined. It does NOT use `equals()` — which matters when an entity's `equals()` intentionally excludes transient fields. Use `withEqualsForType(BiPredicate, class)` to customize comparison for specific types.

**[community] — `usingRecursiveComparison()` does NOT recurse into `Optional<T>` fields by default — it calls `Optional.equals()`, which internally calls `equals()` on the wrapped value. If the wrapped type doesn't override `equals()` (e.g., a non-record domain class), comparison uses identity equality and gives false negatives. Unwrap `Optional` values before comparison or register a custom comparator with `.withEqualsForType(...)` targeting `Optional.class`.**

---

### Java Streams — Testing Stream Pipelines with AssertJ Extractors

Stream pipelines are often tested incorrectly because intermediate operations are lazy. The correct pattern is to materialize results before asserting, and to use AssertJ extractors rather than ad-hoc manual checks.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ProductCatalogServiceTest {

    record Product(String sku, String category, int price, boolean inStock) {}

    private final List<Product> catalog = List.of(
        new Product("A1", "Electronics", 999, true),
        new Product("A2", "Electronics", 499, false),
        new Product("B1", "Books", 29, true),
        new Product("B2", "Books", 39, true),
        new Product("C1", "Clothing", 79, true)
    );

    @Test
    void filterInStockByCategory_returnsOnlyMatchingProducts() {
        List<Product> result = catalog.stream()
            .filter(Product::inStock)
            .filter(p -> "Electronics".equals(p.category()))
            .toList();

        assertThat(result)
            .hasSize(1)
            .extracting(Product::sku)
            .containsExactly("A1");
    }

    @Test
    void sortedByPrice_producesCorrectOrder() {
        List<String> skus = catalog.stream()
            .filter(Product::inStock)
            .sorted(java.util.Comparator.comparingInt(Product::price))
            .map(Product::sku)
            .toList();

        assertThat(skus).containsExactly("B1", "B2", "C1", "A1"); // ascending price
    }

    @Test
    void groupByCategory_countsCorrectly() {
        var byCategory = catalog.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Product::category,
                Collectors.counting()));

        assertThat(byCategory)
            .containsEntry("Electronics", 2L)
            .containsEntry("Books", 2L)
            .containsEntry("Clothing", 1L);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Always materialize streams to `List` or `Map` before asserting — never assert on an unconsumed `Stream<T>`. AssertJ's `extracting(Function)` and `flatExtracting(Function)` are the idiomatic way to drill into stream results. Avoid calling `.stream()` inside `assertThat()` — it consumes the stream and you lose the reference.

**[community] — A frequent test smell is wrapping `Stream.forEach` in an `AtomicInteger` counter to verify element count. Use `assertThat(list).hasSize(N)` instead. Another common mistake is testing `Stream.distinct()` behavior by asserting on the stream directly — always `.toList()` first or the assertion silently consumes the stream with no verifiable result.**

---

### Mockito — Strict Stubbing and `UnnecessaryStubbingException` Patterns

Mockito's strict stubbing (default in `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`) throws `UnnecessaryStubbingException` for stubs that are set up but never called. This is a correctness feature that catches test drift.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoSettings;
import org.mockito.quality.Strictness;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyString;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyLong;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderProcessorTest {

    @Mock private PaymentGateway paymentGateway;
    @Mock private EmailService emailService;

    // CORRECT: Only stub what this specific test actually exercises
    @Test
    void chargePayment_returnsSuccessResult() {
        given(paymentGateway.charge("tok-123", 5000L))
            .willReturn(ChargeResult.success("txn-abc"));
        // emailService is NOT stubbed because this code path does not call it

        ChargeResult result = new OrderProcessor(paymentGateway, emailService)
            .charge("tok-123", 5000L);

        assertThat(result.isSuccess()).isTrue();
    }

    // CORRECT: Use lenient() per-method for conditionally invoked stubs
    @Test
    @MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT)
    void conditionalFlow_mayOrMayNotSendEmail() {
        given(paymentGateway.charge(anyString(), anyLong()))
            .willReturn(ChargeResult.success("txn-xyz"));
        // Email sending is conditional — not guaranteed to be called every invocation
        given(emailService.sendReceipt(anyString()))
            .willReturn(true);

        // test body covering multiple branches where email may or may not fire
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Strict stubbing catches "dead" stubs that mask refactors — if a method is removed from production code but the test still stubs it, strict mode reveals the drift. Use `@MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT)` only at the method level for tests covering conditional logic, not at the class level (which silences the safety net entirely).

**[community] — The most common cause of `UnnecessaryStubbingException` in teams migrating from JUnit 4 is copy-pasting stubs into `@BeforeEach` that configure all mocks for every test in the class. Only stubs that are exercised by EVERY test method in the class belong in `@BeforeEach`. Move test-specific stubs into individual test methods. Misuse of `@BeforeEach` for stubbing is the leading cause of `UnnecessaryStubbingException` in large test suites.**

---

### Testcontainers — Reusable Containers Across Test Classes

Testcontainers' `withReuse(true)` keeps containers alive between test class runs in the same JVM session, dramatically reducing integration test suite time when the same container type is used across many test classes.

```java
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertyRegistry;
import org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertySource;

/**
 * Base class providing a shared, reusable PostgreSQL container for all
 * integration test subclasses. The container starts once per JVM session.
 */
public abstract class PostgresIntegrationTest {

    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> POSTGRES;

    static {
        POSTGRES = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("testdb")
            .withUsername("test")
            .withPassword("test")
            .withReuse(true);  // requires testcontainers.reuse.enable=true in ~/.testcontainers.properties
        POSTGRES.start();
    }

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void postgresProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", POSTGRES::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", POSTGRES::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", POSTGRES::getPassword);
    }
}

// Concrete test class just extends the base — no container startup overhead
@org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest
class UserRepositoryTest extends PostgresIntegrationTest {

    @org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;

    @org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
    @org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional
    void findByEmail_returnsUser() {
        userRepository.save(new User("alice@example.com", "Alice"));
        assertThat(userRepository.findByEmail("alice@example.com")).isPresent();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `withReuse(true)` requires `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true` in `~/.testcontainers.properties` on the running host. Without this property, `withReuse(true)` is silently ignored and containers are NOT reused. This means CI environments need this property configured, or the performance optimization has no effect. The reuse mechanism is based on container label hashing — any configuration change (e.g., different image version) creates a new container.

**[community] — A critical gotcha with reusable containers is test isolation: data written in one test class persists into the next class run if transactions are not properly rolled back. Always annotate integration tests with `@Transactional` (for JPA tests) or use `@Sql` with `BEFORE_TEST_METHOD` execution phase to truncate tables before each test. Reusable containers that accumulate state are a leading cause of flaky tests that fail in certain execution orders but pass when run in isolation.**

---

### Spring Boot — `@TestBean` for Replacing Beans Without Mockito

Spring Framework 6.2 (Spring Boot 3.4+) introduced `@TestBean` as a Bean Override mechanism that replaces a real bean with a custom implementation defined in the test — without requiring Mockito.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.convention.TestBean;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
class NotificationServiceTest {

    // @TestBean replaces the EmailSender bean with the result of the static factory method below
    @TestBean
    EmailSender emailSender;

    // The static factory method must have the same name as the field (or <fieldName>TestOverride)
    static EmailSender emailSender() {
        return new RecordingEmailSender();
    }

    // Custom test double that records sent messages — no Mockito needed
    static class RecordingEmailSender implements EmailSender {
        final List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>();

        @Override
        public void send(String to, String subject, String body) {
            sent.add(to + "|" + subject);
        }
    }

    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService;

    @Test
    void sendWelcome_dispatchesEmailWithCorrectSubject() {
        notificationService.sendWelcome("alice@example.com");

        RecordingEmailSender recorder = (RecordingEmailSender) emailSender;
        assertThat(recorder.sent)
            .hasSize(1)
            .first()
            .asString()
            .startsWith("alice@example.com|Welcome");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@TestBean` is appropriate when you want a custom test double with real domain logic (recording calls, simulating partial failures) that Mockito stubs would make verbose. It does NOT require Mockito, making it suitable for teams that want to minimize mock library dependencies. For simple "return this value" cases, `@MockitoBean` is less boilerplate. The factory method MUST be `static` — an instance method is silently ignored and the real bean is used.

**[official] — `@TestBean` was introduced in Spring Framework 6.2 as part of the Bean Override API. The factory method name must match the field name or be named `<fieldName>TestOverride`. If neither naming convention matches a static method in the test class, Spring throws a `BeanOverrideException` at context startup.**

**[community] — The most common mistake with `@TestBean` is declaring the factory method as a non-static instance method. Spring's Bean Override processor silently skips non-static methods and falls back to the real bean, so the test runs against production code without any error at startup. CI may show false green. Always `static` the factory method and verify replacement with a quick assertion on the injected bean type.**
