### Sealed Classes — Exhaustive Switch Testing and Missing Subtype Detection

Sealed class hierarchies combined with `switch` expressions create a compile-time guarantee of exhaustiveness. Testing sealed hierarchies requires a deliberate strategy to ensure all permitted subtypes are tested and serializers/handlers stay in sync with the hierarchy.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

sealed interface PaymentEvent
    permits PaymentEvent.Charged, PaymentEvent.Declined, PaymentEvent.Refunded {
    record Charged(String txnId, long amountMillis) implements PaymentEvent {}
    record Declined(String reason) implements PaymentEvent {}
    record Refunded(String txnId, long refundMillis) implements PaymentEvent {}
}

class PaymentEventSerializerTest {

    static Stream<PaymentEvent> allPermittedSubtypes() {
        return Stream.of(
            new PaymentEvent.Charged("txn-1", 9999L),
            new PaymentEvent.Declined("Insufficient funds"),
            new PaymentEvent.Refunded("txn-1", 5000L)
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("allPermittedSubtypes")
    void serialize_thenDeserialize_roundTrip(PaymentEvent event) {
        String json = PaymentEventSerializer.serialize(event);
        PaymentEvent restored = PaymentEventSerializer.deserialize(json);

        // Exhaustive switch — compile error if a new permitted subtype is added
        // but not handled here, making test gaps visible at compile time
        String typeTag = switch (restored) {
            case PaymentEvent.Charged c   -> "Charged:"  + c.txnId();
            case PaymentEvent.Declined d  -> "Declined:" + d.reason();
            case PaymentEvent.Refunded r  -> "Refunded:" + r.txnId();
        };

        assertThat(typeTag).isNotEmpty();
        assertThat(restored).isEqualTo(event);
    }

    @Test
    void serializer_registersAllPermittedSubtypes() {
        // Architecture-style check: all permitted subtypes must be registered
        var permittedClasses = Arrays.asList(PaymentEvent.class.getPermittedSubclasses());
        assertThat(permittedClasses)
            .as("PaymentEventSerializer must handle all permitted subtypes")
            .allSatisfy(cls ->
                assertThat(PaymentEventSerializer.isRegistered(cls))
                    .as("Missing serializer registration for %s", cls.getSimpleName())
                    .isTrue()
            );
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `allPermittedSubtypes()` factory method must be manually updated when a new `permits` type is added — use the architecture-style test (`getPermittedSubclasses()`) to automatically detect handler gaps. Without this, new sealed subtypes added by a developer are silently untested, and the production `switch` handler (if non-exhaustive) throws `MatchException` at runtime.

**[community] — Adding a new permitted subtype to a sealed interface does NOT cause a compile error in test setup code that uses `instanceof` chains instead of exhaustive switch. Only pattern `switch` expressions enforce exhaustiveness at compile time. If test fixture methods use `if (event instanceof Charged c)` chains, new subtypes silently produce null/default behavior in tests. Use exhaustive `switch` in test fixture methods to make coverage gaps compile-time visible.**

### Mockito — `ArgumentCaptor` with Java Records and Generic Types

`ArgumentCaptor` works correctly with records but has a subtle behavior with generic types: the captor captures the erased type. Modern usage patterns leverage record accessor methods for field-level assertions.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.ArgumentCaptor;
import org.mockito.Captor;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.time.Instant;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.verify;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class AuditLogServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private AuditRepository auditRepository;

    @Captor
    private ArgumentCaptor<AuditEntry> entryCaptor;

    record AuditEntry(String userId, String action, Instant timestamp, String metadata) {}

    @Test
    void logAction_persistsCorrectAuditEntry() {
        AuditLogService service = new AuditLogService(auditRepository);
        Instant before = Instant.now();

        service.log("user-42", "DELETE_ORDER", "orderId=99");

        // Captor has a value only AFTER verify() runs
        verify(auditRepository).save(entryCaptor.capture());
        AuditEntry captured = entryCaptor.getValue();

        assertThat(captured.userId()).isEqualTo("user-42");
        assertThat(captured.action()).isEqualTo("DELETE_ORDER");
        assertThat(captured.metadata()).isEqualTo("orderId=99");
        assertThat(captured.timestamp())
            .isAfterOrEqualTo(before)
            .isBeforeOrEqualTo(Instant.now());
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    @Test
    void publishBatch_capturesList() {
        // Generic types require raw-class cast with @SuppressWarnings
        ArgumentCaptor<java.util.List<AuditEntry>> listCaptor =
            ArgumentCaptor.forClass((Class<java.util.List<AuditEntry>>) (Class<?>) java.util.List.class);

        EventBus mockBus = org.mockito.Mockito.mock(EventBus.class);
        AuditBatchPublisher publisher = new AuditBatchPublisher(mockBus);
        publisher.publishBatch(java.util.List.of(
            new AuditEntry("u1", "LOGIN", Instant.now(), ""),
            new AuditEntry("u2", "LOGOUT", Instant.now(), "")
        ));

        verify(mockBus).publish(listCaptor.capture());
        assertThat(listCaptor.getValue()).hasSize(2);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@Captor` annotation with field injection is cleaner than `ArgumentCaptor.forClass(...)` inline. For records, captured values can be compared field-by-field using record accessors, which is more readable than equals-based assertions on complex objects. For generic types, raw-type casting with `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` is the accepted Mockito idiom — no fully type-safe alternative exists at the capture site.

**[community] — The most common `ArgumentCaptor` bug is calling `entryCaptor.getValue()` BEFORE `verify(...)` executes. The captor only has a value after the `verify(mock).method(captor.capture())` call completes. Calling `getValue()` prematurely returns `null` (or throws `MockitoException`), but no compile error prevents this. Always structure the test as: arrange stubs → act → `verify(...).method(captor.capture())` → assert on `captor.getValue()`.**

### Spring Boot — `@DataJpaTest` with JPA Auditing and `TestEntityManager`

`@DataJpaTest` starts an in-memory H2 database by default. Testing entities with JPA audit fields (`@CreatedDate`, `@LastModifiedDate`) requires `@EnableJpaAuditing` on a test-scoped configuration, not just the main configuration.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.TestEntityManager;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaAuditing;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.time.Instant;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Import a test-only JPA config that enables auditing for the @DataJpaTest slice
@DataJpaTest
@Import(JpaAuditingTestConfig.class)
class ProductRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    private TestEntityManager em;

    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;

    @Test
    void save_populatesCreatedAtAndUpdatedAt() {
        Instant before = Instant.now();
        Product saved = productRepository.save(new Product("Widget", 999));
        em.flush();

        assertThat(saved.getCreatedAt()).isAfterOrEqualTo(before);
        assertThat(saved.getUpdatedAt()).isAfterOrEqualTo(before);
    }

    @Test
    void update_changesUpdatedAtButNotCreatedAt() throws InterruptedException {
        // persistFlushFind: persist + flush + reload from DB (bypasses L1 cache)
        Product saved = em.persistFlushFind(new Product("Gadget", 499));
        Instant originalCreated = saved.getCreatedAt();
        Thread.sleep(5);

        saved.setPrice(599);
        productRepository.save(saved);
        em.flush();
        em.clear();

        Product reloaded = productRepository.findById(saved.getId()).orElseThrow();
        assertThat(reloaded.getCreatedAt()).isEqualTo(originalCreated);  // unchanged
        assertThat(reloaded.getUpdatedAt()).isAfter(originalCreated);    // bumped
    }
}

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing
class JpaAuditingTestConfig {}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@DataJpaTest` does NOT load `@EnableJpaAuditing` from the main `@SpringBootApplication` class — the annotation scanner is narrowed to the JPA slice. Without the imported audit config, `@CreatedDate` and `@LastModifiedDate` fields remain `null`, and tests silently pass with null timestamps. This is the most common cause of "works in production, fails in tests" for audited entities.

**[community] — `TestEntityManager.persistFlushFind()` is the canonical pattern for persistence testing: it persists, flushes to the database, and reloads from the database in one call, bypassing the first-level (L1) cache. Using `entityManager.persist(entity)` without flush leaves the entity in the persistence context, and reads return the in-memory object — missing database constraint violations, generated column values, and trigger-populated fields entirely. If a test never calls `flush()`, it may assert against stale in-memory state.**

### Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 27 Additions [community]

**`@ParameterizedClass` in JUnit 6 requires the test class constructor parameter count to exactly match the source arity — mismatch causes `ParameterResolutionException` at test discovery, not at test execution [community]** — If a `@CsvSource` row has 3 columns but the test class constructor accepts 2 parameters, JUnit 6 fails the entire test class at discovery time, reporting zero tests executed rather than N test failures. The error message references the constructor signature but not the source row index, making large `@CsvSource` tables hard to diagnose. Always verify constructor arity matches source column count before running.

**Spring Boot `@ServiceConnection` silently falls back to `application.properties` when the container image name does not match the expected prefix [community]** — `@ServiceConnection` uses the Docker image name (e.g., `postgres:16-alpine`) to select a `ConnectionDetailsFactory`. A container using a custom registry image (`myregistry.io/company/postgres:16`) does not match the default prefix matcher and silently falls back to using whatever `spring.datasource.url` is configured in `application-test.properties`. The test does not fail at startup — it connects to the wrong database. Always use canonical Docker Hub image names in test containers, or register a custom `ConnectionDetailsFactory` for internal registries.

**Mockito strict stubbing with `@ParameterizedTest` throws `UnnecessaryStubbingException` when a `@BeforeEach` stub is not exercised by every parameterized test case [community]** — If `@BeforeEach` stubs `mockPayment.charge(...)` but one parameterized case exercises the rejection path (which never calls `charge`), strict mode throws `UnnecessaryStubbingException` for that invocation. The fix is to move stubs into each test method, or use `@MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT)` on the specific method covering the non-stubbed path. Do not apply `LENIENT` at the class level.

**`usingRecursiveComparison()` in AssertJ does NOT recurse into `Optional<T>` fields — it compares `Optional` instances using their `equals()` method [community]** — For an entity record with an `Optional<Address>` field, recursive comparison stops at the `Optional` boundary and calls `Optional.equals()` on the wrapped `Address`. If `Address` does not override `equals()`, comparison falls back to identity equality, giving false positives (both `null` cases) or false negatives (different objects with identical field values). Unwrap `Optional` values explicitly before comparison or register a custom comparator for `Optional.class`.

**`@TestBean` factory methods must be `static` — a non-static factory method is silently ignored and Spring uses the real bean, giving a false green test [community]** — Spring's Bean Override processor only discovers `static` methods matching the field name or `<fieldName>TestOverride` convention. A non-static instance method with the correct name compiles without error, starts without an exception, and results in the production bean being injected. The test appears to pass but exercises real dependencies. Add a quick `assertThat(emailSender).isInstanceOf(RecordingEmailSender.class)` guard assertion in `@BeforeEach` to catch this mistake in CI.

**`TestEntityManager.persistFlushFind()` does NOT execute `@PreUpdate` auditing callbacks if the entity was never in the persistence context — use save+flush+find separately for update-path auditing tests [community]** — `persistFlushFind` is a shortcut for the create path. For update-path tests (change a field, save, verify `@LastModifiedDate` changed), you must: (1) persist and flush the initial entity, (2) clear the persistence context (`em.clear()`), (3) load the entity fresh, (4) mutate it, (5) call `repository.save()`, (6) `flush()`, (7) `clear()`, and (8) reload. Skipping the `em.clear()` between persist and update means the entity never leaves the L1 cache and the `@PreUpdate` callback may not fire.

## Cycle 28 — 2026-05-14

### 1. jqwik — Property-Based Testing for JUnit 5 [community]

Property-based testing generates hundreds of random inputs automatically, uncovering edge cases that hand-crafted examples miss. jqwik 1.9.x integrates natively as a JUnit 5 test engine — no extra runner annotation needed.

**When to use:** Domain logic with non-trivial invariants (encoding, validation, arithmetic). Pure functions with well-defined postconditions.
**When NOT to use:** Tests that require a Spring context, database, or external network — jqwik's lifecycle conflicts with Spring Boot's test infrastructure unless you add the `jqwik-spring` bridge module.

```java
// build.gradle: testImplementation 'net.jqwik:jqwik:1.9.0'
import net.jqwik.api.*;
import net.jqwik.api.constraints.*;

class SlugPropertyTest {

    @Property(tries = 500)
    void slugIsIdempotent(@ForAll @AlphaChars @StringLength(min = 1, max = 80) String input) {
        String once = Slug.of(input);
        String twice = Slug.of(once);
        Assertions.assertEquals(once, twice,
            "Slug must be idempotent but was not for input: " + input);
    }

    @Property
    void slugContainsOnlyLowercaseAlphanumericAndHyphens(
            @ForAll @StringLength(min = 1, max = 120) String input) {
        String slug = Slug.of(input);
        Assertions.assertTrue(slug.matches("[a-z0-9-]*"),
            "Slug contains illegal characters: " + slug);
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<String> validProductCodes() {
        return Arbitraries.strings()
            .withCharRange('A', 'Z')
            .ofMinLength(3).ofMaxLength(10)
            .map(s -> s + "-" + Arbitraries.integers().between(100, 999).sample());
    }
}
```

### 2. PIT Mutation Testing — Verifying Test Suite Effectiveness [official]

PIT (Pitest) 1.17.x injects source mutations (negate conditionals, remove returns, replace constants) and measures what percentage the test suite kills. A high line-coverage metric with a low mutation score reveals tests that execute code but make no meaningful assertions.

**When to use:** After reaching stable line coverage, as a second-pass quality gate. Integrate in CI with `<mutationThreshold>80</mutationThreshold>` to block PRs that introduce under-tested code.
**When NOT to use:** Do not run PIT on every commit in large projects — full analysis can take 10–30 minutes. Use incremental mode (`withHistory`) or scope it to changed modules only.

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
  <artifactId>pitest-maven</artifactId>
  <version>1.17.0</version>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
      <artifactId>pitest-junit5-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>1.2.1</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
  <configuration>
    <mutationThreshold>80</mutationThreshold>
    <withHistory>true</withHistory>
    <targetClasses><param>com.example.pricing.*</param></targetClasses>
    <targetTests><param>com.example.pricing.*Test</param></targetTests>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```java
// Boundary test that kills the CONDITIONAL_BOUNDARY mutant
@Test
void discountAppliesAtExactly100Units() {
    assertThat(Pricing.discount(99)).isEqualTo(0);    // kills < → <= mutant
    assertThat(Pricing.discount(100)).isEqualTo(10);  // kills == → != mutant
    assertThat(Pricing.discount(101)).isEqualTo(10);  // confirms range
}
```

### 3. Spring Boot `@TestBean` — Lightweight Test-Specific Bean Replacement [official]

`@TestBean` (Spring Boot 3.4+) replaces a production bean for the duration of a test without requiring `@MockitoBean` (which creates a Mockito mock). It is ideal when you want a hand-crafted test double (a recording stub, a counter, an in-memory implementation) rather than a mock.

**When to use:** When the real bean has side effects (sends email, writes to S3) and you want a simple recording double that Spring can autowire normally.
**When NOT to use:** When you need dynamic per-test stubbing behavior — use `@MockitoBean` instead. Also avoid when you need to verify call order; `@TestBean` does not integrate with Mockito's verification API.

```java
@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceNotificationTest {

    @TestBean
    EmailSender emailSender;  // field name must match bean name

    // Factory method MUST be static — non-static is silently ignored
    static EmailSender emailSender() {
        return new RecordingEmailSender();
    }

    @Autowired
    OrderService orderService;

    @BeforeEach
    void guardAgainstSilentMiss() {
        // Catch the non-static mistake early
        assertThat(emailSender).isInstanceOf(RecordingEmailSender.class);
    }

    @Test
    void placingOrderSendsConfirmationEmail() {
        orderService.place(new Order("user@example.com", List.of("SKU-1")));
        RecordingEmailSender recorder = (RecordingEmailSender) emailSender;
        assertThat(recorder.sent()).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(recorder.sent().get(0).to()).isEqualTo("user@example.com");
    }
}
```

---

### 4. JUnit 5 `@Nested` BDD-Style Tests [official]

`@Nested` inner classes partition tests into logical contexts (Given/When/Then or state-machine states) sharing setup via `@BeforeEach` at each level. This avoids long method names like `given_emptyCart_when_addItem_then_sizeIsOne` and makes test intent readable as a hierarchy.

**When to use:** Domain-rich services with multiple precondition states. Use `@DisplayName` on both the inner class and test methods for readable test reports.
**When NOT to use:** Simple CRUD tests with a single happy path — the nesting overhead adds noise. Also avoid deeply nested hierarchies (>3 levels) which become hard to follow.

```java
@DisplayName("ShoppingCart")
class ShoppingCartTest {

    ShoppingCart cart;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() { cart = new ShoppingCart(); }

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("when cart is empty")
    class WhenCartIsEmpty {

        @Test @DisplayName("size is zero")
        void sizeIsZero() { assertThat(cart.size()).isZero(); }

        @Test @DisplayName("total is zero")
        void totalIsZero() { assertThat(cart.total()).isEqualByComparingTo(BigDecimal.ZERO); }
    }

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("when cart has items")
    class WhenCartHasItems {

        @BeforeEach
        void addItem() { cart.add(new Item("SKU-1", new BigDecimal("9.99"), 2)); }

        @Test @DisplayName("size reflects added quantity")
        void sizeReflectsQuantity() { assertThat(cart.size()).isEqualTo(2); }

        @Nested
        @DisplayName("and applying a valid coupon")
        class AndApplyingCoupon {

            @Test @DisplayName("reduces total by coupon percentage")
            void reducesTotal() {
                cart.applyCoupon(new Coupon("SAVE10", 10));
                assertThat(cart.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("17.98");
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### 5. AssertJ Soft Assertions — Collect All Failures Before Reporting [official]

`SoftAssertions.assertSoftly()` runs all assertions even when earlier ones fail, collecting every failure into a single report. This is critical for form validation tests, API response shape tests, and any scenario where seeing all failures at once saves re-run cycles.

**When to use:** When a test validates multiple fields on the same object and you want a complete failure report. Use the `@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)` approach for repeated use across methods.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use soft assertions when a later assertion depends on an earlier one succeeding (e.g., assert list is non-null, then assert list size). A `NullPointerException` inside the lambda leaves partial state in the `SoftAssertions` object and may mask the real failure.

```java
import org.assertj.core.api.SoftAssertions;
import org.assertj.core.api.junit.jupiter.SoftAssertionsExtension;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;

@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)
class UserRegistrationResponseTest {

    @Test
    void responseContainsAllRequiredFields(SoftAssertions softly) {
        UserRegistrationResponse response = registrationService.register(
            new RegistrationRequest("alice", "alice@example.com", "P@ssw0rd!"));

        softly.assertThat(response.userId()).isNotNull();
        softly.assertThat(response.email()).isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
        softly.assertThat(response.createdAt()).isBeforeOrEqualTo(Instant.now());
        softly.assertThat(response.verificationEmailSent()).isTrue();
        softly.assertThat(response.roles()).containsExactly("ROLE_USER");
    }

    @Test
    void inlineStyle() {
        SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {
            softly.assertThat(1 + 1).isEqualTo(2);
            softly.assertThat("hello").startsWith("he");
        });
    }
}
```

### 6. `@JsonTest` — Focused JSON Serialization / Deserialization Tests [official]

`@JsonTest` loads only the Jackson (or Gson) slice of the application context — no services, no repositories. Use it to verify `@JsonProperty` mappings, custom serializers, date format configuration, and JSON schema shape without loading the full application.

**When to use:** Any time you add a custom `@JsonSerialize`/`@JsonDeserialize`, a `@JsonNaming`, or a Jackson module. Essential for API contracts where field naming conventions matter.
**When NOT to use:** When the DTO has no custom serialization logic and uses only standard Jackson defaults — a plain unit test is sufficient and faster.

```java
@JsonTest
class OrderDtoJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    JacksonTester<OrderDto> json;

    @Test
    void serialisesOrderIdAsSnakeCase() throws Exception {
        OrderDto dto = new OrderDto("ORD-001", "alice@example.com",
            BigDecimal.valueOf(49.99), List.of("SKU-A", "SKU-B"));

        JsonContent<OrderDto> written = json.write(dto);

        assertThat(written).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.order_id")
            .isEqualTo("ORD-001");
        assertThat(written).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.customer_email")
            .isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
        assertThat(written).extractingJsonPathNumberValue("$.total_amount")
            .isEqualByComparingTo(49.99);
    }

    @Test
    void roundTripPreservesAllFields() throws Exception {
        OrderDto original = new OrderDto("ORD-002", "bob@example.com",
            BigDecimal.valueOf(9.99), List.of("SKU-C"));
        String serialized = json.write(original).getJson();
        OrderDto deserialized = json.parseObject(serialized);
        assertThat(deserialized).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(original);
    }
}
```

---

### 7. `@RestClientTest` — Isolated HTTP Client Tests [official]

`@RestClientTest` loads only the `RestTemplate` / `RestClient` slice and auto-configures a `MockRestServiceServer`. It lets you test your own HTTP client code (the service class that calls an external API) without spinning up a real server or using Testcontainers.

**When to use:** For service classes that wrap `RestTemplate` or `RestClient` to call external APIs. Verify request construction (headers, path params, body serialization) and response parsing in isolation.
**When NOT to use:** When testing reactive WebClient — use `@WebFluxTest` with `WebTestClient` instead. Also not suitable when the HTTP client is buried inside a large service with non-HTTP dependencies.

```java
@RestClientTest(GithubClient.class)
class GithubClientTest {

    @Autowired
    GithubClient client;

    @Autowired
    MockRestServiceServer server;

    @Test
    void fetchesRepositoryByOwnerAndName() throws Exception {
        server.expect(requestTo("https://api.github.com/repos/octocat/Hello-World"))
              .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
              .andExpect(header("Accept", "application/vnd.github+json"))
              .andRespond(withSuccess(
                  "{\"id\":1296269,\"name\":\"Hello-World\",\"full_name\":\"octocat/Hello-World\"}",
                  MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        GithubRepo repo = client.getRepo("octocat", "Hello-World");

        assertThat(repo.id()).isEqualTo(1296269L);
        assertThat(repo.fullName()).isEqualTo("octocat/Hello-World");
        server.verify();
    }
}
```

---

### 8. Mockito `thenAnswer` — Dynamic Return Values and Retry Simulation [official]

`thenAnswer` gives access to the invocation's arguments and call count at stubbing time, enabling retry simulation, echo patterns, and stateful mock behavior that `thenReturn` cannot express.

**When to use:** Retry logic tests (fail N times, succeed on attempt N+1), transformer services (return input transformed), and scenarios where the returned value depends on an argument's content.
**When NOT to use:** When a fixed return value or `thenThrow` sequence suffices — `thenAnswer` lambdas hide intent and are harder to read during review. Prefer `thenReturn(...).thenReturn(...)` for simple two-state sequences.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class PaymentGatewayRetryTest {

    @Mock
    PaymentGateway gateway;

    @InjectMocks
    RetryingPaymentService service;

    @Test
    void succeedsOnThirdAttemptAfterTransientFailures() {
        AtomicInteger callCount = new AtomicInteger();
        when(gateway.charge(any())).thenAnswer(inv -> {
            int attempt = callCount.incrementAndGet();
            if (attempt <= 2) throw new TransientGatewayException("timeout attempt " + attempt);
            return new ChargeResult("TXN-" + attempt, "SUCCESS");
        });

        ChargeResult result = service.chargeWithRetry(new ChargeRequest("tok_test", 100_00));

        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo("SUCCESS");
        assertThat(callCount).hasValue(3);
        verify(gateway, times(3)).charge(any());
    }

    @Test
    void echoPatternReturnsTransformedArgument() {
        when(gateway.tokenize(anyString()))
            .thenAnswer(inv -> "tok_" + inv.getArgument(0, String.class).toLowerCase());

        assertThat(gateway.tokenize("VISA-4242")).isEqualTo("tok_visa-4242");
    }
}
```

---

### 9. Testcontainers Network — Multi-Service Integration Tests [official]

`Network.newNetwork()` allows multiple containers to communicate by hostname inside a shared Docker bridge network. This is essential for testing a consumer against a real Kafka broker, or a service against a sidecar proxy, without exposing ports on the host.

**When to use:** Integration tests where service A must call service B by DNS name (e.g., a Kafka consumer connecting to `kafka:9092`, or an app connecting to a Redis sentinel). Avoids the complexity of `docker-compose` in CI.
**When NOT to use:** When a single container with `@ServiceConnection` is sufficient — `Network` adds setup complexity. Do not create a new `Network` per test method; share it as a `static` field to avoid Docker resource exhaustion.

```java
class KafkaConsumerIntegrationTest {

    static final Network NETWORK = Network.newNetwork();

    @Container
    static final KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer(
            DockerImageName.parse("confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.1"))
        .withNetwork(NETWORK)
        .withNetworkAliases("kafka");

    @Container
    static final GenericContainer<?> consumer = new GenericContainer<>(
            DockerImageName.parse("myregistry/order-consumer:latest"))
        .withNetwork(NETWORK)
        .withEnv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "kafka:9092")
        .dependsOn(kafka)
        .waitingFor(Wait.forLogMessage(".*Consumer started.*", 1));

    @Test
    void consumerProcessesProducedMessage() throws Exception {
        try (KafkaProducer<String, String> producer = buildProducer(kafka.getBootstrapServers())) {
            producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", "k1", "{\"id\":\"ORD-1\"}")).get();
        }
        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
               .untilAsserted(() ->
                   assertThat(consumer.getLogs()).contains("Processed order ORD-1"));
    }
}
```

---

### 10. JUnit 5 Custom `ParameterResolver` — Injecting Domain Objects into Tests [official]

`ParameterResolver` extensions let you inject arbitrary objects (clocks, fake-time providers, database connections, generated keys) into test method parameters. This avoids thread-local hacks and keeps test setup explicit in the method signature.

**When to use:** When multiple test methods in a class need a consistently-initialized domain object that is expensive to construct inline. Common for fixed `Clock` injection in time-sensitive tests.
**When NOT to use:** When Spring's `@Autowired` or a simple `@BeforeEach` factory field suffices. The extension pattern adds indirection — only justified when the same resolver is reused across many test classes.

```java
// Annotation
@Target(ElementType.PARAMETER)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface FrozenClock {
    String value() default "2026-01-15T10:00:00Z";
}

// Extension
public class FrozenClockExtension implements ParameterResolver {

    @Override
    public boolean supportsParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        return pc.isAnnotated(FrozenClock.class)
            && pc.getParameter().getType().equals(Clock.class);
    }

    @Override
    public Object resolveParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        String instant = pc.findAnnotation(FrozenClock.class)
                           .map(FrozenClock::value)
                           .orElse("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z");
        return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse(instant), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    }
}

// Usage
@ExtendWith(FrozenClockExtension.class)
class InvoiceDueDateTest {

    @Test
    void dueDateIsThirtyDaysFromIssue(@FrozenClock("2026-03-01T00:00:00Z") Clock clock) {
        Invoice invoice = Invoice.issue(clock);
        assertThat(invoice.dueDate())
            .isEqualTo(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31));
    }
}
```

---

### 11. WireMock Stateful Scenarios — Simulating Multi-Step Protocol Flows [community]

WireMock 3.x stateful scenarios (`inScenario`) model multi-state server behavior: initial token issue, token expiry, token refresh. Each `MappingBuilder` transitions the scenario to the next state, letting you test retry-with-refresh logic in a single test without test doubles.

**When to use:** OAuth2 token refresh, idempotency key flows, rate-limit + backoff, any multi-step protocol where the server's response changes based on prior calls.
**When NOT to use:** Simple request/response testing where state is unnecessary — stateful scenarios are hard to debug when assertions fail mid-scenario. Always call `wm.resetScenarios()` in `@AfterEach`.

```java
@WireMockTest
class TokenRefreshIntegrationTest {

    static final String SCENARIO = "token-lifecycle";

    @Test
    void clientRefreshesExpiredToken(WireMockRuntimeInfo wm) {
        WireMock wireMock = wm.getWireMock();

        // State 1: initial valid token
        wireMock.register(get("/api/resource")
            .inScenario(SCENARIO).whenScenarioStateIs(STARTED)
            .willReturn(ok("{\"data\":\"value\"}"))
            .willSetStateTo("token-expired"));

        // State 2: token expired — 401
        wireMock.register(get("/api/resource")
            .inScenario(SCENARIO).whenScenarioStateIs("token-expired")
            .willReturn(unauthorized())
            .willSetStateTo("token-refreshed"));

        // State 3: refreshed token succeeds
        wireMock.register(get("/api/resource")
            .inScenario(SCENARIO).whenScenarioStateIs("token-refreshed")
            .willReturn(ok("{\"data\":\"refreshed-value\"}")));

        wireMock.register(post("/oauth/token")
            .willReturn(ok("{\"access_token\":\"new-tok\",\"expires_in\":3600}")));

        ApiClient client = new ApiClient(wm.getHttpBaseUrl());
        ApiResponse first  = client.fetchResource();  // 200
        ApiResponse second = client.fetchResource();  // 401 → refresh → retry 200

        assertThat(first.data()).isEqualTo("value");
        assertThat(second.data()).isEqualTo("refreshed-value");
        wireMock.verifyThat(1, postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/oauth/token")));
    }
}
```

---

### 12. AssertJ `extracting` + `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` — Per-Element Assertions on Collections [official]

`satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` asserts that a collection has exactly N elements and each element satisfies exactly one of the provided consumer assertions (in any order). Combined with `extracting` for multi-field tuples, it replaces fragile `containsExactlyInAnyOrder` calls that require complete `equals()` implementations.

**When to use:** Asserting a list of domain objects returned from a query or transformation, where order is non-deterministic and `equals()` is not overridden. Particularly useful for paginated API response assertions.
**When NOT to use:** When order is deterministic and elements implement `equals()` — `containsExactly` is more readable and failure messages are clearer. Do not use for single-element collections; prefer `singleElement()`.

```java
@Test
void queryReturnsAllActiveProductsWithCorrectFields() {
    List<Product> products = productRepository.findAllActive();

    assertThat(products)
        .extracting(Product::sku, Product::name, Product::price)
        .satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(
            tuple -> assertThat(tuple).containsExactly("SKU-A", "Widget", new BigDecimal("9.99")),
            tuple -> assertThat(tuple).containsExactly("SKU-B", "Gadget", new BigDecimal("24.99"))
        );
}

@Test
void filteredAssertionOnSubset() {
    List<Order> orders = orderService.findAll();

    assertThat(orders)
        .filteredOn(o -> o.status() == OrderStatus.PENDING)
        .extracting(Order::customerId)
        .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("CUST-1", "CUST-3");
}
```

---

### 13. Virtual Thread Testing with Awaitility — Concurrency Without Race Conditions [community]

Java 21 virtual threads enable massive concurrency but introduce new testing challenges: `CountDownLatch` coordination, ensuring the thread pool is not exhausted by blocking operations, and detecting carrier thread pinning. Awaitility's `untilAsserted` replaces fragile `Thread.sleep()` waits.

**When to use:** Services using `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or `Thread.ofVirtual()`. Verifying that blocking I/O in virtual threads does not pin carrier threads.
**When NOT to use:** Simple sequential service logic that happens to run inside a virtual thread — standard JUnit assertions are sufficient. Do not use Awaitility with a timeout shorter than the slowest operation under test; it produces flaky CI failures.

```java
class VirtualThreadServiceTest {

    @Test
    void processesAllItemsConcurrentlyWithVirtualThreads() throws InterruptedException {
        int itemCount = 1000;
        ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String> processed = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
        CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(itemCount);

        try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < itemCount; i++) {
                final int idx = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    try {
                        processed.add(itemProcessingService.process("ITEM-" + idx));
                    } finally {
                        latch.countDown();  // MUST be in finally — exception cannot skip it
                    }
                });
            }
        }

        boolean completed = latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        assertThat(completed).as("All items processed within timeout").isTrue();
        assertThat(processed).hasSize(itemCount);
    }

    @Test
    void asyncResultAvailableWithinSla() {
        CompletableFuture<String> future = asyncService.processAsync("ITEM-X");

        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
               .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(50))
               .untilAsserted(() ->
                   assertThat(future).isCompletedWithValueMatching(
                       r -> r.startsWith("PROCESSED-"), "result must start with PROCESSED-"));
    }
}
```

---

### Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 28 Additions [community]

**`@TestBean` factory method must be `static` on the enclosing test class — a default interface method or method in a `@Configuration` inner class is NOT discovered [community]** — Spring Boot's `BeanOverrideProcessor` scans only `static` methods declared directly on the test class (not inherited, not on inner `@Configuration` classes). A developer who moves the factory into a nested `@TestConfiguration` class to keep the test class tidy ends up with the real bean injected silently. The compiler and Spring startup both succeed. Add `assertThat(emailSender).isInstanceOf(RecordingEmailSender.class)` in `@BeforeEach` — this guard catches the mistake at the earliest assertion, before any domain logic executes. WHY: Because `BeanOverrideProcessor` registration happens during context post-processing, not bean creation, there is no "bean not found" exception to surface the misconfiguration.

**jqwik's `@Property` methods are incompatible with `@SpringBootTest` without the `jqwik-spring` module — combining them causes "no test engine found" errors or silent skip [community]** — jqwik runs as its own JUnit Platform test engine. When a class annotated with `@SpringBootTest` also uses `@Property`, the Spring test runner does not recognise the jqwik annotations and skips them without reporting skipped tests. The fix is to add `net.jqwik:jqwik-spring:1.9.0` and annotate the class with `@JqwikSpringSupport` (which proxies Spring context management). WHY: The two engines manage test lifecycle independently; without the bridge, neither engine claims the test method.

**WireMock stateful scenarios are global to the WireMock server instance — failing to call `wm.resetScenarios()` in `@AfterEach` leaves the scenario in a terminal state and causes the next test to start in the wrong state [community]** — `@WireMockTest` resets mappings between tests but does NOT reset scenario state by default. A test that runs first succeeds; the identical test run second starts in state `token-refreshed` instead of `STARTED` and gets the wrong response. The symptom is a test that passes in isolation but fails when run as part of a suite (ordering-dependent flake). WHY: WireMock separates mapping lifecycle from scenario lifecycle intentionally, to allow scenario replay in multi-request tests; the implication is that `resetScenarios()` must be called explicitly.

**`SoftAssertions.assertSoftly()` continues executing the lambda after an assertion fails, which means a `NullPointerException` thrown by downstream code (not AssertJ) propagates and masks all collected soft failures [community]** — If the first soft assertion is `softly.assertThat(response).isNotNull()` and it fails (response IS null), AssertJ records the failure but continues. The next line `softly.assertThat(response.status())` throws a real `NullPointerException` (not an AssertJ failure), which terminates the lambda and causes the test to report only the NPE — hiding the root cause. WHY: AssertJ can only intercept its own `AssertionError`s; it cannot intercept `RuntimeException`s thrown by your code. Fix: guard with an early hard assertion for null-safety checks before entering the soft block.

**`@DataJpaTest` + `@Import(JpaAuditingConfig.class)` causes Spring to create a separate application context per import combination, defeating the shared context cache [community]** — Each unique set of `@Import` annotations is part of the context cache key. A test with `@DataJpaTest` + `@Import(JpaAuditingConfig.class)` and another with only `@DataJpaTest` load two separate contexts even though the entities and schema are identical. In a large project with 20+ `@DataJpaTest` variants, this multiplies context load time. WHY: Spring cannot prove that importing an additional configuration class leaves the DataJpa slice unchanged. Fix: create a single `@DataJpaTest` base class with the shared `@Import` and inherit from it, collapsing all variants to one cache entry.

**`CountDownLatch.countDown()` inside a virtual thread task MUST be in a `try-finally` block — an unchecked exception in the task body prevents `latch.await()` from ever returning, hanging the test until timeout [community]** — Virtual threads do not propagate unchecked exceptions to the submitter (unlike `Future.get()`). If a task throws a `RuntimeException` before reaching `latch.countDown()`, the latch count never reaches zero. `latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` returns `false` after the timeout, and the test fails with a misleading "timeout" message rather than the original exception. WHY: `ExecutorService.submit()` wraps the task in a `FutureTask`; the exception is stored internally and never rethrown unless you call `future.get()`. Fix: always put `latch.countDown()` in `finally`, and log or rethrow the exception from the catch block so the root cause is visible.
