## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### 1. JUnit 5 `@ClassTemplate` — Reusable Test Class Skeletons with Injected Variants [official]

`@ClassTemplate` (JUnit 5.14+) marks a top-level test class as a template that is instantiated multiple times — once per `ClassTemplateInvocationContext` produced by a registered `ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider`. This extends the `@TestTemplate` concept from methods to entire classes, enabling a single test class to run against different configurations (e.g., multiple database dialects, API versions, or transport protocols) without copy-paste duplication.

**When to use:** When the same set of test methods must execute identically against two or more variants of a collaborator (e.g., `PostgreSQLContainer` vs `MySQLContainer`; REST vs gRPC transport). Eliminates the base-class-per-variant pattern while keeping test code DRY.
**When NOT to use:** Avoid when variant differences are large enough to require different test logic per variant — `@ClassTemplate` instantiates the *same* test body for each variant. Do not use when `@ParameterizedTest` at the method level is sufficient. Alternative: abstract base class with concrete subclasses per variant (classic pattern, more IDE-navigable); `@ParameterizedTest` for method-level variation.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.ClassTemplate;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// --- ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider ---
public class DatabaseVariantProvider
        implements ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider {

    @Override
    public boolean supportsClassTemplate(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        return true;
    }

    @Override
    public Stream<ClassTemplateInvocationContext> provideClassTemplateInvocationContexts(
            ExtensionContext ctx) {
        return Stream.of(
            new DbVariantContext("postgres:16-alpine"),
            new DbVariantContext("mysql:8.4")
        );
    }
}

// --- Shared test template class ---
@ClassTemplate
@ExtendWith(DatabaseVariantProvider.class)
class RepositoryContractTest {

    @Test
    void save_thenFind_roundTrip(DataSource dataSource) {
        var repo = new UserRepository(dataSource);
        repo.save(new User("alice@example.com"));
        assertThat(repo.findByEmail("alice@example.com")).isPresent();
    }

    @Test
    void delete_nonExistent_doesNotThrow(DataSource dataSource) {
        var repo = new UserRepository(dataSource);
        assertThat(repo.delete("unknown@example.com")).isFalse();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ClassTemplate` requires a custom `ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider` — more boilerplate than `@ParameterizedTest`. IDE support (navigation, test count) was limited in early JUnit 5.14 builds; verify with your IDE version. All test methods in the template class must accept the same injected parameters from the context. Alternative: `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` for per-method variation; abstract base class pattern for complex setup differences per variant.

[official]

---

### 2. AssertJ 4.0 `isSealed()` / `isRecord()` — Native Type-Shape Assertions [official]

AssertJ 4.0.0-M1 (Java 17 minimum baseline) added `isSealed()`, `isNotSealed()`, `isRecord()`, and `isNotRecord()` as first-class assertions on `AbstractClassAssert`. These avoid the boilerplate of `assertThat(MyClass.class.isSealed()).isTrue()` and produce assertion failure messages that name the class under test.

**When to use:** Architecture tests that enforce domain model conventions — e.g., verifying that all value objects in a package are records, or that event types are sealed. Pairs well with ArchUnit class-level predicates and `ClassFileImporter`.
**When NOT to use:** Do not gate critical production behaviour on these assertions — they are structural/architectural checks, not behavioural. Avoid in projects that must compile on Java < 17 (AssertJ 4.0 requires Java 17+). Alternative: AssertJ 3.x `satisfies(c -> assertThat(c.isSealed()).isTrue())` for Java 11/17 mixed projects; ArchUnit `classes().that().areSealed()` for bulk package-level rules.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Domain model classes under test
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

class DomainModelStructureTest {

    @Test
    void shape_isSealed() {
        assertThat(Shape.class).isSealed();
    }

    @Test
    void circle_isRecord() {
        assertThat(Circle.class).isRecord();
        assertThat(Circle.class).isNotSealed();
    }

    @Test
    void shape_permittedSubclasses_areAllRecords() {
        for (Class<?> permitted : Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
            assertThat(permitted)
                .as("Permitted subclass %s should be a record",
                    permitted.getSimpleName())
                .isRecord();
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** These assertions require AssertJ 4.0+ and Java 17+. Using `isRecord()` does not verify the record's components — follow up with `assertThat(myRecord).extracting("field1", "field2").containsExactly(...)` to assert component values. Alternative: AssertJ 3.27 `satisfies` with manual reflection; ArchUnit `haveModifier(JavaModifier.SEALED)` for package-wide bulk checks.

[official]

---

### 3. Spring Boot 4.0 `RestTestClient` — Typed Fluent HTTP Testing for `@SpringBootTest` [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 introduced `RestTestClient` in the new `spring-boot-resttestclient` module as a first-class alternative to `WebTestClient` for servlet-based integration tests. It wraps `RestClient` (Spring Framework 6.1+) in a test-aware fluent API, providing `.get()`, `.post()`, `.exchange()`, `.assertThat()` chaining without requiring a reactive server.

**When to use:** `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` or `DEFINED_PORT` tests against servlet-based (non-reactive) Spring Boot 4.x applications. Preferred over `TestRestTemplate` for new code — fluent assertions are more readable and composable.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use in Spring WebFlux/reactive applications — `WebTestClient` remains the correct choice there. Avoid mixing `RestTestClient` and `TestRestTemplate` in the same test suite. Alternative: `TestRestTemplate` (still available in Boot 4.x, but considered legacy); `MockMvcTester` for controller-layer slice tests without a real server.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.client.RestTestClient;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class OrderControllerIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    RestTestClient restTestClient;

    @Test
    void createOrder_returns201WithLocation() {
        var body = new CreateOrderRequest("PRODUCT-42", 3);
        restTestClient.post()
            .uri("/orders")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .body(body)
            .exchange()
            .assertThat()
            .hasStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
            .hasHeader("Location")
            .bodyJson()
            .hasPath("$.orderId");
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_notFound_returns404() {
        restTestClient.get()
            .uri("/orders/99999")
            .exchange()
            .assertThat()
            .hasStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `RestTestClient` is only available in the `spring-boot-resttestclient` module added in Boot 4.0 — add `testImplementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-resttestclient'` explicitly. It does not support streaming responses (use `WebTestClient` there). The fluent API does not yet support multipart file uploads as cleanly as `TestRestTemplate`. Alternative: `TestRestTemplate` for simple synchronous tests; `WebTestClient` bound to a non-reactive server via `WebTestClient.bindToServer()` for richer assertion support.

[official]

---

### 4. Mockito 5.23 `@Nullable`-Aware Default Answer — Preventing NPE from Unstubbed Methods [official]

Mockito 5.23 introduced improved handling of `@Nullable`-annotated return types in the default `RETURNS_DEFAULTS` answer. When a mocked method's return type is annotated with a nullability annotation (JSR-305 `@Nullable`, Jakarta `@Nullable`, or JSpecify `@Nullable`), the default answer returns `null` explicitly rather than triggering a smart-null proxy. Additionally, `ReturnsEmptyValues` now respects `@Nullable` on Android mock makers.

**When to use:** When integrating Mockito with codebases that use nullability annotations pervasively (JSpecify, Checker Framework, Spring's null-safety annotations). Prevents accidental NPE in tests caused by unstubbed methods returning smart-null proxies when `null` is the semantically correct default.
**When NOT to use:** Do not rely on `@Nullable` default-answer behaviour as a substitute for explicit stubs — if a method's return value matters for the test, always stub it explicitly. Do not use if your project does not use nullability annotations. Alternative: `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` with `strictness = STRICT_STUBS` to fail on unstubbed invocations regardless of nullability; `RETURNS_SMART_NULLS` answer for non-nullable return types.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

interface ProfileService {
    @Nullable String findDisplayName(String userId);   // explicitly nullable
    String getDefaultRole(String userId);              // non-nullable
}

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class UserGreetingServiceTest {

    @Mock
    ProfileService profileService;

    @Test
    void greet_usesDefaultName_whenDisplayNameIsNull() {
        // @Nullable return — Mockito 5.23 returns null for unstubbed call
        // (null is the documented valid return, no NPE thrown)
        String displayName = profileService.findDisplayName("user-42");
        assertThat(displayName).isNull();

        var service = new UserGreetingService(profileService);
        String greeting = service.greet("user-42");
        // fallback path tested: display name absent, default greeting used
        assertThat(greeting).isEqualTo("Hello, user!");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** This behaviour only activates when the JVM can see the nullability annotation at runtime (annotation retention must be `RUNTIME`). `@org.springframework.lang.Nullable` has `RUNTIME` retention; JSpecify's `@Nullable` 1.0+ also does. If annotations are `CLASS`-retention only, Mockito cannot see them. Alternative: `RETURNS_SMART_NULLS` global answer; explicit `lenient()` stubs for nullable returns.

[official]

---

### 5. AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields()` — Deep Equality Without `equals()` [official]

`assertThat(actual).usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields("id", "createdAt").isEqualTo(expected)` performs a deep field-by-field equality check while skipping fields that are auto-generated or non-deterministic. This avoids having to implement `equals()`/`hashCode()` on DTOs, JPA entities, or API response objects just for test purposes.

**When to use:** Asserting persistence round-trips where `id` and `createdAt` are database-assigned; comparing API response DTOs where `requestId` or `timestamp` fields are dynamic; comparing complex nested objects where only a subset of fields is meaningful for the test.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use as a substitute for implementing `equals()` when equality is a domain concept — tests that rely on recursive comparison hide the absence of a proper `equals()` implementation. Do not use when the object graph has cycles (Hibernate proxy chains). Alternative: AssertJ `extracting("field1", "field2").containsExactly(...)` for a subset of fields; `isEqualToComparingOnlyGivenFields` (deprecated in AssertJ 3.x, replaced by recursive comparison).

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@DataJpaTest
class ProductRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    ProductRepository productRepo;

    @Test
    void save_persistsAllMutableFields_ignoringGeneratedIds() {
        var product = new Product(null, "Widget Pro",
                new BigDecimal("29.99"), "Electronics", null);
        var saved = productRepo.saveAndFlush(product);

        assertThat(saved)
            .usingRecursiveComparison()
            .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt", "updatedAt", "version")
            .isEqualTo(product);

        assertThat(saved.getId()).isPositive();
        assertThat(saved.getCreatedAt()).isNotNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `usingRecursiveComparison()` traverses the entire object graph — with Hibernate lazy proxies, this can trigger unexpected SQL queries. Use `@Transactional` on the test method and access only eagerly-fetched associations, or detach the entity before asserting. Also, the recursive comparator uses `equals()` for leaf types (String, Integer, etc.) — custom value objects still need `equals()`. Alternative: MapStruct DTO mapping to a flat structure before asserting; `assertThat(saved).isEqualToIgnoringGivenFields(product, "id", "createdAt")` (deprecated AssertJ 3.x API).

[official]

---

### 6. Spring Boot 3.5 `print-condition-evaluation-report` — Debuggable Auto-Configuration in Tests [official]

`@SpringBootTest` combined with `spring.test.print-condition-evaluation-report=true` (Spring Boot 3.5+) prints the `ConditionEvaluationReport` to the test output when a context fails to load. Previously this report was only printed on application startup failure, not on test context failure. This makes `@SpringBootTest` context-load failures dramatically easier to diagnose.

**When to use:** Any `@SpringBootTest` that fails with `ApplicationContextException` or `BeanCreationException` and the cause is unclear. Add to `src/test/resources/application.properties` for all integration tests, or set per-test via `@TestPropertySource`.
**When NOT to use:** Disable in production CI where test output size is a concern — the report can produce hundreds of lines per test class. Avoid in slice tests (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`) where the condition report is less useful since slices intentionally exclude most auto-configuration. Alternative: `--debug` flag on `SpringApplication` startup; logging `org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure` at `DEBUG` level.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.TestPropertySource;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import org.springframework.cache.CacheManager;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
@TestPropertySource(properties = {
    "spring.test.print-condition-evaluation-report=true"
})
class FullContextSmokeTest {

    @Autowired(required = false)
    DataSource dataSource;

    @Autowired(required = false)
    CacheManager cacheManager;

    @Test
    void contextLoads_withExpectedBeans() {
        // If this fails, the condition evaluation report in test output
        // will show exactly which auto-configuration was skipped and why
        assertThat(dataSource)
            .as("DataSource must be auto-configured")
            .isNotNull();
    }

    @Test
    void cacheManager_isConfigured() {
        assertThat(cacheManager)
            .as("CacheManager should be auto-configured from cache.type property")
            .isNotNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The condition evaluation report is emitted only on context-load failure in Boot 3.5 — if the context loads successfully but a bean is wrong, you do not get the report. Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG` for successful-context diagnostics. Alternative: `SpringApplication.run()` with `setLogStartupInfo(true)` in a manual test launcher; `ConditionEvaluationReport.get(applicationContext)` for programmatic access.

[official]

---

### 7. Testcontainers 2.0 Module Renaming — `tc-` Prefix and Package Migration [official]

Testcontainers 2.0 renamed all technology-specific artifact IDs from `testcontainers-<tech>` to `tc-<tech>` (e.g., `testcontainers-postgresql` → `tc-postgresql`, `testcontainers-kafka` → `tc-kafka`). The `@Testcontainers` JUnit 5 extension and `@Container` annotation were moved from `org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter` to `org.testcontainers.junit5` as part of the package restructure.

**When to use:** Any project migrating from Testcontainers 1.x to 2.0. Apply the rename mechanically using your IDE's refactoring tools. Update `build.gradle` / `pom.xml` artifact IDs simultaneously with import updates.
**When NOT to use:** If you are not yet migrating to TC 2.0, remain on the 1.x artifact names and packages. Do not apply partial migrations — mixing 1.x and 2.0 artifacts in the same project causes `ClassNotFoundException` at runtime.

```java
// build.gradle (Testcontainers 2.0 dependency names)
// testImplementation "org.testcontainers:tc-postgresql:2.0.0"
// testImplementation "org.testcontainers:tc-kafka:2.0.0"

// TC 1.x imports (DELETE)
// import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
// import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;

// TC 2.0 imports (ADD)
import org.testcontainers.junit5.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit5.Testcontainers;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class OrderPersistenceTest {

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("orders")
            .withUsername("test")
            .withPassword("secret");

    @Test
    void container_startsAndAcceptsConnections() {
        assertThat(postgres.isRunning()).isTrue();
        assertThat(postgres.getJdbcUrl())
            .startsWith("jdbc:postgresql://");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** TC 2.0 also dropped the deprecated `ContainerState.getMappedPort(int)` overload in favour of `getMappedPort(Integer)` — port lookups that silently auto-boxed will now require explicit casts. The `DockerComposeContainer` API also changed: `withExposedService(name, port, waitStrategy)` now returns `ServiceBuilder`. Budget dedicated migration time. Alternative: remain on TC 1.21.x (still maintained); use the `testcontainers-bom` to align versions across modules.

[official]

---

### 8. JUnit 5 `@EnabledOnJre` with `JRE.OTHER` — Forward-Compatible JRE Gating [official]

`@EnabledOnJre(JRE.OTHER)` enables a test only on JRE versions not explicitly enumerated in the `JRE` enum — i.e., any version newer than the highest constant defined in the installed JUnit 5 release. This allows tests targeting unreleased or preview JDK features to be gated to "any future JRE" without binding to a specific version constant that may not yet exist.

**When to use:** Tests for preview features (JEP 488 Primitive Types in Patterns, JEP 502 Stable Values) on JDK 24+/25+ where the corresponding `JRE.JAVA_24` constant is not yet present in your pinned JUnit version. Also useful for skipping tests on end-of-life JREs without enumerating every version.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use `JRE.OTHER` as the sole gating for production-important tests — if the test should run on JDK 21 LTS, enumerate `JRE.JAVA_21` explicitly. Avoid in tests where the "future JRE" meaning is ambiguous to future maintainers. Alternative: `@EnabledForJreRange(min = JRE.JAVA_21)` for inclusive range gating; `Assumptions.assumeTrue(Runtime.version().feature() >= 25)` for explicit programmatic gating.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.EnabledOnJre;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DisabledOnJre;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.JRE;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class JreFeaturesTest {

    // Runs ONLY on JREs newer than the highest JRE enum constant
    // in this JUnit build (e.g., JDK 25+ when running JUnit 5.11)
    @Test
    @EnabledOnJre(JRE.OTHER)
    void primitiveTypePatternsPreview_smokeTest() {
        Object value = 42;
        // Preview: primitive type patterns (JEP 488)
        boolean result = value instanceof int i && i > 0;
        assertThat(result).isTrue();
    }

    // Explicitly skip LTS versions with incomplete virtual-thread support
    @Test
    @DisabledOnJre({JRE.JAVA_11, JRE.JAVA_17})
    void virtualThreads_supportedOnJdk21Plus() {
        var thread = Thread.ofVirtual().name("test-vt").unstarted(() -> {});
        assertThat(thread.isVirtual()).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `JRE.OTHER` semantics depend on the JUnit version — as JUnit upgrades add new `JRE` constants, the set of versions matched by `OTHER` shrinks. A test that matched `OTHER` on JUnit 5.11 (covering JDK 24+) may stop matching on JUnit 5.14 if `JRE.JAVA_24` was added. Keep `@EnabledOnJre(JRE.OTHER)` tests under active review when upgrading JUnit. Alternative: `@EnabledForJreRange(min = JRE.JAVA_21, max = JRE.OTHER)` for inclusive range; manual `Assumptions.assumeTrue` for fine-grained version strings.

[official]

---

### 9. Spring Boot `@AutoConfigureRestDocs` + `MockMvcRestDocumentation` — Contract-Tested API Documentation [official]

`@AutoConfigureRestDocs` (Spring REST Docs + Spring Boot Test integration) auto-configures Spring REST Docs to capture request/response snippets from `MockMvc` test interactions. Combined with `document("operation-name", ...)` in `MockMvc` calls, it produces AsciiDoc snippets that serve as living documentation — documentation that fails the test if the API contract changes.

**When to use:** REST APIs that require published developer documentation (OpenAPI specs, developer portals). The documentation is generated from actual test interactions, guaranteeing it is always accurate. Best used alongside `@WebMvcTest` for controller slice testing.
**When NOT to use:** Do not add REST Docs to every test — only to dedicated contract test classes. Avoid when the API is internal-only and not consumer-facing. Overhead of snippet generation slows individual test runs. Alternative: OpenAPI/Swagger annotation-based generation (`springdoc-openapi`) for automated spec generation without test coupling; WireMock contract stubs for consumer-driven contract testing.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.restdocs.AutoConfigureRestDocs;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.restdocs.mockmvc.MockMvcRestDocumentation;
import org.springframework.restdocs.payload.PayloadDocumentation;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
@AutoConfigureRestDocs(outputDir = "build/generated-snippets")
class ProductControllerRestDocsTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvc mockMvc;

    @Test
    void getProduct_generatesDocumentationSnippets() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/products/{id}", 1L))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andDo(MockMvcRestDocumentation.document("get-product",
                PayloadDocumentation.responseFields(
                    PayloadDocumentation.fieldWithPath("id")
                        .description("Unique product identifier"),
                    PayloadDocumentation.fieldWithPath("name")
                        .description("Product display name"),
                    PayloadDocumentation.fieldWithPath("price")
                        .description("Current retail price in USD")
                )));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** REST Docs tests fail when the response structure does not match the documented fields — undocumented fields cause `SnippetException`. This is intentional (documentation completeness enforcement) but can be surprising. Generated AsciiDoc snippets must be manually included in your documentation build (Asciidoctor Gradle/Maven plugin). Alternative: `restdocs-api-spec` library to generate OpenAPI specs from REST Docs tests; Springdoc + `@Operation` annotations for annotation-driven docs without test coupling.

[official]

---

### 10. Mockito `RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS` — Fluent Chained Mock Traversal [official]

`Mockito.mock(HttpClient.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` makes every intermediate method call on the mock return another mock rather than `null`, enabling chained calls like `client.request().headers().get("Authorization")` to be stubbed end-to-end. This is useful for mocking deeply nested builder or fluent API chains without hand-crafting intermediate mocks.

**When to use:** Mocking deeply chained fluent APIs (HTTP clients, query builders, Spring `ServerRequest`/`ServerResponse`) where stubbing every intermediate return type separately would be more verbose than the test logic. Useful for legacy integration boundaries with complex builder chains.
**When NOT to use:** Frequent need for deep stubs is a code smell — if production code drills through four levels of chained calls, the real fix is encapsulation. Never use on classes with complex generics or circular references — the auto-stubbing can produce infinite recursion. Alternative: refactor production code to depend on a smaller interface; hand-craft a single intermediate mock with explicit `when` stubs.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.mockito.Answers.RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class BearerTokenExtractorTest {

    @Test
    void extractBearerToken_fromNestedRequestHeaders() {
        // Deep stub: request.getHeaders().getFirst("Authorization")
        // chains without NPE at each intermediate call
        var request = mock(ExternalApiRequest.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);
        when(request.getHeaders().getFirst("Authorization"))
            .thenReturn("Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9.payload.sig");

        var extractor = new BearerTokenExtractor();
        String token = extractor.extract(request);

        assertThat(token)
            .isEqualTo("eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9.payload.sig");
    }

    @Test
    void extractBearerToken_missingHeader_returnsEmpty() {
        var request = mock(ExternalApiRequest.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);
        when(request.getHeaders().getFirst("Authorization"))
            .thenReturn(null);

        var extractor = new BearerTokenExtractor();
        assertThat(extractor.extract(request)).isEmpty();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS` creates a mock for every return type at every chain level — including `Optional`, `List`, and other containers. Chaining through `Optional.get()` bypasses the empty check and returns another mock (not throwing `NoSuchElementException`), which can mask bugs. `MockitoExtension` strict stubs mode (`STRICT_STUBS`) treats unstubbed deep-stub calls as errors, which is recommended. Alternative: Facade/wrapper class over the complex API; hand-written fake/stub for the integration boundary.

[official]

---

### 11. JUnit 5 `@ResourceLock` with Shared Write Locks — Concurrent Test Suite Safety [official]

`@ResourceLock(value = "database", mode = ResourceAccessMode.READ_WRITE)` on a test class or method tells JUnit's parallel execution engine to hold an exclusive lock on the named resource. Tests that declare `READ` mode run concurrently with each other; tests that declare `READ_WRITE` run exclusively. This prevents data-race failures in parallel test suites that share a Testcontainers database.

**When to use:** Parallel test execution (`junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled=true`) with shared stateful resources — databases, message brokers, file system paths, caches. Declare a `READ` lock on read-only tests and `READ_WRITE` on write-heavy tests to maximise parallelism while protecting shared state.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use `@ResourceLock` as a substitute for proper test isolation (rollback, separate schemas, unique IDs). In non-parallel execution, `@ResourceLock` has no effect and adds noise. Do not lock at the class level when only one method modifies shared state — method-level locks are more granular. Alternative: `@Isolated` (JUnit 5 shorthand for `@ResourceLock(GLOBAL, READ_WRITE)`) for tests that must not run concurrently with anything; unique per-test schemas via Flyway tenant isolation.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.parallel.Execution;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.parallel.ExecutionMode;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.parallel.ResourceAccessMode;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.parallel.ResourceLock;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Execution(ExecutionMode.CONCURRENT)
class OrderDatabaseTest {

    // Read-only: can run in parallel with other READ tests
    @Test
    @ResourceLock(value = "orders-db", mode = ResourceAccessMode.READ)
    void listOrders_returnsPagedResults() {
        var orders = orderRepo.findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 10));
        assertThat(orders.getTotalElements()).isPositive();
    }

    // Write: exclusive — no other test accesses orders-db concurrently
    @Test
    @ResourceLock(value = "orders-db", mode = ResourceAccessMode.READ_WRITE)
    void cancelOrder_updatesStatusToCANCELLED() {
        var order = orderRepo.save(Order.draft("customer-1"));
        orderService.cancel(order.getId());
        assertThat(orderRepo.findById(order.getId()))
            .map(Order::getStatus)
            .hasValue(OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The resource name is a raw `String` — typos silently create independent locks that never contend. Extract lock names to a shared `TestResources` constants class. JUnit's parallel executor respects `@ResourceLock` only within the same JVM; if Surefire/Gradle forks test classes into separate JVMs, the lock has no cross-process effect. Alternative: `@Transactional` on write tests for automatic rollback; Testcontainers `withReuse(false)` per fork to give each JVM its own container.

[official]

---

### 12. AssertJ `CompletableFuture` Assertions — Non-Blocking Async Verification [official]

AssertJ 3.27 added first-class `CompletableFutureAssert` methods including `succeedsWith(Duration, Consumer)`, `failsWithin(Duration)`, `hasCompleted()`, and `isCompletedWithValueMatching(Predicate)`. These replace the pattern of `.get()` + `assertThat(value)` and produce readable failure messages that describe the expected async outcome.

**When to use:** Testing service methods that return `CompletableFuture<T>` — caches, async enrichment pipelines, HTTP client wrappers. Prefer over `future.get()` in tests because the failure message names the expected completion outcome rather than throwing a raw timeout exception.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use `hasCompleted()` before the future is done — it returns `false` for in-progress futures, not an assertion failure. For `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>` (Reactor), use `StepVerifier` instead — `CompletableFutureAssert` does not understand reactive types. Alternative: `Awaitility.await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(() -> future.isDone())` + plain assertion for conditional polling; `StepVerifier.create(mono).expectNext(value).verifyComplete()` for reactive types.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InjectMocks;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class AsyncEnrichmentServiceTest {

    @Mock
    ProfileClient profileClient;

    @InjectMocks
    AsyncEnrichmentService enrichmentService;

    @Test
    void enrichUser_completesWithFullProfile() {
        given(profileClient.fetchAsync("user-42"))
            .willReturn(CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
                new Profile("Alice", "Senior Engineer")));

        CompletableFuture<EnrichedUser> future =
            enrichmentService.enrich("user-42");

        assertThat(future)
            .succeedsWith(Duration.ofSeconds(2), enriched -> {
                assertThat(enriched.name()).isEqualTo("Alice");
                assertThat(enriched.title()).isEqualTo("Senior Engineer");
            });
    }

    @Test
    void enrichUser_failsGracefully_onClientError() {
        given(profileClient.fetchAsync("user-99"))
            .willReturn(CompletableFuture.failedFuture(
                new ProfileNotFoundException("user-99")));

        CompletableFuture<EnrichedUser> future =
            enrichmentService.enrich("user-99");

        assertThat(future)
            .failsWithin(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
            .withThrowableThat()
            .hasCauseInstanceOf(ProfileNotFoundException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("user-99");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `succeedsWith(Duration, Consumer)` blocks the test thread for up to `duration` — this is intentional but in a slow CI environment with many async tests, cumulative blocking adds up. Batch short-running futures together and use `allOf` to await them collectively. `CompletableFutureAssert` does not currently support `thenApply`/`thenCompose` chain introspection. Alternative: `Awaitility` for polling-based async assertion; `StepVerifier` for Project Reactor; plain `future.get(5, SECONDS)` + AssertJ value assertion for simple cases.

[official]

---

### 13. Spring Boot `@TestBean` Static Factory Guard Assertion — Validating Test Override Activation [official]

`@TestBean` (Spring Boot 3.2+) overrides a Spring bean in the test context using a static factory method in the test class. A defensive practice is to add a `@BeforeEach` guard assertion verifying that the `@TestBean` actually replaced the real bean — not a different bean of the same type introduced by a misconfigured `@Import` or mismatched return type.

**When to use:** Any `@SpringBootTest` or slice test that uses `@TestBean` to replace a bean with a test double. The guard assertion prevents silent test-double-miss failures where the real bean runs instead of the fake and the test produces a false positive.
**When NOT to use:** Skip the guard in small `@WebMvcTest` slices where the context is small and bean replacement is visually obvious. Do not add guards to every bean in a large context — only the ones whose replacement is critical for test correctness. Alternative: `@MockitoBean` (which fails fast if the target bean is absent); constructor injection + pure unit testing (no Spring context, no ambiguity).

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.TestBean;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
class PaymentServiceIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    PaymentGateway paymentGateway;  // will be replaced by @TestBean

    // Static factory — Spring replaces the real PaymentGateway with this fake
    @TestBean
    static PaymentGateway fakePaymentGateway() {
        return new FakePaymentGateway();
    }

    @BeforeEach
    void guardTestBeanReplacement() {
        // Guard: verify injected bean is the test double, not the real impl
        assertThat(paymentGateway)
            .as("@TestBean must inject FakePaymentGateway, not the real gateway")
            .isInstanceOf(FakePaymentGateway.class);
    }

    @Test
    void processPayment_succeeds_withFakeGateway() {
        var result = paymentGateway.charge("tok_test_visa", 4999);
        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo(PaymentStatus.SUCCESS);
        assertThat(result.transactionId()).startsWith("fake-");
    }

    @Test
    void processPayment_insufficientFunds_returnsDeclined() {
        var result = paymentGateway.charge("tok_test_decline", 99999);
        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo(PaymentStatus.DECLINED);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@TestBean` static factory must return the exact type (or subtype) of the bean being replaced. If multiple beans of the same type exist, `@TestBean` requires `name` disambiguation via `@TestBean(name = "emailNotificationService")`. The static factory method cannot inject Spring dependencies — for dependency-injected test doubles, use `@MockitoBean` instead. Alternative: `@Primary` + conditional `@Profile("test")` bean definition; `@Import(FakeGatewayConfig.class)` for shared fake configurations.

[official]

---

### 14. Testcontainers `HttpWaitStrategy` — Custom Health-Check Container Readiness [official]

`new HttpWaitStrategy().forPath("/actuator/health").forStatusCode(200).withStartupTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))` waits for a container's HTTP endpoint to return the expected status before declaring it ready. This is more reliable than the default `Wait.forListeningPort()` which only waits for the TCP port to open — the application may accept connections before Spring Boot is fully initialised.

**When to use:** Any container running a Spring Boot application (microservice dependencies in integration tests), custom application containers, or any container with an HTTP health endpoint. Prevents flaky test failures caused by requests arriving before the application is ready.
**When NOT to use:** Do not use for databases and message brokers that expose their native protocol (not HTTP) — use `Wait.forSuccessfulCommand("pg_isready")` or `Wait.forLogMessage(".*ready to accept.*", 1)` instead. Avoid extremely short timeouts in CI where startup times vary. Alternative: `Wait.forLogMessage` pattern matching for log-based readiness; `Wait.forHealthcheck()` if the container has a Docker `HEALTHCHECK` instruction.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.wait.strategy.Wait;
import org.testcontainers.junit5.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit5.Testcontainers;
import java.time.Duration;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class ExternalServiceContainerTest {

    @Container
    static GenericContainer<?> externalService =
        new GenericContainer<>("my-registry/order-service:latest")
            .withExposedPorts(8080)
            .withEnv("SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE", "integration")
            .waitingFor(
                Wait.forHttp("/actuator/health")
                    .forStatusCode(200)
                    .forResponsePredicate(
                        body -> body.contains("\"status\":\"UP\""))
                    .withStartupTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(90))
            );

    @Test
    void externalService_isHealthy_onStartup() {
        assertThat(externalService.isRunning()).isTrue();
        String baseUrl = "http://localhost:"
            + externalService.getMappedPort(8080);
        assertThat(baseUrl).startsWith("http://localhost:");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `HttpWaitStrategy` creates an HTTP client inside Testcontainers connecting from the test JVM to the container's mapped port. If your container requires HTTPS with a self-signed certificate, configure `.usingTls()` and trust the certificate in the wait strategy's HTTP client. The strategy polls every 100ms by default — reduce with `.withPollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(500))` to lower CI overhead for slow-starting services. Alternative: `Wait.forLogMessage` for containers without HTTP health endpoints; `WaitAllStrategy` combining log and HTTP checks for belt-and-suspenders readiness.

[official]

---

### 15. JUnit 6 `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` — Locale-Safe Parameterised Tests [official]

JUnit 6 (via JUnit Pioneer, now merged into JUnit 6 core) introduced `@DefaultLocale("en-US")` and `@DefaultTimeZone("UTC")` class/method-level annotations that temporarily replace `Locale.getDefault()` and `TimeZone.getDefault()` for the duration of a test. This eliminates the `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach` boilerplate of saving and restoring the default locale, and prevents locale-sensitive failures when tests run on CI agents with non-English system locales.

**When to use:** Any test that formats numbers, dates, currencies, or error messages where the output depends on the JVM's default `Locale`. Essential for tests with `String.format()`, `DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate()`, `NumberFormat.getInstance()`, or Jackson locale-sensitive serialisation.
**When NOT to use:** Do not set `@DefaultLocale` globally on a base class for all tests — this hides locale bugs that would surface in production. Reserve it for tests that intentionally assert locale-sensitive output under a known locale. Do not use as a substitute for explicitly passing a `Locale` argument to production formatting methods. Alternative: Pass `Locale.US` explicitly to all formatting calls in production code (preferred); `Locale.setDefault()` in `@BeforeEach` with manual restore in `@AfterEach` for JUnit 5.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import org.junitpioneer.jupiter.DefaultLocale;
import org.junitpioneer.jupiter.DefaultTimeZone;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.time.format.FormatStyle;
import java.util.Locale;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class CurrencyFormatterTest {

    @Test
    @DefaultLocale("de-DE")
    @DefaultTimeZone("Europe/Berlin")
    void formatAmount_usesGermanLocale() {
        assertThat(Locale.getDefault().toLanguageTag()).isEqualTo("de-DE");
        var formatter = new CurrencyFormatter();
        assertThat(formatter.format(1234.56)).isEqualTo("1.234,56 €");
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @DefaultLocale("en-US")
    @CsvSource({
        "2026-01-15, January 15, 2026",
        "2026-12-31, December 31, 2026"
    })
    void formatDate_inEnglish(LocalDate date, String expected) {
        String formatted = DateTimeFormatter
            .ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.LONG)
            .withLocale(Locale.getDefault())
            .format(date);
        assertThat(formatted).isEqualTo(expected);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Thread-safety caveat: if tests run in parallel, setting `Locale.setDefault()` affects all threads in the JVM — JUnit Pioneer / JUnit 6 uses `InheritableThreadLocal` internally to scope the locale to the test thread, but some third-party libraries read `Locale.getDefault()` on background threads and may pick up the test locale. In JUnit 6, verify whether the annotation is in `org.junit.api` or still in `org.junitpioneer.jupiter` depending on your RC build. Alternative: JUnit Pioneer `@DefaultLocale` for JUnit 5 projects; explicit `Locale` constructor injection in all production formatting methods.

[official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 32 [community]

**`@TestBean` static factory methods silently fail to replace the bean when the factory return type is an interface and the Spring context registers the concrete class — `@Autowired` then injects the real bean with no error [community]** — A developer declares `@TestBean static NotificationService fakeNotificationService()` returning a `FakeNotificationService` that implements `NotificationService`. However, the Spring context registers `EmailNotificationService` (the concrete class). Since `@TestBean` resolves by type and `FakeNotificationService` does not extend `EmailNotificationService`, the replacement fails silently; the test proceeds with the real `EmailNotificationService` potentially sending real emails. WHY: `@TestBean` replacement matches the factory return type against the registered bean type using `isAssignableFrom` — if the registered bean type is more specific than the factory return type, Spring cannot confirm a safe replacement and skips it without throwing. Fix: declare the factory as `static EmailNotificationService fakeNotificationService()` (concrete return type matching the registered bean), or add the `@BeforeEach` guard assertion from Pattern 13 above to detect silent replacement failures early.

**`usingRecursiveComparison()` silently traverses into Hibernate proxy collections and issues N+1 SQL queries during assertion — the test passes but the `@DataJpaTest` transaction log shows unexpected SELECT statements [community]** — When `assertThat(savedEntity).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(expectedEntity)` runs inside a `@DataJpaTest`, AssertJ's recursive comparator calls `equals()` on every reachable field, including `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` collections. Hibernate's `PersistentBag` initialises lazily on the `equals()` call, issuing a SELECT per collection. The test passes but produces N+1 queries that indicate production performance regressions. WHY: `usingRecursiveComparison()` has no knowledge of JPA lazy loading semantics — it treats a proxy object like any other object and eagerly traverses it. Fix: use `ignoringFields("lazyCollection1", "lazyCollection2")` to exclude lazy relations from recursive comparison, or call `Hibernate.initialize(entity.getRelation())` explicitly before asserting.

**`@ResourceLock` names are `String` literals scoped per JVM classloader — two test classes using `"database"` as a lock name in different Gradle test forks do NOT contend on the same lock, defeating concurrency protection [community]** — A team enables `junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled=true` with Gradle parallel builds. Gradle's `--max-workers` flag can launch independent JVM forks, each with its own JUnit executor and lock registry. The lock name `"database"` is local to each JVM; there is no cross-process lock. Both forks hit the same Testcontainers database simultaneously causing data-corruption test failures that appear only in parallel CI runs. WHY: JUnit's `ResourceLock` is an in-process synchronization primitive using a `ConcurrentHashMap` within the JUnit launcher — it has no IPC mechanism. Fix: disable Gradle test worker forking (`maxParallelForks = 1`) or assign each Gradle worker a unique database schema via `@DynamicPropertySource` reading a worker-specific property.

**`CompletableFuture.failedFuture(exception)` passed to an AssertJ `failsWithin()` assertion wraps the exception in `ExecutionException` — asserting `withThrowableThat().isInstanceOf(MyException.class)` fails because the actual throwable is the wrapper [community]** — A test asserts `assertThat(future).failsWithin(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).withThrowableThat().isInstanceOf(AppException.class)`. The `failedFuture` stores the original exception, but `CompletableFuture.get()` (called internally by AssertJ) always wraps the completion exception in `ExecutionException` per the Java spec. AssertJ's `failsWithin()` surfaces the `ExecutionException`, so `isInstanceOf(AppException.class)` fails. WHY: `CompletableFuture.get()` specification mandates wrapping in `ExecutionException`; AssertJ cannot unwrap it automatically without changing the assertion contract. Fix: chain `.havingCause().isInstanceOf(AppException.class)` — or `withThrowableThat().hasCauseInstanceOf(AppException.class)` to reach the wrapped cause.

**`Testcontainers` `HttpWaitStrategy.forResponsePredicate(body -> ...)` receives the raw response body decoded with the JVM default charset — if the JVM default charset is `ISO-8859-1`, non-ASCII characters in health response bodies cause predicate mismatches silently [community]** — A health endpoint returns `{"status":"UP","region":"münchen"}`. The `forResponsePredicate(body -> body.contains("münchen"))` fails on JVM instances where `Charset.defaultCharset()` is `ISO-8859-1` (common on some Linux CI images), because `"münchen"` is decoded as mojibake. The container starts anyway if `contains("UP")` passes, masking the encoding bug. WHY: `HttpWaitStrategy` reads the response body via a `BufferedReader` using `Charset.defaultCharset()` in TC 1.x; TC 2.0 fixes this to always use `UTF-8`. Fix: on TC 1.x, set `-Dfile.encoding=UTF-8` in test JVM args, or upgrade to TC 2.0; avoid non-ASCII characters in health response predicates.

**`BDDMockito.then(mock).shouldHaveNoMoreInteractions()` at the end of a test causes double-verification errors when `STRICT_STUBS` mode is active — the `MockitoExtension` already calls `verifyNoMoreInteractions()` on teardown and the manual call re-counts stubbing invocations [community]** — A developer adds explicit `then(repo).shouldHaveNoMoreInteractions()` to a `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` test with `strictness = Strictness.STRICT_STUBS`. The extension's `AfterEachCallback` already runs `Mockito.verifyNoMoreInteractions()` for all mocks automatically. Running both can cause false failures in Mockito versions where `STRICT_STUBS` accounts for stub invocations differently from a raw `verifyNoMoreInteractions()` call. WHY: `STRICT_STUBS` performs automatic post-test verification as part of the extension lifecycle; a subsequent manual `shouldHaveNoMoreInteractions()` replays the check against an already-verified mock, with invocation-count state that may differ. Fix: in `STRICT_STUBS` mode, omit explicit `shouldHaveNoMoreInteractions()` and trust the extension; add it only in `LENIENT` mode.

**`@AutoConfigureRestDocs` with `outputDir` pointing to `build/generated-snippets` throws `FileNotFoundException` after `gradle clean` because the directory does not exist and REST Docs does not create it automatically [community]** — The REST Docs snippet writer expects `outputDir` to exist at write time. After `gradle clean` deletes `build/`, the first test execution throws `FileNotFoundException: build/generated-snippets/get-product/response-body.adoc (No such file or directory)`. WHY: Spring REST Docs delegates directory creation to the first snippet write — there is no mkdir-on-startup step, and Gradle's test task does not automatically create the output directory before tests run. Fix: add `test.doFirst { mkdir("$buildDir/generated-snippets") }` to your Gradle build file, or configure a Maven `generate-test-resources` phase step to create the directory before `test` runs.

**`SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(...)` inside a `@ParameterizedTest` collects failures per invocation but CI log truncation can hide which parameter set caused which failure — add `as(...)` labels to every assertion [community]** — A `@ParameterizedTest` with 20 rows and a `SoftAssertions` block inside can produce a failure report with up to 20 × N assertion failures concatenated. When multiple indices fail the messages stack in the output and CI log truncation hides individual assertion details. WHY: `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly` collects all failures in a single `SoftAssertionError` per invocation — JUnit reports one failure per parameterized index, but if the error message is long, truncation hides details. Fix: keep the number of assertions inside the soft block small (5 or fewer); use descriptive `as("field X for input %s", param)` labels so each failure is self-describing even in truncated CI output.
