### 1. JUnit 6 `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` — Declarative Locale/Timezone Scoping for Tests [official]

JUnit 6 introduces `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` annotations that temporarily override the JVM's default locale and timezone for the duration of a test method or class. Before these annotations, tests that depended on locale-sensitive formatting (e.g., currency display, date parsing) required manual `Locale.setDefault()` and teardown calls in `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`, which was fragile and leaked state if an exception occurred before teardown. The annotations are handled by a built-in JUnit extension that saves the original default, applies the requested value before the test, and restores the original in an `AfterEach`-equivalent callback even when the test throws. This makes locale-sensitive tests self-contained and safe for parallel execution in different test classes.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultLocale;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DefaultTimeZone;
import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.time.ZonedDateTime;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.time.format.FormatStyle;
import java.util.Locale;

// All tests in this class see Locale.US and UTC
@DefaultLocale("en-US")
@DefaultTimeZone("UTC")
class PriceFormatterTest {

    private final PriceFormatter formatter = new PriceFormatter();

    @Test
    void formats_price_in_us_dollars() {
        // NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance() uses Locale.getDefault()
        String result = formatter.formatPrice(1234.56);
        assertThat(result).isEqualTo("$1,234.56");
    }

    @Test
    @DefaultLocale("de-DE")  // Method-level overrides class-level
    void formats_price_in_german_locale() {
        String result = formatter.formatPrice(1234.56);
        // German locale: period as thousands separator, comma as decimal
        assertThat(result).isEqualTo("1.234,56 €");
    }

    @Test
    void formats_utc_timestamp() {
        ZonedDateTime dt = ZonedDateTime.parse("2026-05-14T12:00:00Z");
        String result = formatter.formatTimestamp(dt);
        assertThat(result).isEqualTo("May 14, 2026, 12:00:00 PM");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` apply to the test thread's JVM default, not to `DateTimeFormatter` instances that have been pre-built with an explicit `Locale` argument — those are unaffected. When tests run in parallel on multiple threads, setting a JVM-wide default in one thread is visible to other threads until the extension restores it; use `@Isolated` (requires `junit-platform-isolation`) or limit parallel execution to class level when mixing locale-sensitive tests with parallel execution. Alternative: constructor-inject `Locale` and `ZoneId` into production code to avoid JVM defaults entirely.

[official]

---

### 2. JUnit 6 `MethodOrderer.Default` — Resetting Custom Ordering on Nested Classes [official]

When an enclosing test class declares `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Alphanumeric.class)`, JUnit 6 propagates that ordering to all `@Nested` inner classes by default. This is useful for systematic suite ordering but undesirable when a specific nested class requires a different ordering policy. `MethodOrderer.Default` is a built-in no-op orderer that resets method ordering to JUnit's deterministic but unspecified default — it explicitly cancels the inherited ordering without replacing it with any specific strategy. Using `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Default.class)` on a nested class effectively says "I opt out of the parent's ordering policy."

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.MethodOrderer;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Nested;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.TestMethodOrder;

@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Test
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.Order(1)
    void createOrder_succeeds_when_stock_available() { /* ... */ }

    @Test
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.Order(2)
    void createOrder_fails_when_stock_exhausted() { /* ... */ }

    // This nested class opts out of @Order annotation ordering:
    // its methods run in JUnit's deterministic default order
    @Nested
    @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Default.class)
    class ValidationTests {

        @Test
        void rejects_negative_quantity() { /* ... */ }

        @Test
        void rejects_null_product_id() { /* ... */ }

        @Test
        void rejects_quantity_exceeding_max() { /* ... */ }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The "deterministic but intentionally nonobvious" default order is stable across runs on the same JVM/OS but is not alphabetical and is not guaranteed across JDK upgrades — do not rely on it for tests that share mutable state. `ClassOrderer.Default` serves the same reset purpose at the class level for `@TestClassOrder`-annotated suites. Alternative: explicitly annotate each method in the nested class with `@Order` if you need a specific known ordering; use `MethodOrderer.Random` to actively detect hidden order dependencies.

[official]

---

### 3. Spring Boot 4.0 `RestTestClient` — Fluent Integration-Test HTTP Client [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 introduces `RestTestClient`, a fluent HTTP client for integration testing that bridges the gap between the reactive `WebTestClient` API and the synchronous `TestRestTemplate`. It supports both mock-environment testing (backed by `MockMvc`) and running-server testing (backed by a real HTTP client) through the same fluent API, making test code portable across both modes. Auto-configuration exposes `RestTestClient` as a bean when `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` or `spring-boot-resttestclient` is on the classpath; for `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` the client automatically targets the running port.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.client.AutoConfigureRestTestClient;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment;
import org.springframework.test.web.client.RestTestClient;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import java.util.List;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureRestTestClient
class ProductApiIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private RestTestClient restTestClient;

    @Test
    void getProducts_returns_paginated_list() {
        restTestClient
            .get().uri("/api/products?page=0&size=5")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectHeader().contentType("application/json")
            .expectBody()
                .jsonPath("$.content.length()").isEqualTo(5)
                .jsonPath("$.totalElements").value(v ->
                    assertThat((Integer) v).isGreaterThan(0))
                .jsonPath("$.content[0].id").exists();
    }

    @Test
    void createProduct_returns_201_with_location() {
        restTestClient
            .post().uri("/api/products")
            .bodyValue(new CreateProductRequest("Widget", 9.99))
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isCreated()
            .expectHeader().exists("Location");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `RestTestClient` uses the same exchange API style as `WebTestClient` but is synchronous — blocking I/O under the hood. For reactive (WebFlux) applications, prefer `WebTestClient` which natively supports reactive response streaming and SSE assertions. The `RestTestClient` module ships in `spring-boot-resttestclient` (separate artifact in Boot 4.0) — it is not automatically included by `spring-boot-starter-test`; add it explicitly to the test classpath. Mock-environment mode is faster but does not exercise the full HTTP stack (filter chains run, but no actual TCP). Alternative: `MockMvcTester` for AssertJ-first mock-environment assertions; `WebTestClient` for reactive stacks.

[official]

---

### 4. Spring Boot 4.0 `@SpringBootTest(useMainMethod = UseMainMethod.ALWAYS)` — Testing Real Application Startup [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 exposes `UseMainMethod.ALWAYS` on `@SpringBootTest` to instruct the test framework to invoke the application's actual `main(String[] args)` method when creating the `ApplicationContext`, rather than the standard `SpringApplication.run()` path. This catches startup customisations placed in `main()` — such as custom `SpringApplication` builder configuration, banner-mode overrides, environment post-processors registered via `main()`, or Quarkus-style programmatic initializers — that are silently skipped by the normal test context loading path.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest.UseMainMethod;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Uses the actual main() method — catches customisations in main()
@SpringBootTest(
    webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.NONE,
    useMainMethod = UseMainMethod.ALWAYS
)
class ApplicationStartupTest {

    @Autowired
    private Environment env;

    @Test
    void main_method_customisations_are_applied() {
        // Verify that a property registered by a SpringApplicationRunListener
        // or ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent handler inside main() is present
        assertThat(env.getProperty("app.startup.customised")).isEqualTo("true");
    }

    @Test
    void context_loads_without_exception() {
        // If context fails to load, this test fails with a clear message
        assertThat(env.getActiveProfiles()).doesNotContain("disabled");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `UseMainMethod.ALWAYS` fails the test if no `main(String[] args)` method is found on the `@SpringBootApplication` class — use `UseMainMethod.WHEN_AVAILABLE` to silently fall back to the standard path when no `main()` exists (e.g. in library projects). Running the full `main()` path increases startup time and exercises more global state — reserve this for dedicated "smoke test" integration tests rather than all `@SpringBootTest` tests. `NEVER` (the default) preserves backward-compatible behaviour. Alternative: `ApplicationContextRunner` for lightweight auto-configuration unit tests that do not require the full application startup.

[official]

---

### 5. Mockito 5.22 Kotlin Singleton Object Mocking — `mockSingleton()` [official]

Mockito 5.22 adds first-class support for mocking Kotlin `object` singletons via `mockSingleton(MySingleton::class.java)` (Java) or the Kotlin extension `mockSingleton<MySingleton>()`. Kotlin objects are JVM singletons backed by a static `INSTANCE` field — they cannot be replaced by standard `mock()` or `spy()` because no instance injection point exists. `mockSingleton` uses Mockito's static mocking machinery to intercept method calls on the singleton, replacing them with configurable mock answers for the duration of the `MockedSingleton` auto-closeable scope.

```java
import org.mockito.Mockito;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;

// Assumes Kotlin object: object FeatureFlags { fun isEnabled(flag: String): Boolean }
class FeatureFlagsTest {

    @Test
    void checkout_flow_uses_new_payment_when_flag_enabled() {
        // mockSingleton returns an AutoCloseable — use try-with-resources
        try (var mockedFlags = Mockito.mockSingleton(FeatureFlags.class)) {
            // Stub the Kotlin object's method
            when(FeatureFlags.INSTANCE.isEnabled("new-payment-flow")).thenReturn(true);

            var service = new CheckoutService();
            var result = service.processPayment(sampleCart());

            assertThat(result.getProcessor()).isEqualTo("new-payment-flow");
        }
        // After close: FeatureFlags.INSTANCE.isEnabled() resumes real implementation
    }

    @Test
    void checkout_flow_uses_legacy_payment_when_flag_disabled() {
        try (var mockedFlags = Mockito.mockSingleton(FeatureFlags.class)) {
            when(FeatureFlags.INSTANCE.isEnabled("new-payment-flow")).thenReturn(false);

            var service = new CheckoutService();
            var result = service.processPayment(sampleCart());

            assertThat(result.getProcessor()).isEqualTo("legacy-payment-flow");
        }
    }

    private Cart sampleCart() { return new Cart(List.of(new CartItem("SKU-1", 2))); }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `mockSingleton` relies on Mockito's byte-buddy/inline mock maker and requires the JVM to be launched with `--add-opens` flags for the module containing the Kotlin `object` — projects using JPMS strict mode must add explicit opens declarations. Do not use `mockSingleton` for objects that hold shared mutable state across threads — the singleton replacement is global and non-thread-safe. The `StackOverflowError` with `AbstractList` (fixed in 5.22) revealed that `mockSingleton` with abstract supertype implementations can recurse infinitely; always apply to the concrete singleton type. Alternative: refactor Kotlin objects to interfaces with companion objects for production-safe dependency injection.

[official]

---

### 6. Spring Boot 4.1 `@GrpcTest` Slice — Testing gRPC Service Implementations [official]

Spring Boot 4.1 introduces a `@GrpcTest` test slice that loads only the gRPC service layer — service implementations, `@GrpcAdvice` exception handlers, and gRPC interceptors — without starting the full application context. It pairs with a generated in-process `GrpcServer` and a `GrpcChannelFactory` that routes calls to the in-process server, eliminating the need for `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = DEFINED_PORT)` with a real gRPC port for unit-level service tests. The `@GrpcAdvice` exception handling annotation (also new in 4.1) mirrors `@ControllerAdvice` semantics for gRPC — annotated classes handle `StatusRuntimeException` and domain exceptions thrown from gRPC service methods.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.grpc.GrpcTest;
import org.springframework.grpc.test.LocalGrpcPort;
import io.grpc.ManagedChannel;
import io.grpc.ManagedChannelBuilder;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

@GrpcTest(classes = OrderServiceGrpc.class)
class OrderServiceGrpcTest {

    @MockitoBean
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Autowired
    private OrderServiceGrpc.OrderServiceBlockingStub stub;

    @Test
    void getOrder_returns_order_when_found() {
        var expected = OrderProto.Order.newBuilder()
            .setId("ORD-001").setStatus("CONFIRMED").build();
        when(orderRepository.findById("ORD-001"))
            .thenReturn(Optional.of(toEntity(expected)));

        var response = stub.getOrder(
            OrderProto.GetOrderRequest.newBuilder().setId("ORD-001").build());

        assertThat(response.getId()).isEqualTo("ORD-001");
        assertThat(response.getStatus()).isEqualTo("CONFIRMED");
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_throws_NOT_FOUND_when_missing() {
        when(orderRepository.findById("MISSING")).thenReturn(Optional.empty());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> stub.getOrder(
            OrderProto.GetOrderRequest.newBuilder().setId("MISSING").build()))
            .isInstanceOf(io.grpc.StatusRuntimeException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("NOT_FOUND");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@GrpcTest` loads only the service layer — it does not configure Spring Security, Spring Data repositories, or message converters; use `@SpringBootTest` for integration tests that need the full stack. The in-process channel bypasses network serialization/deserialization — tests will not catch protobuf marshalling bugs that would surface with a real TCP connection. The `@GrpcAdvice` annotation requires `spring-grpc` on the classpath (separate from `spring-boot-starter-grpc`). Alternative: Testcontainers with a real gRPC-capable container for full-stack verification; `grpcMock` library for contract-test style mocking.

[official]

---

### 7. JUnit 6 `@CsvSource` `commentCharacter` — Custom CSV Comment Delimiters [official]

JUnit 6.0.1 adds a `commentCharacter` attribute to `@CsvSource` and `@CsvFileSource`. Prior to this change the `#` character was the only supported comment delimiter, which conflicted with CSV data that legitimately used `#` as a field value (e.g., colour hex codes, GitHub issue references, URL fragments). The new attribute accepts any single character as the comment prefix; lines starting with that character are ignored when parsing the CSV data. Setting `commentCharacter = '\0'` disables comment processing entirely, allowing `#` to appear freely in test data.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class HexColorParserTest {

    @ParameterizedTest
    // Use % as comment char so # can appear freely in test data
    @CsvSource(
        commentCharacter = '%',
        textBlock = """
            % Valid hex colors
            #FF0000, 255, 0, 0
            #00FF00, 0, 255, 0
            #0000FF, 0, 0, 255
            % Edge cases
            #000000, 0, 0, 0
            #FFFFFF, 255, 255, 255
            % Mixed case
            #aAbBcC, 170, 187, 204
            """
    )
    void parses_hex_color(String hex, int r, int g, int b) {
        var color = HexColorParser.parse(hex);
        assertThat(color.red()).isEqualTo(r);
        assertThat(color.green()).isEqualTo(g);
        assertThat(color.blue()).isEqualTo(b);
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    // Disable comment processing so # is treated as data
    @CsvSource(
        commentCharacter = '\0',
        value = {
            "#FF0000, red",
            "#00FF00, green",
            "#issue-123, unknown"  // '#' in data, no comment stripping
        }
    )
    void classifies_color_string(String input, String expectedClass) {
        assertThat(HexColorParser.classify(input)).isEqualTo(expectedClass);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `commentCharacter` attribute defaults to `#` for backward compatibility — existing `@CsvSource` tests that happen to pass hex codes beginning with `#` only work if those values are quoted (CSV quoting rules still apply). The `'\0'` (null character) sentinel to disable comments is counterintuitive and may confuse readers; add a comment explaining the intent. For CSV files loaded via `@CsvFileSource`, the same `commentCharacter` attribute applies and disables `#`-prefixed comment lines in the external file. Alternative: quote hex values with `'#FF0000'` to avoid conflict with the default `#` comment character without needing to change `commentCharacter`.

[official]

---

### 8. Spring Boot 4.0 `@SpringBootTest` with Jackson 3 Migration — Testing with Modern Jackson [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 upgrades to Jackson 3.0 and ships Jackson 2 support in deprecated form. Jackson 3 is not backward-compatible — it repackaged `com.fasterxml.jackson` to `tools.jackson` and removed several legacy serialisation features. Test code that directly instantiates `ObjectMapper` or relies on deprecated Jackson 2 modules must be migrated; `@JsonTest` slices auto-configure the Jackson 3 `ObjectMapper` bean and JUnit test classes that use the deprecated `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper` type will fail to compile unless the old artifact is explicitly kept on the test classpath alongside the new one.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.json.JsonTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.json.JacksonTester;
// Jackson 3 packages (tools.jackson, not com.fasterxml.jackson)
import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@JsonTest
class ProductDtoJsonTest {

    // JacksonTester is auto-configured by @JsonTest with Jackson 3 ObjectMapper
    @Autowired
    private JacksonTester<ProductDto> json;

    @Autowired
    private ObjectMapper objectMapper; // Jackson 3 ObjectMapper bean

    @Test
    void serializes_product_without_null_fields() throws Exception {
        var product = new ProductDto("SKU-001", "Widget", null, 9.99);

        assertThat(json.write(product))
            .doesNotHaveJsonPath("$.description") // null excluded
            .hasJsonPathStringValue("$.sku", "SKU-001")
            .hasJsonPathNumberValue("$.price", 9.99);
    }

    @Test
    void deserializes_product_with_unknown_fields_ignored() throws Exception {
        String input = """
            {
              "sku": "SKU-001",
              "name": "Widget",
              "price": 9.99,
              "legacyField": "ignored"
            }
            """;

        var product = json.parseObject(input);

        assertThat(product.sku()).isEqualTo("SKU-001");
        assertThat(product.price()).isEqualTo(9.99);
    }

    @Test
    void round_trip_preserves_all_fields() throws Exception {
        var original = new ProductDto("SKU-002", "Gadget", "A great gadget", 29.99);
        String serialized = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(original);
        var deserialized = objectMapper.readValue(serialized, ProductDto.class);
        assertThat(deserialized).isEqualTo(original);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Projects using custom Jackson 2 modules (e.g., `jackson-datatype-jsr310`) must migrate to Jackson 3 equivalents — many `jackson-datatype-*` artifacts have Jackson 3 counterparts but not all community modules have been ported. The `@JsonTest` slice picks up only `@JsonComponent` beans and auto-configured modules; a custom `ObjectMapper` bean defined in `@Configuration` is NOT picked up by `@JsonTest` by default — override with `@Import(MyJacksonConfig.class)`. Alternative: `ApplicationContextRunner` with `JacksonAutoConfiguration` to unit-test custom Jackson 3 module registration without starting the full web layer.

[official]

---

### 9. Mockito 5.21 `SequencedCollection` Default Answer — Empty Returns for Ordered Collections [official]

Mockito 5.21 enhanced `ReturnsEmptyValues` (the default answer for mocks created via `mock()`) to return sensible empty defaults for `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet`, and `SequencedMap` types introduced in Java 21. Prior to 5.21, methods returning these types received `null` from the default answer, causing `NullPointerException` in production code that called `.getFirst()` or `.getLast()` on the result without a null check. The fix makes mock methods returning `SequencedList`, `SequencedSet`, and `SequencedMap` return empty ordered-collection implementations by default, consistent with the existing behavior for `List`, `Set`, and `Map`.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.mockito.Mockito;
import java.util.SequencedCollection;
import java.util.SequencedMap;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatNoException;

interface ProductRepository {
    SequencedCollection<Product> findRecentlyAdded(int limit);
    SequencedMap<String, Product> findBySkuOrdered(List<String> skus);
}

class ProductServiceTest {

    private final ProductRepository repo = Mockito.mock(ProductRepository.class);
    private final ProductService service = new ProductService(repo);

    @Test
    void recent_products_returns_empty_list_when_no_products_exist() {
        // Mockito 5.21+: returns empty SequencedCollection, not null
        var result = service.getRecentProducts(10);

        // No NullPointerException — safe to call .size(), .isEmpty(), iterate
        assertThat(result).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void service_handles_empty_sku_map_without_null_check() {
        // SequencedMap also returns empty by default in 5.21+
        var result = service.getProductsBySkus(List.of("SKU-1", "SKU-2"));

        assertThat(result).isEmpty();
        // Calling .firstEntry() on the empty SequencedMap returns null —
        // but the map itself is not null, so no NPE on the returned reference
        assertThatNoException().isThrownBy(() -> result.isEmpty());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The empty `SequencedCollection` returned by the default answer is a `LinkedList`-backed implementation; calling `.getFirst()` or `.getLast()` on it throws `NoSuchElementException` (correct contract). Code that relied on `null` being returned to detect "not configured" state in tests will silently break — those tests will now proceed past the null check into downstream logic. When upgrading to 5.21, run the full test suite and look for newly passing tests that were previously correctly failing. Alternative: explicitly stub the method with `when(repo.findRecentlyAdded(10)).thenReturn(emptyList())` to make the intent explicit rather than relying on default answer behaviour.

[official]

---

### 10. JUnit 6 JSpecify Nullability Annotations — IDE-Assisted Null Safety in Tests [official]

JUnit 6 annotates all public API members with JSpecify nullability annotations (`@Nullable`, `@NonNull`, `@NullMarked`) across all modules. Test code that passes `null` to a `@NonNull` parameter now receives an IDE warning or a compiler error (with `-Xjspecify` enabled) rather than a `NullPointerException` at runtime in a CI pipeline. Extension implementors benefit most — `@ExtendWith` implementations that override methods like `beforeEach(ExtensionContext)` can now see which parameters the framework guarantees non-null versus which may be null depending on the invocation context.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.BeforeEachCallback;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtensionContext;
import org.jspecify.annotations.NonNull;

// JUnit 6 extension implementing BeforeEachCallback
// ExtensionContext is @NonNull per JUnit's JSpecify annotations
class DatabaseCleanupExtension implements BeforeEachCallback {

    @Override
    public void beforeEach(@NonNull ExtensionContext context) {
        // context is guaranteed non-null by JUnit's contract
        String testName = context.getDisplayName(); // @NonNull return — no null check needed
        String className = context.getTestClass()
            .map(Class::getSimpleName)
            .orElse("Unknown"); // getTestClass() returns Optional<@NonNull Class<?>>

        DatabaseCleaner.forClass(className).truncate();
        System.out.printf("DB cleaned before [%s] in %s%n", testName, className);
    }
}

// Test class using the extension
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ExtendWith(DatabaseCleanupExtension.class)
class UserRepositoryTest {

    @Test
    void findById_returns_user_after_insert() {
        // DatabaseCleanupExtension ensures clean state before each test
        UserRepository repo = new JdbcUserRepository(dataSource());
        repo.save(new User("u1", "Alice"));
        assertThat(repo.findById("u1")).isPresent()
            .get().extracting(User::name).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** JSpecify annotations are only enforced at build time when the compiler plugin or lint tool is configured — they are runtime-invisible meta-annotations and do not add null checks at the bytecode level. Teams without JSpecify tooling see no change in behavior; teams with tooling enabled in the IDE see warnings that may flag previously-acceptable test code (e.g., intentionally passing `null` to test null-handling). The annotation applies to all 6.x releases, including backports to Jupiter 5.14.x; check the release notes of your version. Alternative: Checker Framework or NullAway for stricter compile-time null safety enforcement across the whole project.

[official]

---

### 11. Spring Boot 4.1 `@ServiceConnection` on `@Bean` Methods — SSL-Enabled Container Connections [official]

Spring Boot 4.1 RC1 fixes `@ServiceConnection` support on `@Bean` methods in `@TestConfiguration` classes, including support for SSL-configured container connections. Prior to this fix, `@ServiceConnection` on a `@Bean`-annotated container method in a test configuration was silently ignored — the framework only recognized `@ServiceConnection` on `@Container`-annotated fields. This restriction made it impossible to conditionally define containers (e.g., reuse a singleton container instance across test classes) using `@Bean` factory methods and still benefit from auto-wired connection properties.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.TestConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.wait.strategy.Wait;

@TestConfiguration
class SharedPostgresConfig {

    // @ServiceConnection now works on @Bean methods in Spring Boot 4.1+
    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgresContainer() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("testdb")
            .withUsername("test")
            .withPassword("test")
            .waitingFor(Wait.forListeningPort());
    }

    // Also works with SSL-enabled containers
    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection(name = "redis")
    // In Boot 4.1, @ServiceConnection picks up SSL certificates from
    // the container if the container exposes a TLS port
    org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer<?> redisContainer() {
        return new org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine")
            .withExposedPorts(6379);
    }
}

// Multiple test classes can import the config to share the container
@SpringBootTest
@Import(SharedPostgresConfig.class)
class UserRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired UserRepository userRepository;
    @Test void saves_user() { /* ... */ }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ServiceConnection` on `@Bean` methods only works in `@TestConfiguration` classes that are imported or detected in the test slice — it does not work in production `@Configuration` classes. The bean must return a `Container` type that has a registered `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory`; custom container types require a custom factory. The SSL certificate auto-detection (fixed in 4.1-RC1) requires the container to expose a TLS port via `withExposedPorts`; Testcontainers containers that use port mapping rather than fixed ports need explicit SSL configuration via `@ServiceConnection(ssl = true)`. Alternative: `@DynamicPropertySource` for finer control over which container properties are published to the `Environment`.

[official]

---

### 12. Mockito 5.23 `@Nullable` on `Mockito.when()` — Safe Stubbing of Nullable Returns [official]

Mockito 5.23 adds `@Nullable` parameter annotations to the `Mockito.when(T methodCall)` static method. Previously, the Java type system treated the `methodCall` argument as `@NonNull`, causing IDE null-safety inspections to warn whenever developers stubbed methods that intentionally return `null`. The `@Nullable` annotation makes `when(null)` semantically valid for stubbing void-equivalent or null-returning expressions, and it allows code like `when(service.findByIdOrNull(id))` (a common Kotlin `OrNull` extension pattern) to compile without suppression.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.NONE)
class NotificationServiceTest {

    @MockitoBean
    UserPreferenceRepository prefRepo;

    @Autowired
    NotificationService notificationService;

    @Test
    void sends_default_channel_when_preference_not_found() {
        // Mockito 5.23: @Nullable on when() — no IDE warning when stubbing
        // a method that legitimately returns null (null = "no preference set")
        when(prefRepo.findPreferenceOrNull("user-1")).thenReturn(null);

        var channel = notificationService.resolveChannel("user-1");

        assertThat(channel).isEqualTo(NotificationChannel.EMAIL); // default
    }

    @Test
    void respects_explicit_sms_preference() {
        when(prefRepo.findPreferenceOrNull("user-2"))
            .thenReturn(new UserPreference("user-2", NotificationChannel.SMS));

        var channel = notificationService.resolveChannel("user-2");

        assertThat(channel).isEqualTo(NotificationChannel.SMS);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `@Nullable` annotation on `when()` is a documentation/tooling annotation — it does not change runtime behavior. Calling `when(null)` directly (passing a literal `null` rather than a method call) produces an `InvalidUseOfMockitoException` at runtime just as before; the annotation only suppresses IDE warnings for nullable method call expressions. Teams using IntelliJ with NullAway or the Kotlin compiler null-safety checker benefit most. Alternative: use `lenient().when(...)` for optional stubs that may or may not be invoked; use explicit `@SuppressWarnings("NullAway")` at the call site if tooling cannot be updated to recognize Mockito 5.23's annotation.

[official]

---

### 13. Spring Boot 4.0 `@WebFluxTest` with `WebTestClient` — Reactive Controller Slice Testing [official]

`@WebFluxTest` is the reactive counterpart to `@WebMvcTest` — it loads only the WebFlux controller layer, auto-configures a `WebTestClient`, and excludes `@Service`, `@Repository`, and full auto-configuration. In Spring Boot 4.0, `@WebFluxTest` works without an embedded Netty or Undertow server — it uses a `MockReactiveWebApplicationContext` with a virtual HTTP server, making tests faster than `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` for controller-level verification. `@MockitoBean` injects reactive dependencies (services returning `Mono` and `Flux`) into the context with full Mockito stubbing support.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.reactive.WebFluxTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.reactive.server.WebTestClient;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import reactor.core.publisher.Flux;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyString;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;

@WebFluxTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerFluxTest {

    @Autowired
    private WebTestClient webClient;

    @MockitoBean
    private ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void getProduct_returns_200_with_product_body() {
        when(productService.findById("prod-1"))
            .thenReturn(Mono.just(new ProductDto("prod-1", "Widget", 9.99)));

        webClient.get().uri("/products/prod-1")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBody(ProductDto.class)
            .value(p -> {
                assertThat(p.id()).isEqualTo("prod-1");
                assertThat(p.name()).isEqualTo("Widget");
            });
    }

    @Test
    void listProducts_streams_items_as_ndjson() {
        when(productService.findAll())
            .thenReturn(Flux.just(
                new ProductDto("p1", "Widget", 9.99),
                new ProductDto("p2", "Gadget", 19.99)
            ));

        webClient.get().uri("/products")
            .accept(org.springframework.http.MediaType.APPLICATION_NDJSON)
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBodyList(ProductDto.class)
            .hasSize(2)
            .contains(new ProductDto("p1", "Widget", 9.99));
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_returns_404_when_not_found() {
        when(productService.findById(anyString())).thenReturn(Mono.empty());

        webClient.get().uri("/products/missing")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@WebFluxTest` uses a mock reactive container — it does not test actual Netty I/O, connection pooling, or backpressure under real load. SSE and WebSocket endpoints require `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with a real server for end-to-end streaming tests. Stubbing `Mono.empty()` vs `Mono.error()` vs returning a hot `Flux` can produce subtly different error propagation results between the mock container and a real Netty deployment. Alternative: `ReactorTestScheduler` from Project Reactor for fine-grained reactive scheduling in unit tests; `@SpringBootTest` + `WebTestClient` for full-stack reactive integration tests.

[official]

---

### 14. JUnit 6 `ConsoleLauncher` `--fail-fast` Mode — Stopping on First Failure in CI [official]

JUnit 6 adds a `--fail-fast` flag to the `ConsoleLauncher` that stops the entire test execution after the first test failure, reporting all tests that did not run as `SKIPPED`. This is distinct from `@Tag`-based filtering or test-count limits — it is a runtime execution strategy particularly useful in CI pipelines where the first broken test is a signal to abort, build a fix, and re-run rather than accumulating failures in a long report. It is also available programmatically via `LauncherDiscoveryRequest.Builder.failFast(true)` for embedding in custom launchers.

```java
// Usage in build scripts (Maven Surefire / Gradle) via JVM argument
// -Djunit.platform.output.capture.stdout=true
// -Djunit.jupiter.execution.failfast=true   (property-based activation)

// Programmatic activation in a custom test runner:
import org.junit.platform.launcher.Launcher;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.LauncherDiscoveryRequest;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.LauncherDiscoveryRequestBuilder;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.LauncherFactory;
import org.junit.platform.engine.discovery.DiscoverySelectors;
import org.junit.platform.launcher.listeners.SummaryGeneratingListener;

class FailFastTestRunner {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var request = LauncherDiscoveryRequestBuilder.request()
            .selectors(DiscoverySelectors.selectPackage("com.example"))
            // JUnit 6: fail-fast stops after first failure
            .configurationParameter(
                "junit.jupiter.execution.failfast.enabled", "true")
            .build();

        var launcher = LauncherFactory.create();
        var listener = new SummaryGeneratingListener();
        launcher.discover(request);
        launcher.execute(request, listener);

        var summary = listener.getSummary();
        if (summary.getTotalFailureCount() > 0) {
            System.err.println("FAIL-FAST triggered after: "
                + summary.getFailures().get(0).getException().getMessage());
            System.exit(1);
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `--fail-fast` is most effective in developer-inner-loop CI (pre-merge checks) where speed matters more than full coverage reporting. For nightly or release-gate pipelines, always run to completion to capture the full failure set and avoid masking multiple independent failures. The `SKIPPED` status for un-run tests can mislead coverage tools that count only executed tests — adjust coverage enforcement to ignore `SKIPPED` results when `--fail-fast` is active. The JUnit 5 equivalent (`--fail-if-no-tests`) is different — `--fail-fast` is a JUnit 6-only feature. Alternative: Surefire `<failFast>true</failFast>` configuration for Maven; Gradle's `--fail-fast` flag for the `test` task.

[official]

---

### 15. Spring Boot 4.0 `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` with `MockMvc` Backing — Unified Mock + Real Server Tests [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 allows `RestTestClient` to be backed by `MockMvc` (mock environment) or a real HTTP client (running server), selected automatically based on the `webEnvironment`. When `webEnvironment = MOCK`, `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` wires `RestTestClient` through `MockMvc`, bypassing the network stack but executing the full filter chain. When `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT`, the same annotation wires `RestTestClient` to target the running server. This means the same test body can run in both modes — teams can parameterize on the environment for fast-feedback (mock) and slow-validation (real server) runs without duplicating test code.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.test.web.client.RestTestClient;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Change to WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT for real-server mode —
// the test body is identical
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.MOCK)
@AutoConfigureMockMvc           // enables MockMvc backing in MOCK mode
class OrderApiTest {

    // RestTestClient is auto-wired regardless of webEnvironment
    @Autowired
    private RestTestClient restTestClient;

    @Test
    void list_orders_returns_200() {
        restTestClient
            .get().uri("/api/orders")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBodyList(OrderSummaryDto.class)
            .value(orders -> assertThat(orders).isNotNull());
    }

    @Test
    void create_order_returns_201_and_location() {
        restTestClient
            .post().uri("/api/orders")
            .bodyValue(new CreateOrderRequest("CUST-1", "SKU-A", 2))
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isCreated()
            .expectHeader().exists("Location");
    }

    @Test
    void get_order_returns_404_for_unknown_id() {
        restTestClient
            .get().uri("/api/orders/nonexistent")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `RestTestClient` in mock mode does not exercise serialization/deserialization the same way a real server does — the request body is processed in-memory without HTTP framing. This means content-negotiation edge cases (e.g., unsupported media type handling, charset detection) may behave differently between mock and real-server modes. The auto-configuration chooses the backing implementation based on `webEnvironment`; explicitly setting `@AutoConfigureWebTestClient` alongside `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` creates two separate clients — only one is needed. Alternative: `MockMvcTester` for AssertJ-first mock-environment tests with chained assertions; `WebTestClient` for reactive apps or when streaming assertions are needed.

[official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 36 [community]

**`Mockito.mockSingleton()` corrupts `UUID.randomUUID()` under JDK 25 when the `AbstractList`-backed mock is not properly closed — all subsequent calls to `UUID.randomUUID()` return the same value within the same class loader [community]** — A developer mocks a Kotlin singleton that extends `AbstractList` using `mockSingleton`. The mock is created in a `@BeforeEach` but accidentally not closed (the `try` block is omitted). Under JDK 25, Mockito's static mocking infrastructure intercepts `AbstractList`'s internal call to `UUID.randomUUID()` to generate stable mock IDs, and the global interception leaks across test methods. Every subsequent `UUID.randomUUID()` call in the test JVM returns the same intercepted value. WHY: `mockSingleton` uses `MockedStatic` under the hood, which patches the static method in the class loader's constant pool; if `close()` is never called, the patch persists for the lifetime of the class loader. The fix in Mockito 5.22 avoids patching `UUID` but the underlying issue (not closing `MockedStatic`) can still corrupt other static methods. Fix: always use `mockSingleton` in a `try-with-resources` block; add `Mockito.validateMockitoUsage()` in `@AfterEach` to detect unclosed mock resources.

**`RestTestClient` with `WebEnvironment.MOCK` silently swallows `Content-Type: text/plain` responses when the controller method returns `ResponseEntity<String>` — the response body is empty in `RestTestClient` assertions even though `MockMvc.perform()` returns the correct body [community]** — A developer migrates from `MockMvc` to `RestTestClient` and notices that `.expectBody(String.class).isEqualTo("Hello")` fails with an empty body. The controller method returns `ResponseEntity.ok("Hello")` with `text/plain` content type. The `RestTestClient` message converter chain in mock mode does not register a plain `StringHttpMessageConverter` by default — it expects JSON or application-type responses. The `MockMvc` converter chain is separate and does register `StringHttpMessageConverter`. WHY: `RestTestClient`'s mock backing uses a different converter stack than raw `MockMvc`; the default converter set is optimized for JSON API testing. Fix: add `.accept(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)` to the request and configure `RestTestClient` with an explicit `StringHttpMessageConverter`; or convert the endpoint to return `application/json` for API tests.

**`@SpringBootTest(useMainMethod = UseMainMethod.ALWAYS)` does not work with test classes nested inside the main application class — JUnit's nested test discovery and Spring's main-method context loading interact incorrectly, creating duplicate contexts [community]** — A developer places `@Nested` integration tests inside the main `@SpringBootApplication` class to co-locate smoke tests with the application. With `UseMainMethod.ALWAYS`, Spring calls `MyApp.main()`, which invokes `SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args)`. The test context loader then wraps this in a second context loading call, creating two independent contexts — the second context starts a second server on the same port, causing a port conflict. WHY: `UseMainMethod.ALWAYS` does not understand that the test is nested inside the `@SpringBootApplication` class and interprets the class as both the test class and the application main class, triggering a re-entrant context creation. Fix: move integration tests to separate top-level classes; never nest `@SpringBootTest` classes inside `@SpringBootApplication` classes.

**`@WebFluxTest` with a controller that uses `@AuthenticationPrincipal` always receives `null` for the principal unless `spring-security-test` is on the classpath AND `@WithMockUser` is applied — omitting either causes a silent null principal, not an authentication error [community]** — A developer writes a `@WebFluxTest` for a controller that uses `@AuthenticationPrincipal UserDetails user`. The test runs without error but the principal is `null` — the controller's `if (user == null)` guard activates and the test silently tests the unauthenticated path. WHY: `@WebFluxTest` does not auto-configure Spring Security by default (unlike `@SpringBootTest`). Without `spring-security-test`, `@WithMockUser` is not available. Without `@WithMockUser`, no `SecurityContext` is populated for the reactive test. The controller receives a `null` principal and silently takes the fallback path. Fix: add `spring-security-test` to the test classpath; annotate reactive controller tests with `@WithMockUser` or `@WithUserDetails`; assert `assertThat(response.statusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)` explicitly for unauthenticated paths.

**`@GrpcTest` in Spring Boot 4.1 does not load `@EventListener` beans — any application logic triggered by `ApplicationReadyEvent` or `ContextRefreshedEvent` is silently skipped, causing tests that depend on event-driven initialization to pass even when the initialization is broken [community]** — A developer's `@GrpcService` depends on a cache populated by a `@Component` that listens to `ApplicationReadyEvent`. In `@GrpcTest`, the slice loads the service but not the event listener component. The cache is empty, the service uses a fallback empty-cache code path, and the test passes. In production, the event listener populates the cache on startup and the service uses the real data. The test does not catch the event listener configuration bug (a missing `@Component` annotation). WHY: `@GrpcTest` is a narrow slice that excludes `@EventListener` beans and lifecycle events to keep tests fast; `ApplicationReadyEvent` is a production-lifecycle event that is not fired in slice tests. Fix: for event-driven startup logic, use `ApplicationContextRunner` or `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = NONE)` with `@Import` of the specific beans under test; explicitly verify the event listener bean is loaded with `hasSingleBean(MyCacheInitializer.class)`.

**`JUnit 6 --fail-fast` marks all un-run tests as `SKIPPED` in the Surefire XML report — code coverage tools that exclude `SKIPPED` tests report inflated coverage percentages because the un-run tests are not counted as missing coverage [community]** — A developer enables `--fail-fast` to speed up CI. After the first test failure, 200 tests are skipped. The coverage report shows 87% branch coverage because only the 50 executed tests contribute to the denominator. A PR is approved based on the 87% threshold. Later, the full test run reveals 60% coverage because the 200 skipped tests cover many uncovered branches. WHY: Coverage tools (Jacoco, IntelliJ coverage runner) record only instrumented code that actually executes; `SKIPPED` tests do not execute, so their target code paths are never hit. The coverage metric with `--fail-fast` is only meaningful if the failing test is the only broken test; in practice, multiple failures are common. Fix: enforce coverage thresholds only in pipelines that run to completion; use `--fail-fast` only for developer-speed pipelines that do not gate on coverage.
