### 1. JUnit 6 `@ParameterizedClass` — Class-Level Parameterization for Entire Test Classes [official]

JUnit 6 introduces `@ParameterizedClass`, a class-level counterpart to `@ParameterizedTest` that parameterizes an entire test class rather than individual methods. When a class is annotated with `@ParameterizedClass`, every test method in the class is executed once per argument set supplied by the configured `@MethodSource`, `@CsvSource`, or other argument providers. Arguments are injected into the class via constructor parameters or annotated fields, and the class is instantiated fresh for each argument set according to the active lifecycle mode. This eliminates the pattern of repeating `@ParameterizedTest` and source annotations on every method in a suite that must run against multiple configurations (e.g., testing the same REST controller against multiple security profiles).

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedClass;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

@ParameterizedClass
@MethodSource("provideLocales")
class OrderServiceMultiLocaleTest {

    // Field injection: each locale is injected before each class instantiation
    final String locale;

    OrderServiceMultiLocaleTest(String locale) {
        this.locale = locale;
    }

    static Stream<String> provideLocales() {
        return Stream.of("en-US", "de-DE", "ja-JP", "fr-FR");
    }

    @Test
    void formatted_price_uses_locale_decimal_separator() {
        OrderService svc = new OrderService(locale);
        String price = svc.format(1234.56);
        // en-US -> "1,234.56", de-DE -> "1.234,56", etc.
        assertThat(price).isNotNull().isNotEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void order_confirmation_message_is_localized() {
        OrderService svc = new OrderService(locale);
        String msg = svc.confirmationMessage(42L);
        assertThat(msg).contains(String.valueOf(42));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ParameterizedClass` multiplies execution count by the number of argument sets, so a class with 10 test methods and 4 locales produces 40 test executions — CI time scales linearly with both. Unlike `@ParameterizedTest`, there is no per-method argument granularity; if only one method requires parameterization, extracting that method into a separate class or keeping `@ParameterizedTest` at the method level is more appropriate. The display name for each class instantiation defaults to `[index] argValue`; use `@ParameterizedClass(name = "{0}")` to produce readable names in CI reports. Alternative: `@TestFactory` with `DynamicTest.stream()` for fully dynamic argument sets generated at runtime.

[official]

---

### 2. JUnit 6 `CancellationToken` API — Cooperative Test Execution Cancellation [official]

JUnit 6 introduces a `CancellationToken` API that allows test engines, extensions, and build tools to cooperatively cancel in-progress test execution without relying on thread interruption. A `CancellationToken` can be obtained from `ExtensionContext.getCancellationToken()` inside any `BeforeEachCallback`, `AfterEachCallback`, or `InvocationInterceptor`, and the token's `isCancellationRequested()` method can be checked at critical points in long-running tests. When `--fail-fast` is active in the `ConsoleLauncher`, JUnit automatically triggers cancellation after the first failure; custom `TestExecutionListener` implementations can also trigger cancellation programmatically. This enables graceful shutdown of parameterized test loops, in-container setup operations, or external resource acquisition without leaving dangling resources.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtensionContext;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.BeforeEachCallback;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.junit.platform.engine.CancellationToken;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assumptions.assumeTrue;

class CancellationAwareExtension implements BeforeEachCallback {
    @Override
    public void beforeEach(ExtensionContext context) {
        CancellationToken token = context.getCancellationToken();
        // Cooperatively skip remaining tests if cancellation was requested
        // (e.g., by --fail-fast or a custom TestExecutionListener)
        assumeTrue(
            !token.isCancellationRequested(),
            "Test execution cancelled -- skipping remaining tests"
        );
    }
}

@ExtendWith(CancellationAwareExtension.class)
class BatchProcessingTest {

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(ints = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5})
    void process_batch_item(int itemId) {
        // If cancellation is requested after item 2 fails, items 3-5
        // are skipped via the extension rather than running to failure
        BatchProcessor processor = new BatchProcessor();
        processor.process(itemId);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `CancellationToken` is a cooperative mechanism — a test method that does not check the token will run to completion even after cancellation is requested, so long-running compute loops inside test methods must explicitly poll the token or periodically yield. The token does not interrupt blocked threads (e.g., a test sleeping or waiting on a lock); for truly interruptible tests, combine `CancellationToken` with thread interruption via a custom `InvocationInterceptor`. Cancellation state is propagated from the `TestPlan` down through the execution hierarchy, meaning cancellation of a parent class also cancels all child methods. Alternative: `@Timeout` annotation for individual time-bounded tests; `--fail-fast` ConsoleLauncher flag for CI-wide cancellation after first failure.

[official]

---

### 3. JUnit 6 `@AutoClose` — Declarative AutoCloseable Field Cleanup [official]

JUnit 6 adds the `@AutoClose` annotation for fields that implement `AutoCloseable`, causing JUnit to call `close()` on annotated fields automatically at the end of the appropriate lifecycle scope. Applied to a `static` field, the resource is closed after all tests in the class complete (`@AfterAll` timing); applied to an instance field, it is closed after each test (`@AfterEach` timing). This removes the need for boilerplate `@AfterEach`/`@AfterAll` methods that exist solely to close resources, and it works with any `AutoCloseable` including JDBC connections, file handles, `WireMockServer`, and Testcontainers `GenericContainer` (which implements `Closeable`). The annotation accepts a `closeMethod` attribute for classes that use a non-standard close method name (e.g., `stop()` instead of `close()`).

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AutoClose;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.TestInstance;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.TestInstance.Lifecycle;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.DriverManagerDataSource;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class RepositoryIntegrationTest {

    // Container is shared across all tests; @AutoClose calls container.close() after all tests
    @AutoClose
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("testdb");

    // DataSource created per test; closed automatically after each @Test
    @AutoClose
    DataSource dataSource;

    @Test
    void save_and_retrieve_order() {
        dataSource = new DriverManagerDataSource(
            postgres.getJdbcUrl(),
            postgres.getUsername(),
            postgres.getPassword()
        );
        OrderRepository repo = new JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource);
        long id = repo.save(new Order("CUST-1", "SKU-A"));
        assertThat(repo.findById(id)).isNotNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@AutoClose` silently swallows `close()` exceptions by default — if cleanup fails, the test method result is not affected, and the failure may go unnoticed unless JUnit logs a warning. For cleanup operations that must not fail silently (e.g., confirming a transaction is rolled back), keep an explicit `@AfterEach` method with assertions. The `closeMethod` attribute requires the method to have no parameters; multi-argument close methods (rare but present in some legacy `AutoCloseable` implementations) are not supported. Static `@AutoClose` fields are closed in reverse declaration order, which matters when multiple resources have dependency ordering (e.g., a connection pool must be closed before the database container). Alternative: try-with-resources in `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`; `ExtensionContext.Store.CloseableResource` for extension-managed cleanup.

[official]

---

### 4. Mockito 5.20 Generic Type Construction Mocking — `mockConstruction` with Generics [official]

Mockito 5.20 adds support for mocking the construction of generic types via `mockConstruction(GenericClass.class, ...)`, where previously only raw types were supported. When a class under test constructs a generic container (e.g., `new ResponseEntity<List<Order>>(...)`) internally, Mockito can now intercept the constructor call and return a configured mock regardless of the type parameter. The mock is scoped to the `try-with-resources` block; construction calls outside the block proceed normally. This closes a common gap where testing methods that internally construct typed collections or generic wrappers required either refactoring to inject the wrapper or accepting a real constructed instance.

```java
import org.mockito.MockedConstruction;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.mockConstruction;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class PaymentProcessorTest {

    @Test
    void process_payment_wraps_result_in_response_envelope() {
        // Mock construction of the generic ResponseEnvelope<T> regardless of T
        try (MockedConstruction<ResponseEnvelope> mocked =
                mockConstruction(ResponseEnvelope.class, (mock, ctx) -> {
                    // ctx.arguments() contains constructor args at call time
                    when(mock.isSuccess()).thenReturn(true);
                    when(mock.getCorrelationId()).thenReturn("CORR-001");
                })) {

            PaymentProcessor processor = new PaymentProcessor();
            ResponseEnvelope<PaymentResult> result =
                processor.process(new PaymentRequest("4111111111111111", 99.99));

            assertThat(result.isSuccess()).isTrue();
            assertThat(result.getCorrelationId()).isEqualTo("CORR-001");
            // Verify exactly one envelope was constructed
            assertThat(mocked.constructed()).hasSize(1);
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Generic type construction mocking uses the raw class token at the bytecode level — Mockito cannot distinguish `new ResponseEnvelope<List<Order>>()` from `new ResponseEnvelope<String>()` at construction time because of type erasure. If a method constructs multiple generic instances of the same raw class with different type parameters, all constructions are intercepted by the same `MockedConstruction` scope. Use `ctx.arguments()` in the `MockitoSettings` lambda to differentiate instances by constructor argument values. This feature is not supported on Android (which lacks inline mock maker support for generic construction). Alternative: dependency injection to pass pre-constructed instances; factory method extraction for testable construction.

[official]

---

### 5. AssertJ 3.27 `actual()` Method — Direct Access to the Object Under Test [official]

AssertJ 3.27.0 adds an `actual()` method to all assertion objects, providing direct access to the wrapped object under test without breaking the fluent chain. Previously, to both assert on an object and pass it to a separate assertion or utility method, developers had to either break the chain to retrieve the reference separately or use `satisfies()`. The `actual()` method eliminates the need to store the subject in a local variable before calling `assertThat(subject)`, and it is particularly useful when the object needs to be passed to a third-party matcher, a custom assertion, or stored for later verification within a single fluent expression. The method returns the exact type of the object under test, preserving generic type information.

```java
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.assertj.core.api.AbstractStringAssert;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;

class OrderDtoAssertionTest {

    @Test
    void order_summary_has_correct_structure_and_is_loggable() {
        OrderDto order = new OrderDto("ORD-123", "CUST-1",
            List.of(new LineItem("SKU-A", 2), new LineItem("SKU-B", 1)));

        // actual() retrieves the wrapped object for use outside the chain
        AbstractStringAssert<?> summaryAssert = assertThat(order.getSummary())
            .isNotBlank()
            .startsWith("ORD-");

        // Use actual() to extract the string for additional processing
        String summary = summaryAssert.actual();
        assertThat(summary.length()).isBetween(5, 50);

        // Combined: assert on value, then use actual() inline
        List<LineItem> items = assertThat(order.getLineItems())
            .hasSize(2)
            .actual();  // returns the list for further use

        assertThat(items.get(0).getSku()).isEqualTo("SKU-A");
    }

    @Test
    void order_total_is_correctly_formatted() {
        OrderDto order = new OrderDto("ORD-456", "CUST-2", List.of());
        // actual() used to get the double value after bounding assertion
        double total = assertThat(order.getTotal())
            .isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0.0)
            .actual();
        // Pass the raw value to a domain-specific formatter test
        assertThat(CurrencyFormatter.format(total)).matches("^\\$[0-9]+\\.[0-9]{2}$");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `actual()` returns the object without type narrowing beyond the assertion's declared type parameter — for complex generic types, the caller may still need an unchecked cast if the assertion class is parameterized at a base type. Overusing `actual()` to retrieve the subject and then write entirely separate assertions defeats the purpose of the fluent API and reduces failure message clarity (since the separate assertion's message lacks the context accumulated by the preceding chain). Use `satisfies()` or `extracting()` instead when the goal is to assert on derived properties within the chain. Alternative: local variable before `assertThat()`; `satisfies(consumer)` for in-chain side-effecting assertions.

[official]

---

### 6. AssertJ 3.27 `usingEquals(BiPredicate)` — Custom Comparison Logic for Equality Assertions [official]

AssertJ 3.27.0 adds `usingEquals(BiPredicate<T, T> equals)` and `usingEquals(BiPredicate<T, T> equals, String description)` to `AbstractAssert`, allowing callers to supply a custom equality function for `isEqualTo`, `isIn`, `containsExactly`, and other equality-based assertions. Previously, custom equality required either implementing `Comparator` (which imposes ordering) or using `usingComparatorForType` (which required a class token and did not support lambdas). The new method accepts any `BiPredicate`, making it straightforward to use method references, lambdas, or external equality libraries (e.g., comparing DTOs by a business key while ignoring audit fields).

```java
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

class CustomerDtoEqualityTest {

    // DTO with audit fields that should be ignored in business equality
    record CustomerDto(String id, String name, String email,
                       Instant createdAt, Instant updatedAt) {}

    @Test
    void customers_are_equal_by_business_key_ignoring_audit_fields() {
        CustomerDto expected = new CustomerDto(
            "CUST-1", "Alice", "alice@example.com",
            Instant.EPOCH, Instant.EPOCH);

        CustomerDto actual = new CustomerDto(
            "CUST-1", "Alice", "alice@example.com",
            Instant.now(), Instant.now()); // different audit timestamps

        // BiPredicate compares only id, name, email
        assertThat(actual)
            .usingEquals(
                (a, b) -> a.id().equals(b.id())
                    && a.name().equals(b.name())
                    && a.email().equals(b.email()),
                "business-key equality (id + name + email)"
            )
            .isEqualTo(expected);
    }

    @Test
    void list_of_customers_compared_by_id_only() {
        List<CustomerDto> result = fetchCustomers();
        List<CustomerDto> expected = List.of(
            new CustomerDto("A", "Alice", "a@e.com", Instant.EPOCH, Instant.EPOCH),
            new CustomerDto("B", "Bob",   "b@e.com", Instant.EPOCH, Instant.EPOCH));

        assertThat(result)
            .usingElementComparator(
                (a, b) -> a.id().compareTo(b.id()))
            .containsExactlyElementsOf(expected);
    }

    List<CustomerDto> fetchCustomers() {
        return List.of(
            new CustomerDto("A", "Alice", "a@e.com", Instant.now(), Instant.now()),
            new CustomerDto("B", "Bob",   "b@e.com", Instant.now(), Instant.now()));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `usingEquals(BiPredicate)` applies globally to the single assertion call — it does not propagate into nested collections or recursive comparisons automatically. For deep object graph comparisons ignoring specific fields, `usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields(...)` is the more ergonomic choice. The `description` parameter in `usingEquals(BiPredicate, String)` is used in failure messages to label the custom equality function; omitting it produces cryptic messages referencing the lambda's synthetic class name. The `BiPredicate` must be consistent (i.e., symmetric and transitive) to avoid confusing assertion failures; inconsistent predicates can produce false positives in collection assertions like `containsExactly`. Alternative: `usingRecursiveComparison()` for field-level ignoring; `usingComparatorForType()` for type-scoped comparison.

[official]

---

### 7. Spring Boot `@MockitoBean` with `@Primary` Resolution — Replacing Beans in Multi-Candidate Contexts [official]

Spring Boot's native `@MockitoBean` (from Spring Framework 7.0, replacing the deprecated `@MockBean`) can be combined with `@Primary` semantics when multiple beans of the same type exist in the test context. When `@MockitoBean` is declared for a type that has more than one registered bean, Spring applies the standard bean resolution rules: if no `@Primary` candidate exists among real beans, the mock registered by `@MockitoBean` becomes the `@Primary` candidate for injection. This allows targeted replacement of a specific bean in a multi-datasource or multi-service context without needing `@Qualifier` on every injection site, by ensuring the mock is the only `@Primary` candidate.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyString;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
class OrderFulfillmentServiceTest {

    // @MockitoBean replaces the primary NotificationService bean
    // the backup NotificationService (SMS) is NOT replaced
    @MockitoBean
    NotificationService emailNotificationService;

    @Autowired
    OrderFulfillmentService fulfillmentService;

    @Test
    void fulfillment_sends_email_notification_on_success() {
        given(emailNotificationService.send(anyString(), anyString()))
            .willReturn(NotificationResult.sent("NOTIF-001"));

        FulfillmentResult result = fulfillmentService.fulfill(
            new Order("ORD-100", "CUST-1"));

        assertThat(result.isSuccess()).isTrue();
        assertThat(result.getNotificationId()).isEqualTo("NOTIF-001");
    }

    @Test
    void fulfillment_continues_when_notification_fails() {
        given(emailNotificationService.send(anyString(), anyString()))
            .willThrow(new NotificationException("SMTP unavailable"));

        FulfillmentResult result = fulfillmentService.fulfill(
            new Order("ORD-101", "CUST-2"));

        // Service should tolerate notification failure
        assertThat(result.isSuccess()).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@MockitoBean` without a `name` attribute replaces beans by type; if multiple beans of the same type exist and none is `@Primary`, Spring will fail with a `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` at context startup — adding `name = "emailNotificationService"` to `@MockitoBean` resolves this. Unlike the deprecated `@MockBean`, `@MockitoBean` does not reset mocks automatically between tests in the same context; configure `MockitoSession` or use `@DirtiesContext` if stateful mock verification across tests is required. The annotation is in package `org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito`, so import paths differ from the old `org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito` package — search-replace during migration. Alternative: `@TestConfiguration` with a `@Bean` returning `Mockito.mock(NotificationService.class)` for contexts where `@MockitoBean` is unavailable.

[official]

---

### 8. Spring Boot `@DataJpaTest` with `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` and Testcontainers `@ServiceConnection` — Production-Parity JPA Slice Tests [official]

Spring Boot's `@DataJpaTest` defaults to replacing the production `DataSource` with an in-memory H2 database, which masks dialect differences (JSON columns, `RETURNING` clause, PostgreSQL-specific functions) that are invisible in H2 but fail in production. Combining `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)` with a Testcontainers `@ServiceConnection`-annotated `PostgreSQLContainer` static field configures the JPA slice to use a real PostgreSQL instance without any manual `@DynamicPropertySource` wiring. Spring Boot's `@ServiceConnection` auto-detects the container type and registers the correct datasource URL, username, and password properties before the application context starts.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.jdbc.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class ProductRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired
    ProductRepository productRepository;

    @Test
    void save_product_with_jsonb_attributes() {
        Product product = new Product("SKU-001", "Widget");
        product.setAttributes(Map.of("color", "blue", "weight", "1.5kg"));
        Product saved = productRepository.save(product);

        assertThat(saved.getId()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(saved.getAttributes()).containsEntry("color", "blue");
    }

    @Test
    void find_products_by_attribute_uses_postgres_jsonb_operator() {
        // This query uses the @> (contains) operator -- fails on H2
        List<Product> found = productRepository
            .findByAttributeContaining("color", "blue");
        assertThat(found).isNotEmpty();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Using Testcontainers in `@DataJpaTest` slices means each test class starts a container, adding 5-15 seconds of startup time compared to H2. Share the container across test classes using a `static` field combined with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` or a shared `AbstractIntegrationTest` base class with a `static @Container` — JUnit's container lifecycle management will start the container once per JVM for `static` fields. `@ServiceConnection` only works for container types that have a registered `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory`; for exotic databases, fall back to `@DynamicPropertySource`. The `@DataJpaTest` slice does not load `@Service` or `@Controller` beans, so this pattern is strictly for repository and entity testing. Alternative: `@SpringBootTest` with `@Testcontainers` for full-context integration tests; Flyway/Liquibase-initialized containers for schema migration testing.

[official]

---

### 9. Mockito `MockedConstruction.constructed()` Assertion — Verifying Number of Constructed Instances [official]

`MockedConstruction.constructed()` returns an immutable list of all mock instances created during the scope of the `mockConstruction` block, allowing tests to assert not just that a method was called on the mock but that the correct number of instances were constructed and each received the expected constructor arguments. This closes the verification gap where a method might create multiple instances of a class (e.g., a factory loop creating `Thread` instances) and the test could only stub the behavior of the first instance. Combined with `ctx.arguments()` in the construction settings lambda, each constructed instance can be configured individually based on the arguments it was constructed with.

```java
import org.mockito.MockedConstruction;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.mockConstruction;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.verify;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;

class TaskDispatcherTest {

    @Test
    void dispatcher_creates_one_worker_per_task() {
        try (MockedConstruction<TaskWorker> mocked =
                mockConstruction(TaskWorker.class, (mock, ctx) -> {
                    String taskId = (String) ctx.arguments().get(0);
                    when(mock.execute()).thenReturn(
                        new TaskResult(taskId, "DONE"));
                })) {

            TaskDispatcher dispatcher = new TaskDispatcher();
            List<TaskResult> results = dispatcher.dispatch(
                List.of("TASK-1", "TASK-2", "TASK-3"));

            // Assert exactly 3 workers were constructed
            assertThat(mocked.constructed()).hasSize(3);

            // Assert each worker was asked to execute
            for (TaskWorker worker : mocked.constructed()) {
                verify(worker).execute();
            }

            // Assert results aggregated correctly
            assertThat(results).extracting(TaskResult::status)
                .containsOnly("DONE");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `constructed()` returns instances in construction order, but the order in which `verify()` or `when()` calls apply to each instance still depends on the test code's iteration order — if the class under test constructs workers in a non-deterministic order (e.g., via parallel streams), `constructed().get(0)` may not correspond to the first task. Use `ctx.arguments()` in the constructor settings lambda to configure each mock by its construction arguments rather than relying on index order. The `constructed()` list is only valid within the `try-with-resources` block; accessing it after the block closes returns an empty list. Alternative: argument captor on factory methods; refactoring to inject a `WorkerFactory` that can be mocked normally.

[official]

---

### 10. Spring Boot `MockMvcTester` AssertJ Integration — Chained Mock MVC Assertions [official]

Spring Boot's `MockMvcTester` provides an AssertJ-native API for `MockMvc`, replacing the static `MockMvcRequestBuilders`/`MockMvcResultMatchers` pattern with a fluent, type-safe chain. Unlike `MockMvc.perform(...).andExpect(...)`, `MockMvcTester` returns an `MvcTestResult` that implements `AssertProvider<AbstractMvcTestResultAssert>`, enabling direct use with `assertThat()`. The result object is lazy — the HTTP exchange is executed when `assertThat()` is first called on the builder, not when `.get().uri(...)` is invoked, which makes it safe to compose assertions before triggering execution. Spring Boot's `@WebMvcTest` auto-configures a `MockMvcTester` bean.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;

    @MockitoBean
    ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void get_product_returns_200_with_json_body() {
        given(productService.findById("SKU-001"))
            .willReturn(new ProductDto("SKU-001", "Widget", 9.99));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/products/SKU-001")
                      .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.sku").isEqualTo("SKU-001");
    }

    @Test
    void get_unknown_product_returns_404() {
        given(productService.findById("MISSING"))
            .willThrow(new ProductNotFoundException("MISSING"));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/products/MISSING"))
            .hasStatus(404)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.errorCode").isEqualTo("PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND");
    }

    @Test
    void create_product_validates_sku_format() {
        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/products")
                      .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                      .content("{\"sku\": \"!invalid\", \"name\": \"Bad\"}"))
            .hasStatus(400)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.violations[0].field").isEqualTo("sku");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `MockMvcTester` is backed by `MockMvc` and does not start a real HTTP server — edge cases involving servlet container behavior (e.g., async dispatch with Tomcat NIO, chunked transfer encoding) are not tested. The lazy execution model means exceptions thrown during the request (e.g., a handler that throws `RuntimeException`) are captured in the `MvcTestResult` rather than propagating to the test method; use `.hasStatus(500)` and `.failure()` assertions to verify error handling rather than expecting a thrown exception. `bodyJson()` returns a `JsonPathResultAssert` that uses JSONPath under the hood; for Spring's `@JsonTest` assertions (`assertThat(json.write(...)).isEqualToJson(...)`) the `JacksonTester` API is still preferred. Alternative: `WebTestClient` for reactive applications; `RestTestClient` for full-stack (mock or real server) integration tests.

[official]

---

### 11. JUnit 6 `MethodOrderer.Default` — Resetting Ordering on Nested Classes Without Explicit Override [official]

JUnit 6's `MethodOrderer.Default` and `ClassOrderer.Default` are placeholder implementations that signal "revert to the default execution order" for a class or nested class that would otherwise inherit a custom ordering from an enclosing class. In JUnit 6, `@TestMethodOrder` and `@TestClassOrder` are inherited by `@Nested` classes, which can cause inner classes to unintentionally inherit alphabetical or annotation-based ordering. Applying `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Default.class)` on a `@Nested` class explicitly resets ordering to JUnit's deterministic-but-unspecified default, preventing inheritance without requiring knowledge of the parent's ordering strategy.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.TestMethodOrder;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.MethodOrderer;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Order;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Nested;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Top-level class runs tests in declaration order (annotated)
@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)
class CheckoutFlowTest {

    @Test @Order(1)
    void step1_add_items_to_cart() {
        assertThat(CartService.addItem("SKU-A")).isTrue();
    }

    @Test @Order(2)
    void step2_apply_coupon() {
        assertThat(CartService.applyCoupon("SAVE10")).isTrue();
    }

    // This nested class needs its own unordered (default) execution
    // @TestMethodOrder is inherited in JUnit 6, so we reset it explicitly
    @Nested
    @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Default.class)
    class CouponValidationTests {

        @Test
        void coupon_is_case_insensitive() { /* ... */ }

        @Test
        void expired_coupon_is_rejected() { /* ... */ }

        @Test
        void coupon_applies_correct_discount() { /* ... */ }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `MethodOrderer.Default.class` produces a deterministic but implementation-defined execution order — it is not guaranteed to be the same as declaration order, alphabetical order, or any other human-readable sequence. If a specific order is needed in the nested class, use `MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class` with `@Order` annotations even if the enclosing class does not use them. The inheritance of `@TestMethodOrder` to `@Nested` classes is a JUnit 6 behavioral change from JUnit 5 (where `@Nested` classes did not inherit the annotation), so existing JUnit 5 test suites migrated to JUnit 6 may see ordering changes in nested classes. Alternative: `MethodOrderer.DisplayName.class` for alphabetical ordering; `MethodOrderer.Random.class` to detect order dependencies.

[official]

---

### 12. Testcontainers `@DynamicPropertySource` vs `@ServiceConnection` — Choosing the Right Property Injection Strategy [community]

Testcontainers offers two strategies for injecting container connection properties into Spring Boot test contexts: `@DynamicPropertySource` (explicit property registration) and `@ServiceConnection` (automatic convention-based registration). `@ServiceConnection`, introduced in Spring Boot 3.1, uses `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory` SPI to auto-register datasource URL, username, password, and driver class from recognized container types (`PostgreSQLContainer`, `RedisContainer`, `KafkaContainer`, etc.) without any boilerplate. `@DynamicPropertySource` remains necessary for custom containers, containers not yet registered with a `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory`, or when the property key differs from the Spring Boot convention (e.g., a custom queue URL key).

```java
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertyRegistry;
import org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertySource;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest {

    // @ServiceConnection: Spring auto-injects datasource.url/username/password
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    // Custom container: @DynamicPropertySource required because
    // GenericContainer has no registered ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory
    @Container
    static GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void redisProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.data.redis.host", redis::getHost);
        registry.add("spring.data.redis.port",
            () -> redis.getMappedPort(6379));
    }

    @Test
    void order_is_cached_after_retrieval() {
        // test uses both postgres and redis
        assertThat(true).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ServiceConnection` only works for container types where a `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory` has been registered — the list grows with each Spring Boot release but custom or niche containers always require `@DynamicPropertySource`. Mixing both strategies in the same test class is valid and common in real applications. `@ServiceConnection` does not support configuring which Spring Boot property key to map to; if the application uses a non-standard key (e.g., `app.db.url` instead of `spring.datasource.url`), `@DynamicPropertySource` is required regardless of container type. Alternative: a shared `AbstractIntegrationTest` base class that declares all containers and `@DynamicPropertySource` methods, inherited by all integration test classes.

[community]

---

### 13. AssertJ `CompletableFuture` Timing Assertions — `isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin` and `completesExceptionallyWithin` [official]

AssertJ 3.27.0 adds timing-aware assertions for `CompletableFuture`: `isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin(Duration, Predicate)` and `completesExceptionallyWithin(Duration, Class)`. These replace the pattern of calling `future.get(timeout, unit)` in a try-catch block — a pattern that produces opaque `TimeoutException` messages and requires additional assertions to verify the value. The new assertions produce descriptive failure messages including the timeout, the actual completion state, and the assertion predicate or exception type. They integrate with AssertJ's soft assertion support, allowing multiple future assertions to be batched in a single `assertSoftly` block.

```java
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.assertj.core.api.SoftAssertions;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

class AsyncOrderProcessorTest {

    private final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
    private final AsyncOrderProcessor processor = new AsyncOrderProcessor(executor);

    @Test
    void order_is_processed_within_2_seconds() {
        CompletableFuture<ProcessingResult> future =
            processor.processAsync(new Order("ORD-200", "CUST-1"));

        // Replaces: ProcessingResult r = future.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        //           assertThat(r).isNotNull(); assertThat(r.isSuccess())...
        assertThat(future)
            .isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin(
                Duration.ofSeconds(2),
                result -> result.isSuccess() && result.orderId().equals("ORD-200")
            );
    }

    @Test
    void invalid_order_fails_with_validation_exception_within_1_second() {
        CompletableFuture<ProcessingResult> future =
            processor.processAsync(new Order(null, "CUST-1")); // null id invalid

        assertThat(future)
            .completesExceptionallyWithin(
                Duration.ofSeconds(1),
                OrderValidationException.class
            );
    }

    @Test
    void multiple_futures_checked_with_soft_assertions() {
        SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {
            CompletableFuture<ProcessingResult> f1 =
                processor.processAsync(new Order("ORD-301", "CUST-2"));
            CompletableFuture<ProcessingResult> f2 =
                processor.processAsync(new Order("ORD-302", "CUST-3"));

            softly.assertThat(f1).isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin(
                Duration.ofSeconds(3), r -> r.isSuccess());
            softly.assertThat(f2).isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin(
                Duration.ofSeconds(3), r -> r.isSuccess());
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** These assertions block the test thread until the future completes or the timeout elapses — they are not non-blocking assertions. If the future never completes (e.g., a deadlock in the processor), the test thread blocks for the full duration of the timeout, which can cause CI build timeouts if the timeout is long. For truly non-blocking assertions on async systems, use `Awaitility` with `await().atMost(...).until(...)` which polls without blocking. The `Predicate` passed to `isCompletedWithValueMatchingWithin` is evaluated inline in the test thread after the future completes; complex predicate logic should be extracted into named `Predicate` constants for readability in failure messages. Alternative: `Awaitility.await()` for polling-based async assertions; `StepVerifier` for Project Reactor `Flux`/`Mono` testing.

[official]

---

### 14. JUnit 6 `@ResourceLock` on `@ParameterizedClass` — Shared Resource Coordination Across Parameterized Instances [official]

JUnit 6.0.2 promotes `@ResourceLock` support on classes annotated with `@ParameterizedClass` or `@ClassTemplate` from experimental to maintained status. When parallel test execution is enabled and multiple parameterized class instances run concurrently, `@ResourceLock` prevents race conditions on shared resources (databases, files, singletons) by serializing access. The lock is identified by a string key; all class instances that declare the same key acquire a shared or exclusive lock before executing. This enables safe parallel parameterization of tests that share a single container or a limited connection pool — instances requiring write access use `ResourceAccessMode.READ_WRITE`, while read-only instances use `ResourceAccessMode.READ`.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.parallel.ResourceLock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.parallel.ResourceAccessMode;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedClass;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

// Multiple parameterized instances run concurrently; READ_WRITE lock
// ensures write tests are serialized against other write and read tests
@ParameterizedClass
@MethodSource("databaseConfigurations")
@ResourceLock(value = "integration-database", mode = ResourceAccessMode.READ_WRITE)
@SpringBootTest
class DatabaseMigrationTest {

    final String migrationScript;

    DatabaseMigrationTest(String migrationScript) {
        this.migrationScript = migrationScript;
    }

    static Stream<String> databaseConfigurations() {
        return Stream.of(
            "migrations/V1__create_orders.sql",
            "migrations/V2__add_customer_index.sql",
            "migrations/V3__add_audit_columns.sql"
        );
    }

    @Autowired MigrationRunner migrationRunner;
    @Autowired SchemaValidator schemaValidator;

    @Test
    void migration_script_applies_without_errors() {
        MigrationResult result = migrationRunner.run(migrationScript);
        assertThat(result.hasErrors()).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void schema_is_valid_after_migration() {
        migrationRunner.run(migrationScript);
        assertThat(schemaValidator.validate()).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ResourceLock` with `READ_WRITE` mode on a `@ParameterizedClass` serializes all write-mode instances, which can negate the parallelism benefit if all parameterized class instances need write access. Use `READ_WRITE` only for truly mutating tests; read-only parameterized instances can use `READ` mode to run concurrently with each other while still blocking write-mode instances. The lock granularity is per class instance, not per method — a single long test method in a parameterized class holds the write lock for the entire method duration. For finer-grained locking, apply `@ResourceLock` on individual `@Test` methods within the class. Alternative: separate test classes for read and write scenarios; `@Isolated` annotation to run a single test class without any concurrency.

[official]

---

### 15. Mockito 5.18 `UnfinishedStubbingException` Multi-Threading Hint — Detecting Cross-Thread Stubbing Bugs [official]

Mockito 5.18 enhances `UnfinishedStubbingException` messages to suggest multi-threading as a potential cause when the exception is thrown outside of a `when()` or `BDDMockito.given()` call. The classic cause of `UnfinishedStubbingException` is forgetting to complete a `when(mock.method()).thenReturn(...)` call, but a less obvious cause is a background thread calling a stubbed mock method while the main thread is in the middle of an unrelated `when()` expression — the background thread's call interrupts the stubbing state machine and causes a spurious `UnfinishedStubbingException` in the next test. The improved message now reads: "Note: This may also occur when a mock is accessed from multiple threads — ensure mock stubbing is thread-safe or use per-thread mocks."

```java
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ThreadSafeStubbingTest {

    @Mock
    InventoryService inventoryService;

    // ANTI-PATTERN: background thread accesses mock during stubbing
    @Test
    void anti_pattern_background_thread_interferes_with_stubbing() throws Exception {
        // This can cause UnfinishedStubbingException -- the executor
        // starts calling inventoryService.getStock() while the main
        // thread is in the middle of when(...).thenReturn(...)
        var executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
        executor.submit(() -> inventoryService.getStock("SKU-A")); // races with stubbing

        // WRONG: background thread may interrupt this stubbing sequence
        when(inventoryService.getStock("SKU-A")).thenReturn(10);
        executor.shutdown();
        executor.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }

    // CORRECT PATTERN: complete all stubbing before starting background threads
    @Test
    void correct_pattern_stub_before_spawning_threads() throws Exception {
        // Stub first, before any background threads access the mock
        given(inventoryService.getStock("SKU-A")).willReturn(10);
        given(inventoryService.getStock("SKU-B")).willReturn(0);

        var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        var f1 = executor.submit(() ->
            new StockChecker(inventoryService).isAvailable("SKU-A"));
        var f2 = executor.submit(() ->
            new StockChecker(inventoryService).isAvailable("SKU-B"));

        executor.shutdown();
        executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        assertThat(f1.get()).isTrue();
        assertThat(f2.get()).isFalse();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Mockito mocks are not thread-safe by design — concurrent access to the same mock from multiple threads can corrupt the internal stubbing state machine even when the `UnfinishedStubbingException` hint suggests otherwise. The improved error message is diagnostic only; it does not prevent the race condition. For truly concurrent tests, create separate mock instances per thread via a `ThreadLocal<MockedObject>` or use a `ConcurrentHashMap` to map thread IDs to dedicated mock instances. `@MockitoBean` in Spring Boot creates a single shared mock bean — avoid background thread access to `@MockitoBean` instances during stubbing setup in `@BeforeEach`. Alternative: `Mockito.reset(mock)` between parameterized invocations when a single mock is shared across concurrent executions (use with extreme caution — resetting in multi-threaded contexts has its own race window).

[official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 37 [community]

**`@AutoClose` on a `static` field that is also annotated with `@Container` (Testcontainers) causes a double-close: Testcontainers closes the container in its `afterAll` callback, and JUnit's `@AutoClose` processor also calls `close()`, resulting in a second `close()` on an already-stopped container and a spurious `IllegalStateException` in the test log [community]** — A developer adds `@AutoClose` to a `static PostgreSQLContainer` field that is already managed by the `@Testcontainers` JUnit extension. JUnit processes `@AutoClose` in the `afterAll` phase after all extensions have executed; the Testcontainers extension already called `container.stop()` during its own `afterAll` callback. The second `close()` call attempts to stop a container that is already in `EXITED` state and throws `IllegalStateException: Container is not running`. WHY: `@AutoClose` is a JUnit-level lifecycle mechanism that does not inspect existing extensions managing the same resource; it blindly calls `close()` without checking if the resource is already closed. Fix: do not annotate `@Container`-managed fields with `@AutoClose` — Testcontainers' extension is the authoritative lifecycle manager for `@Container` fields; use `@AutoClose` only for resources that are NOT managed by another JUnit extension.

**`@MockitoBean` (Spring Framework 7.0) does not support the `answer` attribute that `@MockBean` (deprecated) supported, so mocks that relied on `@MockBean(answer = Answers.RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` silently fall back to the default `RETURNS_DEFAULT` answer when migrated [community]** — A developer migrates from `@MockBean(answer = Answers.RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` to `@MockitoBean`. The `@MockitoBean` annotation does not have an `answer` attribute. The mock is created with `RETURNS_DEFAULT`, breaking chains like `given(service.getConfig().getTimeout()).willReturn(100)` with a `NullPointerException` when `.getConfig()` returns `null`. The test passes compilation but fails at runtime with an NPE on the chained stub. WHY: `@MockitoBean` was redesigned to keep the annotation API minimal and delegate configuration to `MockitoSettings`-based customization; deep stubs require explicit programmatic configuration. Fix: replace the `@MockitoBean`-annotated field with a `@TestConfiguration` `@Bean` that calls `Mockito.mock(Service.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` and inject it via `@Autowired`.

**`@ParameterizedClass` with `@SpringBootTest` creates a separate Spring application context for each parameterized instance by default — a class parameterized with 10 argument sets starts 10 application contexts, multiplying CI memory usage tenfold [community]** — A developer parameterizes a `@SpringBootTest`-annotated test class to run the same integration tests against multiple API version configurations. Each `@ParameterizedClass` instance creates a new application context because JUnit instantiates a new test class instance per parameter set, and Spring's `@SpringBootTest` creates a new context per instance unless the context cache key matches. With 10 parameter sets, 10 contexts start, each consuming ~500 MB of heap. WHY: Spring's context caching is keyed by the full set of `@SpringBootTest` attributes including any `properties` or `args`; parameterized instances that differ only in non-Spring fields (Java fields, not Spring properties) still produce identical cache keys and DO share the context — but adding `@DynamicPropertySource` or varying `properties` per parameter set breaks caching. Fix: extract varying configuration to a shared `ApplicationContextCustomizer` registered via `@ContextCustomizerFactory`; or use a single `@SpringBootTest` with a `@ParameterizedTest` method instead of `@ParameterizedClass`.

**AssertJ 3.27.0 `extracting(Function...)` with the propagated common basetype breaking change converts multi-function extractions from `ListAssert<Object>` to `ListAssert<CommonSupertype>`, causing compile errors in projects that chain `asInstanceOf(InstanceOfAssertFactories.LIST)` after extracting [community]** — A developer upgrades AssertJ from 3.26.x to 3.27.0 and sees compilation errors on lines like `assertThat(orders).extracting(Order::getId, Order::getStatus).asInstanceOf(LIST)`. In 3.26.x, `extracting(Function...)` returned `AbstractListAssert<?, List<Object>, ...>`, so `asInstanceOf(LIST)` narrowed it. In 3.27.0, the return type is narrowed to the common supertype of `getId()` (String) and `getStatus()` (OrderStatus enum), which is `Comparable & Serializable`; `asInstanceOf(LIST)` type parameters no longer match. WHY: The 3.27.0 breaking change was intended to improve compile-time type safety for single-type extractions but introduced a type parameter mismatch for multi-function extractions with heterogeneous return types. Fix: replace `asInstanceOf(LIST)` with `.satisfiesExactly(...)` or use separate `extracting(Function)` calls for each field.

**`MockedConstruction` scopes do not nest safely in JUnit 5 `@ParameterizedTest` — if a parameterized test method opens a `mockConstruction` block and the construction settings lambda throws an unchecked exception, the `MockedConstruction` scope leaks into subsequent parameterized test iterations, causing every subsequent `new ClassName()` call in the test JVM to be intercepted by the leaked scope [community]** — A developer uses `try-with-resources` for `MockedConstruction` inside a `@ParameterizedTest` method, but the construction settings lambda throws a `ClassCastException` for one of the parameter values while casting `ctx.arguments().get(0)`. The `try-with-resources` block does not execute `close()` if the exception occurs during mock instantiation (inside the `MockedConstruction` constructor), before the `try` body is entered. The `MockedConstruction` scope leaks into subsequent parameterized test iterations. WHY: `mockConstruction(Class, MockitoSettings)` throws during the settings lambda before the `AutoCloseable` scope is established, so `close()` is never registered. Fix: use a defensive construction settings lambda that validates argument types before casting; wrap the `mockConstruction` call itself in a try-catch to ensure cleanup if settings throw.
