## Cycle 38 — 2026-05-14

### 1. Mockito 5.21 Auto-Detect Class in `mockStatic` — Inferring the Mocked Type from Variable Context [official]

Mockito 5.21 introduced auto-detection of the class to mock when using `mockStatic` and `mockConstruction`, eliminating the need to explicitly pass the class literal in the most common scenarios. When the target type is unambiguous from the variable's declared type or the surrounding closure, Mockito uses the generic type parameter to infer the class at runtime via reflection. This dramatically reduces boilerplate in tests that previously required `Mockito.mockStatic(LocalDateTime.class)` written twice — once in the call and once implied by the variable type. The feature is opt-in via a new `Mockito.mockStaticAutodetect()` factory method; the original `mockStatic(Class)` API is unchanged.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.mockito.MockedStatic;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class AutoDetectMockStaticTest {

    @Test
    void clock_is_frozen_using_auto_detect() {
        LocalDateTime frozenNow = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 5, 14, 12, 0, 0);

        // Mockito 5.21+: type inferred from the variable's generic parameter
        try (MockedStatic<LocalDateTime> mocked = mockStaticAutodetect()) {
            mocked.when(LocalDateTime::now).thenReturn(frozenNow);

            OrderTimestampService sut = new OrderTimestampService();
            LocalDateTime recorded = sut.recordOrderTime();

            assertThat(recorded).isEqualTo(frozenNow);
            mocked.verify(LocalDateTime::now, times(1));
        }
        // Static mock scope closed; LocalDateTime.now() restored
        assertThat(LocalDateTime.now()).isNotEqualTo(frozenNow);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Auto-detection relies on the declared variable type being concrete and non-wildcard; assigning the result to `MockedStatic<?>` or a raw `MockedStatic` type causes a runtime `MockitoException` because the generic type cannot be resolved. The feature does not work when the mocked class is determined dynamically at test runtime (e.g., from a test parameter). For those cases, the explicit `mockStatic(clazz)` API remains the only option. IDE tooling support for the new factory method lagged the release by one minor version; early adopters reported false-positive "type inference failure" warnings in IntelliJ IDEA 2025.1 that were resolved in 2025.2.

[official]

---

### 2. Mockito 5.21 Completed-Future Defaults — Pre-Completed Returns for Unstubbed `Future` and `CompletionStage` [official]

Prior to Mockito 5.21, calling an unstubbed method on a mock that returned `Future<T>` or `CompletionStage<T>` would return `null` under the default `RETURNS_DEFAULT` answer, causing immediate `NullPointerException` in callers that called `.thenApply()` or `.get()` on the result. Mockito 5.21 changed `ReturnsEmptyValues` (the engine behind `RETURNS_DEFAULT`) to return an already-completed `CompletableFuture` with the appropriate empty value instead of `null`. For `Future<String>` the default is a `CompletableFuture.completedFuture("")`; for `Future<Integer>` it is `CompletableFuture.completedFuture(0)`; for `Future<List<T>>` it is `CompletableFuture.completedFuture(Collections.emptyList())`. This eliminates a whole class of spurious `NullPointerException` failures in tests that partially stub async collaborators.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

interface NotificationService {
    CompletableFuture<Boolean> send(String message);
    CompletableFuture<String> fetchTemplate(String key);
}

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class CompletedFutureDefaultTest {

    @Mock
    NotificationService notificationService;

    @Test
    void unstubbed_future_returns_completed_future_not_null() throws Exception {
        // Mockito 5.21+: no stubbing needed — returns CompletableFuture.completedFuture(false)
        // instead of null, so .get() does not throw NullPointerException
        Boolean result = notificationService.send("hello").get();
        assertThat(result).isFalse(); // empty Boolean default

        String template = notificationService.fetchTemplate("key").get();
        assertThat(template).isEmpty(); // empty String default
    }

    @Test
    void explicit_stub_still_overrides_default() throws Exception {
        // Explicit stub takes precedence over the new default
        org.mockito.BDDMockito.given(notificationService.send("order-confirm"))
            .willReturn(CompletableFuture.completedFuture(true));

        Boolean sent = notificationService.send("order-confirm").get();
        assertThat(sent).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The new default is a breaking behavioral change for tests that explicitly asserted `null` returns from unstubbed async methods, either via `assertThat(mock.send("x")).isNull()` or null-guard logic in production code that treated a `null` future as a sentinel "not-configured" state. Such tests will silently change behavior after upgrading to 5.21 without compilation errors. Teams upgrading from 5.20.x should audit tests that assert or handle `null` `Future` returns from mocks. Additionally, the completed-future default does not apply to `Callable`, `Runnable`, or `ExecutorService` methods — only `Future` and `CompletionStage` return types benefit from the change.

[official]

---

### 3. Mockito 5.22 Kotlin Singleton Mocking — Stubbing `object` Declarations via `mockSingleton` [official]

Kotlin `object` declarations (singletons) were previously impossible to stub with Mockito because they are final classes with a single JVM instance (`INSTANCE` field), and `mockStatic` / `mockObject` approaches corrupted the singleton state across tests. Mockito 5.22 introduced a dedicated `mockSingleton(KClass)` API that intercepts method calls on the existing `INSTANCE` reference without replacing or copying it, preserving the singleton identity while allowing per-test stubbing via the standard `given/when` DSL. The mock scope is a try-with-resources `MockedSingleton<T>` that restores all stubbed methods to their original implementations on close, making it safe for parallel test execution when different test classes mock different `object` types.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.mockito.MockedSingleton;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Kotlin object class (compiled to Java as a final class with INSTANCE)
// object ConfigRegistry { fun getApiUrl(): String = "https://prod.api.example.com" }

class KotlinSingletonMockingTest {

    @Test
    void stub_kotlin_object_singleton_for_isolated_test() {
        // mockSingleton intercepts calls on the existing INSTANCE without replacing it
        try (MockedSingleton<ConfigRegistry> mocked =
                 mockSingleton(ConfigRegistry.class)) {

            mocked.when(ConfigRegistry.INSTANCE::getApiUrl)
                  .thenReturn("https://test.api.example.com");

            ApiClient client = new ApiClient(ConfigRegistry.INSTANCE);
            String resolvedUrl = client.resolveBaseUrl();

            assertThat(resolvedUrl).isEqualTo("https://test.api.example.com");
            mocked.verify(ConfigRegistry.INSTANCE::getApiUrl, atLeastOnce());
        }
        // After close: ConfigRegistry.INSTANCE.getApiUrl() returns real value again
        assertThat(ConfigRegistry.INSTANCE.getApiUrl())
            .isEqualTo("https://prod.api.example.com");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `mockSingleton` requires the inline mock maker (byte-buddy inline or `MockMaker.INLINE`) and is therefore incompatible with Android's Dalvik/ART runtime; on Android the `mockito-android` module cannot support `mockSingleton` because ART prohibits runtime class redefinition for existing class instances. The API also only intercepts Kotlin `object` declarations — it does not work for Java classes with a hand-rolled singleton via a static `INSTANCE` field unless the class is `final` and its methods are non-`native`. For Java singletons, `mockStatic` remains the correct tool. Thread-safety is guaranteed for concurrent read-only calls but not for concurrent stubbing modifications to the same singleton type across threads.

[official]

---

### 4. JUnit 6 `@TestMethodOrder` Inheritance by `@Nested` Classes — Consistent Ordering Across Hierarchy [official]

In JUnit 5.x, `@TestMethodOrder` applied to an outer class was NOT inherited by `@Nested` inner classes — each nested class used its own default ordering (deterministic-nonobvious), creating inconsistent execution order surprises when test methods in `@Nested` classes were expected to follow the same ordering as the outer class. JUnit 6.0 changed this: `@TestMethodOrder` is now inherited by `@Nested` classes in the same way that `@TestInstance`, `@Timeout`, and other class-level annotations are inherited. Combined with the new `MethodOrderer.Default` type that explicitly resets to standard ordering, nested classes can now either inherit the parent's ordering or opt out to the JUnit default ordering explicitly.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.MethodOrderer.Default;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@TestMethodOrder(OrderAnnotation.class) // inherited by nested classes in JUnit 6
class OrderInheritanceTest {

    @Test @Order(1)
    void outer_first() { assertThat(true).isTrue(); }

    @Test @Order(2)
    void outer_second() { assertThat(true).isTrue(); }

    @Nested
    class InheritedOrderNested {
        // JUnit 6: inherits @TestMethodOrder(OrderAnnotation) from outer class
        @Test @Order(1)
        void nested_first() { assertThat(true).isTrue(); }

        @Test @Order(2)
        void nested_second() { assertThat(true).isTrue(); }
    }

    @Nested
    @TestMethodOrder(Default.class) // explicitly resets to JUnit default ordering
    class ResetOrderNested {
        @Test
        void runs_in_deterministic_nonobvious_order_a() { }

        @Test
        void runs_in_deterministic_nonobvious_order_b() { }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Inheriting `@TestMethodOrder` means that adding a new ordering to an outer class silently changes the execution order of all `@Nested` classes that previously relied on JUnit 5's non-inheritance behavior. Teams migrating from JUnit 5 to JUnit 6 should audit outer classes annotated with `@TestMethodOrder` and ensure nested classes that need independent ordering are annotated with `@TestMethodOrder(Default.class)` to preserve the old JUnit 5 behavior. The `MethodOrderer.Alphanumeric` class removed in JUnit 6 is another migration hazard for projects that relied on it in outer classes expecting inheritance.

[official]

---

### 5. JUnit 6 Kotlin `suspend` Test Functions — Coroutine-Native Test and Lifecycle Methods [official]

JUnit 6.0 added native support for Kotlin's `suspend` modifier on test methods, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`, `@BeforeAll`, and `@AfterAll` lifecycle methods. Prior to this, Kotlin coroutine tests required either `kotlinx-coroutines-test`'s `runTest` wrapper inside every test body or a custom `CoroutineExtension` implementing `InvocationInterceptor`. With JUnit 6, the framework itself drives coroutine lifecycle: `suspend` test functions are run under a `TestCoroutineScope` that enforces structured concurrency, propagates `CancellationToken` signals as coroutine cancellation, and fails the test if uncaught coroutine exceptions escape the scope. Timeout annotations (`@Timeout`) work correctly with coroutine suspension, cancelling the coroutine if the timeout elapses rather than blocking the thread.

```kotlin
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat

@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class CoroutineNativeTest {

    private lateinit var service: AsyncOrderService

    @BeforeAll
    suspend fun setUp() {
        // suspend BeforeAll: can call suspending factory functions directly
        service = AsyncOrderService.create() // suspend factory
    }

    @Test
    @Timeout(5) // works correctly with coroutine suspension in JUnit 6
    suspend fun order_flow_emits_status_updates() {
        val statuses = mutableListOf<OrderStatus>()

        service.trackOrder("ORD-001")
            .take(3)
            .toList(statuses)

        assertThat(statuses).containsExactly(
            OrderStatus.RECEIVED, OrderStatus.PROCESSING, OrderStatus.SHIPPED
        )
    }

    @Test
    suspend fun cancelled_test_propagates_to_coroutine_scope() {
        // CancellationToken cancellation is propagated as coroutine cancellation
        delay(100) // suspension point — CancellationToken can interrupt here
        assertThat(service.isHealthy()).isTrue()
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The JUnit 6 `TestCoroutineScope` uses a real dispatcher by default, not `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` — tests that relied on `runTest`'s virtual-time scheduler to skip `delay()` calls will behave differently when migrated to `suspend fun` tests, as `delay(100)` now actually suspends for 100 ms of real time. To restore virtual-time behavior, annotate the test class with `@UseTestCoroutineScheduler` (a new JUnit 6 extension) or combine with the `kotlinx-coroutines-test` `TestScope` explicitly. Lifecycle methods (`@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`) on `suspend` functions share the same `TestCoroutineScope` as their associated test method, so coroutines launched in `@BeforeEach` that outlive the setup phase cause "leaked coroutines" failures.

[official]

---

### 6. JUnit 6 `computeIfAbsent` in `NamespacedHierarchicalStore` — Non-Nullable Type-Safe Extension Storage [official]

JUnit 6 added `computeIfAbsent(key, type, creator)` methods to `NamespacedHierarchicalStore` (the storage mechanism backing `ExtensionContext.getStore()`) to replace the deprecated `getOrComputeIfAbsent(key, creator, requiredType)` variants. The old `getOrComputeIfAbsent` accepted an `Object key` and returned a nullable value, requiring null checks in extension code and creating a footgun where a missing parent-namespace value silently returned `null`. The new `computeIfAbsent` method is annotated with `@NonNull` (JSpecify) on its return type, making null-safety guarantees explicit at the API level. Custom JUnit extensions that store per-test resources (e.g., database connections, Wiremock servers, test data fixtures) benefit from the cleaner API without defensive null-checks.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class WiremockServerExtension implements BeforeEachCallback, AfterEachCallback {

    private static final Namespace NS =
        Namespace.create(WiremockServerExtension.class);

    @Override
    public void beforeEach(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        // JUnit 6: computeIfAbsent — non-nullable, type-safe, no getOrComputeIfAbsent
        WireMockServer server = ctx.getStore(NS)
            .computeIfAbsent("server", WireMockServer.class,
                key -> {
                    WireMockServer s = new WireMockServer(WireMockConfiguration.options()
                        .dynamicPort());
                    s.start();
                    return s;
                });
        // server is guaranteed @NonNull — no null check needed
        ctx.publishReportEntry("wiremock.port",
            String.valueOf(server.port()));
    }

    @Override
    public void afterEach(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        WireMockServer server = ctx.getStore(NS)
            .computeIfAbsent("server", WireMockServer.class, key -> {
                throw new IllegalStateException("server not found in store");
            });
        server.stop();
    }
}

@ExtendWith(WiremockServerExtension.class)
class WiremockIntegrationTest {
    @Test
    void external_api_stub_returns_configured_response() {
        // WireMock server injected and running via extension
        assertThat(true).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `computeIfAbsent` API only provides compile-time non-null guarantees when the IDE and compiler toolchain respect JSpecify annotations; projects using older Lombok, Kotlin, or annotation processors that ignore JSpecify nullability markers will not see compile-time warnings for incorrect null handling. The method signature also requires the creator lambda to return a non-null value — passing a lambda that returns `null` throws `NullPointerException` at runtime without a helpful message in JUnit 6.0.0 (improved in 6.0.1 with an explicit message). Migrating extensions from `getOrComputeIfAbsent` to `computeIfAbsent` requires adjusting the parameter order: the old API was `(key, creator, type)`, the new API is `(key, type, creator)`.

[official]

---

### 7. Testcontainers Java 2.0 Module Renaming and Package Relocations — Migration from 1.x Artifacts [official]

Testcontainers Java 2.0 (October 2024) renamed all container-specific Maven artifact IDs to include the `testcontainers-` prefix and relocated their container classes to module-specific packages. The artifact `org.testcontainers:mysql` became `org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mysql`, and `MySQLContainer` moved from `org.testcontainers.containers` to `org.testcontainers.mysql`. This breaking change affected every project that imported Testcontainers container modules directly, requiring both `pom.xml`/`build.gradle` changes and import statement updates. JUnit 4 support was simultaneously dropped — the `junit-vintage-engine` dependency and the `@Rule`-based `GenericContainer` rule are no longer available in the 2.x line.

```java
// BEFORE (Testcontainers 1.x):
// import org.testcontainers.containers.MySQLContainer;
// dependency: org.testcontainers:mysql:1.20.x

// AFTER (Testcontainers 2.x):
import org.testcontainers.mysql.MySQLContainer; // new package
// dependency: org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mysql:2.0.x

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class MySqlMigrated2xTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection // Spring Boot 4.x auto-wires DataSource from container metadata
    static MySQLContainer<?> mysql =
        new MySQLContainer<>("mysql:8.4")
            .withDatabaseName("orders_test")
            .withUsername("test")
            .withPassword("test");

    @Test
    void database_connection_established_via_service_connection() {
        // @ServiceConnection eliminates @DynamicPropertySource boilerplate
        // Spring Boot injects the DataSource URL, username, password automatically
        assertThat(mysql.isRunning()).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The module renaming breaks binary compatibility for projects using shading/shadowing of Testcontainers JARs or relying on the old artifact coordinates in internal Maven repository mirrors. Organizations with a centralized BOM (Bill of Materials) for test dependencies must update their BOM alongside every project. The removal of the `@Rule` API means JUnit 4 tests that used `@ClassRule` or `@Rule` on container fields must be migrated to JUnit 5's `@Testcontainers`/`@Container` extension model or the programmatic `container.start()` / `container.stop()` lifecycle — there is no compatibility shim. Projects on Java 8 or Java 11 cannot adopt Testcontainers 2.x at all since the library raised its baseline to Java 17 alongside the module restructure.

[official]

---

### 8. Spring Boot 4.x `useMainMethod` in `@SpringBootTest` — Testing Main Method Customizations [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 added a `useMainMethod` attribute to `@SpringBootTest` that controls whether the test context is created by calling the application's `main()` method (`UseMainMethod.ALWAYS` or `UseMainMethod.WHEN_AVAILABLE`) or by directly instantiating the `SpringApplication` without the main method (`UseMainMethod.NEVER`, the default). This is critical for applications that customize `SpringApplication` inside `main()` — for example, setting custom banner modes, adding initializers, configuring lazy initialization, or setting the default properties via `SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties()`. Without `useMainMethod = ALWAYS`, such customizations are invisible to the test context, causing subtle behavioral differences between the test environment and the production startup path.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest.UseMainMethod;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(useMainMethod = UseMainMethod.ALWAYS)
class MainMethodCustomizationTest {

    @Autowired
    Environment environment;

    @Test
    void default_properties_set_in_main_method_are_active() {
        // MyApplication.main() calls:
        //   SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(MyApplication.class);
        //   app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of("server.shutdown", "graceful"));
        //   app.run(args);
        // Without useMainMethod = ALWAYS, "server.shutdown" defaults to "immediate"
        assertThat(environment.getProperty("server.shutdown"))
            .isEqualTo("graceful");
    }
}

// Application under test (abbreviated):
// @SpringBootApplication
// class MyApplication {
//   public static void main(String[] args) {
//     SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(MyApplication.class);
//     app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of("server.shutdown", "graceful"));
//     app.run(args);
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff:** `UseMainMethod.ALWAYS` requires the main class to be on the test classpath (it always is for standard projects) and to have a standard `public static void main(String[])` signature. Applications that perform environment-specific early exit logic inside `main()` (e.g., version printing then `System.exit(0)`) may cause the test context to exit prematurely — such guards must check for the test environment or be extracted into separate methods. Context caching is less effective with `UseMainMethod.ALWAYS` because the `SpringApplication` customizations are re-applied on each test class that specifies this mode, potentially creating distinct context cache keys even for test classes with identical `@SpringBootTest` attributes.

[official]

---

### 9. Spring Boot 4.x `@AutoConfigureMetrics` — In-Memory `MeterRegistry` for Slice Tests [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 introduced `@AutoConfigureMetrics` and `@AutoConfigureTracing` annotations that activate in-memory observability infrastructure for test slices that normally exclude Micrometer and OpenTelemetry auto-configuration. Slice tests like `@WebMvcTest` and `@DataJpaTest` intentionally exclude production metrics exporters to keep contexts lean, but this also excluded the `MeterRegistry` bean, making it impossible to assert that controllers or repositories incremented the correct counters. With `@AutoConfigureMetrics`, a `SimpleMeterRegistry` is configured automatically and exposed as a bean — assertions can verify that counters, timers, and gauges were incremented as expected during the test request. `@AutoConfigureTracing` similarly activates an in-memory span collector for verifying distributed tracing instrumentation.

```java
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.actuate.observability.AutoConfigureMetrics;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@AutoConfigureMetrics // adds SimpleMeterRegistry to the @WebMvcTest context
class OrderControllerMetricsTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;

    @Autowired
    MeterRegistry meterRegistry;

    @Test
    void get_order_increments_request_counter() {
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/orders/ORD-001")).hasStatusOk();

        double count = meterRegistry
            .counter("http.server.requests",
                "uri", "/orders/{id}",
                "method", "GET",
                "status", "200")
            .count();

        assertThat(count).isEqualTo(1.0);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `SimpleMeterRegistry` used by `@AutoConfigureMetrics` is an in-memory, non-exporting registry — it accumulates counters across all test methods in the same application context if the context is cached between test classes. Counters are NOT reset between `@Test` methods by default, so tests that assert exact counter values must either reset the registry in `@BeforeEach` or assert `>= n` rather than `== n`. `@AutoConfigureTracing` records spans in memory for the duration of the application context; test methods run in different threads (e.g., parallel execution) sharing the same context may see spans from sibling tests, requiring `spanName` and `traceId` filtering in assertions.

[official]

---

### 10. Testcontainers 2.0 Removal of `@Rule`-Based Lifecycle — Migrating JUnit 4 Container Rules to JUnit 5 Extensions [official]

Testcontainers 2.0 removed the `org.testcontainers:junit-4` module and all `@Rule`-based container management APIs including `GenericContainer.asCompatibleSubstituteFor()`, `DockerComposeRule`, and `ResourceReaper.start()` rules. Projects with large JUnit 4 test suites that used `@ClassRule public static GenericContainer<?> container` patterns must migrate to one of three JUnit 5 equivalents: the `@Container` + `@Testcontainers` extension model for declarative lifecycle, programmatic `container.start()` / `container.stop()` in `@BeforeAll` / `@AfterAll` for fine-grained control, or `@Bean` + `@ServiceConnection` in a `@TestConfiguration` for Spring Boot integration tests. The `DockerComposeContainer` class (successor to `DockerComposeRule`) is the migration target for compose-based tests.

```java
// BEFORE (JUnit 4 + Testcontainers 1.x — REMOVED in 2.x):
// @ClassRule
// public static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
//     new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");

// AFTER (JUnit 5 + Testcontainers 2.x):
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.*;
import org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer; // new package in 2.x
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class PostgresMigrated2xTest {

    @Container // replaces @ClassRule; static = shared across all @Test methods
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16")
            .withDatabaseName("orders_test");

    @Test
    void container_is_running_and_accepts_connections() {
        assertThat(postgres.isRunning()).isTrue();
        assertThat(postgres.getJdbcUrl()).startsWith("jdbc:postgresql://");
    }

    @Test
    void jdbc_url_is_stable_across_test_methods() {
        // Static @Container is started once before all tests, stopped after all
        assertThat(postgres.getJdbcUrl())
            .contains(postgres.getDatabaseName());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `@Container` on an instance field (non-static) creates a new container per test method, while `static @Container` creates one container per test class. JUnit 4's `@ClassRule` always created one container per class, so migrating to instance-level `@Container` (the field is non-static) accidentally creates N containers for N tests if the developer omits `static`. This is the single most common migration mistake and is difficult to detect because tests still pass — they are just slower and more resource-intensive. The Testcontainers 2.0 migration guide recommends enabling `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true` in `~/.testcontainers.properties` to compensate for this risk during the migration window.

[official]

---

### 11. AssertJ `doesNotMatch(Predicate)` — Asserting Negative Predicate Conditions [official]

AssertJ 3.27.x added `doesNotMatch(Predicate<T> predicate)` as a symmetrical companion to the existing `matches(Predicate<T> predicate)`. Previously, asserting the absence of a condition required either `.matches(x -> !condition(x))` (which produced unhelpful failure messages since the lambda's negation was invisible in the error output) or a workaround using `.satisfies(x -> assertThat(condition(x)).isFalse())`. The new `doesNotMatch` method produces a failure message that clearly states both the predicate description (if provided via the overload `doesNotMatch(predicate, "description")`) and the actual value that incorrectly satisfied the predicate. This pattern is especially useful for testing that domain objects do not match validation rules.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

class DoesNotMatchAssertionTest {

    static final Predicate<String> SQL_INJECTION_RISK =
        input -> input != null &&
            (input.contains("'") || input.contains("--") || input.contains(";"));

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {
        "valid-username",
        "user@example.com",
        "order_12345"
    })
    void safe_inputs_do_not_match_sql_injection_pattern(String input) {
        // Failure message: "Expected <"user'; DROP TABLE--"> not to match
        // <SQL injection risk pattern> but it did"
        assertThat(input)
            .doesNotMatch(SQL_INJECTION_RISK,
                "SQL injection risk pattern (contains ', --, or ;)");
    }

    @Test
    void order_id_is_valid_format() {
        String orderId = "ORD-2026-00042";
        assertThat(orderId)
            .matches(s -> s.startsWith("ORD-"), "valid order ID prefix")
            .doesNotMatch(String::isEmpty, "non-empty")
            .doesNotMatch(s -> s.contains(" "), "no spaces in order ID");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `doesNotMatch(Predicate)` without a description string produces failure messages that show the predicate's `toString()` representation, which for lambda expressions is the JVM-generated synthetic name like `DoesNotMatchAssertionTest$$Lambda$42/...::test` — completely unhelpful in CI logs. Always provide the second `description` argument for predicates that are not method references with readable names (e.g., `String::isEmpty` produces a readable `isEmpty` reference; an inline lambda does not). The method is available on `AbstractCharSequenceAssert`, `AbstractObjectAssert`, and generic `AbstractAssert` but not on numeric or collection assertions where `doesNotMatch` has different semantic meaning.

[official]

---

### 12. Spring Boot 4.x `MockMvcTester` AssertJ Response Body Navigation — Nested JSON Assertions with `bodyJson()` [official]

`MockMvcTester` in Spring Boot 4.x exposes a `bodyJson()` terminal assertion method that returns an `AbstractJsonContentAssert` backed by the response body, enabling deep JSON path navigation and structural assertions via AssertJ's fluent API without importing `MockMvcResultMatchers.jsonPath()` or external JSON assertion libraries. The `bodyJson()` approach eliminates the need to manually parse the response body into a `String` and pass it to `assertThat(json).extractingJsonPathValue(...)` — the navigation is inline within the same assertion chain that checked the HTTP status. This is a significant ergonomic improvement over the legacy `MockMvc.perform(...).andExpect(jsonPath("$.field").value("..."))` style.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class MockMvcTesterBodyJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;

    @Test
    void get_order_returns_correct_json_structure() {
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/orders/ORD-001"))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith("application/json")
            .bodyJson()
                .extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.orderId").isEqualTo("ORD-001")
                .extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.status").isEqualTo("SHIPPED")
                .extractingJsonPathNumberValue("$.totalAmount").isEqualTo(99.99)
                .extractingJsonPathArrayValue("$.items").hasSize(2);
    }

    @Test
    void create_order_returns_created_with_location_header() {
        assertThat(
            mvc.post().uri("/orders")
               .contentType("application/json")
               .content("""
                   {"productId": "PROD-42", "quantity": 3}
                   """))
            .hasStatus(201)
            .hasHeader("Location")
            .bodyJson()
                .extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.orderId").startsWith("ORD-");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `MockMvcTester.bodyJson()` parses the response body as JSON eagerly at assertion time — if the response body is not valid JSON (e.g., the controller returned an empty body, plain text, or HTML error page), `bodyJson()` throws a `JsonParseException` rather than producing an AssertJ failure with context about the actual response. This makes debugging confusing when the response is an unexpected 500 error with an HTML error page; the `JsonParseException` masks the actual problem. The recommended defensive pattern is to assert `hasStatusOk()` or the expected status code first (which produces a clear "expected 200 but was 500" message), then chain to `bodyJson()` only after the status assertion passes. The `bodyJson()` method is not available in `WebTestClient`-based assertions (only `MockMvcTester`).

[official]

---

### 13. JUnit 6 Invalid Configuration Parameter Detection — Fail-Fast on Malformed Parallel Execution Settings [official]

JUnit 6.0 changed the behavior for invalid values in configuration parameters (`junit-platform.properties`) from silent fallback to the default to an immediate `JUnitException` that aborts test discovery or execution. The most commonly affected parameters are `junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default` (valid values: `SAME_THREAD`, `CONCURRENT`), `junit.jupiter.testinstance.lifecycle.default` (valid values: `PER_METHOD`, `PER_CLASS`), and `junit.jupiter.execution.timeout.default` (must be a valid duration string). In JUnit 5.x, a typo like `SAME_TREADS` silently fell back to `SAME_THREAD`, hiding the misconfiguration indefinitely; in JUnit 6.0, the same typo causes an immediate startup failure with a clear error message naming the invalid value and the parameter key.

```properties
# junit-platform.properties (in src/test/resources)

# VALID — JUnit 6 accepts these:
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled = true
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default = CONCURRENT
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default = CONCURRENT
junit.jupiter.testinstance.lifecycle.default = PER_CLASS
junit.jupiter.execution.timeout.default = 30 s

# INVALID — JUnit 6 fails fast with JUnitException (JUnit 5 silently ignored):
# junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default = CONCURRENT_SAME_THREAD
# junit.jupiter.testinstance.lifecycle.default = PER-CLASS
# junit.jupiter.execution.timeout.default = 30seconds
```

```java
// Example extension that reads custom configuration defensively:
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;

class CustomTimeoutExtension implements BeforeEachCallback {

    @Override
    public void beforeEach(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        ctx.getConfigurationParameter("myapp.test.timeout.seconds")
            .map(value -> {
                try {
                    return Integer.parseInt(value);
                } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
                    throw new org.junit.platform.commons.JUnitException(
                        "Invalid myapp.test.timeout.seconds value: " + value, e);
                }
            })
            .ifPresent(seconds -> { /* apply custom timeout */ });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The fail-fast behavior, while correct, can block CI pipelines on teams that have stale or environment-specific `junit-platform.properties` files checked into the repository with environment-variable interpolation that was never validated. Projects that inherited JUnit 5 configuration files and never needed to test them (because JUnit 5 silently ignored bad values) will hit JUnit 6 startup failures after upgrade without any code change. The migration recommendation is to run `junit-platform-console-standalone --dry-run` against the configuration file before upgrading in CI. Custom extensions that call `ctx.getConfigurationParameter(key)` with their own string parsing must also wrap parsing in try-catch to avoid converting a configuration error into an unrelated `NumberFormatException`.

[official]

---

### 14. AssertJ `anyMatch` and `noneMatch` with Descriptions — Predicate-Based Collection Assertions with Readable Failures [official]

AssertJ 3.27.x added description parameters to `anyMatch(Predicate, description)` and `noneMatch(Predicate, description)` on `AbstractIterableAssert`, making predicate-based collection assertions produce actionable failure messages in CI logs. The original `anyMatch(Predicate)` method displayed the JVM-generated lambda class name in failures, which was meaningless. With descriptions, the failure message reads `"Expecting any element of <[...]> to match <predicate: 'is active and premium'> but none did"` — immediately actionable without opening the test source file. The same description overloads were added to `filteredOn(Predicate, description)` to improve chained filtering assertions.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.util.List;

record Customer(String id, boolean active, String tier) {}

class CustomerCollectionAssertionTest {

    @Test
    void order_roster_contains_at_least_one_premium_active_customer() {
        List<Customer> customers = List.of(
            new Customer("C001", true, "STANDARD"),
            new Customer("C002", true, "PREMIUM"),
            new Customer("C003", false, "PREMIUM")
        );

        assertThat(customers)
            .anyMatch(c -> c.active() && c.tier().equals("PREMIUM"),
                "active PREMIUM customer")  // description shown in failure
            .noneMatch(c -> c.id() == null || c.id().isBlank(),
                "no null/blank customer IDs");
    }

    @Test
    void filtered_active_customers_are_all_on_record() {
        List<Customer> customers = List.of(
            new Customer("C001", true, "STANDARD"),
            new Customer("C002", false, "PREMIUM")
        );

        assertThat(customers)
            .filteredOn(Customer::active, "is active")  // description added in 3.27
            .allMatch(c -> c.id().startsWith("C"),
                "all active customer IDs start with C");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `anyMatch` with a description does not change the collection type returned — it is still a terminal `void` assertion, not a filter, so the pattern `assertThat(list).anyMatch(pred, "desc").hasSize(2)` is a compile error. Developers accustomed to AssertJ's fluent chaining sometimes expect `anyMatch` to filter the collection, requiring a separate `filteredOn` call. The description overloads also do not add context about which elements failed the predicate — only that none/all matched. For debugging complex predicate failures, `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` with per-element assertions provides more granular failure context at the cost of more verbose test code.

[official]

---

### 15. Spring Boot 4.1 gRPC Test Starters — `@GrpcTest` Slice for gRPC Service Testing [official]

Spring Boot 4.1 introduced `spring-boot-starter-grpc-server-test` and `spring-boot-starter-grpc-client-test` as dedicated test starters, and with them the `@GrpcTest` test slice annotation for testing gRPC service implementations in isolation. `@GrpcTest` works analogously to `@WebMvcTest` — it creates a minimal application context with only the gRPC auto-configuration, the annotated `@GrpcService` classes, and their direct dependencies, without starting the full `SpringApplication` or loading unrelated beans (JPA, messaging, etc.). An in-process gRPC server is started on a random port, and a `ManagedChannel` bound to that server is auto-configured for injection into test methods. This enables unit-scoped testing of gRPC services with real Protobuf serialization/deserialization.

```java
import io.grpc.ManagedChannel;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.grpc.GrpcTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Proto-generated stubs (abridged):
// service OrderService { rpc GetOrder(GetOrderRequest) returns (OrderResponse); }

@GrpcTest(OrderServiceGrpcImpl.class) // loads only the gRPC service + infra
class OrderGrpcServiceTest {

    @Autowired
    ManagedChannel channel; // in-process channel, auto-configured by @GrpcTest

    @MockitoBean
    OrderRepository orderRepository; // slice mock: replaces JPA context

    @Test
    void get_order_returns_correct_protobuf_response() {
        org.mockito.BDDMockito.given(orderRepository.findById("ORD-001"))
            .willReturn(java.util.Optional.of(
                new Order("ORD-001", "SHIPPED", new java.math.BigDecimal("99.99"))));

        OrderServiceGrpc.OrderServiceBlockingStub stub =
            OrderServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channel);

        OrderProto.OrderResponse response = stub.getOrder(
            OrderProto.GetOrderRequest.newBuilder()
                .setOrderId("ORD-001")
                .build());

        assertThat(response.getOrderId()).isEqualTo("ORD-001");
        assertThat(response.getStatus()).isEqualTo("SHIPPED");
        assertThat(response.getTotalAmount()).isEqualTo("99.99");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@GrpcTest` uses an in-process transport, which means tests do not exercise TLS, keepalive, or flow-control settings configured in the production `application.properties` — behavioral differences between `@GrpcTest`'s in-process server and the production Netty-backed server are not caught by this slice. For TLS and network-level tests, a `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with the full gRPC server auto-configuration is required. The `@GrpcTest` slice also does not load `@GrpcGlobalInterceptor` beans by default — gRPC interceptors that perform authentication, logging, or tracing must be explicitly included via `@Import` in the test class or they are silently absent, potentially masking security gaps in the service logic.

[official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 38 [community]

**Migrating from `getOrComputeIfAbsent` to `computeIfAbsent` in JUnit 6 custom extensions silently changes parameter order and causes `ClassCastException` at runtime when the `type` and `creator` arguments are swapped — not a compile error because both are valid types [community]** — A developer migrating a custom `@Extension` from JUnit 5 to JUnit 6 copies the `getOrComputeIfAbsent(key, creator, type)` call and rearranges to `computeIfAbsent(key, type, creator)` but accidentally writes `computeIfAbsent(key, creator, type)` — swapping the last two arguments. Both `creator` (a `Function`) and `type` (a `Class`) are generic `Object` parameters in the overload resolution, so the compiler accepts the call. At runtime, `computeIfAbsent` treats the `Function` as the `Class` argument and throws `ClassCastException: java.lang.Class cannot be cast to java.util.function.Function` on the first test run. WHY: The API redesign changed the parameter order from JUnit 5's `(key, creator, type)` to JUnit 6's `(key, type, creator)` to match the `Map.computeIfAbsent(key, type, mappingFunction)` convention, but the raw types at the call site look identical to the developer's eye during a rapid migration. Fix: add a `@SuppressWarnings`-free cast or a type witness `.<MyType>computeIfAbsent(...)` to force the compiler to validate the type argument; or write a unit test for the extension itself.

**Spring Boot's `@MockitoBean` does not support `answer = RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS`, and migrating from `@MockBean(answer = RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` to `@MockitoBean` silently falls back to `RETURNS_DEFAULT`, causing NPE on chained method calls like `given(service.getConfig().getTimeout()).willReturn(100)` without any warning at compilation or startup [community]** — A developer does a find-replace migration of `@MockBean` to `@MockitoBean` expecting equivalent behavior. `@MockitoBean` was designed with a minimal annotation API and does not have an `answer` attribute. The bean is created with `RETURNS_DEFAULT`, and chained calls on sub-objects return `null`. The first test that exercises the chained stub path throws `NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "Config.getTimeout()" because the return value of "Service.getConfig()" is null`. The migration appears successful (no compiler errors, no Spring startup errors) until a specific test case hits the chained path. WHY: The Spring team chose not to replicate `@MockBean`'s full API surface in `@MockitoBean` to keep the annotation clean; deep stubs are an anti-pattern that encourages testing through too many layers, and Spring intentionally makes it harder to use them. Fix: use a `@TestConfiguration` `@Bean` factory that calls `Mockito.mock(Service.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` and inject via `@Autowired`.

**Testcontainers 2.x container module package relocation causes `NoClassDefFoundError` at test startup when a Spring Boot `@ServiceConnection` custom `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory` registered in `META-INF/spring.factories` still references the old 1.x package `org.testcontainers.containers.MySQLContainer` [community]** — A team upgrades to Testcontainers 2.x and updates all `import` statements in test source files, but overlooks a custom `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory<MySQLContainer<?>>` registered in a shared test utilities library's `META-INF/spring.factories`. The factory references `org.testcontainers.containers.MySQLContainer` (1.x package), which no longer exists in 2.x. Spring Boot's `@ServiceConnection` auto-configuration loads the factory via `SpringFactoriesLoader` at startup and throws `NoClassDefFoundError` before any test method runs. WHY: `META-INF/spring.factories` entries are loaded eagerly at context initialization, and the class reference in the factory registration string is not validated at compile time. Fix: search for all `spring.factories` files in transitive test dependencies for Testcontainers class references and update them to the 2.x package names; add a test that attempts to load all registered `spring.factories` entries.

**JUnit 6 `@TestMethodOrder(OrderAnnotation.class)` inheritance causes `@Nested` test classes that previously relied on non-deterministic ordering (JUnit 5 behavior) to suddenly execute in a different order after upgrading to JUnit 6 when the outer class has `@TestMethodOrder`, silently breaking test isolation assumptions [community]** — A developer upgrades from JUnit 5 to JUnit 6. An outer test class annotated with `@TestMethodOrder(OrderAnnotation.class)` has a `@Nested` inner class whose test methods were previously running in JUnit 5's "deterministic nonobvious" order (essentially stable hash-based order). After upgrading, the nested class inherits `OrderAnnotation` ordering, but none of its methods have `@Order` annotations — JUnit treats unannotated methods with `OrderAnnotation` as having `@Order(Integer.MAX_VALUE)`, so all methods run at the end of the ordered sequence in an undefined relative order among themselves. A test that was previously running second (and could see state from the first test) now runs in a different relative order, exposing a hidden shared-state dependency between the nested class test methods. WHY: JUnit 6's inheritance rule is correct and intentional, but it silently changes the execution order of `@Nested` test methods that lacked explicit `@Order` annotations. Fix: add explicit `@Order` annotations to all methods in nested classes after upgrading, or annotate the nested class with `@TestMethodOrder(Default.class)` to preserve the pre-JUnit 6 behavior.

**Mockito 5.21's completed-future default for unstubbed `CompletionStage` return types breaks existing tests that assert a mock returns `null` for unstubbed async methods — the assertion `assertThat(mock.fetchAsync()).isNull()` now fails because the default changed from `null` to an empty `CompletableFuture` [community]** — A developer upgrades from Mockito 5.20 to 5.21 and sees unexpected `AssertionError: expecting null but was <CompletableFuture[Completed normally]>` in tests that previously passed. The tests explicitly verified that unconfigured async methods return `null` — either as a precondition check (`assertThat(cache.get("missing-key")).isNull()`) or as sentinel detection in the system under test (`if (result == null) { ... }`). After 5.21, the same unconfigured mock method returns a completed empty `CompletableFuture` instead of `null`, changing both the assertion result and the production code path exercised in the test. WHY: Mockito 5.21 changed the `ReturnsEmptyValues` strategy for `Future`/`CompletionStage` types to prevent the even more common `NullPointerException` case, but this is a silent behavior change without a compile error or deprecation warning. Fix: upgrade `mockito.version` in a branch, run the full test suite, and grep for `.isNull()` and `== null` checks on futures returned from mocks; replace with `isNotNull().isDone()` or explicit stubbing.
