## Cycle 39 — 2026-05-14

### 16. JUnit 6 `@ParameterizedClass` — Class-Level Parameterization Without Test Factory Boilerplate [official]

JUnit 6.0 introduced `@ParameterizedClass`, which allows an entire test class to be instantiated multiple times with different argument sets — one instance per argument combination. This eliminates the need for the `@TestFactory` + `DynamicContainer` boilerplate that JUnit 5 teams used to achieve class-level parameterization. Each `@ParameterizedClass` test class declares one or more `@FieldSource`, `@MethodSource`, or `@ValueSource` argument providers at the class level; JUnit instantiates the class once per argument row and runs all `@Test` methods inside it with that row's values injected into `@Parameter`-annotated fields. Display names are auto-generated from the argument values, making CI reports readable without custom naming logic.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedClass;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.Parameter;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ParameterizedClass
@MethodSource("locales")
class DateFormatterParameterizedTest {

    @Parameter
    Locale locale;

    @Parameter(1)
    String expectedPattern;

    static java.util.stream.Stream<org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments> locales() {
        return java.util.stream.Stream.of(
            org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments.of(Locale.US, "M/d/yy"),
            org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments.of(Locale.GERMANY, "dd.MM.yy"),
            org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments.of(Locale.JAPAN, "yy/MM/dd")
        );
    }

    @Test
    void format_shortDate_matchesLocalePattern() {
        DateFormatter formatter = new DateFormatter(locale);
        String result = formatter.formatShort(java.time.LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 5));
        assertThat(result).matches(expectedPattern.replace("M","\\d+")
                                                   .replace("d","\\d+")
                                                   .replace("y","\\d"));
    }

    @Test
    void parse_formattedDate_roundtrips() {
        DateFormatter formatter = new DateFormatter(locale);
        java.time.LocalDate original = java.time.LocalDate.of(2026, 6, 15);
        String formatted = formatter.formatShort(original);
        assertThat(formatter.parseShort(formatted)).isEqualTo(original);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ParameterizedClass` creates N class instances in memory simultaneously when parallel execution is enabled, which multiplies the per-class setup cost (static containers, extension state, `@BeforeAll` connections) by N. Teams running heavy integration tests with `@ParameterizedClass` over a large argument matrix should measure JVM heap and container startup overhead before enabling parallel execution at the class level. Unlike `@TestFactory`-based DynamicContainers, `@ParameterizedClass` tests are visible to the IDE's test navigator as separate class entries, improving discoverability but making the test tree larger.

[official]

---

### 17. JUnit 6 `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` — Deterministic Locale/TZ in Tests Without JVM Flag Hacks [official]

JUnit 6.1 introduced `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` as test-scoped annotations that temporarily change `Locale.getDefault()` and `TimeZone.getDefault()` for the duration of a test class or method, then restore the original values in `afterEach`/`afterAll`. This replaces the fragile pattern of `Locale.setDefault(...)` in `@BeforeEach` with a manual restore in `@AfterEach`, which left the JVM in the wrong locale if the test threw before cleanup. The annotations accept a BCP 47 language tag string (`"de-DE"`, `"ja-JP"`, `"ar-SA"`) for locale and an IANA time zone ID (`"Europe/Berlin"`, `"America/New_York"`) for time zone, and compose safely with `@Nested` test classes by stacking overrides per scope.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Nested;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.DefaultLocale;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.DefaultTimeZone;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.time.*;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.Locale;

@DefaultLocale("en-US")
@DefaultTimeZone("America/New_York")
class InvoicePdfFormatterTest {

    @Test
    void format_amount_usesEnglishDecimalSeparator() {
        String formatted = InvoicePdfFormatter.formatCurrency(1_234.56);
        assertThat(formatted).isEqualTo("$1,234.56");
    }

    @Nested
    @DefaultLocale("de-DE")
    @DefaultTimeZone("Europe/Berlin")
    class WhenGermanLocale {

        @Test
        void format_amount_usesGermanDecimalSeparator() {
            String formatted = InvoicePdfFormatter.formatCurrency(1_234.56);
            assertThat(formatted).isEqualTo("1.234,56 €");
        }

        @Test
        void format_date_usesDdMmYyyyPattern() {
            String formatted = InvoicePdfFormatter.formatDate(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 5));
            assertThat(formatted).isEqualTo("05.01.2026");
        }
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {"ja-JP", "zh-CN", "ar-SA"})
    void format_amount_withExplicitLocale_doesNotExplode(String localeTag) {
        Locale locale = Locale.forLanguageTag(localeTag);
        assertThat(InvoicePdfFormatter.formatCurrency(locale, 99.99)).isNotBlank();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@DefaultLocale` and `@DefaultTimeZone` call `Locale.setDefault()` and `TimeZone.setDefault()` under the hood, which are global JVM mutations. When tests run in parallel within the same JVM, a thread from one test class can observe the locale set by a concurrently-running test class even though `@DefaultLocale` is supposed to scope it to one class lifecycle. The annotations are safe only under `PER_CLASS` test instance lifecycle with parallel execution set to `SAME_THREAD` for affected classes. Teams running full parallel concurrency must instead pass `Locale` and `ZoneId` explicitly to the system under test rather than relying on JVM defaults.

[official]

---

### 18. Mockito 5.23 `@Nullable`-Aware Stubbing — Stricter Null Argument Matching with Annotation Respect [official]

Mockito 5.23 added awareness of `@Nullable` and `@NonNull` annotations (from `org.jspecify`, `jakarta.annotation`, and `org.springframework.lang`) to the argument matching engine for `when(...)` / `given(...)`. Previously, passing `null` to a stubbed method parameter annotated `@NonNull` was accepted silently by Mockito and produced a matched stub. From 5.23, if strict stubs are enabled (the default with `MockitoExtension`), Mockito logs a warning when a `when(mock.method(null))` argument matches a parameter declared `@NonNull`, and the `UnnecessaryStubbingException` check now treats `when(mock.method(null)).thenReturn(x)` as an unnecessary stub if the SUT never calls the method with `null` under the `@NonNull` contract. This tightens the feedback loop on tests that accidentally stub null paths that the production code will never reach.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InjectMocks;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import org.jspecify.annotations.NonNull;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

public interface UserRepository {
    // @NonNull contract: callers must not pass null
    User findByEmail(@NonNull String email);
    User findById(long id);
}

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class UserServiceTest {

    @Mock UserRepository userRepository;
    @InjectMocks UserService userService;

    @Test
    void findUser_byEmail_delegatesToRepository() {
        User expected = new User(1L, "alice@example.com");
        // Mockito 5.23: non-null argument is fine for @NonNull param
        given(userRepository.findByEmail("alice@example.com")).willReturn(expected);

        User result = userService.findByEmail("alice@example.com");

        assertThat(result).isEqualTo(expected);
    }

    // Use nullable(String.class) matcher explicitly when testing null-handling paths:
    @Test
    void findUser_nullEmail_isHandledByService() {
        given(userRepository.findByEmail(org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.nullable(String.class)))
            .willReturn(null);

        assertThat(userService.findByEmail(null)).isNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The nullability awareness is advisory in Mockito 5.23 — warnings are emitted, not failures, for `@NonNull` violations in stubs, because annotations may not reflect the actual runtime contract in all codebases. Teams relying heavily on `@NonNull` as documentation rather than enforcement may find the warnings noisy without actionable benefit. The feature requires `jspecify` or `jakarta.annotation` on the test classpath; if neither is present, the behavior is identical to 5.22. The `nullable(String.class)` matcher idiom is the correct explicit opt-in for testing null-handling code paths that the `@NonNull` annotation technically prohibits.

[official]

---

### 19. AssertJ 4.0.0-M1 Native `isSealed()` and `isRecord()` Assertions — Type-System Assertions Without Reflection Boilerplate [official]

AssertJ 4.0.0-M1 (targeting Java 17 minimum) introduced first-class assertion methods `isSealed()`, `isNotSealed()`, `isRecord()`, `isNotRecord()`, and `permittedSubclasses()` on `AbstractClassAssert`. Prior to this, teams testing sealed class hierarchies and record types had to write `assertThat(MyClass.class.isSealed()).isTrue()` — producing an unhelpful failure message of `expected true but was false`. The new methods produce messages like `Expecting class <com.example.Shape> to be sealed but it was not`. The `permittedSubclasses()` assertion chains allow asserting the exact set of permitted subtypes, protecting sealed hierarchies from accidental expansion via code review misses.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Domain model under test
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
public record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape {}
public record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

class ShapeDomainModelTest {

    @Test
    void shape_isSealedInterface_withExactPermittedSubtypes() {
        assertThat(Shape.class)
            .isSealed()
            .permittedSubclasses(Circle.class, Rectangle.class, Triangle.class);
    }

    @Test
    void circle_isRecord_withExpectedComponents() {
        assertThat(Circle.class)
            .isRecord()
            .isNotSealed();
    }

    @Test
    void rectangle_recordComponents_matchExpectedNames() {
        // AssertJ 4.0 adds recordComponents() chain
        assertThat(Rectangle.class)
            .isRecord()
            .recordComponents()
            .extracting(java.lang.reflect.RecordComponent::getName)
            .containsExactly("width", "height");
    }

    @Test
    void shapeHierarchy_isNotExpandedAccidentally() {
        // Fails if someone adds a new permitted subtype without updating this test
        assertThat(Shape.class)
            .permittedSubclasses()
            .hasSize(3);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `permittedSubclasses()` assertions make the test suite a living enforcer of the sealed hierarchy contract, which is both a strength and a fragility. Every new permitted subtype requires updating this assertion — teams moving fast may treat this as friction rather than a safety net. The assertions require AssertJ 4.0.0-M1 or later, which requires Java 17 at minimum; projects still on Java 11 must continue using the reflection-based `isSealed()` boolean check. AssertJ 4.0.0-M1 is a milestone release and its APIs may change before GA.

[official]

---

### 20. Spring Boot 3.5 `print-condition-evaluation-report` Test Property — Debugging Auto-Configuration Failures in CI [official]

Spring Boot 3.5 added the `spring.test.print-condition-evaluation-report` property (default `false`), which, when set to `true`, prints the full auto-configuration conditions report — equivalent to the `--debug` startup output — to the test log whenever an `ApplicationContext` fails to load. Previously, diagnosing `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` or unexpected auto-configuration decisions in a CI test run required either reproducing locally with `--debug` or adding `@ImportAutoConfiguration` annotations speculatively. With this property enabled, the full `ConditionEvaluationReport` appears inline in the test failure output, showing exactly which auto-configurations were applied, which were skipped, and which conditions were not met.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.TestPropertySource;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(classes = PaymentServiceApplication.class)
@TestPropertySource(properties = {
    "spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb",
    "stripe.api.key=sk_test_dummy",
    // Enable condition evaluation report for context load failure diagnosis:
    "spring.test.print-condition-evaluation-report=true"
})
class PaymentServiceContextLoadTest {

    @Autowired(required = false)
    StripePaymentGateway stripeGateway;

    @Autowired
    PaymentService paymentService;

    @Test
    void contextLoads_stripeGatewayIsPresent() {
        // If this fails in CI, the auto-config report in the logs explains why
        assertThat(stripeGateway).isNotNull();
    }

    @Test
    void paymentService_isInitializedWithGateway() {
        assertThat(paymentService).isNotNull();
        assertThat(paymentService.getGateway()).isInstanceOf(StripePaymentGateway.class);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Enabling `spring.test.print-condition-evaluation-report=true` globally in a shared test properties file makes every context load failure verbose, which helps debugging but significantly increases log volume on CI pipelines with many failing tests (e.g., after a large refactor). The report is only printed on context load failure — it is silent on successful starts, so enabling it globally is low-noise in a green build. The property was introduced specifically for test contexts; setting it in production `application.properties` has no effect. Teams should consider enabling it only in a developer-specific `application-test-debug.properties` activated by a CI environment variable rather than permanently in the shared test properties file.

[official]

---

### 21. Testcontainers 2.x `@ServiceConnection` with SSL Bundle Propagation — Secure Database Connections in Integration Tests [official]

Testcontainers 2.x and Spring Boot 4.1 fixed a long-standing gap where `@ServiceConnection` auto-configured plain TCP connections to containers but did not propagate TLS/SSL certificates generated by the container to the Spring datasource connection properties. The fix (Spring Boot 4.1 RC1) introduced `SslBundleServiceConnectionDetailsFactory`, which reads the container's `getSslBundle()` when available and registers it with Spring's `SslBundleRegistry`. The datasource `@ServiceConnection` auto-configuration then references this bundle via `spring.datasource.ssl.bundle`, enabling mutual TLS tests against containerized databases without manual `KeyStore`/`TrustStore` configuration in test code.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
@SpringBootTest
class SecurePostgresIntegrationTest {

    // PostgreSQLContainer with SSL enabled — generates a self-signed cert
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection  // Spring Boot 4.1 propagates the SSL bundle automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withSslMode(org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer.SslMode.VERIFY_CA);

    @Autowired
    DataSource dataSource;

    @Test
    void dataSource_connectsOverSsl() throws Exception {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            // Verify TLS via pg_stat_ssl system view
            var stmt = conn.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT ssl FROM pg_stat_ssl WHERE pid = pg_backend_pid()");
            var rs = stmt.executeQuery();
            assertThat(rs.next()).isTrue();
            assertThat(rs.getBoolean("ssl"))
                .as("DataSource connection should use SSL")
                .isTrue();
        }
    }

    @Test
    void manualDatasource_withoutSslBundle_failsToConnect() {
        // A manually constructed datasource without the SSL bundle should fail
        var rawDs = org.springframework.boot.jdbc.DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url(postgres.getJdbcUrl().replace("ssl=true", "sslmode=disable"))
            .username(postgres.getUsername())
            .password(postgres.getPassword())
            .build();
        assertThat(org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.catchThrowable(rawDs::getConnection))
            .isInstanceOf(Exception.class);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The SSL bundle auto-propagation works only when the container module implements `getSslBundle()` — custom container images or older Testcontainers modules that do not implement this interface fall back to plain TCP, silently skipping TLS validation. Teams must verify at test startup that the expected SSL mode is active (as shown above with `pg_stat_ssl`) rather than assuming `@ServiceConnection` SSL wiring succeeded. The feature requires Spring Boot 4.1+ and Testcontainers 2.x; backporting to Spring Boot 3.x requires manual `SslBundleRegistry` registration.

[official]

---

### 22. JUnit 6 `@ClassTemplate` for Multi-Invocation Test Classes — Extension-Driven Configuration Matrices [official]

JUnit 6 introduced `@ClassTemplate` as a more general mechanism than `@ParameterizedClass` for running a test class multiple times under different extension-controlled configurations — not just with different parameter values. Where `@ParameterizedClass` is data-driven (argument rows), `@ClassTemplate` is extension-driven: a `ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider` extension controls how many times the class is instantiated and what context each invocation receives. The canonical use cases are cross-environment test matrices (run the same suite against PostgreSQL 15 and PostgreSQL 16), security configuration variants (run with RBAC enabled vs. disabled), and backwards-compatibility matrices. `@ClassTemplate` replaces the JUnit 4 `@RunWith(Parameterized.class)` pattern without its static field and constructor constraints.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.ClassTemplate;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

// Extension that runs the template class against two database flavors
public class DatabaseFlavorExtension
        implements ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider {

    record DbFlavor(String name, String jdbcUrl) {}

    @Override
    public boolean supportsTestClass(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        return ctx.getTestClass()
                  .map(c -> c.isAnnotationPresent(ClassTemplate.class))
                  .orElse(false);
    }

    @Override
    public Stream<ClassTemplateInvocationContext> provideClassTemplateInvocationContexts(
            ExtensionContext ctx) {
        return Stream.of(
            new DbFlavorContext(new DbFlavor("PostgreSQL-15", "jdbc:tc:postgresql:15:///testdb")),
            new DbFlavorContext(new DbFlavor("PostgreSQL-16", "jdbc:tc:postgresql:16:///testdb"))
        );
    }

    record DbFlavorContext(DbFlavor flavor)
            implements ClassTemplateInvocationContext {
        @Override public String getDisplayName(int idx) { return flavor.name(); }
        @Override public List<Extension> getAdditionalExtensions() {
            return List.of(new DbUrlInjector(flavor.jdbcUrl()));
        }
    }
}

@ClassTemplate
@ExtendWith(DatabaseFlavorExtension.class)
class OrderRepositoryCompatibilityTest {

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;  // gets the flavor-specific DataSource

    @Test
    void save_and_find_order_roundtrips() {
        Order saved = repo.save(new Order("ORD-TEST", "PENDING", java.math.BigDecimal.TEN));
        assertThat(repo.findById(saved.id())).hasValueSatisfying(o ->
            assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo("PENDING"));
    }

    @Test
    void find_by_status_returns_matching_orders() {
        repo.save(new Order("ORD-A", "SHIPPED", java.math.BigDecimal.ONE));
        repo.save(new Order("ORD-B", "PENDING", java.math.BigDecimal.ONE));
        assertThat(repo.findByStatus("SHIPPED")).hasSize(1);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ClassTemplate` requires implementing `ClassTemplateInvocationContextProvider`, which is more boilerplate than `@ParameterizedClass` for simple data-driven cases. Each template invocation is a fully independent context, so expensive setup (container startup, schema migration) happens N times — teams should use Testcontainers `reuse = true` or singleton containers to amortize startup cost. Unlike `@ParameterizedClass`, display names show `[1] PostgreSQL-15` and `[2] PostgreSQL-16` rather than parameter values, which is less intuitive in IDE test navigators when the invocation index is the only differentiator visible.

[official]

---

### 23. Mockito 5.22 Kotlin Singleton Object Mocking — `mockSingleton` API for `object` Declarations [official]

Mockito 5.22 introduced `mockSingleton(KClass)` and `unmockSingleton(KClass)` in `mockito-kotlin` as a first-class API for temporarily replacing Kotlin `object` singletons in tests. Previously, Kotlin `object` instances were effectively unmockable through standard `mockStatic` mechanisms because the Kotlin compiler generates an `INSTANCE` field with final semantics that Mockito's byte-buddy instrumentation could not replace. The `mockSingleton` API uses a dedicated Kotlin-aware mock maker that cooperates with the Kotlin object initialization protocol to swap the `INSTANCE` field for the duration of the test and restore it in `afterEach`. This is essential for testing code that delegates to Kotlin singleton services or `companion object` factory methods.

```kotlin
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith
import org.mockito.kotlin.MockitoExtension
import org.mockito.kotlin.mockSingleton
import org.mockito.kotlin.whenever
import org.mockito.kotlin.verify
import org.mockito.kotlin.any
import org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat

object MetricsCollector {
    fun recordLatency(operationName: String, millis: Long) {
        // Real impl sends to Prometheus
    }
}

class OrderProcessorService {
    fun processOrder(orderId: String): Boolean {
        val start = System.currentTimeMillis()
        // ... process ...
        val elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start
        MetricsCollector.recordLatency("processOrder", elapsed)
        return true
    }
}

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension::class)
class OrderProcessorServiceTest {

    @Test
    fun processOrder_recordsLatencyMetric() {
        // mockSingleton replaces MetricsCollector.INSTANCE for this test only
        val mockMetrics = mockSingleton(MetricsCollector::class)

        val service = OrderProcessorService()
        service.processOrder("ORD-99")

        verify(mockMetrics).recordLatency(
            org.mockito.kotlin.eq("processOrder"),
            any()
        )
        // unmockSingleton called automatically by MockitoExtension afterEach
    }

    @Test
    fun processOrder_whenMetricsFails_doesNotAffectResult() {
        val mockMetrics = mockSingleton(MetricsCollector::class)
        whenever(mockMetrics.recordLatency(any(), any()))
            .thenThrow(RuntimeException("metrics unavailable"))

        val service = OrderProcessorService()
        // Should not propagate the metrics exception to the caller
        assertThat(service.processOrder("ORD-100")).isTrue()
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `mockSingleton` works only with Kotlin `object` declarations compiled by the Kotlin compiler — it does not work with Java singleton patterns (enum singleton, double-checked locking) or `@Singleton`-annotated Spring beans. Because `mockSingleton` mutates the global JVM state (`INSTANCE` field), running tests with `mockSingleton` in parallel without `@Isolated` or per-class lifecycle causes data races that produce intermittent `ClassCastException` failures extremely hard to reproduce. Always pair `mockSingleton` tests with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` and disable parallel execution at the class level.

[official]

---

### 24. JUnit 6 `WorkerThreadPool` SPI — Named Virtual-Thread Executors for Parallel Test Execution [official]

JUnit 6 replaced the `ForkJoinPool`-based parallel execution backend with a configurable `WorkerThreadPool` SPI. The default implementation uses a `ForkJoinPool` (same behavior as JUnit 5), but teams can provide a custom `WorkerThreadPool` via `ServiceLoader` to run parallel tests on virtual threads, bounded thread pools, or observability-instrumented executors. The primary driver is virtual-thread adoption: a `VirtualThreadWorkerPool` implementation using `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` allows unlimited test parallelism without the blocking-thread exhaustion of the JUnit 5 fork-join backend, while named virtual threads (via `Thread.Builder`) make JFR/JMC profiler traces readable per-test.

```java
import org.junit.platform.launcher.core.WorkerThreadPool;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

// Register in META-INF/services/org.junit.platform.launcher.core.WorkerThreadPool
public class NamedVirtualThreadWorkerPool implements WorkerThreadPool {

    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public NamedVirtualThreadWorkerPool() {
        // Thread.Builder.OfVirtual gives virtual threads readable names for JFR
        ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofVirtual()
            .name("junit-worker-", 0)
            .factory();
        this.executor = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory);
    }

    @Override
    public void execute(Runnable task) {
        executor.execute(task);
    }

    @Override
    public void close() throws Exception {
        executor.shutdown();
        executor.awaitTermination(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }
}

// junit-platform.properties to enable parallel mode:
// junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled = true
// junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default = CONCURRENT
// junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default = CONCURRENT

// Test that verifies virtual-thread execution is active:
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class WorkerPoolVerificationTest {

    @Test
    void testMethod_runsOnNamedVirtualThread() {
        Thread current = Thread.currentThread();
        assertThat(current.isVirtual())
            .as("Parallel tests should run on virtual threads when NamedVirtualThreadWorkerPool is active")
            .isTrue();
        assertThat(current.getName())
            .as("Thread name should follow the junit-worker- prefix for JFR observability")
            .startsWith("junit-worker-");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `WorkerThreadPool` SPI is loaded via `ServiceLoader`, so multiple test dependencies that each register a `WorkerThreadPool` implementation cause non-deterministic loading order — only one implementation is used. Teams must ensure only one implementation is present on the `META-INF/services` path; shared test utility libraries should not register a `WorkerThreadPool` unconditionally. The virtual-thread pool has no built-in backpressure — with thousands of parallel tests each running heavy setup (containers, schema migration), the host machine CPU/memory can be saturated. Use `junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.config.fixed.parallelism` to cap concurrency even with a virtual-thread pool.

[official]

---

### 25. AssertJ `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` — Order-Agnostic Per-Element Consumer Assertions [official]

`AbstractIterableAssert.satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(Consumer<? super T>... consumers)` verifies that a collection of N elements satisfies N specified consumer assertions — one consumer per element — matching each consumer to exactly one element in any order, with no element left over and no consumer unfulfilled. The failure message shows which consumers were satisfied and which found no matching element, making diagnosis faster than the previously common pattern of `containsExactlyInAnyOrder` on extracted fields. It was promoted to a primary recommendation in AssertJ 3.25+ for asserting heterogeneous collections where order is undefined.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;

record OrderSummary(String id, String status, BigDecimal total) {}

class OrderSummaryAssertionTest {

    @Test
    void processedOrders_containExpectedEntriesInAnyOrder() {
        List<OrderSummary> processed = orderService.processAll(List.of(
            new OrderRequest("REQ-1", BigDecimal.TEN),
            new OrderRequest("REQ-2", BigDecimal.ONE),
            new OrderRequest("REQ-3", new BigDecimal("99.99"))
        ));

        assertThat(processed)
            .satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(
                o -> {
                    assertThat(o.id()).startsWith("ORD-");
                    assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo("PROCESSED");
                    assertThat(o.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("10.00");
                },
                o -> {
                    assertThat(o.id()).startsWith("ORD-");
                    assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo("PROCESSED");
                    assertThat(o.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("1.00");
                },
                o -> {
                    assertThat(o.id()).startsWith("ORD-");
                    assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo("PROCESSED");
                    assertThat(o.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("99.99");
                }
            );
    }

    @Test
    void eventStream_containsAuditAndNotificationEventsInAnyOrder() {
        List<DomainEvent> events = eventCapture.getEvents();

        assertThat(events)
            .hasSize(2)
            .satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(
                e -> assertThat(e).isInstanceOf(OrderAuditedEvent.class),
                e -> assertThat(e).isInstanceOf(CustomerNotifiedEvent.class)
            );
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` has O(N!) worst-case matching complexity for N elements and N consumers — the implementation tries all permutations to find the best assignment. For small collections (under 20 elements) this is imperceptible, but asserting on 100+ elements with complex consumers can cause the assertion itself to take seconds. The failure message lists satisfied consumers and unmatched consumers but does not show which element was closest to satisfying the failing consumer — additional logging is required to diagnose partial matches. For large collections with simple structural assertions, `usingRecursiveFieldByFieldElementComparatorIgnoringFields` combined with `containsExactlyInAnyOrderElementsOf` is more performant.

[official]

---

### 26. Spring Boot `@RestClientTest` with `MockRestServiceServer` — Slice Testing HTTP Client Components [official]

`@RestClientTest` is the Spring Boot test slice for testing components that use `RestTemplate`, the `RestClient` (Spring 6.1+), or `WebClient` HTTP clients. The slice configures `MockRestServiceServer` for `RestTemplate` and a mock-backed auto-configuration for `RestClient`/`WebClient`, preventing real HTTP calls. Unlike `@SpringBootTest` with a WireMock extension, `@RestClientTest` starts a minimal context containing only the HTTP client bean under test, its Jackson/Gson configuration, and the mock server infrastructure — making tests 5–10× faster and eliminating network dependency entirely. The `mockServer.verify()` call at the end of each test asserts that all expected requests were actually made.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.client.RestClientTest;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.test.web.client.MockRestServiceServer;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.match.MockRestRequestMatchers.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.response.MockRestResponseCreators.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

@RestClientTest(WeatherApiClient.class)  // only WeatherApiClient + HTTP infra loaded
class WeatherApiClientTest {

    @Autowired WeatherApiClient client;
    @Autowired MockRestServiceServer mockServer;

    @Test
    void getCurrentWeather_successResponse_returnsParsedDto() {
        mockServer.expect(requestTo("https://api.weather.example/current?city=Berlin"))
            .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
            .andExpect(header("Accept", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE))
            .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                {"city": "Berlin", "tempC": 18.5, "condition": "CLOUDY"}
                """, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        WeatherDto result = client.getCurrentWeather("Berlin");

        assertThat(result.city()).isEqualTo("Berlin");
        assertThat(result.tempC()).isEqualTo(18.5);
        mockServer.verify();  // assert all expected requests were actually made
    }

    @Test
    void getCurrentWeather_serverError_throwsWeatherApiException() {
        mockServer.expect(requestTo("https://api.weather.example/current?city=Unknown"))
            .andRespond(withServerError());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> client.getCurrentWeather("Unknown"))
            .isInstanceOf(WeatherApiException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("500");
    }

    @Test
    void getCurrentWeather_timeout_throwsRetryableException() {
        mockServer.expect(requestTo("https://api.weather.example/current?city=Timeout"))
            .andRespond(withException(new java.net.SocketTimeoutException("Read timed out")));

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> client.getCurrentWeather("Timeout"))
            .isInstanceOf(RetryableWeatherApiException.class);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `MockRestServiceServer` intercepts at the `ClientHttpRequestFactory` level, so it does not exercise connection pooling, keep-alive negotiation, or TLS handshake behavior. Tests pass even when the production HTTP client has incorrect timeout configuration because the mock bypasses the transport entirely. For TLS and connection-pool correctness, a real WireMock or Testcontainers-based server is required. The `@RestClientTest` slice does not load Spring Security auto-configuration — if the HTTP client uses a `SecurityExchangeFilterFunction` for OAuth2 token exchange, the token exchange is absent in the slice and must be stubbed manually via `@Import`.

[official]

---

### 27. Property-Based Testing with `jqwik` — `@Property` and `@ForAll` for Invariant Testing [community]

`jqwik` (a JUnit Platform test engine) provides property-based testing for Java: instead of writing fixed examples, you declare invariants that must hold for all generated inputs within a defined domain. `@Property` replaces `@Test` and `@ForAll` injects randomly-generated values into test parameters. `jqwik` then shrinks failing inputs to the smallest counterexample automatically. The library integrates with JUnit 5/6's extension model, AssertJ assertions, and Testcontainers — making it additive to existing test suites rather than a replacement framework. Property tests are especially high-value for serialization round-trips, codec implementations, data validation, and pure computation.

```java
import net.jqwik.api.*;
import net.jqwik.api.constraints.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SlugGeneratorPropertyTest {

    @Property(tries = 500)
    void slug_isAlwaysLowercaseAndUrlSafe(
            @ForAll @StringLength(min = 1, max = 200)
            @CharRange(from = 'a', to = 'z')
            @CharRange(from = 'A', to = 'Z')
            @CharRange(from = '0', to = '9')
            @Chars({' ', '-', '_', '!', '?', '.'})
            String input) {
        String slug = SlugGenerator.toSlug(input);
        assertThat(slug)
            .as("Slug of '%s' should be URL-safe", input)
            .matches("[a-z0-9-]*");
    }

    @Property
    void slug_roundTrip_isSameSlug(
            @ForAll @AlphaChars @StringLength(min = 1, max = 50) String word) {
        // Idempotency: slug(slug(x)) == slug(x)
        String once = SlugGenerator.toSlug(word);
        String twice = SlugGenerator.toSlug(once);
        assertThat(twice).isEqualTo(once);
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<String> validIso8601Dates() {
        return Arbitraries.integers().between(2020, 2030)
            .flatMap(year -> Arbitraries.integers().between(1, 12)
            .flatMap(month -> Arbitraries.integers().between(1, 28)
            .map(day -> String.format("%04d-%02d-%02d", year, month, day))));
    }

    @Property
    void date_parser_acceptsAllValidIso8601Dates(
            @ForAll("validIso8601Dates") String dateStr) {
        assertThat(DateParser.parse(dateStr))
            .as("Should parse valid ISO-8601 date '%s'", dateStr)
            .isNotNull();
    }

    @Property
    void email_validator_rejectsAllEmptyLocalParts(
            @ForAll @StringLength(min = 1, max = 100) @AlphaChars String domain) {
        String email = "@" + domain + ".com";
        assertThat(EmailValidator.isValid(email)).isFalse();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Property-based tests with high `tries` values significantly increase test suite runtime — 500 tries × average test time can turn a 20ms unit test into a 10-second property test. Teams should set `tries = 100` as a default and increase only for critical-path properties. `jqwik` runs as a separate JUnit Platform engine, which means some older IDE plugins do not show `@Property` results in the standard test tree. Shrinking to minimal counterexamples adds overhead on failures but is one of the most valuable debugging aids — never disable it. Property tests do not replace example-based tests for specification documentation; use both in tandem.

[community]

---

### 28. PIT Mutation Testing Integration — Measuring Real Test Suite Quality with a Mutation Score Threshold [community]

PIT (Pitest) is a mutation testing tool that systematically introduces small code changes (replace `>` with `>=`, remove a return statement, negate a condition) and checks whether the test suite detects (kills) each mutation. A mutation score of 80%+ indicates that 80% of the code's logic branches are covered by at least one test that would fail if that branch were wrong. PIT integrates with Maven and Gradle, produces HTML reports, and supports incremental mode (`withHistory`) that only re-mutates changed classes, making it practical in CI pipelines with large codebases. Setting `mutationThreshold` in the build fails CI when test quality degrades below the configured bar.

```xml
<!-- pom.xml — PIT Maven plugin configuration -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
    <artifactId>pitest-maven</artifactId>
    <version>1.17.0</version>
    <dependencies>
        <!-- JUnit 5/6 support requires the pitest-junit5-plugin -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
            <artifactId>pitest-junit5-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>1.2.1</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    <configuration>
        <targetClasses>
            <param>com.example.domain.*</param>
            <param>com.example.service.*</param>
        </targetClasses>
        <targetTests>
            <param>com.example.*Test</param>
        </targetTests>
        <!-- Fail build if mutation score drops below 80% -->
        <mutationThreshold>80</mutationThreshold>
        <!-- Only re-mutate classes that changed since last run -->
        <withHistory>true</withHistory>
        <!-- Use stronger mutators for critical financial logic -->
        <mutators>STRONGER</mutators>
        <outputFormats>
            <outputFormat>HTML</outputFormat>
            <outputFormat>XML</outputFormat>
        </outputFormats>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```java
// Service with a boundary that example tests commonly miss:
// PIT mutates >= to > — the boundary test below catches this mutation
public class DiscountCalculator {
    public java.math.BigDecimal apply(java.math.BigDecimal price, int quantity) {
        if (quantity >= 10) {   // PIT mutation: quantity > 10
            return price.multiply(new java.math.BigDecimal("0.9"));
        }
        return price;
    }
}

// Boundary test that kills the PIT mutation:
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"9, 100.00, 100.00", "10, 100.00, 90.00", "11, 100.00, 90.00"})
void applyDiscount_atBoundary(int qty, String price, String expected) {
    DiscountCalculator calc = new DiscountCalculator();
    assertThat(calc.apply(new java.math.BigDecimal(price), qty))
        .isEqualByComparingTo(expected);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** PIT runs all tests against every mutation, multiplying test suite runtime by the number of mutations generated (typically 5–50× slower than a normal test run). For large codebases, full PIT runs are practical only on CI nightly builds or pre-release branches, not on every PR. The `withHistory` incremental mode addresses this by persisting mutation results between runs and only re-mutating changed classes. PIT does not understand `final` fields or native methods — mutations in those paths are skipped and excluded from the denominator, potentially inflating the mutation score. Teams should review excluded classes in the PIT HTML report to ensure critical paths are not silently excluded.

[community]

---

### 29. `@DataJpaTest` with `replace=NONE` and Testcontainers — Real-Database JPA Slice Tests [official]

By default, `@DataJpaTest` uses an in-memory H2 database and replaces the configured `DataSource` with an embedded one. This is fast but misses database-specific behavior: JSON column types, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS` computed columns, partial indexes, and stored procedures. Setting `replace=NONE` disables the DataSource replacement, allowing a Testcontainers-managed PostgreSQL or MySQL container to be used instead. Combined with `@ServiceConnection`, the container URL/credentials are auto-wired into the test's `DataSource` with zero manual property configuration. This pattern gives slice-speed JPA tests (no web layer, no service layer) with production-parity database behavior.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.jdbc.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
class OrderRepositoryPostgresTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Test
    void save_jsonMetadata_persistsAndRetrievesCorrectly() {
        // Tests PostgreSQL JSONB column behavior — H2 treats JSONB as VARCHAR silently
        Order order = new Order(
            "ORD-JSON-01",
            "PENDING",
            new BigDecimal("49.99"),
            Map.of("source", "mobile", "promoCode", "SAVE10")
        );
        orderRepository.save(order);

        List<Order> mobileOrders = orderRepository.findByMetadataSource("mobile");
        assertThat(mobileOrders).hasSize(1)
            .first()
            .extracting(Order::getId)
            .isEqualTo("ORD-JSON-01");
    }

    @Test
    void findByStatus_returnsOnlyMatchingOrders() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            orderRepository.save(new Order("ORD-P-" + i, "PENDING", BigDecimal.TEN, Map.of()));
        }
        orderRepository.save(new Order("ORD-S-1", "SHIPPED", BigDecimal.TEN, Map.of()));

        List<Order> pending = orderRepository.findByStatus("PENDING");
        assertThat(pending).hasSize(5)
            .allMatch(o -> o.getStatus().equals("PENDING"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@DataJpaTest(replace=NONE)` with Testcontainers requires a Docker daemon, making local development on Docker-less environments (some corporate laptops) fail. The Testcontainers `reuse = true` option mitigates startup latency across test runs, but reuse requires `~/.testcontainers.properties` configuration that is not version-controlled. Schema migration (Flyway/Liquibase) runs on each test class start because `@DataJpaTest` creates a fresh application context per class — for large migration histories this adds measurable overhead. Share the context across the test run by using a single `@DataJpaTest` class hierarchy rather than per-class context annotations.

[official]

---

### 30. `@JsonTest` Isolation — Locking Down Jackson Serialization Contracts Without a Running Server [official]

`@JsonTest` is a Spring Boot test slice that loads only the Jackson auto-configuration, custom `ObjectMapper` beans, `@JsonComponent` annotated serializers/deserializers, and no other application beans. It injects `JacksonTester<T>` for fluent JSON round-trip and structure assertions. Use `@JsonTest` to lock down the serialized form of DTOs and API response objects — any accidental renaming, field addition, or format change in a `@JsonProperty` annotation causes an immediate test failure without a running server. This is especially valuable for versioned API contracts and protects against Jackson annotation interpretation changes between library upgrades.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.json.JsonTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.json.JacksonTester;
import org.springframework.boot.jackson.JsonComponent;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.time.Instant;

@JsonComponent
class InstantToEpochSerializer
        extends com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.std.StdSerializer<Instant> {
    public InstantToEpochSerializer() { super(Instant.class); }
    @Override
    public void serialize(Instant value,
                          com.fasterxml.jackson.core.JsonGenerator gen,
                          com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.SerializerProvider p)
            throws java.io.IOException {
        gen.writeNumber(value.toEpochMilli());
    }
}

record OrderResponse(
    @com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty("order_id")   String orderId,
    @com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty("status")     String status,
    @com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty("created_at") Instant createdAt,
    @com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty("total_usd")  java.math.BigDecimal total
) {}

@JsonTest
class OrderResponseJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    JacksonTester<OrderResponse> json;

    @Test
    void serialize_orderResponse_matchesContractShape() throws Exception {
        OrderResponse response = new OrderResponse(
            "ORD-001", "SHIPPED",
            Instant.ofEpochMilli(1_700_000_000_000L),
            new java.math.BigDecimal("99.99")
        );

        assertThat(json.write(response))
            .extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.order_id").isEqualTo("ORD-001")
            .and()
            .extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.status").isEqualTo("SHIPPED")
            .extractingJsonPathNumberValue("$.created_at").isEqualTo(1_700_000_000_000L)
            .extractingJsonPathNumberValue("$.total_usd").isEqualTo(99.99)
            .doesNotHaveJsonPath("$.orderId");  // camelCase field must NOT appear
    }

    @Test
    void deserialize_jsonPayload_roundtripsCorrectly() throws Exception {
        String payload = """
            {
              "order_id": "ORD-002",
              "status": "PENDING",
              "created_at": 1700000001000,
              "total_usd": 12.50
            }
            """;

        OrderResponse result = json.parse(payload).getObject();

        assertThat(result.orderId()).isEqualTo("ORD-002");
        assertThat(result.createdAt())
            .isEqualTo(Instant.ofEpochMilli(1_700_000_001_000L));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@JsonTest` loads `@JsonComponent` beans from the entire application classpath scan, which means global serializer/deserializer registrations from transitive test dependencies can unexpectedly influence the test's `ObjectMapper`. Teams with multiple `@JsonComponent` beans for different API versions must use `@JsonTest(excludeAutoConfiguration = ...)` to scope the test to the specific serializer under test. `JacksonTester.write()` uses the `ObjectMapper` configured by Spring Boot auto-configuration — if production code instantiates `ObjectMapper` directly with custom modules not registered as Spring beans, `@JsonTest` will not see those modules and may produce false positives.

[official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 39 [community]

**Using `@MockitoBean` on a field in a `@Nested` test class causes the parent context to be dirtied on every nested class execution, multiplying Spring context restarts by the number of nested classes — the test suite that ran in 2 minutes now takes 20 minutes with no visible reason** — A developer migrates a large `@SpringBootTest` class to a `@Nested` structure for BDD-style organization, and moves `@MockitoBean` fields into each nested class to scope them to the relevant behavior group. After the migration, CI shows 10× slower test execution. The cause: each `@Nested` class with `@MockitoBean` fields creates a distinct Spring context configuration key (because the set of mock beans is part of the context cache key), so 10 nested classes with different `@MockitoBean` combinations create 10 separate Spring contexts — each starting fresh including Flyway migration, Testcontainers, and full bean initialization. WHY: Spring's test context caching is keyed on the full set of configuration metadata including which beans are mocked; `@MockitoBean` in a nested class is configuration metadata that differs per nested class. Fix: hoist all `@MockitoBean` fields to the outermost test class so all nested classes share one context configuration and thus one context cache entry.

**`@ParameterizedTest` with `@CsvSource` and a value that starts with a leading zero loses the zero silently — `"007"` is parsed as integer `7` and passed to a `String` parameter as `"7"`, breaking tests for order numbers, postal codes, and padded identifiers** — A developer writes `@CsvSource({"007", "010", "042"})` expecting three `String` values with leading zeros. JUnit's CSV parser strips leading zeros from unquoted numeric-looking tokens, converting them to `"7"`, `"10"`, and `"42"`. The parameter type is `String`, so no exception is thrown — the test runs silently with wrong data. WHY: JUnit's `CsvParserSettings` uses Apache Commons CSV with default behavior that trims numeric tokens, mirroring Excel's CSV handling; the stripping happens at the CSV parse layer before type conversion, so even `String` parameters receive the stripped value. Fix: wrap leading-zero values in single quotes in `@CsvSource`: `@CsvSource({"'007'", "'010'"})` — single-quoted values are passed verbatim without numeric parsing.

**Testcontainers `@Container` field declared `static` on an abstract base class is destroyed and recreated for each concrete subclass that inherits it — the team expected one shared container for the entire test suite but gets N containers, exhausting Docker's container limit in CI** — A team extracts a common `static PostgreSQLContainer` field annotated with `@Container` into an abstract `AbstractIntegrationTest` base class to share the Testcontainers instance. They observe that each concrete test class starts a new container, and after 50 test classes Docker daemon reports `cannot create container — too many containers`. WHY: `@Container` lifecycle is bound to the class in which the field is declared — when declared `static` in an abstract base, each concrete subclass's test run triggers Testcontainers' JUnit lifecycle callback for that class, which treats the static field as belonging to the concrete class's lifecycle rather than a shared singleton. Fix: use Testcontainers' singleton pattern without `@Container` — declare the container as a `static final` field with `start()` called in a static initializer; JVM class loading guarantees single initialization across the process.

**`@WebMvcTest` does not load `SecurityFilterChain` beans by default, so tests of secured endpoints return 200 for every request rather than 401 — security is silently absent and the controller appears always accessible, masking authorization gaps** — A team adds Spring Security to their application, annotates the main application class with `@EnableWebSecurity`, and expects that `@WebMvcTest` tests will verify secured endpoints return 401 for unauthenticated requests. The tests pass — but they pass because security is not applied at all in the slice, not because authentication is working. WHY: `@WebMvcTest` loads the MVC layer but scans security configuration only if `@EnableWebSecurity` is present on a bean within the slice's component scan scope; the main `@SpringBootApplication` class is outside the slice scan. Fix: add `@Import(SecurityConfig.class)` to the test class explicitly, or use a `@WebMvcTest` `includeFilters` with `FilterType.ASSIGNABLE_TYPE` pointing to the security configuration class.

**`Awaitility.await().untilAsserted()` passes in isolation but fails intermittently on CI because the condition evaluator uses last-poll-wins semantics — if the state flipped back after passing, the last attempt fails and Awaitility reports a timeout despite the condition having been satisfied earlier** — A developer asserts `await().untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(cache.get("k")).isNotNull())`. In a test environment with aggressive cache eviction under load (common on shared CI agents), the cache entry is populated, Awaitility's poll passes, but then eviction fires before the final confirmation poll and the last attempt fails. Awaitility reports `ConditionTimeoutException: assertion failed` rather than success. WHY: `untilAsserted` semantics require the assertion to pass on the last evaluation, not just on any evaluation — the condition must hold until the polling window closes, not merely transition through a passing state. Fix: structure the test so the assertion targets a durable state change (database record, audit log entry, append-only queue) rather than an evictable or transient signal; or assert on a flag set atomically after population using `AtomicBoolean` that is never unset.
