## Cycle 40 — 2026-05-14

### 31. JUnit 6.1 `@CsvSource` `commentCharacter` — Custom Comment Markers in CSV Parameterized Tests [official]

JUnit 6.1.0-RC1 added a `commentCharacter` attribute to both `@CsvSource` and `@CsvFileSource`, letting teams override the default `#` marker with any character. This solves a real friction point when test data legitimately contains hash characters — URL fragments, hex color codes, markdown headings — that were previously misinterpreted as comments, silently dropping rows from the data set. The attribute accepts a `char` primitive; setting it to `\0` disables comment processing entirely, which is the safest option when importing untrusted CSV exports. Teams that embed SQL fragments in CSV test data will appreciate the ability to use `!` as the comment character so that `-- SQL comments` and `#region` annotations survive unmodified.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ColorCodeParserTest {

    // Default '#' would drop the third row as a comment — commentCharacter='!' fixes it
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource(
        commentCharacter = '!',
        value = {
            "#FF0000, RED",
            "#00FF00, GREEN",
            "#0000FF, BLUE",
            "! this line IS the real comment and will be skipped",
            "#FFFFFF, WHITE"
        }
    )
    void parsesHexColorNames(String hex, String expectedName) {
        ColorParser parser = new ColorParser();
        assertThat(parser.toName(hex)).isEqualTo(expectedName);
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource(
        commentCharacter = '\0',  // disable comment processing entirely
        value = {
            "#000000, BLACK",
            "# not-a-comment, HASH_ROW"  // treated as data, not skipped
        }
    )
    void noRowsDroppedWhenCommentDisabled(String hex, String expectedName) {
        ColorParser parser = new ColorParser();
        assertThat(parser.toName(hex)).isNotNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Changing `commentCharacter` is a test-class-level concern; if the same CSV file is referenced by multiple `@CsvFileSource` annotations in different classes with different `commentCharacter` settings, the same file will be parsed differently per test class, producing inconsistent row counts that are extremely difficult to debug. Teams should standardize on a single comment character per CSV file and document it prominently in the file header. Disabling comments entirely (`'\0'`) is the safest baseline when sharing CSV fixtures across teams.

[official]

---

### 32. JUnit 6.1 `@EnabledOnJre` Integer Attribute — Future-Proof JRE Version Conditions [official]

JUnit 6.1 deprecates the `JRE.OTHER` enum constant and introduces `int`/`int[]` attributes (`versions` and `disabledVersions`) on `@EnabledOnJre`, `@DisabledOnJre`, `@EnabledForJreRange`, and `@DisabledForJreRange`. The `JRE` enum was designed for known LTS releases, but JDK 25, 26, and beyond appeared faster than enum constants could be published, causing tests that used `JRE.OTHER` to match all unknown versions indiscriminately. The new integer-based attributes let teams pin tests to a specific yet-unnamed JDK version number without waiting for a JUnit release to add the corresponding enum constant. The `JRE` enum constants remain valid for backward compatibility; both approaches can coexist in the same annotation.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.EnabledOnJre;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DisabledOnJre;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.EnabledForJreRange;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class JreVersionGatedTest {

    // Pin to JDK 25 specifically without waiting for JRE.JAVA_25 enum constant
    @Test
    @EnabledOnJre(versions = 25)
    void primitiveTypePatternsAreAvailableOnJdk25() {
        // JEP 488 second preview — only available on JDK 25
        int result = computeWithPrimitivePattern(42);
        assertThat(result).isEqualTo(84);
    }

    // Disable on JDK 26+ until the API stabilises
    @Test
    @DisabledOnJre(versions = {26, 27, 28})
    void stableValueApiUnderTest() {
        StableValueHolder holder = StableValueHolder.of(() -> "computed");
        assertThat(holder.get()).isEqualTo("computed");
    }

    // Range from JDK 21 (LTS) up to and including 24
    @Test
    @EnabledForJreRange(minVersion = 21, maxVersion = 24)
    void virtualThreadSchedulerOnLtsRange() {
        Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {});
        assertThat(vt.isVirtual()).isTrue();
    }

    private int computeWithPrimitivePattern(int n) {
        return n * 2;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Integer-based version attributes make tests more forward-compatible, but they sacrifice the self-documenting quality of enum constants — a reviewer reading `versions = 25` must know the JDK version schedule to understand the intent. Teams should add a comment alongside each integer version gate explaining why the test is gated and when to revisit it. The old `JRE.OTHER` pattern still compiles without deprecation warnings on JUnit 6.0, so migration urgency is low — wait until `OTHER` usage actually causes false positives before migrating.

[official]

---

### 33. JUnit 6.1 `Arguments.of(Iterable<?>)` — Building Parameterized Arguments from Runtime Collections [official]

JUnit 6.1 adds `Arguments.of(Iterable<?>)` and `Arguments.argumentSetFrom(String, Iterable<?>)` factory methods that convert any `Iterable` — `List`, `Set`, domain-specific collections — directly into a parameterized test argument row. Previously, teams had to call `Arguments.of(collection.toArray())` or construct arrays manually, which lost type safety and required casting. The named variant `argumentSetFrom(String, Iterable<?>)` also assigns a display name to the argument set, making parameterized test reports readable in CI without custom `@ParameterizedTest(name = "...")` format strings. This is particularly valuable when arguments are built dynamically from a database fixture loader or a YAML test data file at test initialization time.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DynamicArgumentsTest {

    // Arguments built from a runtime collection — no toArray() casting needed
    static Stream<Arguments> orderLineItems() {
        List<String> skus = List.of("SKU-001", "SKU-002", "SKU-003");
        return skus.stream()
            .map(sku -> Arguments.of(List.of(sku, sku + "-variant")));
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("orderLineItems")
    void each_sku_and_variant_are_added_to_cart(List<String> lineItems) {
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        lineItems.forEach(cart::addItem);
        assertThat(cart.size()).isEqualTo(lineItems.size());
    }

    // Named argument sets for readable CI reports
    static Stream<Arguments> namedRegions() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.argumentSetFrom("EU Region", List.of("DE", "FR", "PL")),
            Arguments.argumentSetFrom("APAC Region", List.of("JP", "AU", "SG"))
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("namedRegions")
    void tax_rules_are_applied_per_region(List<String> countryCodes) {
        TaxRuleEngine engine = new TaxRuleEngine();
        countryCodes.forEach(code ->
            assertThat(engine.rateFor(code)).isGreaterThan(0.0));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `Arguments.of(Iterable<?>)` uses the iterable's `toString()` representation for the default test display name, which for `ArrayList` produces `[SKU-001, SKU-002]` — readable but not always meaningful for domain objects with poor `toString()` implementations. Teams passing domain objects via iterable should prefer `argumentSetFrom(String, Iterable<?>)` to set explicit names. The iterable content is eagerly materialized into an `Object[]` at test discovery time, so lazily-generated iterables (database cursors, streams) must be fully buffered in memory before the test framework can proceed.

[official]

---

### 34. JUnit 6.1 `@EmptySource` for `Iterable` and `Iterator` — Exhaustive Empty-Input Testing [official]

JUnit 6.1 expanded `@EmptySource` to cover `Iterable<?>`, `Iterator<?>`, and `ListIterator<?>` parameter types, in addition to the existing `String`, array, `Collection`, and `Map` support. This means a single `@EmptySource`-annotated `@ParameterizedTest` method can now receive an empty instance of whatever type its parameter declares — the framework selects the appropriate empty singleton. Before this change, testing with an empty `Iterable` required either a custom `ArgumentsProvider` or using `@NullAndEmptySource` with a `null` guard inside the test body. The expansion is especially useful for methods that accept `Iterable<T>` at the API boundary and must handle empty traversal gracefully without throwing.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.EmptySource;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.NullAndEmptySource;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatNoException;

class EmptySourceIterableTest {

    @ParameterizedTest
    @EmptySource
    void processItems_emptyIterable_returnsEmptyResult(Iterable<String> items) {
        // @EmptySource now provides Collections.emptyList() adapted as Iterable
        BatchProcessor processor = new BatchProcessor();
        List<String> result = processor.process(items);
        assertThat(result).isEmpty();
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @EmptySource
    void drainIterator_emptyIterator_noExceptionThrown(Iterator<Integer> iter) {
        assertThatNoException().isThrownBy(() -> {
            int count = 0;
            while (iter.hasNext()) {
                iter.next();
                count++;
            }
            assertThat(count).isZero();
        });
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @NullAndEmptySource
    void importRows_nullOrEmpty_treatedAsNoOp(Iterable<String> rows) {
        ImportService service = new ImportService();
        assertThatNoException().isThrownBy(() -> service.importAll(rows));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@EmptySource` for `Iterator` provides an untyped empty iterator — the type parameter `T` is erased at runtime. If the production code performs `instanceof` checks on the iterator's elements during traversal, an empty iterator will never exercise those branches, creating a coverage illusion. Teams must complement `@EmptySource` with at least one `@MethodSource` providing a typed single-element iteration to verify the hot path before the iterator is exhausted. Additionally, `ListIterator` from `@EmptySource` supports `hasPrevious()` returning `false` — implementations that do not call `hasPrevious()` will not notice if this behaviour is incorrect.

[official]

---

### 35. JUnit 6.1 `AssertionFailureBuilder.trimStacktrace()` — Clean Custom Assertion Failures [official]

JUnit 6.1 added `trimStacktrace(Class<?>)` and `retainStackTraceElements(int)` to `AssertionFailureBuilder`, enabling authors of custom assertion helpers to scrub their own internal frames from the stack trace of a generated `AssertionFailedError`. Without trimming, a custom assertion's call stack pollutes the test output with 5-10 internal helper frames before reaching the test method line, making failures look like they originate inside the assertion infrastructure rather than in the test body. The `trimStacktrace(Class<?>)` variant removes all frames at or below the named class, while `retainStackTraceElements(int)` keeps only the top N frames. The feature complements AssertJ's own stack-trace trimming and is the standard mechanism for JUnit extension authors to produce readable failure diagnostics.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AssertionFailureBuilder;

// Custom assertion helper that trims its own frames
public final class DomainAssertions {

    private DomainAssertions() {}

    public static void assertOrderIsPaid(Order order) {
        if (order.getStatus() != OrderStatus.PAID) {
            AssertionFailureBuilder.assertionFailure()
                .message("Expected order to be PAID")
                .expected(OrderStatus.PAID)
                .actual(order.getStatus())
                .trimStacktrace(DomainAssertions.class)
                .buildAndThrow();
        }
    }

    public static void assertInvoiceMatchesOrder(Invoice invoice, Order order) {
        if (!invoice.getOrderId().equals(order.getId())) {
            AssertionFailureBuilder.assertionFailure()
                .message("Invoice does not reference the expected order")
                .expected(order.getId())
                .actual(invoice.getOrderId())
                .trimStacktrace(DomainAssertions.class)
                .buildAndThrow();
        }
        if (invoice.getTotalCents() != order.getTotalCents()) {
            AssertionFailureBuilder.assertionFailure()
                .message("Invoice total does not match order total")
                .expected(order.getTotalCents())
                .actual(invoice.getTotalCents())
                .retainStackTraceElements(3)
                .buildAndThrow();
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `trimStacktrace(Class<?>)` removes all frames at or below the named class, which means if the assertion helper is itself called from another helper (helper chains), the trimming point may cut too aggressively and hide the intermediate helper call that was the actual point of failure. Teams building layered assertion helpers should trim at the outermost helper class and keep intermediate helpers in the stack. `retainStackTraceElements(int)` is more predictable for shallow call stacks but becomes a magic number that breaks if the call depth changes.

[official]

---

### 36. JUnit 6.1 System Properties Extension — `@SetSystemProperty` and `@ClearSystemProperty` [official]

JUnit 6.1 graduated the System Properties extension from JUnit Pioneer into the JUnit Jupiter core as `@SetSystemProperty` and `@ClearSystemProperty`. These annotations temporarily set or clear JVM system properties for the duration of a test method or class, automatically restoring the original value in the `afterEach`/`afterAll` lifecycle. Before this graduation, teams added the JUnit Pioneer dependency solely for this feature, increasing transitive dependency weight. The extension uses `ExtensionContext.Store.CloseableResource` to ensure restoration even when tests throw exceptions, making it more reliable than try-finally `System.setProperty` patterns that fail to restore on assertion errors.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.SetSystemProperty;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ClearSystemProperty;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SystemPropertyDependentTest {

    @Test
    @SetSystemProperty(key = "app.environment", value = "test")
    @SetSystemProperty(key = "app.region", value = "eu-west-1")
    void configLoader_readsSystemProperties_returnsExpectedConfig() {
        ConfigLoader loader = new ConfigLoader();
        AppConfig config = loader.load();

        assertThat(config.getEnvironment()).isEqualTo("test");
        assertThat(config.getRegion()).isEqualTo("eu-west-1");
    }

    @Test
    @ClearSystemProperty(key = "http.proxyHost")
    @ClearSystemProperty(key = "http.proxyPort")
    void httpClient_noProxyConfigured_connectsDirectly() {
        HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().build();
        assertThat(client.proxy()).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    @SetSystemProperty(key = "feature.flag.new-checkout", value = "true")
    void checkoutService_featureFlagEnabled_usesNewFlow() {
        CheckoutService svc = new CheckoutService();
        CheckoutResult result = svc.checkout(Order.sample());
        assertThat(result.getFlow()).isEqualTo("NEW_CHECKOUT_V2");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@SetSystemProperty` / `@ClearSystemProperty` are parallel-execution unsafe by default because system properties are process-wide global state — two tests running concurrently on different threads that both call `@SetSystemProperty(key = "app.environment", value = ...)` with different values will interfere. The extension does not acquire any synchronization lock; it is the test author's responsibility to annotate such tests with `@Execution(SAME_THREAD)` or to structure the test class to run sequentially. Teams running with `junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled = true` must audit all `@SetSystemProperty` usages for cross-test interference before enabling parallelism.

[official]

---

### 37. Spring Boot 4.x `RestTestClient` — AssertJ-Fluent Integration Test HTTP Client [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 introduces `RestTestClient` as a first-class test HTTP client that pairs `RestClient`'s request-building API with AssertJ-based response assertions. Unlike `WebTestClient` (which requires a reactive stack) or `MockMvc` (which requires importing `.andExpect()` chains), `RestTestClient` works with both servlet-based and reactive applications and uses the familiar AssertJ `.satisfies()`, `.hasStatus()`, and `.bodyText()` patterns. It can target a mock environment via `@AutoConfigureMockMvc` or a live server at `RANDOM_PORT`, making it a single test client that works across integration test tiers. The module `spring-boot-resttestclient` is separate from the main starter, allowing teams that prefer `MockMvc` to opt out of the dependency.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.client.RestTestClient;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class OrderControllerIntegrationTest {

    @MockitoBean
    private PaymentGateway paymentGateway;

    @Test
    void createOrder_validRequest_returns201WithOrderId(
            @org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired RestTestClient client) {

        OrderRequest request = new OrderRequest("user-42", List.of("SKU-001"));

        client.post()
            .uri("/api/v1/orders")
            .contentType(org.springframework.http.MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .body(request)
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isCreated()
            .expectHeader().valueMatches("Location", ".*/api/v1/orders/.*")
            .expectBody(OrderResponse.class)
            .satisfies(body -> {
                assertThat(body.getOrderId()).isNotBlank();
                assertThat(body.getStatus()).isEqualTo("PENDING");
            });
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_nonExistentId_returns404(
            @org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired RestTestClient client) {

        client.get()
            .uri("/api/v1/orders/{id}", "does-not-exist")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound()
            .expectBody()
            .bodyText().contains("Order not found");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `RestTestClient` buffers the entire response body in memory by default, which is inappropriate for streaming endpoints or large file downloads — use `WebTestClient` with `returnResult()` and `responseBody()` flux for streaming responses. The module adds a non-trivial compile-time dependency (`spring-boot-resttestclient`) that is separate from `spring-boot-starter-test`; teams that inadvertently add it to production classpath (rather than test scope) will ship unused test infrastructure. `RestTestClient` also does not support WebSocket testing; teams with WebSocket endpoints must continue using `WebSocketStompClient` directly.

[official]

---

### 38. Mockito 5.22 `mockSingleton` for Kotlin `object` Declarations — Stubbing Companion Objects and Service Singletons [official]

Mockito 5.22 introduced `mockSingleton` as a dedicated API for mocking Kotlin `object` declarations — the language's built-in singleton pattern. Regular `mockStatic` works for Java `static` methods but fails silently for Kotlin `object` members because Kotlin's compiler emits `object` fields as JVM instance fields on the singleton class rather than true static methods, causing `mockStatic` to produce stubs that are never invoked. `mockSingleton` resolves this by intercepting method calls on the `INSTANCE` field, which is where Kotlin routes all `object` member invocations at bytecode level. The API follows the same try-with-resources idiom as `mockStatic`, restoring the original singleton behavior when the scope closes.

```kotlin
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.mockito.kotlin.mockSingleton
import org.mockito.kotlin.whenever
import org.mockito.kotlin.verify
import org.mockito.kotlin.any
import org.mockito.kotlin.mock
import org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat

// Production code — Kotlin singleton object
object PaymentRouter {
    fun route(order: Order): PaymentGateway =
        if (order.currency == "EUR") EuroGateway else DefaultGateway
}

class CheckoutServiceTest {

    @Test
    fun `checkout uses mocked router to select gateway`() {
        val mockGateway: PaymentGateway = mock()

        mockSingleton(PaymentRouter::class) {
            whenever(PaymentRouter.route(any())).thenReturn(mockGateway)

            val svc = CheckoutService()
            val order = Order(id = "ORD-1", currency = "EUR", totalCents = 999)
            svc.checkout(order)

            verify(mockGateway).charge(999)
        }
    }

    @Test
    fun `companion object factory method is stubbable`() {
        mockSingleton(DatabaseConnection.Companion::class) {
            whenever(DatabaseConnection.create(any()))
                .thenReturn(FakeDatabaseConnection())

            val repo = UserRepository()
            val user = repo.findById("u-1")

            assertThat(user).isNotNull
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `mockSingleton` replaces the underlying singleton `INSTANCE` for the duration of the scope using JVM instrumentation. If the Kotlin `object` has lazy-initialized fields (`val computed by lazy { ... }`) that were already initialized before `mockSingleton` is called, the mock scope starts with those values pre-computed and cannot intercept their initialization. Teams testing objects with lazy initialization must structure tests to call `mockSingleton` before any code that triggers the `object`'s lazy init chain. `mockSingleton` is only available in the `mockito-kotlin` Kotlin DSL; pure Java codebases with Kotlin companion objects must use the lower-level `Mockito.mockSingleton(class, MockitoSession)` API introduced alongside it.

[official]

---

### 39. Spring Boot 4.x `@WebFluxTest` with `@MockitoBean` — Reactive Controller Slice Testing [official]

`@WebFluxTest` loads only the WebFlux layer — controllers, filters, `WebExceptionHandler`, `RouterFunction` beans — and pairs with `@MockitoBean` (the Spring Boot 4.0 replacement for the removed `@MockBean`) to inject test doubles for service dependencies. Unlike `@SpringBootTest`, `@WebFluxTest` does not start a real server; it uses `WebTestClient` backed by a mock web server that replays the reactive pipeline in the test thread. Spring Boot 4.0 deprecated and then removed `@MockBean` entirely in favour of `@MockitoBean` (from `spring-test`), which has the same semantics but lives in the framework module rather than the boot-specific test module. The combination covers response-body serialization, reactive `Mono`/`Flux` chains, and security filter integration without the weight of a full application context.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.reactive.WebFluxTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.test.web.reactive.server.WebTestClient;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import reactor.core.publisher.Flux;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyString;

@WebFluxTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerWebFluxTest {

    @Autowired
    private WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @MockitoBean
    private ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void getProduct_existingId_returnsProductJson() {
        given(productService.findById("prod-1"))
            .willReturn(Mono.just(new Product("prod-1", "Widget", 1299)));

        webTestClient.get()
            .uri("/products/prod-1")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBody()
            .jsonPath("$.id").isEqualTo("prod-1")
            .jsonPath("$.name").isEqualTo("Widget")
            .jsonPath("$.priceCents").isEqualTo(1299);
    }

    @Test
    void listProducts_serviceReturnsFlux_streamsAllItems() {
        given(productService.listAll())
            .willReturn(Flux.just(
                new Product("p-1", "A", 100),
                new Product("p-2", "B", 200)
            ));

        webTestClient.get()
            .uri("/products")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBodyList(Product.class).hasSize(2);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@WebFluxTest` does not load `@Service`, `@Repository`, or `@Component` beans — only `@Controller`, `@ControllerAdvice`, `@JsonComponent`, `Converter`/`GenericConverter`, and `WebFluxConfigurer` beans are included. If the controller under test injects a `@Component`-annotated validator or converter directly rather than via the declared `@Service` boundary, the slice will fail with a `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` that does not occur in production. Teams must either `@Import` the missing component or move the dependency behind a `@Service` abstraction. `@MockitoBean`-declared fields on a `@WebFluxTest` class that differ between test subclasses create distinct Spring context cache keys, multiplying context startups in test suites with heavy `@Nested` usage.

[official]

---

### 40. Testcontainers 2.x Module Artifact Naming Migration — From Implicit to Explicit Module IDs [official]

Testcontainers 2.0 renamed all database and service modules from the previous unqualified names (`org.testcontainers:mysql`) to explicit `testcontainers-` prefixed artifacts (`org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mysql`). Simultaneously, container classes moved from the shared `org.testcontainers.containers` package to module-specific sub-packages — `MySQLContainer` is now in `org.testcontainers.mysql`, `PostgreSQLContainer` in `org.testcontainers.postgresql`, and so on. The change enables independent versioning per module and avoids classpath collisions in multi-module Gradle/Maven projects where different subprojects use different database versions. Projects that declare Testcontainers via Spring Boot's dependency management BOM will receive the correct artifact IDs automatically; projects that manage versions manually must update all 20+ artifact IDs.

```xml
<!-- pom.xml — Testcontainers 2.x migration -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
            <artifactId>testcontainers-bom</artifactId>
            <version>2.0.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <!-- 1.x: org.testcontainers:mysql          -->
    <!-- 2.x: org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mysql -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
        <artifactId>testcontainers-mysql</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
        <artifactId>testcontainers-postgresql</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

```java
// Java imports also changed:
// 1.x: import org.testcontainers.containers.MySQLContainer;
// 2.x: import org.testcontainers.mysql.MySQLContainer;

import org.testcontainers.mysql.MySQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class DatabaseIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    static MySQLContainer<?> mysql = new MySQLContainer<>("mysql:8.4")
        .withDatabaseName("testdb")
        .withUsername("test")
        .withPassword("test");

    @Test
    void containerStarts_jdbcUrlIsReachable() {
        assertThat(mysql.getJdbcUrl()).startsWith("jdbc:mysql://");
        assertThat(mysql.isRunning()).isTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The 2.x module renaming is a purely mechanical breaking change with no functional benefit for teams that use a single database. Teams with multi-module Gradle projects that relied on the `testcontainers` BOM to manage versions for all modules may find the BOM import simpler now (each module is independently versioned), but the initial migration requires updating every import statement and artifact ID across the entire codebase — tools like IDE structural search-and-replace are essential. Teams that used the `org.testcontainers:testcontainers` core artifact without a database module artifact (for custom containers or `GenericContainer`) see no change other than the package renaming in specific helpers.

[official]

---

### 41. Spring Boot 4.1 `@GrpcTest` Slice — Isolated gRPC Service Testing Without Full Application Context [official]

Spring Boot 4.1 introduces `@GrpcTest`, a dedicated test slice for gRPC services analogous to `@WebMvcTest` for REST controllers. It loads only `@GrpcService`-annotated beans, gRPC interceptors, and the in-process gRPC server infrastructure; it excludes JPA repositories, Kafka consumers, and other non-gRPC components. The slice auto-configures an in-process gRPC channel backed by `InProcessChannelBuilder`, which bypasses the network stack entirely — requests round-trip through memory, making tests fast and deterministic. `@MockitoBean` injects test doubles for service-layer dependencies, and the gRPC cleanup lifecycle is integrated automatically so channels and servers are shut down after each test class.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.grpc.GrpcTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import net.devh.boot.grpc.client.inject.GrpcClient;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.Optional;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

@GrpcTest(OrderServiceGrpc.class)
class OrderGrpcServiceTest {

    @GrpcClient("test")
    private OrderServiceGrpc.OrderServiceBlockingStub stub;

    @MockitoBean
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Test
    void createOrder_validProtoRequest_returnsCreatedResponse() {
        given(orderRepository.save(any()))
            .willReturn(Order.builder().id("ORD-99").build());

        CreateOrderRequest request = CreateOrderRequest.newBuilder()
            .setUserId("user-1")
            .addSkus("SKU-A")
            .build();

        CreateOrderResponse response = stub.createOrder(request);

        assertThat(response.getOrderId()).isEqualTo("ORD-99");
        assertThat(response.getStatus()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.PENDING);
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_notFound_throwsStatusRuntimeException() {
        given(orderRepository.findById("missing"))
            .willReturn(Optional.empty());

        assertThatThrownBy(() ->
            stub.getOrder(GetOrderRequest.newBuilder()
                .setOrderId("missing").build()))
            .isInstanceOf(io.grpc.StatusRuntimeException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("NOT_FOUND");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@GrpcTest` uses an in-process channel, which means network-level errors (TLS handshake failures, connection timeouts, load-balancing round-robin behaviour) cannot be tested with this slice — use `@SpringBootTest` with `RANDOM_PORT` and a real gRPC channel for network fidelity. The `@GrpcAdvice`-annotated exception handler beans added in the same Spring Boot 4.1 release are loaded by the slice, so error-handling logic is testable, but `@GrpcGlobalInterceptor` beans defined in `@Configuration` classes outside the slice's component scan scope must be explicitly imported with `@Import`.

[official]

---

### 42. AssertJ `usingRecursiveAssertion` with `ignoringFields` — Deep Object Graph Validation Without Boilerplate [official]

AssertJ's `usingRecursiveAssertion()` applies a predicate or assertion to every field across an entire object graph, recursively traversing nested objects, collections, and arrays. When combined with `.ignoringFields("createdAt", "updatedAt", "id")` or `.ignoringFieldsMatchingRegexes(".*Timestamp")`, the recursive walk skips volatile or generated fields that would otherwise cause test brittleness. Unlike `usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(expected)` which compares two objects field-by-field, `usingRecursiveAssertion` lets teams assert a property holds for every field — for example that no field is null, or that all `String` fields are non-empty. This pattern eliminates the need for custom `equals()` and `hashCode()` in test domain objects and for per-field null-check assertions that grow with the model.

```java
import org.assertj.core.api.Assertions;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;

class RecursiveAssertionTest {

    @Test
    void savedCustomer_noFieldIsNull_afterPersistence() {
        CustomerRepository repo = new CustomerRepository(dataSource);
        Customer saved = repo.save(Customer.newBuilder()
            .firstName("Ada")
            .lastName("Lovelace")
            .email("ada@example.com")
            .build());

        Assertions.assertThat(saved)
            .usingRecursiveAssertion()
            .ignoringFields("middleName", "deletedAt")
            .allFieldsSatisfy(field -> field != null);
    }

    @Test
    void orderResponse_allStringFieldsAreNonBlank() {
        OrderResponse response = orderService.createOrder(validRequest());

        Assertions.assertThat(response)
            .usingRecursiveAssertion()
            .ignoringFieldsMatchingRegexes(".*Id", ".*At")
            .allFieldsSatisfy(field ->
                !(field instanceof String s) || !s.isBlank());
    }

    @Test
    void productCatalog_deepCollectionAssert_allPricesPositive() {
        List<Product> catalog = catalogService.getAll();

        Assertions.assertThat(catalog)
            .flatExtracting(Product::getVariants)
            .usingRecursiveAssertion()
            .allFieldsSatisfy(field ->
                !(field instanceof Integer i) || i > 0);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `usingRecursiveAssertion` traverses the full object graph including inherited fields from parent classes, which can include framework-injected proxy fields, Hibernate lazy-load enhancement fields, or Jackson internal fields — these synthetic fields will cause the assertion to fail on unexpected nulls unless explicitly ignored. Teams should call `.ignoringFieldsOfTypes(Class<?>...)` to skip known proxy-holder types (`ByteBuddyInterceptor`). The recursive walk is eager; deeply nested object graphs with circular references will cause a `StackOverflowError` unless the graph is bounded, making this pattern unsafe for entities with bidirectional JPA relationships without `ignoringFields` guards.

[official]

---

### 43. Property-Based Testing with `jqwik` `ActionSequence` API — Stateful System Invariant Testing [community]

Beyond simple value-based `@Property` tests, `jqwik` 1.9+ supports stateful property-based testing through the `ActionSequence` API. A stateful property defines a set of valid `Action` implementations (state transitions) and asks `jqwik` to generate and shrink arbitrary sequences of those actions, asserting invariants after every step. This is far more powerful than example-based tests for data structures, state machines, and services with complex valid-state transitions — `jqwik` finds the minimal sequence of operations that violates an invariant and reports the exact replay sequence. The approach mirrors QuickCheck's model-based testing from Haskell and is the gold standard for testing collections, caches, and workflow engines.

```java
import net.jqwik.api.*;
import net.jqwik.api.stateful.*;
import java.util.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class BoundedQueueStatefulTest {

    @Property
    void boundedQueue_invariantsMaintainedUnderArbitraryActions(
            @ForAll("sequences") ActionSequence<BoundedQueue<Integer>> actions) {

        actions.run(new BoundedQueue<>(5));
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<ActionSequence<BoundedQueue<Integer>>> sequences() {
        return Arbitraries.sequences(
            Arbitraries.oneOf(enqueueAction(), dequeueAction(), peekAction())
        );
    }

    private Arbitrary<Action<BoundedQueue<Integer>>> enqueueAction() {
        return Arbitraries.integers().between(0, 999)
            .map(value -> Action.just(
                "enqueue(" + value + ")",
                queue -> {
                    int sizeBefore = queue.size();
                    boolean enqueued = queue.offer(value);
                    if (sizeBefore < 5) {
                        assertThat(enqueued).isTrue();
                        assertThat(queue.size()).isEqualTo(sizeBefore + 1);
                    } else {
                        assertThat(enqueued).isFalse();
                        assertThat(queue.size()).isEqualTo(5);
                    }
                }
            ));
    }

    private Arbitrary<Action<BoundedQueue<Integer>>> dequeueAction() {
        return Arbitraries.just(Action.just("dequeue", queue -> {
            int sizeBefore = queue.size();
            Integer removed = queue.poll();
            if (sizeBefore > 0) {
                assertThat(removed).isNotNull();
                assertThat(queue.size()).isEqualTo(sizeBefore - 1);
            } else {
                assertThat(removed).isNull();
                assertThat(queue.size()).isZero();
            }
        }));
    }

    private Arbitrary<Action<BoundedQueue<Integer>>> peekAction() {
        return Arbitraries.just(Action.just("peek", queue -> {
            int sizeBefore = queue.size();
            queue.peek();
            assertThat(queue.size()).isEqualTo(sizeBefore);
        }));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Stateful property tests are significantly slower than value-based property tests because `jqwik` generates and executes entire action sequences (default 1000 sequences of up to 30 actions each). Teams should configure `@Property(tries = 200)` for local development and reserve the full 1000-try run for CI. When a failing sequence is found, `jqwik` shrinks it to the minimal reproducing sequence — but shrinking can take seconds for complex state machines. The `Action` abstraction does not support preconditions out of the box; actions that are only valid in certain states must be guarded with `assumeThat` inside the action body, which counts invalid action attempts against the `tries` budget.

[community]

---

### 44. Mockito `thenAnswer` with `InvocationOnMock.getArgument(int, Class<T>)` — Type-Safe Argument Capture in Stubs [community]

Mockito's `thenAnswer(Answer<T>)` API allows stubs to compute return values dynamically from the arguments passed to the mocked method. The `InvocationOnMock.getArgument(int, Class<T>)` overload provides generic-safe argument extraction that avoids unchecked casts and returns `null` instead of throwing `ClassCastException` when the argument is absent. Community practitioners use this pattern to implement realistic stub behaviours: echo stubs (return the first argument), transform stubs (apply a function to an argument), or conditional stubs (inspect an argument field to decide the return value). The pattern is particularly effective when replacing `ArgumentCaptor` + verify + separate assertion with a single stub that both acts and implicitly validates call arguments.

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private OrderRepository repository;

    @Test
    void saveOrder_returnsSavedOrderWithGeneratedId() {
        when(repository.save(any(Order.class)))
            .thenAnswer(invocation -> {
                Order incoming = invocation.getArgument(0, Order.class);
                return incoming.toBuilder().id("GENERATED-001").build();
            });

        OrderService svc = new OrderService(repository);
        Order result = svc.placeOrder(Order.draft("user-1", List.of("SKU-A")));

        assertThat(result.getId()).isEqualTo("GENERATED-001");
        assertThat(result.getUserId()).isEqualTo("user-1");
    }

    @Test
    void sendNotification_emailAddressPassedToGateway() {
        NotificationGateway gateway = mock(NotificationGateway.class);
        List<String> capturedRecipients = new ArrayList<>();

        doAnswer(invocation -> {
            String recipient = invocation.getArgument(0, String.class);
            capturedRecipients.add(recipient);
            return null;
        }).when(gateway).send(anyString(), anyString());

        NotificationService svc = new NotificationService(gateway);
        svc.notifyAll(List.of("a@x.com", "b@x.com"));

        assertThat(capturedRecipients)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("a@x.com", "b@x.com");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `thenAnswer` with complex lambdas embeds conditional logic inside the test stub, which can make the test harder to read when the answer lambda grows beyond 5 lines — the stub becomes a second implementation that must itself be tested. Community best practice is to extract multi-line `Answer` implementations into named inner classes or static factory methods to preserve readability. `getArgument(int, Class<T>)` returns `null` for absent arguments rather than throwing, so stubs that depend on argument presence should add explicit null guards or use `getArgument(int)` with an explicit cast if null is never expected.

[community]

---

### 45. `@DataJpaTest` with `@RecordColumn` Projection Assertions — Validating Repository Projections Without Boilerplate [community]

Spring Data JPA projections — interface-based, class-based (DTO constructor), and record projections — are frequently tested insufficiently because developers test the full entity rather than the projected view. A community pattern combines `@DataJpaTest` with a real database (via `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` and Testcontainers) and asserts on the projected record's fields explicitly, verifying that only the declared columns are populated and private fields from the full entity are absent. Records as projections are particularly amenable to asserting with `assertThat(projection).extracting(...)` because their `equals()` is based on all components, making component-wise AssertJ assertions trivially correct. This pattern catches N+1-inducing lazy fetch mismatches that only surface when the projection interface is used instead of the entity.

```java
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.jdbc.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

// Projection — record-based, only id and name
record ProductSummary(String id, String name) {}

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
class ProductRepositoryProjectionTest {

    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository repository;

    @Test
    void findSummariesByCategory_returnsOnlyProjectedFields() {
        // Seed
        repository.saveAll(List.of(
            new Product("p-1", "Widget", "TOOLS", 999),
            new Product("p-2", "Gadget", "TOOLS", 1499),
            new Product("p-3", "Doohickey", "MISC", 299)
        ));

        List<ProductSummary> summaries =
            repository.findSummariesByCategory("TOOLS");

        assertThat(summaries).hasSize(2);
        assertThat(summaries)
            .extracting(ProductSummary::id, ProductSummary::name)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(
                tuple("p-1", "Widget"),
                tuple("p-2", "Gadget")
            );

        // Verify projection does NOT include price — absence is the assertion
        assertThat(summaries)
            .allSatisfy(s -> assertThat(s)
                .hasNoNullFieldsOrPropertiesExcept());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Record-based projections require an exact constructor match between the record's canonical constructor and the JPQL `SELECT new ...` clause column order; a column name typo or order mismatch throws a `QueryException` at test startup rather than a meaningful assertion failure, which can confuse developers who expect the test to fail at the `assertThat` line. Interface-based projections are more resilient to column ordering but do not benefit from `equals()`-based AssertJ assertions. Teams should test both the "happy path" (correct fields returned) and the "exclusion path" (sensitive fields like `password`, `internalNotes` are absent) to catch over-fetching regressions.

[community]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 40 [community]

**`@SpringBootTest` with `@DirtiesContext` on every test class seems safe because the context is always fresh, but it destroys the context cache and forces a full Spring context startup for every single test class — a suite of 200 test classes each starting Testcontainers takes 200 × 15 seconds = 50 minutes instead of the expected 5 minutes with a shared context** — A team adds `@DirtiesContext` to integration test classes to avoid state leakage after database tests that insert rows without cleanup. The suite was previously running in 5 minutes; after adding `@DirtiesContext` to 200 classes it takes 50 minutes in CI. WHY: `@DirtiesContext` destroys the Spring application context after the class completes, which evicts the entry from the test context cache; each subsequent class starts a brand-new context including Testcontainers container startup, Flyway migration, and full bean initialization — the very sharing that made the suite fast is eliminated. Fix: replace `@DirtiesContext` with `@Transactional` on test classes so database changes are rolled back after each test within a shared context, or use `@Sql(scripts = "/cleanup.sql", executionPhase = AFTER_TEST_METHOD)` for cleanup that must happen outside a transaction.

**Using Mockito's `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` together when a production class has a `final` field silently leaves the field `null` — the constructor injection that `@InjectMocks` performs skips fields that Mockito's heuristic does not resolve, and the test throws `NullPointerException` inside the production code at an unrelated location** — A developer adds a new `final EmailValidator validator` field to a service class and marks it `final`. The existing `@InjectMocks`-based test starts throwing `NullPointerException` at an unrelated assertion. WHY: Mockito's `@InjectMocks` uses constructor injection when a matching constructor exists, but only injects mocks it recognizes — if the new `@Mock private EmailValidator validator` field was added but Mockito's constructor-injection heuristic could not match it (due to ambiguous constructors or type overlap), the field is left `null`. Fix: prefer explicit constructor calls over `@InjectMocks` — create the subject manually in `@BeforeEach` with `new OrderService(repository, paymentGateway, validator)` so all dependencies are visible and injection failures become compile-time errors.

**Testcontainers `withReuse(true)` causes the container to persist between test suite runs, but environment-variable-driven configuration changes (like rotating a `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` between runs) are silently ignored because the reused container started with the old configuration** — A developer enables `withReuse(true)` for a `PostgreSQLContainer` to speed up local development iteration. After a security rotation that changes the test database password in environment variables, tests start failing with authentication errors. WHY: `withReuse(true)` marks the container with a label hash derived from its configuration; if the hash matches an already-running container, Testcontainers reuses it without re-applying `withEnv(...)` or `withPassword(...)` — the container was started with the old password and the new password is never applied. Fix: either call `withReuse(false)` when credentials change, or include the credential values in the container's `withLabel(...)` so the hash changes when credentials rotate, forcing a new container to start.

**A `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` that returns a `Stream<Arguments>` from a non-static method compiles and the test class instantiates successfully, but all parameterized test invocations are skipped with the message `"No arguments provided for @ParameterizedTest"` — there is no compilation error and no meaningful error message pointing to the root cause** — A developer writes a factory method `Stream<Arguments> testData()` as an instance method (not `static`) and references it in `@MethodSource("testData")`. JUnit skips all invocations silently. WHY: `@MethodSource` factory methods must be `static` unless the test class is annotated with `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` — without `PER_CLASS`, JUnit cannot call instance methods on a not-yet-created test instance during the test discovery phase, so it falls back to reporting zero arguments instead of throwing. Fix: either declare the factory method `static`, or add `@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` to the test class.

**`Awaitility.await().until(Callable<Boolean>)` does not call `Assertions.fail()` on timeout — it throws `ConditionTimeoutException` which is not an `AssertionError`, so test frameworks that distinguish assertion failures from unexpected exceptions (like Surefire's failure categorization) report the test as an "error" rather than a "failure", hiding flaky timeout patterns in CI dashboards** — A team uses `await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(() -> cache.containsKey("k"))` in integration tests. When the condition times out on an overloaded CI agent, Surefire reports the test as `ERROR` (unexpected exception) rather than `FAILURE` (assertion), and the team's failure-rate dashboard never captures these as flakiness incidents. WHY: `ConditionTimeoutException` extends `RuntimeException`, not `AssertionError`; JUnit and Surefire treat `AssertionError` subclasses as test assertion failures and `RuntimeException` subclasses as test errors — two different categories in the report. Fix: use `await().untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(cache).containsKey("k"))` which internally throws `AssertionFailedError` on timeout, or catch `ConditionTimeoutException` and rethrow as `AssertionFailedError` to normalize the failure category.
