## Cycle 41 — 2026-05-14

### 46. Spring Boot `MockMvcTester` — AssertJ-Native Controller Testing Without Static Imports [official]

`MockMvcTester` is the AssertJ-based entry point for testing Spring MVC controllers introduced in Spring Framework 6.2 and fully promoted in Spring Boot 4.x. Unlike the classic `MockMvc` API which requires `ResultMatcher` lambdas with static imports from `MockMvcResultMatchers`, `MockMvcTester` wraps responses in AssertJ `MvcTestResult` so the full AssertJ assertion vocabulary is available without mixing two assertion styles in the same test. Unresolved handler exceptions do not throw immediately — they are captured and accessible through `.hasFailed()` and `.failure()`, which means tests no longer need `try/catch` blocks around `perform()`. Async responses (from `DeferredResult` or reactive publishers) are handled transparently by default without calling `asyncDispatch()` manually.

```java
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;

    @MockitoBean
    OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void getOrder_returnsOrderJson() {
        given(orderService.findById("ORD-1"))
            .willReturn(new Order("ORD-1", "PLACED", BigDecimal.valueOf(49.99)));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/orders/{id}", "ORD-1"))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.status").asString().isEqualTo("PLACED");
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_unknownId_returns404WithMessage() {
        given(orderService.findById("X")).willThrow(new OrderNotFoundException("X"));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/orders/{id}", "X"))
            .hasFailed()
            .hasStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
            .failure().hasMessageContaining("X");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `MockMvcTester` requires the `spring-test` module at version 6.2+ and the `assertj-core` library on the classpath — projects still on Spring Framework 5.x or using only Hamcrest matchers must migrate both dependencies before adopting it. The failure-capture semantics (no exception thrown on handler error) differ from classic `MockMvc` behavior and can surprise developers who previously relied on the exception propagating to trigger `@ExceptionHandler` verification; teams must explicitly assert `.hasFailed()` rather than expecting a thrown exception.

[official]

---

### 47. Mockito 5.21 Automatic Class Detection in `mockStatic` and `mockConstruction` — Removing Redundant Class Arguments [official]

Mockito 5.21 introduced automatic class detection for `mockStatic` and `mockConstruction` when the mock variable is declared with an explicit generic type at the call site. When the compiler can infer the target class from the left-hand-side type — for example `MockedStatic<FileUtils> mock = mockStatic()` — Mockito uses reflection on the generic type argument to identify the class to mock, eliminating the redundant `.class` argument. This reduces boilerplate in test setup blocks where the mocked class is already declared in the variable type. The change is purely additive; existing code passing an explicit `.class` argument continues to compile and behave identically.

```java
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

class FileProcessorTest {

    @Test
    void process_usesCurrentTimestamp() {
        // Before 5.21: mockStatic(Instant.class)
        // After 5.21: class inferred from generic parameter
        try (MockedStatic<Instant> mockedInstant = mockStatic()) {
            Instant fixed = Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
            mockedInstant.when(Instant::now).thenReturn(fixed);

            FileProcessor processor = new FileProcessor();
            String result = processor.generateFileName();

            assertThat(result).isEqualTo("output-2026-01-01T00:00:00Z.csv");
            mockedInstant.verify(Instant::now, times(1));
        }
    }

    @Test
    void process_constructionInterceptor() {
        // Class inferred from MockedConstruction<DatabaseWriter>
        try (MockedConstruction<DatabaseWriter> mocked = mockConstruction()) {
            new FileProcessor().flush();

            DatabaseWriter constructed = mocked.constructed().get(0);
            verify(constructed).writeAll(any());
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The type-inference shorthand only works when the generic type is declared on the variable — using `var` (Java 10+) with `mockStatic()` produces a raw `MockedStatic` type and the explicit `.class` argument remains required because the compiler has nothing to infer from. Additionally, if a test class needs to mock the same class twice in different scopes, the explicit `.class` form is clearer and avoids accidental shadowing of the inferred type at the variable-declaration level.

[official]

---

### 48. JUnit 6 `@ParameterizedClass` — Parameterizing the Entire Test Class Lifecycle [official]

JUnit 6 introduced `@ParameterizedClass`, which applies parameterization at the class level rather than the method level. Each argument set from a source like `@MethodSource`, `@ValueSource`, or `@CsvSource` causes the entire test class — including `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`, and all `@Test` methods — to be executed once per argument combination. This is useful when the SUT itself has a parameterized constructor and all tests in the class share the same initialization, avoiding the need to repeat identical `@BeforeEach` injection logic across ten `@ParameterizedTest` methods. Unlike `@TestFactory`, `@ParameterizedClass` integrates with the full JUnit 6 extension lifecycle and supports `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` at per-parameter granularity when combined with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`.

```java
@ParameterizedClass
@ValueSource(strings = { "H2", "PostgreSQL", "MySQL" })
class RepositoryCompatibilityTest {

    private final String dialect;
    private EntityRepository repository;

    RepositoryCompatibilityTest(String dialect) {
        this.dialect = dialect;
    }

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        DataSource ds = DataSourceFactory.forDialect(dialect);
        repository = new EntityRepository(ds);
        repository.createSchema();
    }

    @Test
    void save_thenFindById_returnsEntity() {
        Entity e = repository.save(new Entity("e1", "label"));
        assertThat(repository.findById("e1")).contains(e);
    }

    @Test
    void deleteNonExistent_doesNotThrow() {
        assertThatCode(() -> repository.delete("ghost")).doesNotThrowAnyException();
    }

    @AfterEach
    void tearDown() {
        repository.dropSchema();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@ParameterizedClass` requires JUnit 6; there is no equivalent in JUnit 5.x, so projects on JUnit 5 must simulate this with `@TestFactory` or `@ExtendWith` plus a custom `TestInstancePostProcessor`, both of which produce far more boilerplate. Each parameter set creates a full test-class lifecycle instantiation, so `@BeforeAll` static setup still runs once per JVM unless `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` is used — teams that expect per-parameter `@BeforeAll` need to explicitly configure the lifecycle. Reporting tools that do not understand `@ParameterizedClass` may display all tests under a single class name without the parameter discriminator suffix.

[official]

---

### 49. AssertJ `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly` — Collecting All Assertion Failures in One Block [official]

AssertJ's `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly` provides a static factory method that accepts a `ThrowingConsumer<SoftAssertions>` and guarantees `assertAll()` is called at the end even if the consumer throws — previously, forgetting to call `assertAll()` caused soft assertions to silently pass. The lambda syntax is compatible with JUnit 5 extension-injected `SoftAssertions` parameters, and the `@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)` approach auto-injects `SoftAssertions` into test methods, eliminating even the `assertSoftly` wrapper. Teams writing multi-field validations (e.g., verifying 10 fields of a deserialized response) benefit most: all ten failures appear in one test report rather than stopping at the first failed field.

```java
import org.assertj.core.api.SoftAssertions;

@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)
class OrderSummaryTest {

    @Test
    void orderSummary_allFieldsCorrect(SoftAssertions softly) {
        OrderSummary summary = fetchSummary("ORD-99");

        softly.assertThat(summary.id()).isEqualTo("ORD-99");
        softly.assertThat(summary.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.SHIPPED);
        softly.assertThat(summary.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("199.99");
        softly.assertThat(summary.lineItems()).hasSize(3);
        softly.assertThat(summary.shippedAt()).isNotNull();
        softly.assertThat(summary.trackingNumber()).startsWith("1Z");
        // All failures collected; assertAll() called automatically by extension
    }

    @Test
    void orderSummary_staticHelper_style() {
        OrderSummary summary = fetchSummary("ORD-100");

        SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {
            softly.assertThat(summary.id()).isEqualTo("ORD-100");
            softly.assertThat(summary.status()).isNotNull();
            softly.assertThat(summary.total()).isPositive();
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Soft assertions accumulate all failures, which can produce extremely long failure messages when many fields are wrong — this is useful during initial development but can obscure systematic root causes (e.g., a deserialization bug that corrupts every field) that would be more apparent from a single early failure. The `@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)` approach requires a JUnit 5 extension which must be registered globally via `ServiceLoader` or per-class via `@ExtendWith`, adding a configuration step that is easy to forget in new test classes. Teams using `SoftAssertions` with `@ParameterizedTest` should be aware that AssertJ collects failures per test-method invocation, not per parameter set, so a soft assertion failure in one parameter invocation does not bleed into the next.

[official]

---

### 50. Spring Boot `@AutoConfigureObservability` — Testing Tracing and Metrics in Slice Tests [official]

Spring Boot 3.4+ introduced `@AutoConfigureObservability`, a dedicated auto-configuration annotation that can be added to test slices (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, etc.) to bring in a real Micrometer `MeterRegistry` and Micrometer Tracing infrastructure — normally excluded from slice tests to keep them fast. By default, slice tests use no-op implementations of `ObservationRegistry` and `Tracer`, which means `@Observed`-annotated beans and `ObservationHandler` interceptors are not exercised. Adding `@AutoConfigureObservability` to a `@WebMvcTest` class enables asserting on span names, metrics counters incremented by HTTP requests, and custom observation tags without loading the full application context.

```java
@WebMvcTest(PaymentController.class)
@AutoConfigureObservability
class PaymentControllerObservabilityTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;

    @Autowired
    MeterRegistry meterRegistry;

    @MockitoBean
    PaymentService paymentService;

    @Test
    void processPayment_incrementsSuccessCounter() throws Exception {
        given(paymentService.process(any()))
            .willReturn(new PaymentResult("PAY-1", Status.APPROVED));

        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/payments")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .content("{\"amount\":100,\"currency\":\"USD\"}"))
            .hasStatusOk();

        Counter counter = meterRegistry.find("payment.processed")
            .tag("status", "APPROVED")
            .counter();

        assertThat(counter).isNotNull();
        assertThat(counter.count()).isEqualTo(1.0);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@AutoConfigureObservability` initializes Micrometer and a tracing bridge (e.g., Micrometer Tracing with Brave or OTel), which adds measurable overhead to slice test startup — teams observed 200–400 ms additional startup on representative suites. The annotation enables the full `ObservationRegistry` pipeline, so if a custom `ObservationHandler` (such as a log-emitting handler) is also on the classpath and has side effects (writing to an external system in CI), it may be invoked unexpectedly; teams should ensure custom handlers are guarded by `@ConditionalOnNotWebApplication` or similar conditions in test environments.

[official]

---

### 51. Testcontainers `@ImportTestcontainers` with Typed `@ServiceConnection` — Composable Container Interfaces [official]

Testcontainers 1.21+ allows test classes to reference container definitions declared in separate interfaces via `@ImportTestcontainers(MyContainers.class)`, where the interface holds `@Container`-annotated static fields with `@ServiceConnection`. Each interface defines one infrastructure concern (database, cache, messaging), and a test class can import multiple interfaces, composing exactly the containers it needs without copying field declarations. `@ServiceConnection` on a `PostgreSQLContainer` or `RedisContainer` automatically propagates connection properties (`spring.datasource.url`, `spring.redis.host`) into the Spring `Environment`, so no `@DynamicPropertySource` method is required. This pattern replaces the common `abstract AbstractIntegrationTest` base class anti-pattern that forces all integration tests to start every container even when they only need a database.

```java
// Reusable container interfaces — each owns one concern
interface PostgresContainers {
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");
}

interface RedisContainers {
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);
}

// Test only needs Postgres — no Redis startup cost
@SpringBootTest
@ImportTestcontainers(PostgresContainers.class)
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Test
    void save_thenQuery_returnsPersistedOrder() {
        orderRepository.save(new Order("O-1", "DRAFT"));
        assertThat(orderRepository.findById("O-1")).isPresent();
    }
}

// Test needs both — imports both interfaces
@SpringBootTest
@ImportTestcontainers({PostgresContainers.class, RedisContainers.class})
class CachingOrderServiceTest {
    // Both postgres and redis available
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Shared static container fields in interfaces are started once per JVM if all referencing test classes share the Spring context cache key — but if two classes import the same interface while differing in other context configuration, two independent container instances start, negating the sharing benefit. Teams must carefully manage context cache keys (same `@SpringBootTest` configuration, same profiles) to ensure container reuse. Additionally, `@ServiceConnection` auto-propagation supports only officially recognized container types; custom containers or community modules may need a `@DynamicPropertySource` fallback alongside `@ImportTestcontainers`.

[official]

---

### 52. JUnit 6 `@AutoClose` — Declarative Resource Cleanup Without `@AfterEach` Boilerplate [official]

JUnit 6 introduced `@AutoClose`, a field-level annotation that automatically calls `close()` on any `AutoCloseable` test field after each test (or after all tests when combined with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`). This eliminates the common `@AfterEach void tearDown() { resource.close(); }` pattern for resources like database connections, HTTP clients, WireMock servers, or temporary file handles. The annotation respects the JUnit 5 extension lifecycle ordering, so `@AutoClose` fields are closed after all `@AfterEach` methods and extension `afterEach` callbacks have run, ensuring the resource is still accessible during cleanup assertions. Multiple `@AutoClose` fields are closed in reverse declaration order (last declared, first closed), mirroring `try-with-resources` semantics.

```java
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class WireMockIntegrationTest {

    @AutoClose
    WireMockServer wireMock = new WireMockServer(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort());

    @AutoClose
    CloseableHttpClient httpClient = HttpClients.createDefault();

    @BeforeAll
    void startWireMock() {
        wireMock.start();
    }

    @Test
    void fetchUser_mapsJsonToRecord() throws Exception {
        wireMock.stubFor(get("/users/1")
            .willReturn(okJson("{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Alice\"}")));

        HttpGet request = new HttpGet("http://localhost:" + wireMock.port() + "/users/1");
        try (CloseableHttpResponse response = httpClient.execute(request)) {
            String body = EntityUtils.toString(response.getEntity());
            assertThat(body).contains("Alice");
        }
    }

    @Test
    void fetchUser_notFound_returns404() throws Exception {
        wireMock.stubFor(get("/users/99").willReturn(notFound()));

        HttpGet request = new HttpGet("http://localhost:" + wireMock.port() + "/users/99");
        try (CloseableHttpResponse response = httpClient.execute(request)) {
            assertThat(response.getCode()).isEqualTo(404);
        }
    }
    // wireMock and httpClient closed automatically after all tests
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@AutoClose` is only available in JUnit 6; projects still on JUnit 5.x must use `@AfterEach`/`@AfterAll` or `@RegisterExtension` with a custom `CloseableResource` wrapper. The annotation closes fields unconditionally after each test — if a test intentionally leaves a resource in a dirty state for a subsequent test (a common pattern in integration test sequences), `@AutoClose` will close it prematurely; in those cases `@RegisterExtension` with manual lifecycle control is more appropriate. Error propagation during `close()` follows `try-with-resources` suppressed-exception semantics: if the test fails and `close()` also throws, both exceptions appear in the report but the original test failure is the primary cause.

[official]

---

### 53. Spring Boot `@MockitoBean` Scoped Overrides — Replacing Beans Only for Specific Test Classes [official]

Spring Boot 4.x's `@MockitoBean` (the successor to `@MockBean`) supports a `scope` attribute allowing teams to declare that the Mockito replacement applies only to the `@SpringBootTest` class declaring it, not to other test classes sharing the same Spring context cache entry. Previously, two `@SpringBootTest` classes that differed only in their `@MockBean` declarations each got a separate Spring context, doubling Testcontainers startup time. With `@MockitoBean(scope = MockitoBean.Scope.TEST_CLASS)` on every mock declaration, Spring can recognize that the mock is scoped to the declaring class and does not need to create a separate context for it. The bean reverts to the production implementation for test classes that share the context but do not declare the `@MockitoBean`.

```java
// Both classes share the same Spring context (same @SpringBootTest config)
// Only ReportGeneratorTest replaces the NotificationService

@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest {
    @Autowired
    OrderService orderService; // uses real NotificationService

    @Test
    void createOrder_sendNotification() {
        // Full end-to-end: real notification side effect
        assertThatCode(() -> orderService.createOrder(new Order("O-1")))
            .doesNotThrowAnyException();
    }
}

@SpringBootTest
class ReportGeneratorTest {

    @MockitoBean(scope = MockitoBean.Scope.TEST_CLASS)
    NotificationService notificationService; // replaced only for this class

    @Autowired
    ReportGenerator reportGenerator;

    @Test
    void generateReport_doesNotSendNotifications() {
        reportGenerator.generate();
        verify(notificationService, never()).send(any());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `TEST_CLASS` scope reduces context proliferation but introduces a subtle correctness risk: if a real `NotificationService` has a side effect that leaves observable state (e.g., writes to a shared in-memory queue), tests in `OrderServiceIntegrationTest` may see state produced by tests in `ReportGeneratorTest` within the same context, because the context is shared but the mock is not. Teams must ensure that bean state is reset between test classes — either via `@Transactional` rollback, `@Sql` cleanup, or stateless service design — before relying on `TEST_CLASS` scope mocks to share a context. Forgetting the `scope` attribute defaults to the old behavior where each unique mock set creates a new context.

[official]

---

### 54. Mockito 5.21 `ReturnsEmptyValues` with JDK 21 `SequencedCollection` — Correct Default Returns for Modern Collection Types [official]

Mockito 5.20 and 5.21 extended the `RETURNS_EMPTY` and `RETURNS_MOCKS` default answer strategies to recognize JDK 21's new `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet`, and `SequencedMap` interfaces. Before this fix, stubbing a method that returned `SequencedList` with no explicit `thenReturn(...)` caused Mockito to return `null` instead of an empty sequenced collection, resulting in `NullPointerException` inside production code that called `getFirst()` or `getLast()` on the return value. The fix ensures that any method whose declared return type is a subtype of `SequencedCollection` returns an appropriate empty collection by default, matching the existing behavior for `List`, `Set`, and `Map`.

```java
interface OrderRepository {
    SequencedCollection<Order> findRecent(int limit);
    LinkedList<Order> findByCustomer(String customerId); // LinkedList is SequencedCollection
}

class OrderServiceTest {

    OrderRepository repo = mock(OrderRepository.class,
        withSettings().defaultAnswer(RETURNS_EMPTY));

    @Test
    void getRecentOrders_noOrders_returnsEmpty() {
        // Before 5.20: returned null, NullPointerException on .getFirst()
        // After 5.20: returns empty SequencedCollection
        SequencedCollection<Order> orders = repo.findRecent(10);
        assertThat(orders).isNotNull().isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void findByCustomer_linkedList_notNull() {
        LinkedList<Order> orders = repo.findByCustomer("C-1");
        // LinkedList implements SequencedCollection — now returns empty LinkedList
        assertThat(orders).isNotNull();
        assertThatCode(() -> orders.peekFirst()).doesNotThrowAnyException();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `RETURNS_EMPTY` is not appropriate for every mock — services with critical null-checking contracts (e.g., a `findById` that is expected to return `Optional.empty()` on miss, not an empty collection) will silently receive an empty collection from `RETURNS_EMPTY` where `null` was the semantically correct default, masking missing stubs. Teams should reserve `RETURNS_EMPTY` for repository or collection-returning interfaces and keep the strict default (`RETURNS_DEFAULT`, which throws on unstubbed calls with `STRICT_STUBS`) for service mocks to catch incomplete stub setup early.

[official]

---

### 55. WireMock `scenarioState` API — Stateful Stub Sequencing for Multi-Step Protocol Tests [community]

WireMock's scenario state machine allows tests to simulate multi-step protocol flows — such as an idempotency-key retry flow, an OAuth token refresh after 401, or a poll-until-ready pattern — without deploying a real server. Each stub is registered with `inScenario("name").whenScenarioStateIs(STATE)` and optionally transitions to a new state on invocation via `.willSetStateTo(NEXT_STATE)`. The scenario starts in the implicit `Scenario.STARTED` state. This is the correct tool when a test needs to assert that a client makes exactly N retries after receiving error responses, then succeeds — using separate `WireMock.stubFor()` calls for each expected request in a retry loop is unordered and cannot assert sequence.

```java
@WireMockTest
class TokenRefreshIntegrationTest {

    @Test
    void client_refreshesToken_on401_thenSucceeds(WireMockRuntimeInfo wm) {
        // First call returns 401 (token expired)
        stubFor(get("/api/data")
            .inScenario("token-refresh")
            .whenScenarioStateIs(Scenario.STARTED)
            .willReturn(unauthorized())
            .willSetStateTo("REFRESHING"));

        // After refresh, second call returns 200
        stubFor(get("/api/data")
            .inScenario("token-refresh")
            .whenScenarioStateIs("REFRESHING")
            .willReturn(okJson("{\"data\":\"value\"}")));

        stubFor(post("/oauth/token")
            .inScenario("token-refresh")
            .whenScenarioStateIs("REFRESHING")
            .willReturn(okJson("{\"access_token\":\"new-token\"}"))
            .willSetStateTo("REFRESHED"));

        ApiClient client = new ApiClient(wm.getHttpBaseUrl());
        ApiResponse response = client.fetchData();

        assertThat(response.data()).isEqualTo("value");
        verify(exactly(1), postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/oauth/token")));
        verify(exactly(2), getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/api/data")));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** WireMock scenarios are global to the `WireMockServer` instance — if two tests run in parallel against the same server instance, their scenario state transitions can interleave, corrupting both tests. The `@WireMockTest` JUnit 5 extension starts a fresh `WireMockServer` per test method, so parallel test execution at the method level is safe; however, if tests share a static `WireMockServer` field for performance, parallel execution requires manual state reset via `WireMock.resetScenarios()` in `@BeforeEach`. Scenario names are strings and there is no compile-time safety — a typo in a state name silently falls back to the `STARTED` state, causing intermittent stub-not-matched failures that are difficult to diagnose.

[community]

---

### 56. `@DataJpaTest` with `TestEntityManager` — Low-Level Persistence Assertions Without Repository Coupling [official]

Spring Boot's `TestEntityManager` wraps the JPA `EntityManager` with test-friendly flush-and-clear helpers, giving `@DataJpaTest` tests direct control over the persistence context lifecycle without exposing the full `EntityManager` API. `testEntityManager.persistFlushFind(entity)` persists, flushes to SQL, evicts the entity from the first-level cache, and re-loads it from the database in a single call — this verifies that `@Column` mappings, `@Convert` converters, and database constraints are exercised, not just in-memory JPA state. This pattern catches mapping bugs that would otherwise be invisible in `save()` + `findById()` repository tests where the first-level cache returns the original Java object without a round-trip.

```java
@DataJpaTest
class CustomerMappingTest {

    @Autowired
    TestEntityManager em;

    @Test
    void emailAddress_storedAndRetrievedAsLowercase() {
        Customer customer = new Customer();
        customer.setEmail("Alice@Example.COM");
        customer.setName("Alice");

        // persistFlushFind: persist -> flush to DB -> evict from cache -> reload from DB
        Customer reloaded = em.persistFlushFind(customer);

        // Verifies @Column(name="email") + @Convert(EmailLowercaseConverter.class)
        assertThat(reloaded.getEmail()).isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
    }

    @Test
    void nullableForeignKey_storedWithoutConstraintViolation() {
        Order order = new Order();
        order.setStatus("DRAFT");
        order.setCustomer(null); // nullable FK

        Order reloaded = em.persistFlushFind(order);

        assertThat(reloaded.getCustomer()).isNull();
        assertThat(reloaded.getId()).isNotNull(); // DB generated ID
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `TestEntityManager.persistFlushFind()` forces a flush and cache eviction, which makes it stricter than a repository-level test but also means it will trigger deferred constraint checks (e.g., `@UniqueConstraint` violations) at flush time rather than at transaction commit — some databases defer constraint evaluation to commit, and this difference can cause tests to pass with H2 but fail with PostgreSQL where deferred constraints behave differently. Tests written against `TestEntityManager` are tightly coupled to JPA persistence semantics and may not accurately represent query performance; for testing repository query methods (e.g., custom JPQL, `@Query` projections), prefer `@DataJpaTest` with an injected repository over `TestEntityManager`.

[official]

---

### 57. REST Assured with Spring Boot `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` — End-to-End HTTP Assertions on a Live Server [community]

REST Assured provides a BDD-style DSL (`given/when/then`) for making real HTTP requests against a running server, making it the preferred tool for full-stack integration tests where the HTTP layer (filters, interceptors, content negotiation, error handling) must be exercised end-to-end rather than through the mock dispatcher. When combined with `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`, the server starts on a dynamically assigned port, and `RestAssured.port = port` configures the client at `@BeforeEach`. Unlike `MockMvc`, REST Assured exercises the actual Servlet container (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow), HTTP codec, and filter chain, catching bugs in `OncePerRequestFilter`, `HandlerInterceptor`, and content-type negotiation that mock-dispatcher tests miss.

```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class ProductApiEndToEndTest {

    @LocalServerPort
    int port;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        RestAssured.port = port;
        RestAssured.basePath = "/api/v1";
    }

    @Test
    void createProduct_returns201WithLocationHeader() {
        String body = """
            {"name":"Widget","price":9.99,"category":"TOOLS"}
            """;

        given()
            .contentType(ContentType.JSON)
            .body(body)
        .when()
            .post("/products")
        .then()
            .statusCode(HttpStatus.CREATED.value())
            .header("Location", matchesPattern(".*/products/[a-z0-9-]+"))
            .body("name", equalTo("Widget"))
            .body("price", equalTo(9.99f));
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_notFound_returns404ProblemJson() {
        given()
        .when()
            .get("/products/nonexistent-id")
        .then()
            .statusCode(404)
            .contentType("application/problem+json")
            .body("title", equalTo("Not Found"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Running `@SpringBootTest` with `RANDOM_PORT` starts the full application context including all `@Component`-scanned beans, Flyway/Liquibase migrations, and any `@EventListener` beans — startup time can be 5–15 seconds depending on the application, making these tests unsuitable for the fast-feedback unit test tier; they belong in a separate Maven Surefire/Failsafe integration test phase (via `<failsafePlugin>` and `*IT.java` naming) so they run independently from the unit suite. REST Assured's response body matchers use Hamcrest by default, mixing Hamcrest and AssertJ in the same codebase; REST Assured 5.x introduced native AssertJ support via `response.then(AssertJCondition.statusCode(200))` which aligns the styles.

[community]

---

### 58. `@SpringBootTest` `args` Attribute — Testing Application Argument Parsing Without Shell Invocation [official]

`@SpringBootTest(args = {...})` passes command-line argument strings to the Spring Boot application's `ApplicationArguments` bean, enabling tests to verify `CommandLineRunner`, `ApplicationRunner`, and `@Value("${...}")` bindings that depend on command-line options without spawning a subprocess or modifying JVM system properties. Arguments are parsed by Spring Boot's `SimpleCommandLinePropertySource`, which means `--key=value` pairs override `application.properties` values within the test context, allowing teams to test feature-flag behavior, batch job parameters, and multi-tenant routing logic driven by startup arguments.

```java
@SpringBootTest(args = {"--batch.mode=FULL", "--tenant=acme", "--dry-run=true"})
class BatchJobArgumentTest {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationArguments args;

    @Autowired
    Environment env;

    @Test
    void batchModeArg_parsedCorrectly() {
        assertThat(args.getOptionValues("batch.mode"))
            .containsExactly("FULL");
    }

    @Test
    void dryRunFlag_resolvedAsProperty() {
        // args override application.properties via CommandLinePropertySource
        assertThat(env.getProperty("dry-run")).isEqualTo("true");
    }

    @Test
    void tenantArg_available_asOptionName() {
        assertThat(args.getOptionNames()).contains("tenant");
        assertThat(args.getOptionValues("tenant")).containsExactly("acme");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Arguments passed via `@SpringBootTest(args = ...)` participate in the context cache key — two test classes with different `args` arrays will produce separate Spring contexts even if everything else is identical, increasing startup overhead in suites with many argument-variation tests. This is different from `@TestPropertySource(properties = ...)`, which also overrides properties but does not create a separate context when the override set is compatible with a cached context. Teams should prefer `@TestPropertySource` or `@DynamicPropertySource` for simple property overrides and reserve `@SpringBootTest(args = ...)` exclusively for testing `ApplicationArguments`-aware beans (`CommandLineRunner`, `ApplicationRunner`) that specifically read from the `ApplicationArguments` API rather than the `Environment`.

[official]

---

### 59. Mockito `ArgumentCaptor` with `@Captor` and AssertJ — Capturing and Asserting Complex Argument State [official]

Mockito's `ArgumentCaptor` combined with AssertJ's `assertThat` provides a type-safe, readable pattern for asserting on the full state of objects passed to mocks, especially when the argument is a complex domain object with many fields that `eq()` or `any()` matchers cannot inspect. `@Captor` eliminates the `ArgumentCaptor.forClass(...)` boilerplate and works alongside `@Mock`/`@MockitoBean` annotations. Calling `captor.getValue()` after `verify(mock).method(captor.capture())` returns the captured argument, at which point the full AssertJ vocabulary (recursive comparison, extracting fields, satisfies) can be applied. For multiple invocations, `captor.getAllValues()` returns all captured arguments as a `List`.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class NotificationServiceTest {

    @Mock
    EmailGateway emailGateway;

    @Captor
    ArgumentCaptor<EmailMessage> emailCaptor;

    @InjectMocks
    NotificationService notificationService;

    @Test
    void sendWelcomeEmail_includesAllRequiredFields() {
        notificationService.sendWelcome(
            new User("u1", "Alice", "alice@example.com", Locale.ENGLISH));

        verify(emailGateway).send(emailCaptor.capture());
        EmailMessage sent = emailCaptor.getValue();

        assertThat(sent)
            .satisfies(m -> {
                assertThat(m.to()).isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
                assertThat(m.subject()).startsWith("Welcome");
                assertThat(m.templateId()).isEqualTo("welcome-en");
                assertThat(m.variables()).containsEntry("firstName", "Alice");
            });
    }

    @Test
    void sendBulkNotification_capturesAllMessages() {
        notificationService.notifyAll(List.of(
            new User("u1", "Alice", "a@x.com", Locale.ENGLISH),
            new User("u2", "Bob", "b@x.com", Locale.FRENCH)));

        verify(emailGateway, times(2)).send(emailCaptor.capture());
        List<EmailMessage> all = emailCaptor.getAllValues();

        assertThat(all).extracting(EmailMessage::templateId)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("welcome-en", "welcome-fr");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `ArgumentCaptor` captures the argument reference, not a snapshot of its state at call time — if the production code mutates the captured object after the method call (e.g., clears a list, nulls a field), `captor.getValue()` will reflect the mutated state, causing the test to assert on post-mutation values and potentially pass incorrectly. This is a common gotcha with mutable domain objects; the fix is to either use immutable objects (records), copy-on-pass patterns, or assert immediately after the `verify()` before any subsequent production code can mutate the captured reference. Teams should also resist using `ArgumentCaptor` as a substitute for a poorly designed API — if capturing and asserting requires more lines than the production code, the method signature probably needs a dedicated value object.

[official]

---

### 60. `@TestConfiguration` with `@Primary` — Overriding Production Beans in Integration Tests Without `@MockBean` [community]

When the goal is to replace a production bean with a test double that has real behavior (not a Mockito mock), `@TestConfiguration` combined with `@Primary` provides a clean mechanism: a `@TestConfiguration`-annotated inner class declares a `@Bean` method returning the test implementation, and `@Primary` ensures Spring wires it in preference to the production bean in the same context. Unlike `@MockitoBean`, which always produces a Mockito mock, this pattern allows injecting hand-written fakes, in-memory stubs, or test-specific implementations (e.g., an in-memory `EmailService` that collects sent messages instead of calling SendGrid). `@TestConfiguration` beans are only included when the class is explicitly imported or is a nested static class of the test, preventing accidental inclusion in production contexts.

```java
@SpringBootTest
class OrderFulfillmentTest {

    // Nested @TestConfiguration — only active for THIS test class
    @TestConfiguration
    static class FakeEmailConfig {

        @Bean
        @Primary
        EmailService fakeEmailService(FakeEmailInbox inbox) {
            return new InMemoryEmailService(inbox);
        }

        @Bean
        FakeEmailInbox fakeEmailInbox() {
            return new FakeEmailInbox();
        }
    }

    @Autowired
    OrderFulfillmentService fulfillmentService;

    @Autowired
    FakeEmailInbox emailInbox;

    @Test
    void fulfillOrder_sendsConfirmationEmail() {
        fulfillmentService.fulfill(new Order("O-1", "alice@example.com"));

        assertThat(emailInbox.receivedEmails())
            .hasSize(1)
            .first()
            .satisfies(email -> {
                assertThat(email.to()).isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
                assertThat(email.subject()).contains("Confirmation");
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** A `@Primary` bean in a nested `@TestConfiguration` affects all beans in the same Spring context that depend on `EmailService` — if multiple test classes share the same context via the context cache and one class declares a `@TestConfiguration @Primary` fake, all other classes sharing that context will also use the fake, which may cause unintended behavior in tests expecting the real implementation. To avoid context pollution, teams should either use `@MockitoBean(scope = TEST_CLASS)` for mock-style replacements or ensure each test needing a fake imports its own `@TestConfiguration` that forces a unique context cache key. Overly broad `@Primary` on test beans is one of the most common causes of context-cache-related test failures in large Spring test suites.

[community]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 41 [community]

**Using `@ParameterizedTest @MethodSource` with a factory method that references a field initialized in `@BeforeEach` fails with a `NullPointerException` at test discovery — not during test execution — because `@MethodSource` factory methods are called before the test instance is created** — A developer writes a `@MethodSource` factory method that reads `this.config` to build argument sets, where `config` is populated in `@BeforeEach`. The test fails immediately at discovery with `NullPointerException` inside the factory method. WHY: JUnit discovers and calls `@MethodSource` factory methods during the parameterization phase, which happens before any test instance is created and before `@BeforeEach` runs — `this.config` is `null` because the instance fields have not been initialized. Fix: either use `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` so a single test instance is created before discovery, or move the factory method data to a static field or static initializer block.

**`@MockitoBean` (Spring Boot 4.x) does NOT produce the same Spring context cache key as `@MockBean` (Spring Boot 3.x) — migrating a single `@MockBean` to `@MockitoBean` in a test class invalidates the shared context and starts a new one, causing a 10–15 second Testcontainers restart for every test class in a mixed-annotation suite** — A team migrates from Spring Boot 3.x to 4.x and replaces `@MockBean` with `@MockitoBean` in half the test classes during a gradual migration. CI time doubles overnight. WHY: `@MockBean` registers mock definitions under `MockDefinition` metadata in the context cache key, while `@MockitoBean` registers them under `MockitoContextCustomizer` metadata — the two are different cache key components, so a class using `@MockitoBean` cannot share a context with a class using `@MockBean` even if they mock the same type with the same settings. Fix: complete the migration atomically — convert all `@MockBean` usages to `@MockitoBean` in one commit so all test classes share the same cache key structure.

**`assertThat(list).containsExactlyElementsOf(expectedList)` throws `NullPointerException` inside AssertJ when the list contains `null` elements, while `assertThat(list).isEqualTo(expectedList)` handles nulls correctly — the two methods are not equivalent for null-containing lists** — A developer refactors a test from `isEqualTo` to `containsExactlyElementsOf` thinking it is strictly stronger. The test starts failing with `NullPointerException` from inside AssertJ on a list that contains a `null` element. WHY: `containsExactlyElementsOf` iterates through each element and calls `element.equals(expected)` — when `element` is `null`, this dereferences `null.equals(...)` instead of using `Objects.equals(null, expected)`. Fix: use `assertThat(list).isEqualTo(expectedList)` for null-containing lists, or filter out nulls before asserting with `containsExactlyElementsOf`. This issue is fixed in AssertJ 3.27; projects on older versions must work around it explicitly.

**`@WebMvcTest` with Spring Security auto-configuration loads `UserDetailsService` bean definitions from the classpath — if a `@Configuration` class defines a `UserDetailsService` bean that requires a database connection (e.g., `JdbcUserDetailsManager`), `@WebMvcTest` will fail to start with `DataSource` not found** — A team adds a `@WebMvcTest` to a project that uses Spring Security with JDBC-backed user details. The test fails with `DataSource required` before any test method runs. WHY: `@WebMvcTest` loads the security auto-configuration but not `@DataJpaTest` or any database auto-configuration; beans in `@Configuration` classes annotated with `@EnableWebSecurity` are visible to `@WebMvcTest` even if they require infrastructure beans not loaded by the web slice. Fix: either add `@MockitoBean DataSource dataSource` to the test, or move the `UserDetailsService` bean to a `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`-guarded configuration so the test's `@Import(TestSecurityConfig.class)` can override it with an in-memory `UserDetailsService`.

**Testing a `@Scheduled` method by directly calling it from a test gives false confidence — the scheduling trigger, cron expression, `ShedLock` acquisition, and `@Transactional` wrapping applied by the scheduler thread are not exercised** — A team writes unit tests that directly call `scheduler.runDailyReport()` and asserts on its output, achieving 100% line coverage of the scheduled method. On production, the job silently fails to acquire the distributed `ShedLock` and never runs because the lock table was not initialized. WHY: Direct method calls bypass the AOP proxy that applies `@Transactional`, `@ShedLock`, and any `BeanPostProcessor`-applied advice — the test exercises the method body but not the execution environment the scheduler provides. Fix: write a separate integration test using `@SpringBootTest` with `ScheduledTaskRunner` or Awaitility waiting on a flag set by the method body that exercises the full scheduling infrastructure, and separately unit-test the business logic in isolation.
