### 86. ArchUnit `@AnalyzeClasses` with `importOptions` — Excluding Generated and Framework Classes from Architecture Rules [community]

ArchUnit's `@AnalyzeClasses` annotation accepts an `importOptions` array that filters which classes are imported into the analysis scope, preventing generated Protobuf classes, Lombok-generated builders, Spring's CGLIB proxies, and inner anonymous classes from triggering false-positive architecture rule violations. The built-in `ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class` is well known, but `ImportOption.DoNotIncludeJars.class` excludes all classes from JAR dependencies (only project-owned classes are checked), and teams can write custom `ImportOption` implementations by testing `ClassFileLocation.contains("/generated/")` or matching against package patterns. This is essential for Hexagonal Architecture rule suites where auto-generated gRPC stubs in `generated-sources` would otherwise appear to violate the "domain layer must not depend on infrastructure" rule because their package name happens to collide with the domain package.

```java
@AnalyzeClasses(
    packages = "com.example",
    importOptions = {
        ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class,
        HexagonalArchitectureTest.ExcludeGeneratedSources.class,
        HexagonalArchitectureTest.ExcludeMapStructMappers.class
    }
)
public class HexagonalArchitectureTest {

    static class ExcludeGeneratedSources implements ImportOption {
        @Override
        public boolean includes(Location location) {
            return !location.contains("/generated/")
                && !location.contains("/generated-sources/");
        }
    }

    static class ExcludeMapStructMappers implements ImportOption {
        private static final Pattern MAPPER_IMPL =
            Pattern.compile(".*/mapper/.*MapperImpl\\.class");
        @Override
        public boolean includes(Location location) {
            return !location.matches(MAPPER_IMPL);
        }
    }

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_must_not_depend_on_infrastructure =
        layeredArchitecture()
            .consideringAllDependencies()
            .layer("Domain").definedBy("com.example.domain..")
            .layer("Application").definedBy("com.example.application..")
            .layer("Infrastructure").definedBy("com.example.infrastructure..")
            .whereLayer("Domain").mayNotAccessAnyLayer()
            .whereLayer("Application").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Domain")
            .whereLayer("Infrastructure").mayOnlyAccessLayers(
                "Application", "Domain");
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `ImportOption.DoNotIncludeJars.class` also excludes Spring Framework classes from the analysis, which means rules like "no class may directly use `JdbcTemplate` in the domain layer" will silently pass even if a violation exists — the `JdbcTemplate` class itself is not in the analyzed set, so the import dependency cannot be detected. For detecting infrastructure-framework imports in the domain layer, use an explicit `noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("com.example.domain..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("org.springframework.jdbc..")` rule instead of relying on `layeredArchitecture()` checks for cross-JAR imports.

[community]

---

### 87. AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison` with `ignoringFields` and `ignoringFieldsMatchingRegexes` — Robust DTO Equality Without `equals()` Overrides [community]

AssertJ's `usingRecursiveComparison()` performs a deep field-by-field structural comparison without requiring `equals()` to be overridden on the compared objects — critical for JPA entities where `equals()` is based on database identity (primary key) rather than value equality, or for DTOs that are Lombok `@Data` classes where `equals()` is auto-generated but excludes certain fields. Chaining `.ignoringFields("id", "createdAt", "updatedAt")` excludes database-assigned and audit fields from the comparison, while `.ignoringFieldsMatchingRegexes(".*[Vv]ersion.*")` uses regex to ignore whole categories of implementation-detail fields by naming convention. This avoids the brittleness of comparing serialized JSON strings with `isEqualTo("""...""")` which breaks when Jackson reorders fields.

```java
@Test
void createProduct_returnsCorrectlyPopulatedDto() {
    var request = new CreateProductRequest(
        "Ergonomic Chair",
        BigDecimal.valueOf(349.99),
        "FURN",
        List.of("BLUE", "BLACK"));

    ProductDto result = productService.create(request);

    // Build expected value with null placeholders for DB-assigned fields
    ProductDto expected = new ProductDto(
        null,              // id assigned by DB — excluded from comparison
        "Ergonomic Chair",
        BigDecimal.valueOf(349.99),
        "FURN",
        List.of("BLUE", "BLACK"),
        null,              // createdAt — excluded
        null               // updatedAt — excluded
    );

    assertThat(result)
        .usingRecursiveComparison()
        .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt", "updatedAt")
        .ignoringFieldsMatchingRegexes(".*[Vv]ersion.*")
        .withStrictTypeChecking()
        .isEqualTo(expected);

    // Then separately assert excluded fields have meaningful values
    assertThat(result.id()).isPositive();
    assertThat(result.createdAt())
        .isNotNull()
        .isBefore(Instant.now().plusSeconds(5));
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `usingRecursiveComparison()` uses reflection to traverse all fields including private and inherited ones — when comparing large object graphs (e.g., an entity with lazy-loaded JPA collections), the comparison may inadvertently trigger Hibernate proxy initialization for lazily-loaded associations, causing `LazyInitializationException` if the comparison occurs outside a transaction. Scope recursive comparisons to DTOs (plain Java objects with no persistence proxies) rather than raw JPA entities; if you must compare entities, ensure the comparison happens within an active transaction or eagerly load all required associations before the assertion.

[community]

### 88. Mockito `ArgumentCaptor` with `@Captor` vs. `forClass` — Capturing Generic Arguments Without Unchecked-Cast Warnings [community]

`ArgumentCaptor.forClass(SomeClass.class)` produces an `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` warning when the captured type is generic (e.g., `List<Order>` captured as `List.class`) because the raw class token erases the generic type parameter. The idiomatic solution is `@Captor ArgumentCaptor<List<Order>> captor` as a field annotation — Mockito's annotation processor infers the full generic type from the field declaration, producing a properly typed captor with no cast warnings. For test methods that cannot use `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` (e.g., Spring Boot integration tests), `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` in `@BeforeEach` processes `@Captor` fields with the same type inference.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderNotifierTest {

    @Mock
    EmailClient emailClient;

    @Mock
    AuditLogger auditLogger;

    @InjectMocks
    OrderNotifier notifier;

    // Field annotation — full generic type inferred, no unchecked warning
    @Captor
    ArgumentCaptor<List<EmailMessage>> bulkEmailCaptor;

    @Captor
    ArgumentCaptor<AuditEvent<OrderStatus>> auditEventCaptor;

    @Test
    void notifyBulk_sendsCorrectEmailsAndAuditsTransition() {
        var orders = List.of(
            new Order("O-1", "user1@example.com"),
            new Order("O-2", "user2@example.com"));

        notifier.notifyStatusChange(orders, OrderStatus.SHIPPED);

        verify(emailClient).sendBulk(bulkEmailCaptor.capture());
        List<EmailMessage> sent = bulkEmailCaptor.getValue();
        assertThat(sent)
            .hasSize(2)
            .extracting(EmailMessage::to)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(
                "user1@example.com", "user2@example.com");

        verify(auditLogger).record(auditEventCaptor.capture());
        assertThat(auditEventCaptor.getValue().payload())
            .isEqualTo(OrderStatus.SHIPPED);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `@Captor` fields are reset between test methods by `MockitoExtension`, so capturing across multiple `verify()` calls within a single test method accumulates all captured values in `captor.getAllValues()` in invocation order — this is the intended behavior but surprises developers who expect `captor.getValue()` to return the last capture when a method was called multiple times. Always use `getAllValues()` when verifying a method called more than once, and assert with `containsExactly(...)` on the full list to validate the specific sequence rather than indexing with `get(0)`, `get(1)` which is fragile when call order changes.

[community]

### 89. WireMock Response Templating with `jsonPath` Helper — Dynamic Response Bodies Based on Request Content [community]

WireMock's Handlebars response templating engine provides a `jsonPath` helper that extracts values from a JSON request body and injects them into the response, enabling stateless stubs that mirror request data back in the response without requiring a separate stub per input value. This is invaluable for testing flows where the system under test sends a request and then processes the correlated response — a payment gateway stub that echoes the merchant reference and amount back in the authorization response allows a single stub to serve hundreds of different requests without explicit `stubFor` calls for each value combination.

```java
@RegisterExtension
static WireMockExtension wm = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
    .options(WireMockConfiguration.wireMockConfig()
        .dynamicPort()
        .extensions(new ResponseTemplateTransformer(true)))
    .build();

@BeforeEach
void stubPaymentGateway() {
    wm.stubFor(post(urlPathEqualTo("/payments/authorize"))
        .willReturn(aResponse()
            .withStatus(200)
            .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .withBody("""
                {
                  "authorizationId": "AUTH-{{randomValue type='UUID'}}",
                  "approvedAmount": {{jsonPath request.body '$.amount'}},
                  "currency": "{{jsonPath request.body '$.currency'}}",
                  "status": "APPROVED",
                  "merchantRef": "{{jsonPath request.body '$.merchantRef'}}"
                }
                """)
            .withTransformers("response-template")));
}

@Test
void authorizePayment_echoesMerchantRefAndAmount() {
    var response = paymentClient.authorize(
        new PaymentRequest(
            new BigDecimal("59.99"), "USD", "ORDER-42"));

    assertThat(response.approvedAmount())
        .isEqualByComparingTo("59.99");
    assertThat(response.merchantRef())
        .isEqualTo("ORDER-42");
    assertThat(response.authorizationId())
        .matches("AUTH-[0-9a-f-]{36}");
    // Always verify the request reached WireMock with expected structure
    wm.verify(postRequestedFor(urlPathEqualTo("/payments/authorize"))
        .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.amount"))
        .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.merchantRef")));
}
```

**Tradeoff:** WireMock response templating with `jsonPath` evaluates the path at stub-match time on the WireMock server, so failures in the path expression (e.g., a typo like `'$.merhantRef'`) silently produce an empty string in the response rather than a stub error — the test then fails with a confusing assertion mismatch rather than a clear "template evaluation error" message. Always add an explicit `wm.verify(postRequestedFor(...).withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.amount")))` assertion after the call to confirm the request reached WireMock with the expected structure, which surfaces path-expression bugs as a distinct verification failure rather than an assertion on the returned response body.

[community]

### 90. jqwik `@Property` with `@Provide` Named Arbitraries — Reusable Domain-Specific Generators [community]

jqwik's `@Provide` method annotation paired with `@ForAll @From("providerName")` allows teams to define named `Arbitrary<T>` factory methods once in a shared class or `@Group` and reference them by name in multiple `@Property` tests, avoiding copy-paste of complex generator chains across property tests. Domain-specific arbitraries like `validOrderId()`, `euroAmount()`, or `nonEmptyProductSku()` encode the valid-value contract of the domain model, making property tests self-documenting ("given any valid Euro amount, ...") and ensuring that the generator's constraints are maintained centrally when domain validation rules evolve.

```java
class PricingServiceProperties {

    PricingService pricingService = new PricingService();

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<BigDecimal> euroAmount() {
        // Domain rule: prices are 0.01 to 9999.99, exactly 2 decimal places
        return Arbitraries.bigDecimals()
            .between(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.01), BigDecimal.valueOf(9999.99))
            .ofScale(2);
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<String> validPromoCode() {
        return Arbitraries.strings()
            .alpha()
            .numeric()
            .ofMinLength(4)
            .ofMaxLength(12)
            .map(String::toUpperCase)
            .filter(s -> !s.isBlank());
    }

    @Property(tries = 500)
    void applyDiscount_neverExceedsOriginalPrice(
            @ForAll @From("euroAmount") BigDecimal price,
            @ForAll @IntRange(min = 0, max = 100) int discountPercent) {
        BigDecimal discounted =
            pricingService.applyDiscount(price, discountPercent);
        assertThat(discounted)
            .isLessThanOrEqualTo(price)
            .isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(BigDecimal.ZERO);
    }

    @Property(tries = 200)
    void applyPromoCode_alwaysProducesNonNegativePrice(
            @ForAll @From("euroAmount") BigDecimal price,
            @ForAll @From("validPromoCode") String promoCode) {
        BigDecimal result =
            pricingService.applyPromoCode(price, promoCode);
        assertThat(result).isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(BigDecimal.ZERO);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Named arbitraries via `@Provide` are resolved by method name string lookup at runtime — renaming the `@Provide` method without updating all `@From("oldName")` annotations causes a `JqwikException: No provider method found for 'oldName'` at test execution time, not at compile time. Teams using IntelliJ IDEA should install the jqwik plugin which adds compile-time validation of `@From` references; in projects without the plugin, enforce a naming convention (e.g., `@Provide` method name matches the domain type in camelCase: `euroAmount` for `BigDecimal` Euro prices) and add `@SuppressWarnings("unused")` on `@Provide` methods to prevent IDEs from suggesting removal of "unused" methods.

[community]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 43

**JUnit 6 `ClassOrderer.Default` on `@Nested` classes sorts by the Java simple class name — which for `@DisplayName`-annotated nested classes means the execution order differs from alphabetical display-name order shown in the IDE, causing CI suites to run nested classes in an unexpected sequence when relying on `Default` ordering for BDD-style tests** — A team adds `@TestClassOrder(ClassOrderer.Default.class)` expecting nested classes to execute in alphabetical order by their `@DisplayName("A. Create")`, `@DisplayName("B. Pay")`, `@DisplayName("C. Ship")` values. Locally the IDE shows them in the right order because it sorts by display name. But in CI the execution order is alphabetical by Java class name (`CreateOrder`, `PayOrder`, `ShipOrder`) which happens to match in this case — but if the Java names don't align with the display names ("WhenEmailTaken" vs "A. When email taken"), the ordering diverges silently. WHY: `ClassOrderer.Default` compares `testClass.getJavaClass().getSimpleName()`, not `testDescriptor.getDisplayName()` — there is no variant that sorts by `@DisplayName` string. Fix: always use explicit `@Order(1)`, `@Order(2)` annotations on nested classes that must execute in a specific sequence; never rely on naming coincidence.

**Mockito 5.21's auto-completed futures only apply to completely unstubbed methods — explicitly stubbing a `CompletableFuture`-returning method with `when(mock.op()).thenReturn(null)` re-introduces null return behavior, silently breaking callers that chain `.thenApply(...)` assuming the default non-null future** — A developer stubs `when(asyncService.fetchData()).thenReturn(null)` to simulate "no data" semantics, but the caller chains `.thenApply(f -> f.orElse(DEFAULT))` which throws `NullPointerException`. WHY: `thenReturn(null)` overrides Mockito's entire default answer — the `ReturnsEmptyValues` default applies only to completely unstubbed method invocations. Fix: use `thenReturn(CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null))` for "completed with null value" semantics, or `thenReturn(CompletableFuture.completedFuture(Optional.empty()))` when the return type is `CompletableFuture<Optional<T>>`.

**Testcontainers 2.0 module rename from `org.testcontainers:mysql` to `org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mysql` also changed the container class package — projects updating only the artifact ID in `build.gradle` will compile successfully (compatibility shim present in 2.0.0) but fail at runtime with `ClassNotFoundException` on environments that download fresh dependencies without the shim** — A team updates the BOM to 2.0 and renames the Gradle dependency. All tests compile and pass in CI where the old artifact is cached. On a new developer machine with a clean Gradle cache, every test fails with `ClassNotFoundException: org.testcontainers.containers.MySQLContainer`. WHY: The 2.0 migration guide lists both the artifact ID change and the package relocation as separate migration steps; the compatibility shim ships only in 2.0.0 and is removed in 2.1. Fix: perform a project-wide search-and-replace of `org.testcontainers.containers.*Container` imports to their new module-specific packages (`org.testcontainers.mysql.MySQLContainer`, `org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer`, etc.) as part of the same commit that updates the BOM version.

**`@GrpcTest` in Spring Boot 4.1 does not load `@ControllerAdvice` beans — only `@GrpcAdvice` annotated beans are picked up by the gRPC test slice, so teams that handle exceptions in a shared `@ControllerAdvice` believing it applies to both HTTP and gRPC will find that gRPC status-code mapping tests pass in `@GrpcTest` (the exception propagates uncaught) while the actual gRPC service returns `UNKNOWN` status in production** — A developer writes a catch-all `@ControllerAdvice` that maps `EntityNotFoundException` to `NOT_FOUND`. The `@WebMvcTest` passes because HTTP advice is loaded. The developer adds a `@GrpcTest` expecting the same handler and finds the test throws a raw `StatusRuntimeException` with code `INTERNAL` instead of `NOT_FOUND`. WHY: Spring gRPC's test slice uses a dedicated component-scan filter for `@GrpcAdvice` that is entirely separate from Spring MVC's `@ControllerAdvice` discovery. Fix: create a dedicated `@GrpcAdvice` class for gRPC status mapping even if it delegates to the same service-layer exception translator used by the `@ControllerAdvice`.

**AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields(...)` performs exact case-sensitive field name matching with no warning for non-existent field names — a typo like `.ignoringFields("UpdatedAt")` when the actual field is `updatedAt` silently leaves the field included in the comparison, causing a test to fail on the wrong field with a misleading "expected <null> but was <2026-05-14T...>" message that looks like a data-seeding problem rather than a field-name typo** — A developer expects `.ignoringFields("id", "createdAt", "UpdatedAt")` to exclude `updatedAt` from comparison. The test fails intermittently depending on clock skew because `updatedAt` is actually being compared. There is no `IllegalArgumentException` for non-existent field names. WHY: AssertJ's recursive comparison silently ignores unknown field names in `ignoringFields` to allow proactive exclusion of fields that may not exist in all types in a polymorphic comparison. Fix: after adding an `ignoringFields` entry, temporarily write a failing assertion targeting a known wrong value in that field to confirm it is actually excluded — if the outer assertion still passes, the field is being ignored; if it fails, a typo is the likely cause.

## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### 91. JUnit 6 `@ParameterizedClass` — Parameterizing an Entire Test Class Across Multiple Configurations [official]

JUnit 6 introduces `@ParameterizedClass`, which applies parameterization at the class level rather than at individual test methods. When a class is annotated with `@ParameterizedClass`, every test method inside it receives the same parameter values injected via constructor or field injection, allowing an entire suite of test methods to be replayed across a set of configurations — for example, all tests in a database repository test class run once per supported database dialect. The annotation accepts any JUnit argument source (e.g., `@MethodSource`, `@CsvSource`, `@EnumSource`) in the same way `@ParameterizedTest` does. Parameters are injected as constructor arguments by default; annotating a field with `@Inject` makes JUnit inject the argument directly into that field without a constructor change. This eliminates the anti-pattern of duplicating a large test class just to run it against two configurations and dramatically improves readability of cross-cutting scenario matrices.

```java
@ParameterizedClass
@MethodSource("databaseDialects")
class OrderRepositoryContractTest {

    // JUnit injects the argument directly into this field
    @Inject
    DatabaseDialect dialect;

    static Stream<DatabaseDialect> databaseDialects() {
        return Stream.of(DatabaseDialect.POSTGRES, DatabaseDialect.MYSQL,
                         DatabaseDialect.H2);
    }

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        // dialect is already set when @BeforeEach runs
        dataSource = DataSourceFactory.create(dialect);
        repository = new OrderRepository(dataSource);
    }

    @Test
    void save_thenFindById_roundTripsSuccessfully() {
        Order saved = repository.save(new Order("REF-001", Money.of(99, "EUR")));
        assertThat(repository.findById(saved.id()))
            .isPresent()
            .get()
            .extracting(Order::reference)
            .isEqualTo("REF-001");
    }

    @Test
    void findAll_returnsEmptyListWhenNoOrders() {
        assertThat(repository.findAll()).isEmpty();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@ParameterizedClass` multiplies the total test count by the number of argument rows — a class with 20 test methods and 5 dialect values produces 100 test nodes. Build time increases proportionally; use `@Disabled` on slow methods and limit `@MethodSource` to the minimal representative set needed for contract coverage, rather than including every available dialect just because the feature makes it easy to add more.

---

### 92. JUnit 6 `@ParameterizedTest` with `@ConvertWith` — Declarative Custom Argument Conversion [official]

`@ConvertWith` allows a test method parameter to declare its own conversion strategy independently of global implicit converters. Annotating a parameter with `@ConvertWith(MyConverter.class)` causes JUnit to call `MyConverter.convert(source, targetType)` for that argument before invoking the test method, which is especially useful when `@CsvSource` strings need to become domain value objects without modifying global Jackson or Spring `ConversionService` configuration. The converter must implement `TypedArgumentConverter<S, T>` (introduced in JUnit 6) or the legacy `ArgumentConverter` interface; `TypedArgumentConverter` carries source and target type metadata, enabling type-safe conversion and clear error messages when the conversion fails. This complements `@AggregateWith` (which combines all arguments into a single POJO) — use `@ConvertWith` for a single parameter needing a bespoke conversion, and `@AggregateWith` when the entire argument row maps to one domain object.

```java
// Custom converter: "EUR:99.99" -> Money
class MoneyConverter extends TypedArgumentConverter<String, Money> {
    protected MoneyConverter() {
        super(String.class, Money.class);
    }

    @Override
    protected Money convert(String source) throws ArgumentConversionException {
        String[] parts = source.split(":");
        if (parts.length != 2) {
            throw new ArgumentConversionException(
                "Expected format 'CURRENCY:AMOUNT', got: " + source);
        }
        try {
            return Money.of(new BigDecimal(parts[1]), parts[0]);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            throw new ArgumentConversionException("Invalid amount: " + parts[1], e);
        }
    }
}

@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({
    "EUR:0.01, EUR:100.00, false",
    "EUR:50.00, EUR:50.00, true",
    "EUR:100.01, EUR:100.00, true"
})
void isOverBudget_correctlyComparesMoneyValues(
        @ConvertWith(MoneyConverter.class) Money actual,
        @ConvertWith(MoneyConverter.class) Money budget,
        boolean expectedResult) {
    assertThat(budgetChecker.isOverBudget(actual, budget))
        .isEqualTo(expectedResult);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TypedArgumentConverter` performs conversion eagerly at framework entry before `@BeforeEach` runs — a converter that opens a database connection or reads a file per invocation will create N connections for N parameterized rows before any test teardown runs. Keep converters side-effect free and cheap; push any stateful setup into `@BeforeEach` instead.

---

### 93. Mockito 5.22 Kotlin Singleton Mocking with `mockKotlinObject` — Stubbing `object` Declarations in Unit Tests [official]

Mockito 5.22 introduces `mockKotlinObject(MyObject::class)`, which wraps Kotlin `object` singletons in a `MockedStatic`-style scoped mock. Because Kotlin `object` declarations compile to static final singleton instances, they were previously unmockable without PowerMock or heavy instrumentation. The new API intercepts calls on the singleton instance for the duration of the provided lambda scope and restores the original instance after the block, making it compatible with JUnit 5's `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` lifecycle. Combining `mockKotlinObject` with `whenever(MyObject.method()).thenReturn(...)` syntax from `mockito-kotlin` bridges the remaining gap between Kotlin idiomatic code and Mockito's Java-origin API. The feature is available only when `mockito-inline` (or its successor `mockito-subclass`) is on the classpath, and requires the corresponding Kotlin coroutines support module if the singleton function is a `suspend` function.

```kotlin
// Production code
object TaxCalculator {
    fun vatRate(country: CountryCode): BigDecimal =
        ExternalTaxRatesService.fetch(country)
}

// Test
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension::class)
class InvoiceServiceTest {

    @Test
    fun `calculateTotal uses injected vat rate for DE`() {
        mockKotlinObject(TaxCalculator::class) {
            whenever(TaxCalculator.vatRate(CountryCode.DE))
                .thenReturn(BigDecimal("0.19"))

            val invoice = InvoiceService().calculateTotal(
                listOf(LineItem("Widget", Money.of(100, "EUR"))),
                CountryCode.DE
            )

            assertThat(invoice.vatAmount)
                .isEqualByComparingTo(BigDecimal("19.00"))
        }
        // Original TaxCalculator.vatRate behavior is restored here
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `mockKotlinObject` relies on byte-buddy instrumentation at class-load time and is incompatible with GraalVM native image compilation — tests using it must be excluded from native test runs via `@DisabledInNativeImage`. Additionally, mocking Kotlin `object` singletons is a signal that the singleton is doing too much; treat persistent test usage of `mockKotlinObject` as a design smell and prefer injecting the dependency as a constructor parameter or function parameter instead.

---

### 94. Mockito `BDDMockito.will()` with Custom `Answer` — BDD-Style Stubbing of Side-Effect-Heavy Callbacks [community]

`BDDMockito.will(Answer<T>)` is the BDD counterpart to `Mockito.doAnswer(Answer<T>)`, enabling expressive given-style stubbing when the stub must produce a dynamic response or trigger a side effect — such as calling a capture callback, populating an `AtomicReference` passed as argument, or simulating an async notification. Unlike `BDDMockito.given(...).willReturn(...)` which returns a fixed value, `will(answer).given(mock).method(...)` allows the answer to inspect the actual `InvocationOnMock` and return a computed result, making it the idiomatic BDD choice when argument-dependent behavior is required. It has an identical execution model to `doAnswer` but reads better in the given/when/then test structure because the customization appears in the "given" block rather than splitting setup across `doAnswer` before `when()` calls. Teams migrating from classic Mockito to BDD style often overlook `will()` and continue using `doAnswer`, producing inconsistent style within the same test file.

```java
@Test
void processOrder_notifiesObserverWithComputedTotal() {
    // Arrange
    AtomicReference<Money> capturedTotal = new AtomicReference<>();
    OrderObserver mockObserver = mock(OrderObserver.class);

    will(invocation -> {
        // Dynamically inspect and record the argument
        Money total = invocation.getArgument(0, Money.class);
        capturedTotal.set(total);
        return null; // void method
    }).given(mockObserver).onOrderProcessed(any(Money.class));

    OrderProcessor processor = new OrderProcessor(mockObserver);

    // Act
    processor.process(List.of(
        new LineItem("Widget", Money.of(40, "EUR")),
        new LineItem("Gadget", Money.of(60, "EUR"))
    ));

    // Assert
    assertThat(capturedTotal.get())
        .isEqualByComparingTo(Money.of(100, "EUR"));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `will(answer).given(mock).method()` syntax requires the `BDDMockito` static import; mixing `BDDMockito.given` and `Mockito.doAnswer` in the same test file triggers Mockito's strict-stub checker to flag the doAnswer stub as potentially "unnecessary" even when it is intentional — standardize on `will()` throughout the file to avoid false strict-stub violations.

---

### 95. AssertJ `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly()` — Collecting All Assertion Failures Before Reporting [official]

`SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> { ... })` runs all assertions within the lambda and collects every failure instead of stopping at the first one, giving a complete picture of what is wrong in a single test run. Unlike wrapping a test class with `@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)` and injecting `SoftAssertions` as a parameter, `assertSoftly` is self-contained and requires no JUnit extension or class-level annotation — it is the preferred form for single test methods that need soft behavior without coupling the entire class to the extension. The collected failures are reported as a single `MultipleFailuresError` that lists each sub-failure with its index, assertion description, and stack trace, making it far easier to diagnose multiple related field mismatches in a DTO comparison than re-running the test repeatedly. `BDDSoftAssertions.thenSoftly()` is the BDD-flavored equivalent and replaces `assertThat` with `then` inside the lambda for teams following BDD naming conventions.

```java
@Test
void createOrder_responseBodyContainsAllExpectedFields() {
    OrderResponse response = orderService.createOrder(
        new CreateOrderRequest("CUST-1", List.of(
            new LineItemRequest("SKU-A", 2, Money.of(19.99, "EUR")),
            new LineItemRequest("SKU-B", 1, Money.of(5.00,  "EUR"))
        ))
    );

    SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {
        softly.assertThat(response.id()).as("order id").isNotNull();
        softly.assertThat(response.status()).as("status")
              .isEqualTo(OrderStatus.PENDING);
        softly.assertThat(response.total()).as("total")
              .isEqualByComparingTo(Money.of(44.98, "EUR"));
        softly.assertThat(response.lineItems()).as("line item count")
              .hasSize(2);
        softly.assertThat(response.createdAt()).as("createdAt")
              .isNotNull()
              .isBefore(Instant.now());
        softly.assertThat(response.customerId()).as("customerId")
              .isEqualTo("CUST-1");
    });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `assertSoftly` incurs a small performance cost because all lambdas are executed regardless of failures and the error list is assembled at the end; in micro-benchmark tests or tests with thousands of iterations this overhead is measurable. More importantly, soft assertions inside a loop (`for (var item : items) softly.assertThat(item).isNotNull()`) can produce hundreds of collected failures that scroll past the test output limit in CI — use `assertThat(items).doesNotContainNull()` for collection checks rather than per-element soft assertions.

---

### 96. AssertJ `AbstractIterableAssert.satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder()` — Order-Agnostic Element-Wise Predicate Assertions [official]

`satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(Consumer<T>... consumers)` verifies that a collection contains exactly the expected number of elements and that each element satisfies one consumer from the provided set, in any order. Unlike `containsExactlyInAnyOrder(...)` which relies on `equals`, this method accepts arbitrary `Consumer<T>` predicates — useful when the collection contains objects without well-defined equality or when fine-grained field-level checking is needed per element. Each consumer is matched to exactly one element; if two consumers match the same element (while another element goes unmatched), AssertJ reports an assignment failure with a clear diagnostic showing which consumers were unassigned. This is distinct from `allSatisfy(consumer)` (every element must satisfy the same single consumer) and `anySatisfy(consumer)` (at least one element satisfies the consumer); `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` is the right choice when every element must satisfy a distinct expectation.

```java
@Test
void findByOrderStatus_returnsOneOrderPerStatusCorrectly() {
    // Seed three orders with different statuses
    orderRepository.saveAll(List.of(
        Order.of("REF-1", OrderStatus.PENDING,  Money.of(10, "EUR")),
        Order.of("REF-2", OrderStatus.PAID,     Money.of(20, "EUR")),
        Order.of("REF-3", OrderStatus.SHIPPED,  Money.of(30, "EUR"))
    ));

    List<Order> results = orderRepository.findAll();

    assertThat(results)
        .hasSize(3)
        .satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(
            order -> assertThat(order)
                .extracting(Order::reference, Order::status)
                .containsExactly("REF-1", OrderStatus.PENDING),
            order -> assertThat(order)
                .extracting(Order::reference, Order::status)
                .containsExactly("REF-2", OrderStatus.PAID),
            order -> assertThat(order)
                .extracting(Order::reference, Order::status)
                .containsExactly("REF-3", OrderStatus.SHIPPED)
        );
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` uses a brute-force matching algorithm with O(n!) worst-case complexity to find a valid consumer-element assignment — for collections larger than ~10 elements this can make a failing assertion noticeably slow to evaluate because AssertJ must explore all permutations before concluding no valid assignment exists. Limit its use to small, well-bounded collections (typically 2-7 elements) and prefer `containsExactlyInAnyOrderElementsOf` with a custom comparator when the collection may grow unboundedly.

---

### 97. Spring Boot `@RestClientTest` with `MockRestServiceServer` — Testing `RestClient`/`RestTemplate` HTTP Clients in Isolation [official]

`@RestClientTest` is a Spring Boot test slice that auto-configures a `MockRestServiceServer` bound to all `RestTemplate` and `RestClient` beans in the application context, enabling HTTP client logic to be tested without a real network connection. The slice loads only the beans required by the specified client class — it excludes the full web layer, JPA repositories, and non-HTTP infrastructure — making it significantly faster than `@SpringBootTest`. Since Spring Boot 3.2, `RestClient` built via `RestClient.Builder` (auto-configured as `RestClientBuilder` bean) is also intercepted by `MockRestServiceServer` when using `@RestClientTest`, so teams migrating from `RestTemplate` to `RestClient` get the same mock behavior without changing their test setup. The `server.expect(...).andRespond(...)` API supports matching by URI, HTTP method, headers, and request body, and `server.verify()` at the end of the test confirms all expected interactions occurred.

```java
@RestClientTest(ProductCatalogClient.class)
class ProductCatalogClientTest {

    @Autowired
    private ProductCatalogClient client;

    @Autowired
    private MockRestServiceServer server;

    @Test
    void getProduct_returnsDeserializedProductOnSuccess() {
        server.expect(once(), requestTo("/products/SKU-42"))
              .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
              .andExpect(header(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT,
                                MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE))
              .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                  { "sku": "SKU-42", "name": "Widget", "price": 19.99 }
                  """, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        Product product = client.getProduct("SKU-42");

        assertThat(product.sku()).isEqualTo("SKU-42");
        assertThat(product.name()).isEqualTo("Widget");
        assertThat(product.price()).isEqualByComparingTo(new BigDecimal("19.99"));

        server.verify(); // all expected requests were made
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_throwsClientExceptionOn404() {
        server.expect(requestTo("/products/UNKNOWN"))
              .andRespond(withStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> client.getProduct("UNKNOWN"))
            .isInstanceOf(ProductNotFoundException.class);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockRestServiceServer` records expected requests in declaration order and verifies them in the same order by default — if the production code issues requests in a non-deterministic order (e.g., driven by a `ConcurrentHashMap` iteration), the test will fail intermittently. Use `MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(restTemplate).build(false)` with `ignoreExpectOrder(true)` to disable ordered matching, and verify only final outcomes via `server.verify()` counts rather than sequence-sensitive `expect(times(1))` chains.

---

### 98. Testcontainers `Network` with Multiple Containers — Simulating Service-to-Service Communication in Integration Tests [community]

Testcontainers `Network.newNetwork()` creates an isolated Docker bridge network that is shared among multiple `GenericContainer` instances, allowing containers to reference each other by their network alias rather than by host-mapped ports. This is essential when testing microservice interactions (e.g., an app container connecting to a database container via `jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/test`) because the internal service address is stable across test runs, unlike the ephemeral random host port. Both containers must call `.withNetwork(network)` and `.withNetworkAliases("alias")`, and the test must start them in dependency order. Implementing `Network` as a `@Container static` field alongside `@ClassRule` (JUnit 4) or using `@BeforeAll` (JUnit 5) ensures the network is created once per test class and destroyed via `try-with-resources` or the `AutoCloseable` contract when the last container referencing it stops.

```java
@Testcontainers
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest {

    static Network network = Network.newNetwork();

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withNetwork(network)
            .withNetworkAliases("db")
            .withDatabaseName("orders")
            .withUsername("test")
            .withPassword("test");

    @Container
    static GenericContainer<?> app =
        new GenericContainer<>("order-service:latest")
            .withNetwork(network)
            .withEnv("DB_URL",  "jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders")
            .withEnv("DB_USER", "test")
            .withEnv("DB_PASS", "test")
            .withExposedPorts(8080)
            .waitingFor(Wait.forHttp("/actuator/health")
                .forStatusCode(200)
                .withStartupTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60)));

    @Test
    void placeOrder_returns201WithOrderId() {
        String baseUrl = "http://localhost:" + app.getMappedPort(8080);
        given()
            .baseUri(baseUrl)
            .contentType(ContentType.JSON)
            .body("""
                { "customerId": "C1", "sku": "SKU-1", "qty": 2 }
                """)
        .when()
            .post("/orders")
        .then()
            .statusCode(201)
            .body("orderId", notNullValue());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Sharing a `Network` between a database container and an application container means both must start successfully before any test runs — if the application image is large or slow to initialize, the entire test class blocks on startup. Split heavy end-to-end tests into a dedicated `@Tag("integration")` source set and run them in a parallel Gradle subproject to avoid blocking fast unit test feedback.

---

### 99. Testcontainers `@DynamicPropertySource` with `@ServiceConnection` — Zero-Boilerplate Container Property Wiring [official]

Spring Boot 3.1+ recognizes `@ServiceConnection` on `@Container` fields and automatically derives the connection properties (`spring.datasource.url`, `spring.datasource.username`, etc.) from the container without requiring any `@DynamicPropertySource` method. The `ConnectionDetails` abstraction maps container-provided metadata to Spring Boot's connection properties using a `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory` SPI — one is bundled for every first-party Testcontainers module (`PostgreSQLContainer`, `RedisContainer`, `KafkaContainer`, etc.). This eliminates the entire `@DynamicPropertySource` boilerplate method that previously appeared in every `@DataJpaTest` or `@SpringBootTest` integration test, reduces the chance of typos in property key strings, and enables IDE auto-complete for supported container types. When a container type does not yet have a built-in factory, a custom `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory<C, D>` implementation can be registered via `spring.factories` to teach Spring Boot how to extract connection properties from that container type.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryIT {

    // @ServiceConnection eliminates the need for @DynamicPropertySource
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("orders_test");

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static KafkaContainer kafka =
        new KafkaContainer(DockerImageName.parse("confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0"));

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Autowired
    private KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    @Test
    void savedOrder_publishesOrderCreatedEvent() throws Exception {
        Order order = orderRepository.save(Order.of("REF-1", Money.of(50, "EUR")));
        // ... verify Kafka message via embedded consumer
        assertThat(order.id()).isNotNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@ServiceConnection` works only with container types that have a registered `ContainerConnectionDetailsFactory` — using a custom image name (e.g., `DockerImageName.parse("myregistry/postgres-custom:15")`) that does not pattern-match the default factory name prefix will silently skip wiring, producing `DataSourceProperties` with no URL set and a confusing `Cannot load driver class: null` error. Always verify wiring by logging `spring.datasource.url` in a `@BeforeAll` or by running with `--debug` once after adding a new `@ServiceConnection` container to confirm the factory activated.

---

### 100. Spring Boot `@JsonTest` with `JacksonTester` — Isolated JSON Serialization Contract Tests [official]

`@JsonTest` loads only the Jackson (or Gson/Jsonb) configuration from the application context — including custom `@JsonComponent` beans, `JacksonAutoConfiguration`, and `ObjectMapper` customizers — without starting the web server or loading JPA beans, making it the correct slice for testing that `@JsonProperty`, `@JsonSerialize`, `@JsonIgnore`, and custom serializers produce the exact JSON contract consumers depend on. `JacksonTester<T>` is auto-configured by the slice; calling `json.write(object)` returns a `JsonContent<T>` which supports AssertJ-integrated assertions via `hasJsonPath`, `extractingJsonPathStringValue`, and `isEqualToJson`. The same tester supports deserialization via `json.parseObject(content)` and round-trip testing via a single write-then-parse assertion. Using `@JsonTest` instead of manually constructing `ObjectMapper` in unit tests ensures the test uses the exact same `ObjectMapper` configuration (including any production `Module` registrations like `JavaTimeModule`) as the running application.

```java
@JsonTest
class OrderSummaryJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    private JacksonTester<OrderSummary> json;

    @Test
    void serializes_moneyAsNestedObject() throws Exception {
        OrderSummary summary = new OrderSummary(
            "ORD-123",
            Money.of(new BigDecimal("99.99"), "EUR"),
            Instant.parse("2026-05-14T10:00:00Z")
        );

        JsonContent<OrderSummary> content = json.write(summary);

        assertThat(content).hasJsonPathStringValue("$.orderId", "ORD-123");
        assertThat(content).extractingJsonPathNumberValue("$.total.amount")
            .isEqualTo(99.99);
        assertThat(content).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.total.currency")
            .isEqualTo("EUR");
        assertThat(content).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.createdAt")
            .isEqualTo("2026-05-14T10:00:00Z");
    }

    @Test
    void deserializes_roundTripsWithoutDataLoss() throws Exception {
        String json = """
            {"orderId":"ORD-456","total":{"amount":50.00,"currency":"USD"},
             "createdAt":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}
            """;
        OrderSummary parsed = this.json.parseObject(json);
        assertThat(parsed.orderId()).isEqualTo("ORD-456");
        assertThat(parsed.total()).isEqualByComparingTo(Money.of(50, "USD"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@JsonTest` loads `@JsonComponent` beans from the full application component scan by default — if a production `@JsonComponent` depends on a `@Service` or database-querying bean, the slice will fail with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`. Fix by adding `@Import(MyJsonComponent.class)` to the test and removing the `@JsonComponent` annotation from production code (making it a plain `@Component` that is only registered in the test), or by introducing a `@TestConfiguration` that provides the required dependency as a mock.

---

### 101. WireMock `stubFor` with `matchingJsonPath` and `equalToJson` — Request Body Matching in Contract Tests [community]

WireMock's `matchingJsonPath("$.field", equalTo("value"))` and `equalToJson(expectedBody)` request matchers enable precise HTTP request body assertions in stub definitions, which is crucial for contract testing scenarios where the downstream service must receive a correctly formed JSON payload. `matchingJsonPath` uses JSONPath expression syntax and supports the full set of WireMock value matchers (`equalTo`, `containing`, `matching`, `absent`) as the second argument — it evaluates only the specified path, making it resilient to additional fields in the actual request body. `equalToJson(body, IGNORE_ARRAY_ORDER, IGNORE_EXTRA_ELEMENTS)` performs a structural JSON comparison and is the right choice when the entire body must conform to a schema or contract, with `IGNORE_ARRAY_ORDER` handling non-deterministic JSON array serialization from `HashSet` or parallel streams. Combining both matchers with `and()` in a `MappingBuilder` chain creates layered validation: `matchingJsonPath` for critical business fields and `equalToJson` for overall structure.

```java
@WireMockTest
class PaymentGatewayClientTest {

    @Test
    void chargeCard_sendsCorrectlyStructuredPaymentRequest(WireMockRuntimeInfo wm) {
        stubFor(post(urlEqualTo("/v1/charges"))
            .withHeader("Content-Type",
                        containing(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE))
            .withHeader("Idempotency-Key", matching("[a-f0-9-]{36}"))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.amount",
                             equalTo("9999")))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.currency",
                             equalTo("EUR")))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.source",
                             absent().not())) // field must be present
            .willReturn(aResponse()
                .withStatus(200)
                .withHeader("Content-Type", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .withBody("""
                    {"id": "ch_abc123", "status": "succeeded"}
                    """)));

        PaymentClient client = new PaymentClient(wm.getHttpBaseUrl());
        ChargeResult result = client.charge(
            Money.of(99.99, "EUR"), CardToken.of("tok_visa"));

        assertThat(result.id()).isEqualTo("ch_abc123");
        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo(ChargeStatus.SUCCEEDED);
        verify(exactly(1), postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/v1/charges")));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `equalToJson` with `IGNORE_EXTRA_ELEMENTS` silently passes even when the client sends unexpected fields — a schema evolution bug where a field was renamed in the client but the test stub's `expected` body was not updated will go undetected. Use `equalToJson(body)` without `IGNORE_EXTRA_ELEMENTS` in contract tests where the client must send exactly the agreed fields, reserving the lenient mode only for exploratory or resilience tests where downstream schema drift is the scenario being tested.

---

### 102. ArchUnit `DependencyRule.onlyDependOn` with `allowedPackages` — Enforcing Microservice Boundary Compliance [community]

ArchUnit's `noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..internal..").should().beAccessedByClassesThat().resideOutsideOfPackage("..internal..")` pattern, combined with `ClassesThat.resideInAPackage` and `dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage` rules, implements a compile-time microservice boundary check that prevents cross-module internal API leakage without runtime enforcement. For multi-module Maven/Gradle projects, ArchUnit can be configured with `@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example")` to scan across module boundaries if the classpath includes all modules, making it possible to catch inadvertent dependencies on neighboring microservice internals that happen to be on the compile classpath. This is more precise than Gradle's `api` vs `implementation` scope because it can express rules about specific sub-packages (e.g., `..domain.model..` may only be accessed from `..application..` and `..adapters..`, never from another service's package). Combining layer rules with `FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule)` prevents regressions by locking known violations into a stored baseline, allowing teams to work down technical debt without new violations being introduced.

```java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example.orderservice")
class OrderServiceArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainMustNotDependOnAdapters =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage("..adapters..", "..infrastructure..")
            .because("Domain layer must be free of infrastructure concerns");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule internalPackagesMustNotLeakOutside =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideOutsideOfPackage("..orderservice..")
            .should().accessClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("..orderservice..internal..")
            .because("Internal packages are implementation details");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule commandHandlersMustBeInApplicationLayer =
        classes()
            .that().haveNameMatching(".*CommandHandler")
            .should().resideInAPackage("..application.command..")
            .andShould().notBePublic()
            .because("Command handlers are application-internal");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule layeredArchitectureRule = layeredArchitecture()
        .consideringAllDependencies()
        .layer("Domain").definedBy("..orderservice.domain..")
        .layer("Application").definedBy("..orderservice.application..")
        .layer("Adapters").definedBy("..orderservice.adapters..")
        .whereLayer("Domain").mayNotAccessAnyLayer()
        .whereLayer("Application").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Domain")
        .whereLayer("Adapters").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Application", "Domain");
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@AnalyzeClasses` scanning the entire `com.example` package in a monorepo with 30 modules causes ArchUnit to import hundreds of thousands of classes at test startup — on some machines this takes 30-60 seconds, turning architecture tests into a build bottleneck. Scope `@AnalyzeClasses` to the specific module's top-level package and use `importOptions = {DoNotIncludeTests.class, DoNotIncludeJars.class}` to reduce the import set; run architecture tests in a dedicated `verificationTest` source set that is skipped during normal development builds and only runs in CI.

---

### 103. Spring Boot `@DataJpaTest` with `replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE` and Testcontainers — Real-Database JPA Slice Tests [community]

By default `@DataJpaTest` replaces the configured `DataSource` with an in-memory H2 database, which masks database-specific SQL dialect issues — native queries using PostgreSQL-specific syntax (`JSONB`, `RETURNING`, array operators) silently fail or behave differently on H2. Adding `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)` disables this substitution and uses the `DataSource` configured by `@DynamicPropertySource` or `@ServiceConnection`, enabling the JPA slice to run against the real database engine from a Testcontainers container while still limiting the Spring context to only JPA infrastructure beans. This combines the speed advantage of the slice (no web layer, no Kafka, no other infrastructure) with database dialect accuracy, and is the recommended approach for teams who discovered H2 compatibility mode was masking production query failures. The combination `@DataJpaTest` + `replace = NONE` + `@ServiceConnection` is the canonical pattern in Spring Boot 3.1+.

```java
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderJpaRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("orders_test")
            .withReuse(true); // reuse across test runs for speed

    @Autowired
    private TestEntityManager entityManager;

    @Autowired
    private OrderJpaRepository repository;

    @Test
    void findByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc_usesIndexAndReturnsLatestFirst() {
        Instant t1 = Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        Instant t2 = Instant.parse("2026-06-01T00:00:00Z");
        entityManager.persistAndFlush(Order.of("C1", "REF-1", t1));
        entityManager.persistAndFlush(Order.of("C1", "REF-2", t2));
        entityManager.clear();

        List<Order> results = repository.findByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc("C1");

        assertThat(results)
            .extracting(Order::reference)
            .containsExactly("REF-2", "REF-1"); // latest first
    }

    @Test
    void nativeQuery_jsonbContainsFilter_worksOnPostgres() {
        // This test would silently fail or error on H2
        entityManager.persistAndFlush(Order.withMetadata("C2", "{\"tier\":\"gold\"}"));
        entityManager.clear();

        List<Order> goldOrders = repository.findByMetadataContaining("gold");
        assertThat(goldOrders).hasSize(1);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@Container static ... withReuse(true)` keeps the Postgres container alive between JVM runs by fingerprinting the container config — this dramatically speeds up local development cycles but means database state from a previous test run persists if `@Transactional` rollback does not clean up all side effects. Always pair `withReuse(true)` with a Flyway or Liquibase `cleanBeforeRun` property set to `true` in the test `application.properties` to ensure schema drift between version upgrades is caught rather than silently inherited.

---

### 104. Awaitility `await().during()` — Asserting That a Condition Remains True Over a Time Window [community]

Awaitility's `await().during(Duration, TimeUnit).atMost(Duration, TimeUnit).until(callable)` — more precisely expressed as `await().during(200, MILLISECONDS).atMost(2, SECONDS).until(() -> !queue.isEmpty())` — evaluates the condition continuously for the specified duration and fails if the condition becomes false at any point during that window. This is the inversion of the more common `await().atMost(...)` which succeeds on the first true evaluation: `during()` is used to verify stability rather than eventual occurrence, such as confirming that a cache entry is not evicted prematurely, a rate limiter does not allow more than N calls in a window, or a circuit breaker stays open for its configured duration. The less-known companion `await().pollDelay().pollInterval()` configuration is essential when using `during()` — without setting a short `pollInterval` (e.g., 10ms), Awaitility defaults to 100ms polling which means a 200ms stability window gets only 2 evaluations and short-lived violations are missed entirely.

```java
@Test
void rateLimiter_blocksRequestsBeyondAllowedRateForFullWindow() {
    RateLimiter limiter = RateLimiter.of("test",
        RateLimiterConfig.custom()
            .limitForPeriod(5)
            .limitRefreshPeriod(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
            .timeoutDuration(Duration.ZERO)
            .build());

    AtomicInteger permitsAcquired = new AtomicInteger(0);

    // Consume the full permit budget
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        limiter.acquirePermission();
        permitsAcquired.incrementAndGet();
    }

    // Assert the limiter stays exhausted for the full window
    await()
        .pollDelay(Duration.ZERO)
        .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(10))
        .during(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .atMost(1200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .until(() -> !limiter.acquirePermission()); // must stay false (blocked)

    assertThat(permitsAcquired.get()).isEqualTo(5);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `await().during(...)` keeps the test thread alive for at least the `during` duration regardless of the outcome — a 500ms stability window adds a minimum 500ms to each test that uses it, which compounds badly across large test suites. Reserve `during()`-based assertions for tests that explicitly verify temporal guarantees (rate limiters, circuit breakers, TTL caches); for all other async tests where eventual completion is what matters, use `await().atMost(...)` only.

---

### 105. JUnit 6 `@TempDir` with `@TempDir(cleanup = ON_SUCCESS)` — Preserving Test Artifacts for Debugging Failures [official]

JUnit 6's `@TempDir` annotation injects a `Path` or `File` pointing to a fresh temporary directory created before the test and deleted after it, providing file-system isolation between tests without manual directory management. In JUnit 6, the `cleanup` attribute was added to `@TempDir`: `cleanup = CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS` deletes the directory only when the test passes, leaving it intact on failure so that log files, output artifacts, and intermediate results are available for debugging. `CleanupMode.NEVER` preserves the directory unconditionally (useful during active development to inspect outputs), while the default `CleanupMode.ALWAYS` (equivalent to the JUnit 5 behavior) always deletes. When `@TempDir` is declared as a static field with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`, the same directory is shared across all test methods in the class — a useful pattern for sequential pipeline tests where each method processes the output of the previous one, but a footgun if two methods write the same filename.

```java
@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)
class ReportGeneratorTest {

    // Shared across all tests; preserved on failure for debugging
    @TempDir(cleanup = CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS)
    static Path reportDir;

    @Test
    @Order(1)
    void generateCsvReport_createsFileWithHeader() throws Exception {
        ReportGenerator generator = new ReportGenerator(reportDir);
        generator.generateCsv(sampleData());

        Path csvFile = reportDir.resolve("report.csv");
        assertThat(csvFile).exists();
        assertThat(Files.readAllLines(csvFile).getFirst())
            .isEqualTo("id,reference,total,status");
    }

    @Test
    @Order(2)
    void generatePdfReport_embedsCsvData() throws Exception {
        // Relies on the CSV produced by Order(1)
        Path csvFile = reportDir.resolve("report.csv");
        assumeTrue(Files.exists(csvFile), "CSV prerequisite not generated");

        ReportGenerator generator = new ReportGenerator(reportDir);
        generator.generatePdf(csvFile);

        assertThat(reportDir.resolve("report.pdf"))
            .exists()
            .isRegularFile();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS` leaks temporary directories on CI when tests fail — in a busy pipeline running thousands of tests per day, failed tests that write large binary artifacts (PDFs, logs, binary blobs) to `@TempDir` locations will accumulate gigabytes of undiscarded temp files and eventually fill the CI worker disk. Mitigate by setting the `junit.jupiter.tempdir.scope` to `global` in CI properties and pointing `java.io.tmpdir` to an ephemeral path that CI infrastructure cleans between job runs, rather than the default OS temp directory.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 45

**JUnit 6 `@ParameterizedClass` with `@BeforeEach` and non-static `@Container` fields causes a new container instance per parameterized invocation — teams expecting the container to be shared across all parameterized runs of the class are surprised when 5 dialect values spawn 5 separate database containers in parallel, exhausting Docker socket connections and hitting Docker Desktop's default container limit** — A team annotates their test class with `@ParameterizedClass @MethodSource("dialects")` and adds `@Container PostgreSQLContainer postgres` as an instance field. Five dialect values spawn five postgres containers simultaneously. WHY: `@ParameterizedClass` creates a new test class instance per argument row, and `@Container` on an instance field follows the JUnit test lifecycle — a new `GenericContainer` object per instance means Testcontainers starts a new container per parameterized row. Fix: declare the `@Container` field as `static` so it is shared across all parameterized class instances, or use `@Container static Map<Dialect, GenericContainer> containers` with one pre-started container per dialect.

**Mockito `BDDMockito.given(mock.voidMethod()).willDoNothing()` does not compile for void methods — the correct BDD idiom is `willDoNothing().given(mock).voidMethod()` (note the reversed order), which is the opposite of the non-void BDD stubbing syntax `given(mock.nonVoidMethod()).willReturn(value)`, and this syntactic asymmetry causes teams to accidentally call the real method by writing the wrong order** — A developer writes `given(emailService.sendWelcome(any())).willDoNothing()` believing it suppresses the real email call. Because `sendWelcome` is void, Mockito actually calls the real method during the `given(...)` argument evaluation before the stub is registered. WHY: Java evaluates method arguments before passing them to `given()`, so a real void method call occurs inside the `given()` parentheses. The reversed `willDoNothing().given(mock).method()` syntax avoids this by setting up the answer first, then binding it during a synthetic call that does not invoke the real method. Fix: always use `willDoNothing().given(mock).method(args)` — never `given(mock.voidMethod()).willDoNothing()` — for void method stubbing.

**AssertJ `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder` with lambda consumers that themselves throw checked exceptions requires wrapping in `ThrowableAssert.catchThrowable` or declaring the consumer with `ThrowingConsumer` from AssertJ — plain `Consumer<T>` lambdas cannot throw checked exceptions, silently swallowing the checked exception as an unchecked wrapper and causing an obscure `AssertionError: consumers threw unexpected exceptions` message rather than the actual cause** — A developer writes `satisfiesExactlyInAnyOrder(order -> { assertThat(orderRepository.findById(order.id())).isPresent(); })` where `findById` throws `IOException`. The lambda compiles (IOException is swallowed by the AssertJ infrastructure) but at runtime the test fails with a misleading error. WHY: `Consumer<T>` is a functional interface whose `accept` method does not declare checked exceptions; AssertJ catches the wrapped runtime exception internally and surfaces it as an assertion configuration error. Fix: cast or declare the consumer as `ThrowingConsumer<T>` (AssertJ's checked-exception-aware variant) which properly propagates checked exceptions as assertion failures.

**Spring Boot `@RestClientTest` does not auto-configure `RestClient.Builder` beans created via `new RestClient.Builder()` — only `RestClient.Builder` beans obtained from the auto-configured `RestClientBuilder` bean are intercepted by `MockRestServiceServer`, so teams that inject `RestClient.Builder` via constructor but instantiate it manually in production code will find their mock server expectations are never matched** — A production `ProductCatalogClient` has `@Autowired RestClient.Builder builder` in the constructor. Tests pass in `@WebMvcTest` but fail in `@RestClientTest` with `SocketTimeoutException` against `localhost:0`. WHY: Spring Boot's `MockRestServiceServer` is wired to the auto-configured `RestClientBuilder` bean by `RestClientBuilderCustomizer`; a manually instantiated `new RestClient.Builder()` bypasses this customizer entirely and creates a real HTTP client. Fix: always obtain `RestClient.Builder` by injection (`@Autowired`) rather than instantiation; if the client must create its own builder, inject `RestClient.Builder.newInstance()` via a `@Bean` factory so the mock infrastructure can apply its customizer.

**Testcontainers `Network.newNetwork()` declared as a static field without explicit `@AfterAll` cleanup leaks the Docker network when JUnit's `@Container` lifecycle does not call `network.close()` — after several test runs in the same JVM (e.g., Gradle test worker reuse), the Docker daemon accumulates orphan networks and eventually rejects new network creation with `failed to allocate gateway IP: address already in use`** — A CI pipeline reuses JVM workers across test classes. After 50 test classes each creating a `Network.newNetwork()`, the Docker daemon has 50 orphan networks and blocks the 51st with an IP exhaustion error. WHY: `@Container` manages container lifecycle (start/stop) but not `Network` lifecycle — `Network` is just a plain object and Testcontainers only garbage-collects containers, not networks. Fix: declare `static Network network = Network.newNetwork()` with `@AfterAll static void tearDownNetwork() { network.close(); }` in every test class, or use the `@RegisterExtension`-based `NetworkResource` wrapper that implements `CloseableResource` and is cleaned up by JUnit's `ExtensionContext.Store`.

### Pattern 106 — JUnit 5 `ExtensionContext.Store` with `CloseableResource` — Auto-Cleanup of Extension-Managed Resources [official]

JUnit 5's `ExtensionContext.Store` provides a key-value map scoped to a test's lifecycle that automatically calls `CloseableResource.close()` on stored values when the test, method, or class scope closes. Extensions that manage expensive resources — database connections, thread pools, mock servers — should store them in the appropriate `Store` scope rather than using static fields or `@AfterAll` hooks, because `Store` cleanup is guaranteed by the JUnit framework even when exceptions occur during `@BeforeEach` or mid-test. The `ExtensionContext.Namespace` prevents key collisions between unrelated extensions sharing the same `Store`. Storing in `getStore(GLOBAL)` instead of `getStore(namespace)` is a deliberate pattern for truly singleton resources (e.g., a Docker network) that must outlive all tests in a JVM run and be cleaned up only after the last test class finishes.

```java
public class ManagedServerExtension
        implements BeforeAllCallback, AfterAllCallback {

    private static final Namespace NS =
            Namespace.create(ManagedServerExtension.class);
    private static final String KEY = "server";

    @Override
    public void beforeAll(ExtensionContext ctx) throws Exception {
        EmbeddedServer server = EmbeddedServer.start();
        // Stored value implements CloseableResource → closed by JUnit on scope exit
        ctx.getStore(NS).put(KEY, (CloseableResource) server::stop);
        ctx.getStore(NS).put("port", server.port());
    }

    @Override
    public void afterAll(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        // Explicit retrieval proves the resource is accessible to the test class
        int port = ctx.getStore(NS).get("port", Integer.class);
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(getClass()).info("Server ran on port {}", port);
        // CloseableResource.close() is called automatically after this method
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ExtensionContext.Store` cleanup order is not guaranteed when multiple extensions each register `CloseableResource` values in the same scope; if one resource depends on another being alive during its close callback (e.g., a metrics reporter that flushes to a database whose pool is also stored in the same scope), silent data loss occurs. Enforce ordering by nesting resources: the outer resource's `CloseableResource.close()` explicitly closes the inner resource before returning, so the lifecycle chain is explicit rather than JUnit-order-dependent.

### Pattern 107 — Mockito `mockConstruction()` with `MockInitializer` — Stubbing `new` Expressions in Legacy Code [official]

Mockito's `mockConstruction(Type.class, init)` intercepts every `new Type(...)` call within the try-with-resources scope, replacing the constructed instance with a configured mock and calling the `MockInitializer` callback with the mock and the `MockedConstruction.Context` (which exposes the constructor arguments). This is the canonical escape hatch for legacy code that instantiates dependencies inline with `new` rather than injecting them, making the code otherwise untestable without refactoring. The `context.arguments()` list provides the exact constructor arguments so the initializer can apply conditional stubbing based on what the production code actually passed. Each distinct construction call produces its own mock instance, and `mockConstruction.constructed()` returns the ordered list of all mocks created during the scope.

```java
@Test
void processPayment_retriesOnNetworkError_thenSucceeds() {
    AtomicInteger callCount = new AtomicInteger();

    try (MockedConstruction<PaymentGatewayClient> mocked =
             mockConstruction(PaymentGatewayClient.class, (mock, ctx) -> {
                 // ctx.arguments() == [apiKey, timeoutMillis]
                 String apiKey = (String) ctx.arguments().get(0);
                 assertThat(apiKey).startsWith("pk_");

                 when(mock.charge(any())).thenAnswer(inv -> {
                     if (callCount.incrementAndGet() < 2) {
                         throw new NetworkException("timeout");
                     }
                     return ChargeResult.success("ch_123");
                 });
             })) {

        PaymentService service = new PaymentService("pk_live_secret");
        ChargeResult result = service.processPayment(Money.of(100, "USD"));

        assertThat(result.chargeId()).isEqualTo("ch_123");
        assertThat(mocked.constructed()).hasSize(1);
        verify(mocked.constructed().get(0), times(2)).charge(any());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `mockConstruction` is thread-local: the interception applies only to the thread that called `mockConstruction()`, so if the production code under test spawns child threads or uses virtual threads that call `new PaymentGatewayClient(...)`, those constructions are not intercepted and a real instance is created instead. In virtual-thread-heavy code where `new` calls occur inside submitted tasks, restructure the test to use a factory supplier injected via constructor rather than relying on `mockConstruction`.

### Pattern 108 — AssertJ 4.0 `assertThat(record).isEqualByComparingTo()` with `isRecord()` and `isSealed()` — Native Java 17+ Type Assertions [official]

AssertJ 4.0 (Java 17 minimum) adds `isRecord()`, `isSealed()`, `isPermittedSubclassOf(Class)`, and `hasRecordComponents(String...)` as first-class assertion methods on `AbstractClassAssert`, enabling architecture and type-contract tests that previously required reflection. `isRecord()` asserts that a class is a Java record without needing `assertThat(MyRecord.class.isRecord()).isTrue()` — the failure message names the actual class and explains the assertion semantics. `hasRecordComponents("id", "name", "price")` asserts that a record declares exactly those components in that order, catching accidental component reordering in records used as API types where component order determines constructor argument order and CSV/JSON mapping.

```java
// Architecture test: all DTOs in the api.dto package must be records
@Test
void allApiDtos_areRecords() {
    Reflections reflections = new Reflections("com.example.api.dto");
    Set<Class<?>> dtoClasses = reflections.getTypesAnnotatedWith(ApiDto.class);

    for (Class<?> dtoClass : dtoClasses) {
        assertThat(dtoClass)
            .as("DTO class %s must be a record for immutability", dtoClass.getSimpleName())
            .isRecord();
    }
}

// Contract test: OrderSummary record has stable component order for JSON mapping
@Test
void orderSummaryRecord_hasStableComponentOrder() {
    assertThat(OrderSummary.class)
        .isRecord()
        .hasRecordComponents("orderId", "customerId", "totalAmount", "status", "createdAt");
}

// Sealed hierarchy test: Shape hierarchy is complete and sealed
@Test
void shapeHierarchy_isSealedWithExpectedSubtypes() {
    assertThat(Shape.class).isSealed();
    assertThat(Circle.class).isPermittedSubclassOf(Shape.class);
    assertThat(Rectangle.class).isPermittedSubclassOf(Shape.class);
    assertThat(Triangle.class).isPermittedSubclassOf(Shape.class);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `hasRecordComponents` checks component names and order but not component types — a refactoring that changes `long id` to `UUID id` passes the assertion while breaking JSON serialization contracts. Pair `hasRecordComponents` with a `@JsonTest` round-trip test or a `usingRecursiveComparison` assertion on a deserialized instance to also verify type compatibility.
