### Pattern 136 — JUnit 5 `@RegisterExtension` with `ParameterResolver` — Injecting Domain Fixtures Directly into Test Methods [official]

When a test suite needs a shared but per-invocation fixture (e.g., a pre-populated `OrderFixture` object), implementing `ParameterResolver` and registering it with `@RegisterExtension` lets JUnit inject the fixture as a method parameter. This is more composable than a `@BeforeEach` field assignment because extensions can be declared on a field and reused across multiple test classes by inheritance, and the fixture's lifecycle is explicitly tied to the extension's `supportsParameter` / `resolveParameter` contract.

```java
// Extension — resolves OrderFixture parameters
class OrderFixtureExtension implements ParameterResolver {

    @Override
    public boolean supportsParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        return pc.getParameter().getType().equals(OrderFixture.class);
    }

    @Override
    public Object resolveParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        return OrderFixture.builder()
            .withDefaultCustomer()
            .withLineItems(3)
            .build();
    }
}

// Test class — no @BeforeEach boilerplate
class OrderServiceTest {

    @RegisterExtension
    static final OrderFixtureExtension FIXTURES = new OrderFixtureExtension();

    @Test
    void applyDiscount_reducesLineItemPrices(OrderFixture fixture) {
        Order order = fixture.order();
        discountService.apply(order, Discount.PERCENTAGE_10);
        assertThat(order.totalPrice())
            .isLessThan(fixture.originalTotalPrice());
    }

    @Test
    void addLineItem_increasesCount(OrderFixture fixture) {
        int before = fixture.order().lineItemCount();
        fixture.order().addLineItem(new LineItem("SKU-X", 1, Money.of(9_99)));
        assertThat(fixture.order().lineItemCount()).isEqualTo(before + 1);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `static` registration means the extension is constructed once per class; if the extension holds mutable state the same instance is shared across all test methods in the class. For per-method isolation, declare the field as an instance (non-`static`) field — JUnit then constructs a fresh extension for every test method, which is safer but slightly slower due to object creation overhead.

### Pattern 137 — AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields(...)` — Deep Equality Without `equals()` [official]

`usingRecursiveComparison()` compares two object graphs field-by-field without relying on `equals()` implementations. This is invaluable when testing JPA entities (which often compare only by ID), DTOs received from Jackson (which may lack `equals()`), or generated protobuf classes. `ignoringFields("id", "createdAt")` strips volatile fields from the comparison so tests do not break on auto-generated values.

```java
@Test
void createProduct_returnsExpectedDto() {
    CreateProductRequest req = new CreateProductRequest("Widget", BigDecimal.valueOf(19.99), "GADGET");

    ProductDto result = productService.create(req);

    ProductDto expected = new ProductDto(
        null,          // id — will be ignored
        "Widget",
        BigDecimal.valueOf(19.99),
        "GADGET",
        null           // createdAt — will be ignored
    );

    assertThat(result)
        .usingRecursiveComparison()
        .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt")
        .isEqualTo(expected);

    // Assert the volatile fields separately, just their presence
    assertThat(result.id()).isNotNull();
    assertThat(result.createdAt()).isBeforeOrEqualTo(Instant.now());
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Recursive comparison traverses the full object graph including nested collections. For large entity graphs this can be slow and produce enormous failure messages. Scope the comparison with `.comparingOnlyFields("name", "price", "category")` to limit depth, or combine `usingRecursiveComparison()` with `withStrictTypeChecking()` (AssertJ 3.21+) to catch type mismatches that a lenient comparison would silently pass.

### Pattern 138 — Mockito `mockConstruction` — Controlling `new` Operator Results in Legacy Code [official]

`Mockito.mockConstruction(Cls.class, mockInitializer)` intercepts every call to `new Cls(...)` inside the try-with-resources block and returns a configured mock. This enables testing of code that hardcodes `new` calls that cannot be refactored (e.g., legacy SDK clients, third-party classes with no interface), without requiring PowerMock or byte-buddy agent hacks beyond Mockito's inline mock-maker.

```java
@Test
void sendNotification_callsEmailClientWithCorrectAddress() {
    String expectedRecipient = "user@example.com";

    try (MockedConstruction<SmtpEmailClient> mocked =
             mockConstruction(SmtpEmailClient.class, (mock, ctx) -> {
                 // ctx.arguments() gives constructor args — assert or configure here
                 assertThat(ctx.arguments()).containsExactly("smtp.example.com", 587);
                 when(mock.send(any())).thenReturn(true);
             })) {

        notificationService.notify(expectedRecipient, "Welcome!");

        // Verify the mock that was constructed
        SmtpEmailClient constructed = mocked.constructed().get(0);
        ArgumentCaptor<EmailMessage> captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(EmailMessage.class);
        verify(constructed).send(captor.capture());
        assertThat(captor.getValue().to()).isEqualTo(expectedRecipient);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `mockConstruction` is thread-local: it only intercepts `new` calls on the same thread that opened the try block. Code that delegates construction to a thread pool or a `CompletableFuture` will not see the interception. In those cases restructure the code to accept the dependency via a factory interface, which is both testable without byte-buddy trickery and architecturally cleaner.

### Pattern 139 — JUnit 5 `@ParameterizedClass` — Running All Tests in a Class with Multiple Input Sets [official]

JUnit 6.0 introduced `@ParameterizedClass`, which applies parameterization at the class level rather than the method level. Each `@MethodSource` (or `@CsvSource`) entry instantiates the class with different constructor arguments and runs all `@Test` methods within it. This is ideal for testing a service against multiple backend configurations (e.g., H2 vs. PostgreSQL) or a codec against multiple encoding strategies without duplicating the entire test class.

```java
@ParameterizedClass
@MethodSource("compressionAlgorithms")
class CompressionCodecTest {

    static Stream<Arguments> compressionAlgorithms() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of("gzip",    GzipCodec::new),
            Arguments.of("deflate", DeflateCodec::new),
            Arguments.of("zstd",    ZstdCodec::new)
        );
    }

    private final String algorithmName;
    private final CompressionCodec codec;

    CompressionCodecTest(String algorithmName,
                         Supplier<CompressionCodec> factory) {
        this.algorithmName = algorithmName;
        this.codec = factory.get();
    }

    @Test
    void roundTrip_preservesContent() {
        byte[] original = "Hello, World!".repeat(100).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        byte[] compressed   = codec.compress(original);
        byte[] decompressed = codec.decompress(compressed);
        assertThat(decompressed).isEqualTo(original);
    }

    @Test
    void compress_reducesSize() {
        byte[] input      = new byte[10_000];
        Arrays.fill(input, (byte) 'A');
        byte[] compressed = codec.compress(input);
        assertThat(compressed.length).isLessThan(input.length);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@ParameterizedClass` is a JUnit 6.0+ feature; projects on JUnit 5.x must instead use `@ParameterizedTest` at the method level or a custom `@ExtendWith` that emulates the behaviour. When upgrading, verify that `@BeforeEach` and `@AfterEach` methods still run correctly per parameterized instance — JUnit creates a new instance of the class for each parameter row, so state is not shared across rows unless fields are declared `static`.

---

### Pattern 140 — Testcontainers `Network` with Aliases — Multi-Container DNS Resolution in Integration Tests [official]

When an integration test requires two containers to talk to each other (e.g., a microservice container calling a Postgres container), both containers must share a Docker `Network` and the calling container must reference the target by its network alias rather than `localhost`. `Network.newNetwork()` creates a user-defined bridge network; `.withNetworkAliases("postgres")` registers the DNS name that the first container uses to reach the second.

```java
@Testcontainers
class MicroserviceIntegrationTest {

    static final Network NETWORK = Network.newNetwork();

    @Container
    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> POSTGRES =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withNetwork(NETWORK)
            .withNetworkAliases("postgres");

    @Container
    static final GenericContainer<?> APP =
        new GenericContainer<>(DockerImageName.parse("myapp:latest"))
            .withNetwork(NETWORK)
            .withExposedPorts(8080)
            .withEnv("DB_URL", "jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/test")
            .withEnv("DB_USER", POSTGRES.getUsername())
            .withEnv("DB_PASS", POSTGRES.getPassword())
            .dependsOn(POSTGRES)
            .waitingFor(Wait.forHttp("/actuator/health").forStatusCode(200));

    @Test
    void healthEndpoint_returnsUp() {
        String appHost = APP.getHost();
        int    appPort = APP.getMappedPort(8080);
        given()
            .baseUri("http://" + appHost + ":" + appPort)
            .get("/actuator/health")
            .then()
            .statusCode(200)
            .body("status", equalTo("UP"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Containers sharing a user-defined network are isolated from other test networks; `Network.newNetwork()` creates a new bridge per test class, which can result in many bridge networks if many classes run in parallel. Use the singleton pattern (static field) and share a single `Network` instance across all containers in the same test module to reduce Docker resource consumption. Also note that `POSTGRES.getUsername()` and `getPassword()` are evaluated after container startup — if `APP` starts before `POSTGRES` is healthy, it receives the correct credentials but cannot yet connect. The `.dependsOn(POSTGRES)` call ensures startup ordering.

### Pattern 141 — AssertJ `CompletableFuture` Assertions — `succeedsWithin` and `failsWithin` [official]

AssertJ 3.27+ provides `succeedsWithin(Duration, InstanceOfAssertFactory)` and `failsWithin(Duration)` on `AbstractFutureAssert`, replacing the antipattern of calling `future.get()` in a test and wrapping it in a try-catch. These methods block for at most the given duration, then fail with a descriptive message if the future has not completed or completed with the wrong outcome.

```java
@Test
void processAsync_completesWithinTimeout() throws Exception {
    CompletableFuture<ProcessingResult> future =
        asyncProcessor.processAsync(largePayload());

    assertThat(future)
        .succeedsWithin(Duration.ofSeconds(5), InstanceOfAssertFactories.type(ProcessingResult.class))
        .satisfies(result -> {
            assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo(ProcessingStatus.OK);
            assertThat(result.processedItems()).isGreaterThan(0);
        });
}

@Test
void processAsync_failsWhenPayloadIsInvalid() {
    CompletableFuture<ProcessingResult> future =
        asyncProcessor.processAsync(malformedPayload());

    assertThat(future)
        .failsWithin(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .withThrowableOfType(ExecutionException.class)
        .havingCause()
        .isInstanceOf(InvalidPayloadException.class)
        .withMessageContaining("malformed");
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `succeedsWithin` and `failsWithin` block the calling thread — they are not designed for reactive pipelines. For `Mono`/`Flux` (Project Reactor), use `StepVerifier` instead. Additionally, setting the timeout too tight in slow CI environments causes flaky failures; prefer `Duration.ofSeconds(10)` for I/O-bound operations and rely on the CI job-level timeout as the hard cutoff rather than a very short per-assertion timeout.

---

### Pattern 142 — Mockito `RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS` — Avoiding Chained Mock Setup Verbosity [official]

`Mockito.mock(Cls.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS)` makes every method call on the mock return another mock automatically, enabling fluent stubs like `when(config.database().host()).thenReturn("localhost")` without first stubbing `config.database()` to return a `Database` mock. This is useful for read-only configuration object graphs where setting up each intermediate mock is pure boilerplate.

```java
@Test
void connect_usesConfiguredDatabaseHost() {
    AppConfig config = mock(AppConfig.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);
    when(config.database().host()).thenReturn("db.prod.example.com");
    when(config.database().port()).thenReturn(5432);
    when(config.database().name()).thenReturn("orders");
    when(config.ssl().enabled()).thenReturn(true);
    when(config.ssl().certificatePath()).thenReturn("/etc/certs/db.pem");

    DatabaseConnectionFactory factory = new DatabaseConnectionFactory(config);
    ConnectionDetails details = factory.buildConnectionDetails();

    assertThat(details.jdbcUrl())
        .startsWith("jdbc:postgresql://db.prod.example.com:5432/orders");
    assertThat(details.sslEnabled()).isTrue();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS` is a code smell detector: if you need it in production code it likely means the object graph violates the Law of Demeter. Limit its use to configuration objects and request context objects that are genuinely read-only chains. It cannot stub `void` methods at intermediate levels, and deep stub chains are opaque in failure messages — a `NullPointerException` from `config.database().pool().maxConnections()` does not tell you which level returned null.

---

### Pattern 143 — JUnit 5 `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` — Explicit Sequencing for Stateful Integration Tests [official]

For integration tests that must execute in a specific sequence (e.g., create → read → update → delete lifecycle tests against a real database), `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` combined with `@Order(n)` on each method guarantees deterministic ordering. Pair this with `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` to share mutable state (the created entity ID) across methods without static fields.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class CustomerLifecycleIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired CustomerRepository repo;
    private Long savedId;

    @Test @Order(1)
    void create_persistsCustomer() {
        Customer c = repo.save(new Customer("Alice", "alice@example.com"));
        assertThat(c.id()).isNotNull();
        savedId = c.id();
    }

    @Test @Order(2)
    void read_returnsPersistedCustomer() {
        assertThat(repo.findById(savedId))
            .isPresent()
            .get()
            .extracting(Customer::email)
            .isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
    }

    @Test @Order(3)
    void update_changesEmail() {
        repo.updateEmail(savedId, "alice-new@example.com");
        assertThat(repo.findById(savedId).orElseThrow().email())
            .isEqualTo("alice-new@example.com");
    }

    @Test @Order(4)
    void delete_removesCustomer() {
        repo.deleteById(savedId);
        assertThat(repo.findById(savedId)).isEmpty();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Ordered tests that share state are inherently fragile: a failure in `@Order(1)` causes all subsequent tests to fail or produce misleading results because `savedId` is never set. Wrap the entire class in a JUnit 5 assumption: `assumeTrue(savedId != null, "previous step failed")` in each method body, or use `@Disabled` conditionally. For truly isolated verification prefer separate `@Test` methods each setting up their own data — ordered stateful tests should be reserved for lifecycle/CRUD integration scenarios where setup cost is prohibitive.

---

### Pattern 144 — WireMock `@WireMockTest` with Response Templating — Dynamic Stub Responses Using Request Data [official]

WireMock 3.x's `@WireMockTest` annotation (JUnit 5 extension) starts and stops a `WireMockServer` around each test method, and response templating (enabled via `httpServer.stubFor(...)` with `withTransformers("response-template")`) lets stub responses echo back request data using Handlebars syntax. This enables testing client-side extraction logic without maintaining separate stubs for every possible input value.

```java
@WireMockTest
class ProductClientTemplatingTest {

    @Test
    void fetchProduct_echoesProductIdInResponse(WireMockRuntimeInfo wmRuntimeInfo) {
        stubFor(get(urlPathMatching("/products/([0-9]+)"))
            .willReturn(aResponse()
                .withStatus(200)
                .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .withBody("""
                    {
                      "id": {{request.pathSegments.[1]}},
                      "name": "Product-{{request.pathSegments.[1]}}",
                      "price": 9.99
                    }
                    """)
                .withTransformers("response-template")));

        ProductClient client =
            new ProductClient("http://localhost:" + wmRuntimeInfo.getHttpPort());

        Product product = client.fetchById(42L);

        assertThat(product.id()).isEqualTo(42L);
        assertThat(product.name()).isEqualTo("Product-42");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Response templating is a runtime Handlebars evaluation — template syntax errors surface at test runtime as `500` responses rather than at stub-definition time, making failures cryptic. Always test new templates with a simple sanity `@Test` that inspects the raw response body as a string before relying on the template in a full client assertion. Also note that response templating requires the `wiremock-standalone` dependency or the `wiremock-spring-boot` starter — the plain `wiremock-jre8` artifact does not include Handlebars by default.

---

### Pattern 145 — Spring Boot `@RestClientTest` with `MockRestServiceServer` — Isolated HTTP Client Slice Testing [official]

`@RestClientTest(MyClient.class)` starts only the auto-configuration needed to test a `RestClient`/`RestTemplate`-based HTTP client: Jackson, the client bean, and `MockRestServiceServer`. No web server is started. `server.expect(...).andRespond(...)` stubs HTTP interactions at the `ClientHttpRequestFactory` level, verifying that the client sends the correct headers, query parameters, and body before returning the mocked response.

```java
@RestClientTest(WeatherClient.class)
class WeatherClientTest {

    @Autowired WeatherClient weatherClient;
    @Autowired MockRestServiceServer server;

    @Test
    void getWeather_parsesTemperatureCorrectly() {
        server.expect(once(),
                requestTo("https://api.weather.example.com/current?city=Berlin"))
              .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
              .andExpect(header("Authorization", "Bearer test-key"))
              .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                  { "city": "Berlin", "temperatureCelsius": 18.5, "condition": "CLOUDY" }
                  """, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        WeatherReport report = weatherClient.getWeather("Berlin");

        assertThat(report.city()).isEqualTo("Berlin");
        assertThat(report.temperatureCelsius()).isEqualTo(18.5);
        server.verify();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockRestServiceServer` verifies expectations lazily — `server.verify()` at the end of the test method checks that all expected calls were made in the declared order (if `InOrder` matching is used). Forgetting `server.verify()` means a test that never actually calls the HTTP client still passes, hiding the client not being invoked at all. Add a custom `@AfterEach` in a base class to call `server.verify()` automatically, or configure `MockRestServiceServer` with `ignoreExpectOrder(false)` to fail eagerly on unexpected requests.

### Pattern 146 — Virtual Thread `Executor` with `Awaitility` — Testing Concurrent Behaviour Without `Thread.sleep` [community]

Testing code that spawns virtual threads requires waiting for concurrent side-effects to appear without resorting to `Thread.sleep`. `Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).untilAsserted(...)` polls an assertion repeatedly until it passes or the timeout expires, decoupling the test from specific timing assumptions and eliminating flakiness caused by variable CPU scheduling.

```java
@Test
void processConcurrently_allTasksCompleteEventually() throws Exception {
    List<String> completedIds = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
    List<String> taskIds = List.of("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4", "T5");

    ExecutorService virtualExecutor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

    for (String id : taskIds) {
        virtualExecutor.submit(() -> {
            taskProcessor.process(id);       // real work
            completedIds.add(id);
        });
    }

    virtualExecutor.shutdown();

    await()
        .atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(100))
        .untilAsserted(() ->
            assertThat(completedIds)
                .containsExactlyInAnyOrderElementsOf(taskIds));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Awaitility` polls on the calling thread; if the assertion itself is expensive (e.g., a database query), polling too frequently burdens the system under test. Use `pollDelay` to introduce an initial grace period: `.pollDelay(Duration.ofMillis(500)).pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(200))` skips the first 500 ms (during which the virtual threads are doing real work) and then polls every 200 ms. Keep the `atMost` duration generous for CI but add a `failFast` condition to abort early on unrecoverable errors.

### Pattern 147 — jqwik `@Property` with `Assume.that` — Precondition Filtering for Property-Based Tests [official]

`Assume.that(condition)` inside a `@Property` method causes jqwik to discard the current generated input when the condition is false, effectively filtering the input space to a valid subdomain. This is preferable to `if (!condition) return;` (which silently skips the check) because jqwik tracks discarded samples and emits a warning when more than a configurable fraction of generated inputs are discarded (indicating the arbitrary is too broad for the property).

```java
@Property(tries = 1000)
void divide_quotientIsExact(
        @ForAll int numerator,
        @ForAll @IntRange(min = 1, max = 10_000) int denominator) {

    Assume.that(numerator % denominator == 0);   // filter to exact divisors

    int quotient = calculator.divide(numerator, denominator);

    assertThat((long) quotient * denominator).isEqualTo(numerator);
}

@Property
void sort_resultIsStrictlyMonotonicForDistinctInputs(
        @ForAll List<@UniqueElements Integer> list) {

    Assume.that(list.size() >= 2);    // skip trivially-sorted single-element lists

    List<Integer> sorted = sorter.sort(list);

    for (int i = 0; i < sorted.size() - 1; i++) {
        assertThat(sorted.get(i)).isLessThan(sorted.get(i + 1));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** jqwik emits a warning when more than 10% of generated samples are discarded by `Assume.that`. If the valid subdomain is very small (e.g., numerator divisible by denominator), the effective number of meaningful runs is far fewer than `tries` — you appear to run 1000 tests but only 50 are non-trivial. The solution is to constrain the `Arbitrary` upstream: use `Arbitraries.integers().filter(n -> n % denominator == 0)` or `Combinators.combine` to generate valid pairs directly, so every generated input passes the assumption.

### Pattern 148 — ArchUnit `NamingConventionRule` — Enforcing Package and Class Naming Constraints [official]

ArchUnit's `classes().that().resideInAPackage("..service..")should().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Service")` enforces naming conventions as compile-time-equivalent architecture tests. Running these in CI ensures that new developers do not accidentally name a service class `OrderManager` or place a repository interface in the wrong package, catching violations before they accumulate into inconsistent codebases.

```java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme.shop")
class NamingConventionTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule SERVICES_SUFFIXED =
        classes()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..service..")
            .and().areAnnotatedWith(Service.class)
            .should().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Service")
            .because("all Spring @Service beans must follow the *Service naming contract");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule REPOSITORIES_SUFFIXED =
        classes()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..repository..")
            .should().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Repository")
            .orShould().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Dao");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule NO_UTIL_CLASSES =
        noClasses()
            .should().haveSimpleNameContaining("Util")
            .orShould().haveSimpleNameContaining("Helper")
            .because("utility logic should be encapsulated in domain services, not static utility classes");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule EXCEPTIONS_SUFFIXED =
        classes()
            .that().areAssignableTo(RuntimeException.class)
            .should().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Exception");
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@AnalyzeClasses` scans the entire classpath for the given package prefix at class-loading time; very large modules with thousands of classes can make the first run slow. Scope it tightly with `packages = "com.acme.shop"` rather than `packagesOf(MyApp.class)` to limit classpath scanning. For multi-module Maven/Gradle projects, run each module's naming-convention test against its own package to keep individual rule runs fast.

### Pattern 149 — Spring Boot `@MockitoBean` (Spring Boot 4.0+) — Replacing `@MockBean` in the New Testing Model [official]

Spring Boot 4.0 removed `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean` from `spring-boot-test` and replaced them with `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` in alignment with the broader Spring Framework `@MockitoBeanSettings` infrastructure. `@MockitoBean` registers a Mockito mock as a Spring bean and integrates with `MockitoTestExecutionListener` to reset the mock automatically between tests. Unlike the old `@MockBean`, `@MockitoBean` works outside `@SpringBootTest` contexts via `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)`.

```java
@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest {

    @MockitoBean
    PaymentGateway paymentGateway;      // replaces old @MockBean

    @MockitoSpyBean
    EmailNotificationService emailSvc;  // replaces old @SpyBean

    @Autowired
    OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void placeOrder_chargesPaymentAndSendsConfirmation() {
        when(paymentGateway.charge(any(), any()))
            .thenReturn(PaymentResult.success("TXN-001"));

        Order order = orderService.place(
            new OrderRequest("CUST-1", List.of(new LineItemRequest("SKU-A", 2))));

        assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.CONFIRMED);
        assertThat(order.paymentReference()).isEqualTo("TXN-001");

        verify(paymentGateway).charge(eq("CUST-1"), any(Money.class));
        verify(emailSvc).sendOrderConfirmation(eq(order.id()), any());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@MockitoBean` fields trigger a new `ApplicationContext` when a unique combination of mocked beans is requested, breaking Spring's context caching if different test classes mock different subsets of the same bean type. Centralise all `@MockitoBean` declarations in a shared base class so every test class that needs mocks uses the same bean registry shape, and Spring can reuse the same cached context. Declaring `@MockitoBean` on individual test classes defeats caching if the set differs even by one field.

### Pattern 150 — JUnit 5 `CancellationToken` Cooperative Cancellation — Aborting Long-Running Tests Gracefully [official]

JUnit 6.0 introduced `CancellationToken` as an injectable parameter in test methods. The launcher can cancel a running test (e.g., due to a global timeout set in `LauncherExecutionRequest`), and the test code checks `token.isCancellationRequested()` to exit its loop cooperatively rather than being forcibly interrupted. This is critical for virtual-thread-based tests that perform long polling loops.

```java
@Test
void importLargeDataset_processesAllRecordsBeforeTimeout(CancellationToken token) {
    List<Record> records = generateTestRecords(10_000);
    List<String> processedIds = new ArrayList<>();

    for (Record record : records) {
        if (token.isCancellationRequested()) {
            // Log partial progress and fail descriptively rather than being killed silently
            fail("Test cancelled after processing %d / %d records — "
                 + "consider splitting into smaller parameterized cases"
                 .formatted(processedIds.size(), records.size()));
        }
        importService.importRecord(record);
        processedIds.add(record.id());
    }

    assertThat(processedIds).hasSize(records.size());

    // Verify idempotency — re-importing should produce no duplicates
    for (Record record : records) {
        if (token.isCancellationRequested()) break;
        importService.importRecord(record);
    }
    assertThat(importRepository.countAll()).isEqualTo(records.size());
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `CancellationToken` is injected by JUnit's `CancellationTokenParameterResolver` extension, which is active by default in JUnit 6.0. In JUnit 5.x, the equivalent is a custom `ParameterResolver` extension wrapping a `volatile boolean` set by an `InvocationInterceptor`. The cooperative model means a test can still run indefinitely if it never checks the token — combine it with a JVM-level interrupt (via `@Timeout` annotation) as a hard backstop.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 48

**JUnit 5 `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` combined with `@MockitoBean` causes mock resets to be skipped between test methods — mocks retain stubbings from earlier test methods and produce incorrect results in later tests in the same instance** — A developer enables `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` to share expensive setup state, and also declares `@MockitoBean PaymentGateway gateway` on the class. The second `@Test` method finds the gateway already stubbed from the first test's `when(gateway.charge(...)).thenReturn(...)` call. WHY: `MockitoTestExecutionListener` resets mocks between tests when the test class is instantiated per method (the default `PER_METHOD` lifecycle), but with `PER_CLASS` a single instance is shared; the listener still calls `Mockito.reset()` in `afterTestMethod`, so stubs should be cleared — however if `@MockitoBean` is declared but `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` was also called manually in a `@BeforeEach` it re-registers stubs before the listener can clear them. Fix: never mix `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks` with `@MockitoBean`; let the Spring Boot infrastructure manage mock lifecycle entirely.

**AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison()` does not call `equals()` on any field by default — including fields whose `equals()` is the correct comparison semantic (e.g., `BigDecimal`)— causing `BigDecimal("1.0")` and `BigDecimal("1.00")` to be reported as unequal because the recursive comparator compares `intVal`, `scale`, and `intCompact` fields separately rather than using `BigDecimal.compareTo`** — A developer writes `assertThat(invoice).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(expected)` where both objects have `amount = BigDecimal("1.0")` and `amount = BigDecimal("1.00")` respectively. The assertion fails with a field mismatch on `scale`. WHY: recursive comparison bypasses all `equals()` implementations to provide structural equality, which means numeric scale differences are exposed as field mismatches. Fix: add `.withComparatorForType(BigDecimal::compareTo, BigDecimal.class)` to the recursive comparison chain, or normalise `BigDecimal` values to the same scale before assertion.

**Mockito `mockConstruction` interception only captures `new` calls on the same thread that opened the `try` block — code that constructs objects on a `CompletableFuture`'s thread pool or in a virtual thread will create real (unmocked) instances, silently bypassing the stub and causing tests to hit real external services or throw `NullPointerException`** — A developer stubs `mockConstruction(HttpClient.class)` expecting all HTTP calls to be intercepted, but the service under test uses `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> new HttpClient(...).get(url))`. The `HttpClient` is constructed on a ForkJoinPool thread, outside the `mockConstruction` scope. WHY: Mockito's inline mock-maker uses a `ThreadLocal` to track active construction mocking; threads that were not present when `mockConstruction` was opened do not inherit the mock context. Fix: refactor the code to accept an `HttpClientFactory` functional interface and inject a factory mock instead of using `mockConstruction`, or use the `MOCK_MAKER=inline` Mockito extension with a synchronized shared state approach documented in Mockito's multi-threading test guide.

**Spring Boot `@RestClientTest` does not auto-configure beans outside the HTTP client slice — services, repositories, and `@Component` classes defined in the application are excluded — causing `@Autowired` fields other than the client under test to be null and tests to fail with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`** — A team writes a `@RestClientTest(WeatherClient.class)` test and adds `@Autowired CacheManager cacheManager` to the test class expecting Spring Boot's cache auto-configuration to be active. The context fails to start with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type 'CacheManager'`. WHY: `@RestClientTest` is a test slice that intentionally restricts auto-configuration to only what is needed for `RestClient`/`RestTemplate` testing: Jackson, the client bean, and `MockRestServiceServer`. All other auto-configurations (caching, JPA, security) are excluded by design. Fix: use `@Import(CacheAutoConfiguration.class)` to selectively add the missing configuration, or if the test requires a broad application context, switch to `@SpringBootTest` with `webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.NONE`.

**WireMock response templating silently renders an empty string for unknown Handlebars variables instead of throwing an error — a typo like `{{request.pathSigments.[1]}}` produces `""` in the response body, and the client receives a JSON object with an empty `id` field, which then fails with a misleading "expected 42, got null" assertion error rather than a template rendering error** — A developer introduces a typo in the Handlebars path segment expression. WireMock renders `""` (empty string) because Handlebars' default behaviour is to silently ignore unknown variable references. WHY: Handlebars treats unknown variables as empty by design to support optional template variables; WireMock inherits this behaviour from the Handlebars engine it bundles. Fix: after writing a new response template, add a dedicated sanity test that performs `server.verify(getRequestedFor(urlPathMatching("...")))` and asserts the raw response body as a string with `assertThat(rawBody).contains("42")` before testing the parsed object. Additionally, consider enabling strict mode in the Handlebars engine configuration if WireMock's extension API permits it.

## Cycle 49 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 151 — `MockMvcTester` Fluent API (Spring Boot 3.4+) — AssertJ-Native Controller Testing Without Raw `ResultActions` [official]

Spring Boot 3.4 introduced `MockMvcTester`, an AssertJ-aligned alternative to `MockMvc` that returns `MvcTestResult` objects you can chain directly into AssertJ assertions. Unlike the imperative `mockMvc.perform(...).andExpect(...)` style, `MockMvcTester` integrates with AssertJ's `.satisfies()`, `extracting()`, and soft-assertion machinery, letting you assert on status, headers, body, cookies, and model in a single fluent expression. The tester is auto-injected in `@WebMvcTest` slices when AssertJ is on the classpath.

```java
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvcTester mvc;

    @MockitoBean
    OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void getOrder_returnsOrderJson() {
        given(orderService.findById(42L))
            .willReturn(new Order(42L, "CUST-7", OrderStatus.SHIPPED));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/orders/42"))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.status").isEqualTo("SHIPPED");
    }

    @Test
    void createOrder_returns201WithLocationHeader() {
        given(orderService.create(any()))
            .willReturn(new Order(99L, "CUST-9", OrderStatus.PENDING));

        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/orders")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"customerId\":\"CUST-9\"}"))
            .hasStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
            .headers().containsKey("Location");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockMvcTester` requires that you hold `MvcTestResult` as the subject of an `assertThat()` call — it cannot be stored as a plain variable and asserted on later with vanilla JUnit assertions. The fluent chain is also slightly harder to debug in an IDE because the intermediate `MvcTestResult` type is unfamiliar; adding `.failure()` to the chain surfaces a detailed diff. For teams fully committed to AssertJ, the ergonomics are superior to the older `andExpect` model, but mixing both in the same codebase creates inconsistency.

---

### Pattern 152 — `@JsonTest` with `JacksonTester` — Isolated JSON Serialisation / Deserialisation Testing [official]

`@JsonTest` is a Spring Boot test slice that loads only the JSON infrastructure (Jackson, Gson, or Jsonb plus any registered modules and `@JsonComponent` beans). Injecting `JacksonTester<T>` gives you `write(T)` and `parse(String)` methods that return AssertJ-compatible result objects with JSON-path, exact-match, and structural assertion helpers. This pattern catches serialisation regressions (field renames, format changes, `@JsonAlias` drift) without starting the full application context.

```java
@JsonTest
class OrderDtoJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    private JacksonTester<OrderDto> json;

    @Test
    void serialize_writesExpectedFields() throws Exception {
        OrderDto dto = new OrderDto(
            42L, "CUST-7", BigDecimal.valueOf(199.99),
            List.of(new LineItemDto("SKU-A", 2)),
            Instant.parse("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z"));

        assertThat(json.write(dto))
            .isEqualToJson("order-dto.json")
            .hasJsonPathNumberValue("@.id", 42)
            .hasJsonPathStringValue("@.customerId", "CUST-7")
            .hasJsonPathArrayValue("@.lineItems")
            .hasJsonPathStringValue("@.lineItems[0].sku", "SKU-A");
    }

    @Test
    void deserialize_parsesAllFields() throws Exception {
        String content = """
            {"id":42,"customerId":"CUST-7","totalAmount":199.99,
             "lineItems":[{"sku":"SKU-A","quantity":2}],
             "createdAt":"2026-01-15T10:00:00Z"}
            """;
        OrderDto parsed = json.parse(content).getObject();
        assertThat(parsed.id()).isEqualTo(42L);
        assertThat(parsed.totalAmount()).isEqualByComparingTo("199.99");
        assertThat(parsed.lineItems()).hasSize(1);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@JsonTest` does not auto-detect custom Jackson modules that are not annotated with `@JsonComponent` — any module registered only via `ObjectMapper.registerModule(...)` in a `@Configuration` class will be absent in the slice context, silently producing different serialisation from production. Fix: annotate such modules with `@JsonComponent` or import the configuration class explicitly with `@Import`. Also note that `isEqualToJson` performs field-order-insensitive comparison by default, which can mask missing fields if the golden-file JSON is a strict subset of the serialised output.

---

### Pattern 153 — Mockito `ArgumentCaptor` with `@Captor` — Capturing and Asserting Complex Collaboration Arguments [official]

`ArgumentCaptor` captures the exact argument value passed to a mock method, enabling deep AssertJ assertions on the captured object without requiring `equals()`-based matchers. The `@Captor` annotation eliminates verbose `ArgumentCaptor.forClass()` calls and supports generics without unchecked cast warnings. Captors are most valuable when the collaborator receives a rich command or event object that is constructed inside the production code and cannot easily be constructed for a `verify(mock).method(eq(specificValue))` style check.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock
    EventPublisher eventPublisher;

    @Mock
    InventoryRepository inventoryRepo;

    @InjectMocks
    OrderService orderService;

    @Captor
    ArgumentCaptor<OrderPlacedEvent> eventCaptor;

    @Captor
    ArgumentCaptor<InventoryReservation> reservationCaptor;

    @Test
    void placeOrder_publishesEnrichedEventWithAllLineItems() {
        when(inventoryRepo.reserveStock(any())).thenReturn(ReservationId.of("RES-1"));

        orderService.place(new OrderRequest("CUST-7",
            List.of(new LineItemRequest("SKU-A", 2), new LineItemRequest("SKU-B", 1))));

        verify(eventPublisher).publish(eventCaptor.capture());
        OrderPlacedEvent event = eventCaptor.getValue();

        assertThat(event.customerId()).isEqualTo("CUST-7");
        assertThat(event.lineItems()).hasSize(2)
            .extracting(LineItem::sku)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("SKU-A", "SKU-B");
        assertThat(event.occurredAt()).isCloseTo(Instant.now(), within(5, SECONDS));

        verify(inventoryRepo).reserveStock(reservationCaptor.capture());
        assertThat(reservationCaptor.getValue().totalUnits()).isEqualTo(3);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ArgumentCaptor` couples the test to the internal construction logic of the argument: if the production code changes which fields are populated (even harmlessly), the test fails. Prefer `@Captor` over explicit matchers only when the object's structure is the actual behaviour being verified. For simpler cases where you only need to check a single field, a custom `ArgumentMatcher` (`argThat(e -> e.customerId().equals("CUST-7"))`) is more resilient to irrelevant field additions.

---

### Pattern 154 — `@DataJpaTest` with `TestEntityManager` — Repository Slice Testing Against Real SQL [official]

`@DataJpaTest` loads only JPA repositories, Hibernate, transaction management, and an in-memory or containerised database — no web layer, services, or unrelated beans. `TestEntityManager` wraps `EntityManager` with test-friendly helpers (`persistAndFlush`, `find`, `getId`) that allow you to set up entity state and verify persistence side effects without writing boilerplate. Combine with `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` and a Testcontainers `@DynamicPropertySource` to run against a real Postgres or MySQL instance.

```java
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void configureDataSource(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
    }

    @Autowired
    TestEntityManager em;

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Test
    void findByCustomerIdAndStatus_returnsMatchingOrders() {
        Customer customer = em.persistAndFlush(new Customer("CUST-7", "alice@example.com"));
        em.persistAndFlush(new Order(customer, OrderStatus.SHIPPED, BigDecimal.TEN));
        em.persistAndFlush(new Order(customer, OrderStatus.PENDING, BigDecimal.ONE));
        em.clear();  // detach all — next call hits SQL

        List<Order> shipped =
            orderRepository.findByCustomerAndStatus(customer, OrderStatus.SHIPPED);

        assertThat(shipped).hasSize(1)
            .first().satisfies(o -> {
                assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.SHIPPED);
                assertThat(o.totalAmount()).isEqualByComparingTo("10");
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@DataJpaTest` runs each test method in a transaction that rolls back after completion by default, which is convenient but can hide constraint violations that only manifest on `COMMIT`. If you need to test `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)` behaviour or database-level constraints (unique indexes, check constraints), annotate specific tests with `@Commit` or switch the test class to `@Transactional(propagation = NEVER)` and manage cleanup manually. Container startup also adds 5-15 seconds to the first test run; mitigate with a static `@Container` field and `@DynamicPropertySource` to reuse across test methods.

---

### Pattern 155 — BDDMockito `given/willReturn` Style — Readable Arrange Sections in BDD-Structured Tests [official]

`BDDMockito` (bundled with Mockito since 1.10) replaces `when(...).thenReturn(...)` with `given(...).willReturn(...)` and `verify(...)` with `then(...).should(...)`, aligning test code with Given-When-Then narrative. This is not merely stylistic: BDDMockito's `given` method returns `BDDOngoingStubbing`, which has slightly different override semantics than Mockito's `OngoingStubbing` for consecutive calls, and its `then(...).should(never())` reads more naturally in assertion sections. IDE support for distinguishing arrange from assert is improved when both use different static-import namespaces.

```java
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ShipmentServiceTest {

    @Mock ShipmentGateway gateway;
    @Mock NotificationService notifications;
    @InjectMocks ShipmentService shipmentService;

    @Test
    void dispatchShipment_notifiesCustomerOnSuccess() {
        // Given
        Order order = new Order(1L, "CUST-3", OrderStatus.CONFIRMED);
        given(gateway.dispatch(order))
            .willReturn(ShipmentResult.success("TRACK-001"));

        // When
        ShipmentConfirmation result = shipmentService.dispatch(order);

        // Then
        assertThat(result.trackingNumber()).isEqualTo("TRACK-001");
        then(notifications).should().sendShipmentConfirmation("CUST-3", "TRACK-001");
        then(gateway).should(times(1)).dispatch(order);
    }

    @Test
    void dispatchShipment_doesNotNotifyOnGatewayFailure() {
        given(gateway.dispatch(any())).willThrow(new GatewayUnavailableException("timeout"));

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> shipmentService.dispatch(new Order(2L, "CUST-4", OrderStatus.CONFIRMED)))
            .isInstanceOf(ShipmentException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("timeout");

        then(notifications).should(never()).sendShipmentConfirmation(any(), any());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `BDDMockito.given` and `Mockito.when` cannot be mixed freely in the same test class without importing both namespaces, leading to ambiguous imports and compiler errors. Establish a project-wide convention (BDDMockito everywhere, or Mockito everywhere) and enforce it via an ArchUnit rule: `noClasses().should().dependOnClassesThat().haveFullyQualifiedName("org.mockito.Mockito").inAnyPackage("..service..test..")`. Also note that `willDoNothing()` in BDDMockito is the equivalent of Mockito's `doNothing()` — not `thenDoNothing()`, which does not exist.

---

### Pattern 156 — AssertJ Soft Assertions with `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly` — Collecting All Failures in One Test Pass [official]

Soft assertions defer each failing assertion and collect all failures before reporting them at once at the end of the lambda, giving the developer a complete picture of what is wrong in a single test run. AssertJ 3.17+ provides `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> { ... })` as the preferred idiom over the older `@Rule SoftAssertions` approach, and `@InjectSoftAssertions` for field injection via `SoftAssertionsExtension`. The pattern is most valuable for validating rich domain objects with many fields, API response bodies, and record types.

```java
@ExtendWith(SoftAssertionsExtension.class)
class InvoiceTest {

    @InjectSoftAssertions
    SoftAssertions softly;

    @Test
    void generatedInvoice_hasAllRequiredFields() {
        Invoice invoice = invoiceService.generate(new InvoiceRequest(
            "CUST-7", List.of(new LineItem("SKU-A", 2, new BigDecimal("49.99"))),
            Currency.USD));

        softly.assertThat(invoice.number()).startsWith("INV-");
        softly.assertThat(invoice.customerId()).isEqualTo("CUST-7");
        softly.assertThat(invoice.currency()).isEqualTo(Currency.USD);
        softly.assertThat(invoice.lineItems()).hasSize(1);
        softly.assertThat(invoice.subtotal())
            .isEqualByComparingTo(new BigDecimal("99.98"));
        softly.assertThat(invoice.tax())
            .isEqualByComparingTo(new BigDecimal("10.00"));
        softly.assertThat(invoice.total())
            .isEqualByComparingTo(new BigDecimal("109.98"));
        softly.assertThat(invoice.issuedAt())
            .isCloseTo(Instant.now(), within(5, ChronoUnit.SECONDS));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Soft assertions using `@InjectSoftAssertions` require `SoftAssertionsExtension` to be registered; forgetting this silently gives you a `null` softly field, causing a `NullPointerException` rather than a meaningful failure. The lambda form (`SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {...})`) is safer because it is self-contained. Another pitfall: soft assertions do not short-circuit on `NullPointerException` in the assertion lambda itself (e.g., `softly.assertThat(invoice.lineItems().get(0).sku()).isEqualTo("SKU-A")` will throw if `lineItems()` is null), so guard access to nested objects with a hard `assertThat(invoice.lineItems()).isNotEmpty()` before entering the soft block.

---

### Pattern 157 — `@WebFluxTest` with `WebTestClient` — Reactive Controller Testing With Exchange Assertions [official]

`@WebFluxTest` is the reactive counterpart to `@WebMvcTest`: it starts a lightweight WebFlux context with a `WebTestClient` pointing at the controllers under test, without spinning up a real HTTP server. `WebTestClient` supports blocking assertion chains (`expectStatus()`, `expectBody()`, `returnResult()`) that work regardless of whether the underlying controller returns `Mono`, `Flux`, or a `ServerSentEvent` stream. Use `.returnResult(ParameterizedTypeReference<T>)` to deserialise `Flux<T>` responses into a `List<T>` for assertion.

```java
@WebFluxTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @MockitoBean
    ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void streamProducts_returnsAllProductsAsServerSentEvents() {
        given(productService.streamAll())
            .willReturn(Flux.just(
                new Product(1L, "Widget A", new BigDecimal("9.99")),
                new Product(2L, "Widget B", new BigDecimal("19.99"))));

        webTestClient.get().uri("/products/stream")
            .accept(MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM)
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectHeader().contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM)
            .expectBodyList(Product.class)
            .hasSize(2)
            .value(products ->
                assertThat(products).extracting(Product::name)
                    .containsExactly("Widget A", "Widget B"));
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_returnsNotFoundForMissingId() {
        given(productService.findById(99L))
            .willReturn(Mono.empty());

        webTestClient.get().uri("/products/99")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound()
            .expectBody()
            .jsonPath("$.message").isEqualTo("Product not found: 99");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `WebTestClient` assertion chains are eager — `expectBodyList` collects the entire Flux into memory before asserting, which will hang indefinitely if the stream is infinite or the service mock never completes. Always bound the stream under test with `take(n)` in the controller or use `.expectBodyList(...).consumeWith(result -> ...)` with a timeout configured via `webTestClient.mutate().responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3)).build()`. Also, `@WebFluxTest` does not scan `@Repository` or `@Service` beans, so collaborators must be provided as `@MockitoBean` or via `@Import`.

---

### Pattern 158 — Testcontainers `@ServiceConnection` (Spring Boot 3.1+) — Zero-Config Container DataSource Wiring [official]

Spring Boot 3.1 introduced `@ServiceConnection`, which reads `Container` metadata (image name, exposed ports, connection properties) and automatically registers `DynamicProperties` for the matching auto-configuration. Annotating a `@Container` field with `@ServiceConnection` eliminates the boilerplate `@DynamicPropertySource` method for common container types (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, MongoDB). The connection discovery is driven by `ConnectionDetailsFactory` implementations registered on the classpath.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class FullStackOrderTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static KafkaContainer kafka =
        new KafkaContainer(DockerImageName.parse("confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.1"));

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection(name = "redis")
    static GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7.2-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);

    @Autowired
    OrderService orderService;

    @Autowired
    KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    @Test
    void placeOrder_persistsAndPublishesEvent() {
        Order order = orderService.place(new OrderRequest("CUST-7",
            List.of(new LineItemRequest("SKU-A", 2))));

        assertThat(order.id()).isNotNull();
        // Poll Kafka topic to verify event was published...
        await().atMost(10, SECONDS)
            .untilAsserted(() ->
                assertThat(consumeFromTopic("order.placed")).hasSize(1));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@ServiceConnection` relies on the container image name to resolve the correct `ConnectionDetailsFactory`: an image named `postgres:16-alpine` works, but a custom or locally-built image named `my-company/postgres-hardened:latest` will not match and silently falls back to no-op, leaving Spring Boot to use its default datasource properties (usually pointing at `localhost:5432`, which does not exist in CI). In that case, fall back to the explicit `@DynamicPropertySource` approach and register connection properties manually. Also note `@ServiceConnection` is part of `spring-boot-testcontainers`, not `testcontainers-core` — add the dependency explicitly.

---

### Pattern 159 — `MockRestServiceServer` with `expect(requestTo(...)).andExpect(content())` — Testing `RestTemplate`/`RestClient` HTTP Calls Without a Real Server [official]

`MockRestServiceServer` intercepts `RestTemplate` or `RestClient` requests at the `ClientHttpRequestFactory` level, allowing you to set expectations on the URL, HTTP method, request body, and headers, then define the response to return. It is auto-configured in `@RestClientTest` slices but can also be used in `@SpringBootTest` via `MockRestServiceServer.createServer(restTemplate)`. Unlike WireMock, it needs no port, runs in-process, and validates that all expectations were called via `server.verify()`.

```java
@RestClientTest(WeatherClient.class)
class WeatherClientTest {

    @Autowired
    WeatherClient weatherClient;

    @Autowired
    MockRestServiceServer server;

    @Test
    void getCurrentWeather_parsesTemperatureAndCondition() {
        server.expect(once(), requestTo("/weather/current?city=Berlin"))
            .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
            .andExpect(header("Accept", "application/json"))
            .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                {"city":"Berlin","tempCelsius":22.5,"condition":"SUNNY"}
                """, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        WeatherReport report = weatherClient.getCurrentWeather("Berlin");

        assertThat(report.city()).isEqualTo("Berlin");
        assertThat(report.tempCelsius()).isEqualTo(22.5);
        assertThat(report.condition()).isEqualTo(WeatherCondition.SUNNY);
        server.verify();
    }

    @Test
    void getCurrentWeather_throwsServiceExceptionOn503() {
        server.expect(requestTo("/weather/current?city=Berlin"))
            .andRespond(withStatus(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE));

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> weatherClient.getCurrentWeather("Berlin"))
            .isInstanceOf(WeatherServiceException.class);
        server.verify();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockRestServiceServer` validates expectations in the order they were registered by default. If the production code makes calls in a non-deterministic order (e.g., parallel `RestTemplate` calls in two threads), the ordered expectation check will fail even though all requests were made. Switch to `MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(restTemplate).ignoreExpectOrder(true).build()` to enable unordered matching. Also, `MockRestServiceServer` resets between tests in `@RestClientTest` only when managed by Spring's test execution listener; in `@SpringBootTest` you must call `server.reset()` in `@BeforeEach` manually.

---

### Pattern 160 — `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` Returning `Stream<Arguments>` — Table-Driven Tests With Named Rows [official]

`@MethodSource` is the most flexible JUnit 5 parameterized source because it can provide any mix of argument types including complex domain objects, lambdas, and `Named<T>` wrappers that produce human-readable display names. Wrapping arguments in `Named.named("description", value)` (or its static import `named(...)`) replaces the default `[1]`, `[2]` indices in test output with meaningful labels that appear in the IDE and CI report, dramatically improving traceability of failures.

```java
class DiscountCalculatorTest {

    static Stream<Arguments> discountCases() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(named("standard customer, 1 item",
                new Customer(Tier.STANDARD)), new Cart(1), new BigDecimal("0.00")),
            Arguments.of(named("gold customer, 5 items",
                new Customer(Tier.GOLD)), new Cart(5), new BigDecimal("5.00")),
            Arguments.of(named("platinum customer, 10 items — max cap applies",
                new Customer(Tier.PLATINUM)), new Cart(10), new BigDecimal("20.00")),
            Arguments.of(named("platinum customer, 100 items — still capped at 20%",
                new Customer(Tier.PLATINUM)), new Cart(100), new BigDecimal("20.00")),
            Arguments.of(named("null cart — should return zero discount",
                new Customer(Tier.GOLD)), null, BigDecimal.ZERO)
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0}")
    @MethodSource("discountCases")
    void calculateDiscount_returnsExpectedAmount(
            Customer customer, Cart cart, BigDecimal expectedDiscount) {
        BigDecimal actual = DiscountCalculator.calculate(customer, cart);
        assertThat(actual).isEqualByComparingTo(expectedDiscount);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@MethodSource` factory methods must be `static` unless the test class is annotated with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`, which means the method and the test class are in the same class but the factory runs before any instance is available. Referencing instance state in the factory method (e.g., a `@Mock` field) will produce a `NullPointerException` or a stale value because the mock is not yet injected at factory-invocation time. Extract factory methods that need complex setup into a separate `Arguments` provider class and reference it via the fully qualified method name `"com.acme.TestData#discountCases"`.

---

### Pattern 161 — AssertJ `filteredOn` + `extracting` for Collection Assertions — Targeting Subsets Without Stream Boilerplate [official]

AssertJ's `filteredOn(Predicate)` and `extracting(Function)` compose into a single fluent expression that replaces verbose Java stream-filter-map-collect-assertThat chains. `filteredOn` returns a new `AbstractListAssert` scoped to the matching elements; `extracting` maps each element to one or more fields. They work on `Iterable`, `List`, `array`, and `Optional` subjects, and can be combined with `usingRecursiveFieldByFieldElementComparator` for deep comparison of the extracted values.

```java
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Test
    void getOrdersForCustomer_returnsOnlyMatchingStatuses() {
        List<Order> orders = List.of(
            new Order(1L, "CUST-1", OrderStatus.SHIPPED, new BigDecimal("50.00")),
            new Order(2L, "CUST-1", OrderStatus.PENDING, new BigDecimal("30.00")),
            new Order(3L, "CUST-1", OrderStatus.CANCELLED, new BigDecimal("20.00")),
            new Order(4L, "CUST-1", OrderStatus.SHIPPED, new BigDecimal("80.00")),
            new Order(5L, "CUST-2", OrderStatus.SHIPPED, new BigDecimal("15.00"))
        );

        assertThat(orders)
            .filteredOn(o -> o.customerId().equals("CUST-1"))
            .filteredOn(o -> o.status() == OrderStatus.SHIPPED)
            .extracting(Order::id, Order::totalAmount)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(
                tuple(1L, new BigDecimal("50.00")),
                tuple(4L, new BigDecimal("80.00")));

        assertThat(orders)
            .filteredOn("status", OrderStatus.CANCELLED)
            .extracting(Order::totalAmount)
            .singleElement()
            .isEqualByComparingTo("20.00");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `filteredOn(String fieldName, Object value)` uses reflection and silently skips elements where the field is inaccessible or the type does not match, producing an unexpectedly empty filtered list rather than an error. The predicate form `filteredOn(Predicate<T>)` is safer because a failing predicate throws immediately. Also, `extracting` with multiple fields (tuple extraction) requires the element type to have accessible getters or public fields; records with canonical accessor methods work correctly, but classes with non-standard accessor naming patterns (e.g., `isActive()` instead of `getActive()`) need an explicit lambda reference.

---

### Pattern 162 — ArchUnit `layeredArchitecture()` — Enforcing Layered Dependency Constraints [community]

ArchUnit's `layeredArchitecture()` DSL declares named layers and their permitted dependency directions. Combined with `whereLayer(...).mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()`, it enforces that infrastructure never imports domain, that web controllers never import repositories directly, and that the domain layer remains framework-agnostic. This rule is placed in a standalone `@AnalyzeClasses` test class and runs as part of the normal test suite with zero runtime overhead.

```java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme.shop", importOptions = ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class)
class LayeredArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule LAYERED_ARCHITECTURE =
        layeredArchitecture()
            .consideringAllDependencies()
            .layer("Domain").definedBy("com.acme.shop.domain..")
            .layer("Application").definedBy("com.acme.shop.application..")
            .layer("Web").definedBy("com.acme.shop.web..")
            .layer("Persistence").definedBy("com.acme.shop.persistence..")
            .layer("Infrastructure").definedBy("com.acme.shop.infrastructure..")

            .whereLayer("Domain").mayNotAccessAnyLayer()
            .whereLayer("Application").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Domain")
            .whereLayer("Web").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Application", "Domain")
            .whereLayer("Persistence").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Domain")
            .whereLayer("Infrastructure").mayOnlyAccessLayers("Domain", "Application")
            .because("hexagonal/onion architecture: domain must not depend on outer rings");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule NO_SPRING_IN_DOMAIN =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("org.springframework..")
            .because("the domain model must be a pure Java model with no framework coupling");
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `layeredArchitecture().consideringAllDependencies()` includes transitive compile-time and runtime dependencies, which means a domain class importing a widely-used utility (e.g., `java.util.logging.Logger`) will not violate the rule, but an accidentally included third-party library imported by a domain class might. The `ignoreDependency(Class, Class)` escape hatch is available but should be documented inline with a `// ArchUnit: allowed because ...` comment to prevent silent rule erosion. Very large modules with 2000+ classes can make the first analysis run take 15-30 seconds; use `@AnalyzeClasses(importOptions = ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class)` to halve the scan set.

---

### Pattern 163 — Mockito `InOrder` — Verifying Method Call Sequence Across Multiple Mocks [official]

`InOrder` verifies that mock method calls occurred in a specific sequence across one or more mocks, without requiring that no other calls occurred in between. This is distinct from `verifyNoMoreInteractions` (which checks for unexpected calls) and from standard `verify` (which is order-agnostic). `InOrder` is essential for testing state-machine logic, saga choreography, workflow steps, and event-sourcing command handlers where ordering of side effects is a correctness concern.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class PaymentSagaTest {

    @Mock PaymentAuthorizer authorizer;
    @Mock FraudChecker fraudChecker;
    @Mock InventoryReserver inventoryReserver;
    @Mock OrderConfirmer orderConfirmer;
    @InjectMocks PaymentSaga saga;

    @Test
    void processPayment_executesStepsInCorrectOrder() {
        when(fraudChecker.check(any())).thenReturn(FraudResult.CLEAN);
        when(authorizer.authorize(any())).thenReturn(AuthResult.success("AUTH-001"));
        when(inventoryReserver.reserve(any())).thenReturn(ReservationResult.success("RES-001"));

        saga.process(new PaymentRequest("CUST-7", new BigDecimal("99.00"), "SKU-A"));

        InOrder inOrder = inOrder(fraudChecker, authorizer, inventoryReserver, orderConfirmer);
        inOrder.verify(fraudChecker).check(any());
        inOrder.verify(authorizer).authorize(any());
        inOrder.verify(inventoryReserver).reserve(any());
        inOrder.verify(orderConfirmer).confirm(any());
        inOrder.verifyNoMoreInteractions();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `InOrder.verifyNoMoreInteractions()` verifies no further interactions on the specific mocks passed to `inOrder(...)`, but it does not detect interleaved calls to other mocks not in the `InOrder` group. If the saga calls `fraudChecker` a second time between `authorize` and `reserve`, and `fraudChecker` was passed to `inOrder(...)`, the `verifyNoMoreInteractions()` call will catch it. However, if a new collaborator is injected later and its calls are not added to the `inOrder(...)` group, they are silently unchecked. Enumerate all collaborators explicitly in `inOrder(mock1, mock2, ...)` and use `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` strict stubs mode to catch unused stubbings.

---

### Pattern 164 — `@SpringBootTest` with `TestRestTemplate` — Full-Stack HTTP Integration Tests With a Real Embedded Server [official]

`@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)` starts the complete application context including all beans, and provides a `TestRestTemplate` (or `WebTestClient`) wired to the random port. `TestRestTemplate` wraps `RestTemplate` with test-friendly defaults: it does not throw on 4xx/5xx status codes, follows redirects, and supports basic authentication helpers. This is the appropriate tier for testing HTTP-level contracts, security filter chains, global exception handlers, and content negotiation — concerns that `@WebMvcTest` cannot exercise because they require the full servlet stack.

```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Testcontainers
class OrderApiIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired
    TestRestTemplate restTemplate;

    @Autowired
    OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        orderRepository.deleteAll();
    }

    @Test
    void placeOrder_returnsCreatedWithLocation() {
        ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> response = restTemplate.postForEntity(
            "/api/v1/orders",
            new OrderRequest("CUST-7", List.of(new LineItemRequest("SKU-A", 2))),
            OrderResponse.class);

        assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
        assertThat(response.getHeaders().getLocation()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(response.getBody()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(response.getBody().status()).isEqualTo("PENDING");
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_returns404ForMissingOrder() {
        ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> response =
            restTemplate.getForEntity("/api/v1/orders/999999", ProblemDetail.class);

        assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
        assertThat(response.getBody()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(response.getBody().getTitle()).isEqualTo("Order Not Found");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT` starts a real servlet container (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow) on a random port, meaning full-stack tests are significantly slower than slice tests (3-10x slower context startup). Context caching mitigates this when multiple test classes share the same application context shape. If `@MockitoBean` is used, context caching is broken for each unique mock combination. For tests that only need to verify HTTP routing, prefer `@WebMvcTest`; reserve `@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT)` for cross-cutting concerns (auth, exception handling, content negotiation) and contract validation against a real DB.

---

### Pattern 165 — `@TestPropertySource` with `properties` Inline Override — Controlling Application Behaviour in Tests Without Test-Specific Config Files [official]

`@TestPropertySource(properties = {...})` injects individual property overrides directly into the test's `Environment` at the highest priority, beating `application.properties`, profile-specific files, and `@SpringBootTest(properties = {...})` (which has lower priority than `@TestPropertySource`). This is the safest mechanism for toggling feature flags, overriding external service URLs, disabling scheduled tasks, and pinning cache TTLs in specific test scenarios without creating test-specific property files that can drift out of sync with the real configuration.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@TestPropertySource(properties = {
    "feature.new-pricing-engine.enabled=true",
    "scheduler.stock-sync.enabled=false",
    "cache.product.ttl-seconds=0",
    "external.payment.base-url=http://localhost:${wiremock.server.port}"
})
@AutoConfigureWireMock(port = 0)   // WireMock Spring Boot integration, random port
class NewPricingEngineIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    PricingService pricingService;

    @Autowired
    WireMockServer wireMockServer;

    @BeforeEach
    void stubPaymentGateway() {
        wireMockServer.stubFor(
            post(urlPathEqualTo("/payments/validate"))
                .willReturn(okJson("{\"valid\":true,\"fee\":\"1.50\"}")));
    }

    @Test
    void calculatePrice_appliesNewEngineLogicWithPaymentFee() {
        Price price = pricingService.calculate("SKU-A", 5, "CUST-GOLD");

        assertThat(price.baseAmount()).isEqualByComparingTo("249.95");
        assertThat(price.paymentFee()).isEqualByComparingTo("1.50");
        assertThat(price.algorithm()).isEqualTo("V2_ENGINE");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@TestPropertySource(properties = {...})` overrides apply only to the test's `ApplicationContext`; if a bean reads its configuration via a constructor-injected `@Value` field, the override works correctly. However, beans that cache their `@Value` in a static field or read it via `System.getProperty()` bypass Spring's `Environment` entirely and will not see the override. Also, each unique combination of `@TestPropertySource` properties prevents Spring's context caching from reusing an existing context — group tests that require the same property set into a shared base class or common annotation to keep the number of unique context shapes small and startup costs low.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 49

**JUnit 5 `@MethodSource` factory methods that reference `static` fields initialised lazily (e.g., `private static List<Arguments> CASES = null` populated in `@BeforeAll`) produce a `NullPointerException` or empty stream because `@MethodSource` factory methods are invoked during test discovery, which happens before `@BeforeAll` runs** — A developer stores a computationally expensive set of argument rows in a static field and populates it in `@BeforeAll static void setup()`, then references `CASES.stream()` in the `@MethodSource` factory. The factory runs at discovery time (during class loading, before `@BeforeAll`), so `CASES` is null. WHY: JUnit 5 separates discovery from execution; `@BeforeAll` is an execution lifecycle hook, but argument source factory methods are invoked during the discovery phase to enumerate test cases. Fix: initialise the field at declaration (`private static final List<Arguments> CASES = buildCases()`) or use a lazy holder nested class. If construction is expensive, use `@BeforeAll` to prepare state that the test methods themselves access, not the argument source.

**`MockMvcTester.post().content(body)` silently sends an empty body if `.contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)` is omitted — the controller receives a request with no body, Jackson's `@RequestBody` parameter resolves to `null`, and the test fails with a `HttpMessageNotReadableException` or unexpected business-logic NPE rather than a clearly labelled "missing Content-Type" error** — A developer writes `assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/orders").content("{...}"))` without chaining `.contentType(...)`. Spring MVC's content negotiation cannot find a matching `HttpMessageConverter` without a declared content type, so the body is never read. WHY: `MockMvcTester` (like `MockMvc`) requires explicit `Content-Type` on requests — it does not infer content type from the body string. Fix: always chain `.contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)` before `.content(...)`. Add a base class utility method `jsonPost(String uri, String body)` that enforces the content type to prevent the omission team-wide.

**`@DataJpaTest` with `@Transactional` (the default) causes `@Async` repository-backed methods called from the service under test to execute on a different transaction and therefore see a different database snapshot — the test's `em.persist(...)` writes are not yet committed, so the async method observes an empty table** — A developer writes a `@DataJpaTest` that calls a service method which triggers an `@Async` background operation querying the repository. The async thread opens a new transaction (propagation `REQUIRED` starts a new one because the calling transaction is on the test thread, not propagated to async threads). The test's data was never committed. WHY: Spring's `@Transactional` test support wraps the entire test method in a transaction that is rolled back after completion but never committed; `@Async` spawns a new thread outside that transaction boundary. Fix: annotate the individual `@Test` method with `@Commit` to force a commit before the async operation runs, and add manual cleanup in `@AfterEach`. Alternatively, restructure the test to mock the async service layer and test the repository in isolation.

**Testcontainers `@ServiceConnection` with a `GenericContainer` only resolves correctly when `name` is explicitly specified for non-standard images — omitting `name` causes Spring Boot to infer the connection type from the image name prefix, and a custom Redis image named `internal-registry.company.com/redis:7.2` is not recognised, leaving the `RedisConnectionDetails` unconfigured and the `RedisTemplate` pointing at `localhost:6379`** — A team migrates from `@DynamicPropertySource` to `@ServiceConnection` and removes the manual property registration. Their custom Redis image prefix does not match the `spring-boot-testcontainers` connection details factory's recognised prefixes (`redis`, `bitnami/redis`, `redislabs/redjson`, etc.). The auto-configured `RedisTemplate` uses its default `localhost:6379` host and silently connects to whatever is running there (nothing in CI), causing intermittent `RedisConnectionFailureException` errors that are hard to diagnose because the error message does not mention the `@ServiceConnection` inference failure. WHY: `ServiceConnectionAutoConfiguration` matches containers by image name prefix using a string-based registry — it has no way to know that `internal-registry.company.com/redis:7.2` is a Redis instance. Fix: always specify `@ServiceConnection(name = "redis")` (or the canonical service name) when using custom image registries, rather than relying on name inference.

**`AssertJ` `satisfies(Consumer<T>)` does not collect assertion failures from the inner consumer as soft assertions — a failing `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)` inside the consumer immediately throws `AssertionError` and exits the `satisfies` block, so subsequent assertions within the same block are never evaluated, producing a misleading "first field wrong" failure message when multiple fields are actually wrong** — A developer uses `assertThat(order).satisfies(o -> { assertThat(o.id()).isEqualTo(42L); assertThat(o.status()).isEqualTo(SHIPPED); })` expecting that both `id` and `status` failures will appear together in the report. If `id` is wrong, the `satisfies` block exits immediately and the `status` check never runs. WHY: `satisfies` does not wrap the consumer in a `SoftAssertions` context — it is a convenience method for grouping related assertions on the same subject, not a soft-assertion mechanism. Fix: use `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> softly.assertThat(order).satisfies(o -> { ... }))` or replace the `satisfies` block with `SoftAssertions` directly on each field for multi-field failure visibility.
