### Pattern 166 — Mockito `@Spy` + `doReturn` — Partial Mocking Without Calling Real Logic [official]

A `@Spy` wraps a real object instance, delegating all un-stubbed calls to the real implementation while allowing selective stubbing of specific methods. This enables partial mocking of concrete classes — useful for legacy code, template-method hierarchies, and services with one expensive side-effecting method among many cheap ones. The critical idiom is using `doReturn(...).when(spy).method()` instead of `when(spy.method()).thenReturn(...)`: the `when(spy.method())` form calls the real method before Mockito can intercept it, causing side effects or exceptions during test setup.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class InvoiceServiceSpyTest {

    // Mockito creates a real instance then wraps it as a spy
    @Spy
    InvoiceService invoiceService = new InvoiceService(new InMemoryInvoiceRepository());

    @Test
    void generatePdf_skipsRealPdfRendering() {
        // CORRECT: doReturn avoids calling the real renderPdf() during setup
        doReturn(new byte[]{0x25, 0x50, 0x44, 0x46})  // fake PDF bytes
            .when(invoiceService).renderPdf(any(Invoice.class));

        // Real business logic (calculateTotals, applyTax, persist) runs for real
        Invoice invoice = invoiceService.createAndPersist("CUST-99", List.of(
            new LineItem("SKU-A", 2, new BigDecimal("49.99"))));

        byte[] pdf = invoiceService.generatePdf(invoice);

        assertThat(pdf).startsWith(new byte[]{0x25, 0x50, 0x44, 0x46}); // %PDF
        // Verify the real persist path ran (not mocked)
        assertThat(invoiceService.findById(invoice.id())).isPresent();
    }

    @Test
    void doNotUseWhenFormOnSpy_demonstratesThePitfall() {
        // WRONG — this calls the real renderPdf() RIGHT NOW during setup
        // If renderPdf() throws or has side effects, the test breaks here, not at execution
        // when(invoiceService.renderPdf(any())).thenReturn(new byte[0]); // DO NOT DO THIS
        assertThat(true).isTrue(); // placeholder — see gotcha below
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@Spy` partial mocking ties tests to the concrete class's constructor and field layout, making them brittle to refactoring. Prefer designing for full mocking via interfaces; reserve `@Spy` for legacy classes where extracting an interface is not yet feasible, or for spy-on-real-object scenarios (e.g., verifying a method delegates correctly to `super`). Spies also interact poorly with `@Transactional` Spring proxies — you cannot spy on a Spring-managed bean because the proxy wraps the bean, not the other way around; use `@MockitoSpyBean` (Spring Boot 3.4+) for that case.

### Pattern 167 — Mockito `MockedStatic` — Stubbing Static Utility Methods in Isolation [official]

`Mockito.mockStatic(Class<T>)` opens a thread-local `MockedStatic<T>` scope that intercepts static method calls on the target class within the current thread. This enables testing code that calls static utilities (`UUID.randomUUID()`, `LocalDate.now()`, `Files.exists()`, internal security helpers) without refactoring to inject dependencies. The scope must be closed — always use try-with-resources or register cleanup in `@AfterEach`.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderIdGeneratorTest {

    @Test
    void generateOrderId_usesPrefixedUuid() {
        UUID fixedUuid = UUID.fromString("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000042");

        try (MockedStatic<UUID> uuidMock = Mockito.mockStatic(UUID.class)) {
            uuidMock.when(UUID::randomUUID).thenReturn(fixedUuid);

            String orderId = OrderIdGenerator.next();

            assertThat(orderId).isEqualTo("ORD-00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000042");
            uuidMock.verify(UUID::randomUUID, times(1));
        }
        // After the try block, UUID.randomUUID() behaves normally again
    }

    @Test
    void generateOrderId_dateStamped_usesTodaysDate() {
        LocalDate fixed = LocalDate.of(2026, 5, 14);

        try (MockedStatic<LocalDate> dateMock = Mockito.mockStatic(LocalDate.class,
                Mockito.CALLS_REAL_METHODS)) {   // keep all other LocalDate statics real
            dateMock.when(LocalDate::now).thenReturn(fixed);

            String stampedId = OrderIdGenerator.datestamped();

            assertThat(stampedId).startsWith("2026-05-14-");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockedStatic` is thread-local, meaning parallel test execution is safe as long as each test opens its own scope. However, `mockStatic` cannot intercept calls made from the same class being tested when the JVM inlines static calls at bytecode level (rare but possible with `final` methods in JDK classes). Prefer dependency injection (passing a `Supplier<UUID>` or `Clock`) as the primary design; use `MockedStatic` as a last resort for third-party or JDK statics you cannot refactor. Do not leave `MockedStatic` scopes open across test methods — it will silently affect subsequent tests on the same thread.

### Pattern 168 — AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison()` — Deep Field-by-Field Equality Without `equals()` [official]

`assertThat(actual).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(expected)` compares two object graphs field by field, recursively, without requiring `equals()` overrides on domain objects. This is essential for testing DTOs, entities, and response objects where `equals()` is not defined or is identity-based. Configuration options allow ignoring specific fields (e.g., generated IDs, audit timestamps), specifying field comparators, and controlling collection ordering.

```java
@Test
void createProduct_returnsCorrectlyPopulatedResponse() {
    CreateProductRequest request = new CreateProductRequest(
        "Wireless Headphones", "SKU-WH-100", new BigDecimal("149.99"), "ELECTRONICS");

    ProductResponse actual = productService.create(request);

    ProductResponse expected = new ProductResponse(
        null,               // id — generated, ignore it
        "Wireless Headphones",
        "SKU-WH-100",
        new BigDecimal("149.99"),
        "ELECTRONICS",
        null,               // createdAt — generated
        ProductStatus.ACTIVE);

    assertThat(actual)
        .usingRecursiveComparison()
        .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt")          // skip generated fields
        .withStrictTypeChecking()                    // fail if types differ
        .isEqualTo(expected);
}

@Test
void listProducts_orderedByPriceDescending_matchesExpectedShape() {
    List<ProductResponse> products = productService.findAll(Sort.by("price").descending());

    List<ProductResponse> expectedShape = List.of(
        new ProductResponse(null, "Premium Widget", "SKU-P", new BigDecimal("299.99"), "TOOLS", null, ProductStatus.ACTIVE),
        new ProductResponse(null, "Basic Widget",   "SKU-B", new BigDecimal("19.99"),  "TOOLS", null, ProductStatus.ACTIVE));

    assertThat(products)
        .usingRecursiveFieldByFieldElementComparator()
        .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt")
        .containsExactlyElementsOf(expectedShape);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Recursive comparison can produce verbose failure messages for deeply nested objects — the output shows the full path to each differing field, which is helpful but can be overwhelming. Use `.withRepresentation(Representation)` or `.ignoringFields(...)` to narrow the comparison surface when the class graph is large. Be aware that `usingRecursiveComparison()` follows object references and can enter infinite loops on circular object graphs (e.g., bidirectional JPA relationships); use `ignoringFields("children.parent")` or break cycles before asserting.

### Pattern 169 — `TestInterface` + Default Methods — Reusable Test Contracts Across Implementations [official]

JUnit 5 honours `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`, and other lifecycle annotations on interface default methods. This enables defining a reusable contract test as an interface: any class that implements the interface inherits all the contract tests automatically. This is the idiomatic way to ensure multiple implementations of the same interface all pass the same behavioural suite without copy-pasting test code.

```java
// Shared contract for all Cache<K,V> implementations
interface CacheContract<K, V> {

    Cache<K, V> createCache(int maxSize);   // implementors provide the SUT

    @Test
    default void put_andGet_returnsStoredValue() {
        Cache<String, String> cache = createCache(10);
        cache.put("key1", "value1");
        assertThat(cache.get("key1")).contains("value1");
    }

    @Test
    default void get_missingKey_returnsEmpty() {
        Cache<String, String> cache = createCache(10);
        assertThat(cache.get("nonexistent")).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    default void eviction_whenCapacityExceeded_removesOldestEntry() {
        Cache<String, String> cache = createCache(2);
        cache.put("k1", "v1");
        cache.put("k2", "v2");
        cache.put("k3", "v3");  // triggers eviction of k1 (LRU)
        assertThat(cache.get("k1")).isEmpty();
        assertThat(cache.get("k3")).contains("v3");
    }
}

// Each implementation test simply implements the contract interface
class InMemoryCacheTest implements CacheContract<String, String> {
    @Override
    public Cache<String, String> createCache(int maxSize) {
        return new InMemoryLruCache<>(maxSize);
    }
    // All 3 contract tests are inherited automatically
}

class CaffeineCacheTest implements CacheContract<String, String> {
    @Override
    public Cache<String, String> createCache(int maxSize) {
        return new CaffeineBackedCache<>(maxSize);
    }
    // All 3 contract tests also run here
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TestInterface` contracts are powerful for API-based testing but require discipline: the contract must test behaviour at the interface level only — no references to implementation-specific state or internals. If the contract test needs setup that varies per implementation, add `@BeforeEach default void setUp()` with an empty body or make it abstract. JUnit 5 will call the most-specific override, allowing implementors to add their own setup while inheriting the contract tests. Avoid making contract tests too coarse-grained (e.g., full integration scenarios) — keep them focused on the interface's contract, not edge cases specific to one implementation.

---

### Pattern 170 — `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` — Explicit Ordered Test Execution for Stateful Workflows [official]

By default, JUnit 5 runs tests in a deterministic but not alphabetical order. `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` combined with `@Order(n)` annotations enables explicit ordering — essential for integration tests that exercise a stateful workflow (e.g., create → update → delete a resource) where earlier steps produce state consumed by later steps.

```java
@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Testcontainers
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)  // shared state across methods
class CustomerLifecycleOrderedTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired TestRestTemplate rest;

    private Long createdCustomerId;  // shared state — set by step 1, read by steps 2-4

    @Test
    @Order(1)
    void step1_createCustomer_returnsCreatedWithId() {
        ResponseEntity<CustomerResponse> resp = rest.postForEntity(
            "/api/customers",
            new CreateCustomerRequest("Alice", "alice@example.com"),
            CustomerResponse.class);
        assertThat(resp.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
        createdCustomerId = resp.getBody().id();
        assertThat(createdCustomerId).isPositive();
    }

    @Test
    @Order(2)
    void step2_getCustomer_returnsCreatedData() {
        ResponseEntity<CustomerResponse> resp = rest.getForEntity(
            "/api/customers/" + createdCustomerId, CustomerResponse.class);
        assertThat(resp.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK);
        assertThat(resp.getBody().email()).isEqualTo("alice@example.com");
    }

    @Test
    @Order(3)
    void step3_updateCustomer_persistsChange() {
        rest.put("/api/customers/" + createdCustomerId,
            new UpdateCustomerRequest("alice-updated@example.com"));
        CustomerResponse updated = rest.getForObject(
            "/api/customers/" + createdCustomerId, CustomerResponse.class);
        assertThat(updated.email()).isEqualTo("alice-updated@example.com");
    }

    @Test
    @Order(4)
    void step4_deleteCustomer_returns204AndRemovesResource() {
        rest.delete("/api/customers/" + createdCustomerId);
        ResponseEntity<Void> resp = rest.getForEntity(
            "/api/customers/" + createdCustomerId, Void.class);
        assertThat(resp.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Ordered stateful tests violate the principle of test independence — a failure in `@Order(1)` cascades and makes all subsequent steps meaningless or actively misleading. Mitigate this by using `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` to share state within the class and scoping ordered tests to a single workflow concern per class. For unit tests, ordered execution is almost always a smell indicating hidden shared state; refactor to independent tests with `@BeforeEach` setup. Reserve ordered integration tests for end-to-end workflow verification where the cost of setting up the full state from scratch in each test is prohibitive.

---

### Pattern 171 — Mockito `Strictness.STRICT_STUBS` — Eliminating Unnecessary Stubbing and Silent Failures [official]

`MockitoExtension` enables `STRICT_STUBS` by default in Mockito 5.x, which fails the test if any stubbing is declared but never invoked (unnecessary stubbing) or if an interaction happens that was not stubbed and not expected. This catches two major test quality problems: dead stubs left behind after refactoring (which give false confidence) and unexpected interactions that should have been verified.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)  // STRICT_STUBS is the default in Mockito 5
class PaymentProcessorStrictTest {

    @Mock PaymentGateway gateway;
    @Mock NotificationService notifier;
    @InjectMocks PaymentProcessor processor;

    @Test
    void processPayment_success_notifiesCustomer() {
        // Both stubs are USED — strict mode accepts this
        when(gateway.charge("tok_visa", new BigDecimal("99.99")))
            .thenReturn(ChargeResult.success("ch_123"));
        when(notifier.send(anyString(), eq("Payment successful")))
            .thenReturn(true);

        PaymentResult result = processor.process("tok_visa", new BigDecimal("99.99"));

        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo(PaymentStatus.COMPLETED);
        verify(notifier).send("tok_visa", "Payment successful");
    }

    // With STRICT_STUBS, if you add a stub that the test path never reaches,
    // Mockito throws UnnecessaryStubbingException, forcing you to remove it.
    // This is intentional: dead stubs hide the real test scope and mislead readers.

    @Test
    void processPayment_gatewayDecline_doesNotNotify() {
        when(gateway.charge(any(), any()))
            .thenReturn(ChargeResult.declined("Insufficient funds"));
        // Intentionally NO stub for notifier — STRICT_STUBS verifies it is NOT called

        PaymentResult result = processor.process("tok_declined", new BigDecimal("50.00"));

        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo(PaymentStatus.DECLINED);
        verifyNoInteractions(notifier);  // explicit, but STRICT_STUBS would catch it anyway
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `STRICT_STUBS` breaks tests during refactoring when a code path is removed but the test's stubbing is not updated — this is intentional (the stub is now unnecessary). It can feel painful during rapid development where stubs are added speculatively. To opt out for a single test class, annotate with `@MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT)`. Avoid opting out globally — the default strict mode is the most effective single Mockito setting for maintaining test quality over time.

---

### Pattern 172 — Testcontainers `Network` + Multi-Container Dependency Graph — Wiring Service-to-Service Communication in Tests [official]

When integration tests require multiple containers that communicate with each other (e.g., a microservice calling a sidecar, or a service connecting to Redis via an internal hostname), `Network.newNetwork()` creates a Docker bridge network and `withNetworkAliases(...)` assigns DNS names resolvable within that network. Containers that depend on each other can be started in order using `dependsOn()`.

```java
@Testcontainers
@SpringBootTest
class ProductSearchIntegrationTest {

    static final Network NETWORK = Network.newNetwork();

    @Container
    static final GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7.2-alpine")
            .withNetwork(NETWORK)
            .withNetworkAliases("redis-cache")   // resolvable as "redis-cache" inside the network
            .withExposedPorts(6379)
            .waitingFor(Wait.forLogMessage(".*Ready to accept connections.*\\n", 1));

    @Container
    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
            .withNetwork(NETWORK)
            .withNetworkAliases("product-db");

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void configureProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        // Host-side connectivity for Spring Boot to reach redis
        registry.add("spring.data.redis.host", redis::getHost);
        registry.add("spring.data.redis.port", () -> redis.getMappedPort(6379));
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
    }

    @Autowired ProductSearchService searchService;

    @Test
    void search_withCaching_returnsCachedResultOnSecondCall() {
        searchService.index(new Product("SKU-CACHE-1", "Cached Widget", "TOOLS"));

        List<Product> first  = searchService.search("Cached Widget");
        List<Product> second = searchService.search("Cached Widget");

        assertThat(first).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(second).isEqualTo(first);
        // Second call should be served from Redis cache (no DB query)
        // Verify via Micrometer cache metrics or a cache hit counter
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Network-connected multi-container tests dramatically increase startup time (30–90 seconds for a full stack). Use `@Container static` (class-level) containers with context reuse (`testcontainers.reuse.enable=true` in `.testcontainers.properties`) to amortize the cost across test runs. Be aware that `Network` objects are not automatically closed by Testcontainers JUnit 5 integration when declared as static fields — annotate with `@Container` or close them in `@AfterAll`. Each unique network is a Docker resource; excessive network creation in CI can exhaust Docker daemon file descriptors.

---

### Pattern 173 — `@DataRedisTest` — Slice Testing for Redis-Backed Repositories and Caches [official]

`@DataRedisTest` loads only the Redis-related slice of the auto-configuration: `RedisTemplate`, `ReactiveRedisTemplate`, `StringRedisValueOperations`, and `@RedisHash` repositories. It does not load `@Service`, `@Controller`, or JPA infrastructure. Combine with Testcontainers to run against a real Redis instance rather than an embedded substitute.

```java
@DataRedisTest
@Testcontainers
class CartRepositoryRedisTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static final GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7.2-alpine")
            .withExposedPorts(6379)
            .waitingFor(Wait.forLogMessage(".*Ready to accept connections.*\\n", 1));

    @Autowired CartRepository cartRepository;  // Spring Data Redis @RedisHash repository
    @Autowired StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate;

    @AfterEach
    void clearRedis() {
        redisTemplate.getConnectionFactory().getConnection().serverCommands().flushDb();
    }

    @Test
    void save_andFindById_roundTripsCartData() {
        Cart cart = new Cart("SESS-42", List.of(
            new CartItem("SKU-A", 2, new BigDecimal("49.99")),
            new CartItem("SKU-B", 1, new BigDecimal("129.00"))));

        cartRepository.save(cart);
        Optional<Cart> found = cartRepository.findById("SESS-42");

        assertThat(found).isPresent();
        assertThat(found.get().items()).hasSize(2);
        assertThat(found.get().items())
            .extracting(CartItem::sku)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("SKU-A", "SKU-B");
    }

    @Test
    void cart_expiry_isSetCorrectly() {
        Cart cart = new Cart("SESS-TTL", List.of());
        cartRepository.save(cart);

        Long ttl = redisTemplate.getExpire("cart:SESS-TTL");
        assertThat(ttl).isBetween(1L, 3600L);  // cart TTL should be at most 1 hour
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@DataRedisTest` does not start an embedded Redis; a `@ServiceConnection`-wired Testcontainers container is required. The slice only auto-configures Spring Data Redis components — if your repository class uses custom `RedisTemplate<K,V>` beans defined in `@Configuration` classes outside the slice, those beans are not loaded. Use `@Import(RedisConfig.class)` to pull in custom configuration. `flushDb()` in `@AfterEach` is aggressive but necessary to prevent test ordering issues; prefer namespace-prefixed keys (`cart:SESS-*`) so you can use `keys("cart:*")` + `delete` for more surgical cleanup.

---

### Pattern 174 — `Awaitility` `failFast` + `conditionEvaluationListener` — Diagnosable Async Assertion with Early Abort [official]

Awaitility's `await()` retries an assertion until it passes or a timeout is reached. `failFast` adds a short-circuit: if a sentinel condition becomes true (e.g., a thread crashes or a failure flag is set) before the main condition succeeds, Awaitility aborts immediately rather than waiting for the full timeout. `conditionEvaluationListener` logs each evaluation attempt for post-mortem debugging.

```java
@Test
void asyncOrderProcessor_processesAllOrders_withinSla() {
    AtomicBoolean processorCrashed = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    List<String> processedIds = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());

    // Register crash detector — if the processor thread dies, stop waiting immediately
    orderProcessor.onFatalError(() -> processorCrashed.set(true));

    // Submit 5 orders asynchronously
    List<String> orderIds = IntStream.range(0, 5)
        .mapToObj(i -> orderService.submitAsync("CUST-" + i))
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

    orderProcessor.onOrderProcessed(processedIds::add);

    await()
        .failFast("Processor crashed — no point waiting",
            () -> processorCrashed.get())
        .conditionEvaluationListener(condition ->
            log.debug("Awaiting order processing: {}/{} done after {}ms",
                processedIds.size(), orderIds.size(),
                condition.getElapsedTimeInMS()))
        .pollDelay(Duration.ofMillis(50))
        .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(100))
        .atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .untilAsserted(() ->
            assertThat(processedIds)
                .containsExactlyInAnyOrderElementsOf(orderIds));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `failFast` requires a sentinel condition that is independently observable — if the failure mode does not set a detectable flag, `failFast` provides no benefit. In practice, hook the `failFast` predicate to thread `UncaughtExceptionHandler`s or error event listeners. `conditionEvaluationListener` logs on every poll cycle; at `pollInterval(100ms)` over `atMost(5s)` that is up to 50 log lines per test — enable only at DEBUG level or in CI failure analysis mode. Do not use `Awaitility.setDefaultTimeout()` globally in test infrastructure without documenting it; silent global defaults mask individual test SLA requirements.

---

### Pattern 175 — jqwik `@Property` + `@Provide` — Property-Based Testing for Business Invariants [community]

jqwik is the property-based testing framework for JUnit 5. `@Property` methods receive randomly generated arguments supplied by `@Provide`-annotated `Arbitrary` factories or built-in `@ForAll` annotations. Properties express invariants that must hold for all valid inputs, rather than specific example values — this discovers edge cases that example-based tests miss.

```java
class SlugGeneratorPropertyTest {

    @Property(tries = 500)
    void slug_isAlwaysLowercase(@ForAll @AlphaChars @StringLength(min = 1, max = 80) String input) {
        String slug = SlugGenerator.from(input);
        assertThat(slug).isEqualTo(slug.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT));
    }

    @Property(tries = 500)
    void slug_containsNoSpacesOrSpecialChars(
            @ForAll @AlphaChars @Whitespace @StringLength(min = 1, max = 80) String input) {
        String slug = SlugGenerator.from(input);
        assertThat(slug).matches("[a-z0-9-]*");
    }

    @Property(tries = 200)
    void slug_isIdempotent(@ForAll @AlphaChars @StringLength(min = 1, max = 40) String input) {
        String once  = SlugGenerator.from(input);
        String twice = SlugGenerator.from(once);
        assertThat(twice).isEqualTo(once);
    }

    // Custom Arbitrary for domain-specific inputs
    @Provide
    Arbitrary<ProductCode> validProductCodes() {
        return Combinators.combine(
            Arbitraries.strings().withCharRange('A', 'Z').ofLength(3),
            Arbitraries.integers().between(100, 999)
        ).as((prefix, num) -> new ProductCode(prefix + "-" + num));
    }

    @Property(tries = 300)
    void productCode_roundTripsViaJson(@ForAll("validProductCodes") ProductCode code)
            throws Exception {
        String json    = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(code);
        ProductCode rt = new ObjectMapper().readValue(json, ProductCode.class);
        assertThat(rt).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(code);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Property-based tests are significantly more powerful than example tests for invariant verification but require careful `Arbitrary` design — a poorly constrained generator produces inputs that violate preconditions rather than finding real bugs. Use `@Assume` (or `Assume.that(...)`) to filter invalid inputs rather than checking them in the test body, so jqwik's shrinking algorithm can still find minimal failing examples. jqwik integrates with JUnit 5's `@ExtendWith` stack and can share `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach` lifecycle — no separate test runner needed. `tries` defaults to 1000; reduce to 100–200 for tests with expensive setup to keep CI times manageable.

---

### Pattern 176 — ArchUnit `noClasses().that().areAnnotatedWith()` — Banning Deprecated or Forbidden Patterns [official]

ArchUnit's `noClasses()` API complements `layeredArchitecture()` and naming rules with targeted prohibition rules. Use it to enforce team conventions like "no class in the `domain` package may reference Spring annotations", "no `@Transactional` in controllers", or "no test class may use `Thread.sleep`".

```java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example.shop")
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainMustNotDependOnSpring =
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("org.springframework..")
            .because("Domain layer must be framework-agnostic for portability and testability");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule controllersNotTransactional =
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..controller..")
            .should().beAnnotatedWith("org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional")
            .because("Transaction boundaries belong in the service layer, not controllers");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noThreadSleepInTests =
        noClasses().that().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Test")
            .should(callMethod(Thread.class, "sleep", long.class))
            .because("Use Awaitility instead of Thread.sleep for async assertions");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule repositoriesMustBeInterfaces =
        classes().that().resideInAPackage("..repository..")
            .and().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Repository")
            .should().beInterfaces()
            .because("Repository abstractions must be interfaces to enable mocking and multiple implementations");
}
```

**Tradeoff.** ArchUnit rules run during the test suite and add class-loading overhead (typically 1–3 seconds for moderate codebases). Use `@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "...", importOptions = {DoNotIncludeTests.class})` to exclude test classes from architectural rules that should only apply to production code. Rules with `.because(...)` clauses dramatically improve developer experience when rules fail — always include a reason. Be conservative with global `noClasses()` rules early in a project's life; introduce them incrementally as the team agrees on boundaries, to avoid CI failures that block legitimate work.

---

### Pattern 177 — `@TempDir` with `CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS` — Retaining Diagnostic Artifacts on Failure [official]

JUnit 5's `@TempDir` annotation creates a temporary directory for each test. The `cleanup` attribute (added in JUnit 5.9) controls when the directory is deleted: `CleanupMode.ALWAYS` (default), `CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS`, or `CleanupMode.NEVER`. `ON_SUCCESS` keeps the directory intact when a test fails, enabling post-mortem inspection of generated files, logs, or output artifacts.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ReportGeneratorTest {

    // Directory survives when the test fails — inspect report.html for debugging
    @TempDir(cleanup = CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS)
    Path outputDir;

    @InjectMocks ReportGenerator generator;

    @Test
    void generateHtmlReport_producesValidHtml() throws Exception {
        ReportRequest request = new ReportRequest(
            "Q1-2026", List.of(
                new MetricRow("Revenue",    "1,234,567"),
                new MetricRow("Orders",     "4,892"),
                new MetricRow("Conversion", "3.2%")));

        generator.generate(request, outputDir);

        Path report = outputDir.resolve("q1-2026-report.html");
        assertThat(report).exists();

        String content = Files.readString(report, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        assertThat(content)
            .contains("<!DOCTYPE html>")
            .contains("Q1-2026")
            .contains("1,234,567")
            .doesNotContain("<script>")  // XSS guard
            .doesNotContainPattern(Pattern.compile("(?i)javascript:"));
    }

    @Test
    void generateHtmlReport_withNullRequest_throwsIllegalArgument() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> generator.generate(null, outputDir))
            .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
            .hasMessage("request must not be null");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `CleanupMode.ON_SUCCESS` is most valuable in CI environments where the test output directory is archived as an artifact. Set `outputDir` to a path inside the CI workspace's artifact directory for automatic collection. `CleanupMode.NEVER` is useful during local development but should not be committed as the default — it accumulates directories indefinitely. If the test creates large binary files (PDFs, images), consider `ON_SUCCESS` combined with a global `@BeforeAll` teardown that prunes directories older than 24 hours to prevent disk accumulation on long-running CI agents.

---

### Pattern 178 — WireMock Fault Simulation — Testing Resilience to Network Failures and Partial Responses [official]

WireMock's `Fault` enumeration simulates network-level failure modes that are impossible to reproduce with simple stubbing: `CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER`, `EMPTY_RESPONSE`, `MALFORMED_RESPONSE_CHUNK`, and `RANDOM_DATA_THEN_CLOSE`. These test the resilience of retry logic, circuit breakers, and timeout handling in HTTP client code.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureWireMock(port = 0)
@TestPropertySource(properties = "payment.gateway.url=http://localhost:${wiremock.server.port}")
class PaymentGatewayResilienceTest {

    @Autowired WireMockServer wireMockServer;
    @Autowired PaymentGatewayClient client;

    @BeforeEach
    void resetWireMock() {
        wireMockServer.resetAll();
    }

    @Test
    void charge_onConnectionReset_retriesAndSucceedsOnThirdAttempt() {
        // First two calls: connection reset; third call: success
        wireMockServer.stubFor(post(urlPathEqualTo("/v1/charges"))
            .inScenario("retry-on-reset")
            .whenScenarioStateIs(Scenario.STARTED)
            .willReturn(aResponse().withFault(Fault.CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER))
            .willSetStateTo("FIRST_FAILURE"));

        wireMockServer.stubFor(post(urlPathEqualTo("/v1/charges"))
            .inScenario("retry-on-reset")
            .whenScenarioStateIs("FIRST_FAILURE")
            .willReturn(aResponse().withFault(Fault.CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER))
            .willSetStateTo("SECOND_FAILURE"));

        wireMockServer.stubFor(post(urlPathEqualTo("/v1/charges"))
            .inScenario("retry-on-reset")
            .whenScenarioStateIs("SECOND_FAILURE")
            .willReturn(okJson("{\"id\":\"ch_retry_ok\",\"status\":\"succeeded\"}")));

        ChargeResult result = client.charge(
            new ChargeRequest("tok_visa", new BigDecimal("50.00")));

        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo("succeeded");
        wireMockServer.verify(3, postRequestedFor(urlPathEqualTo("/v1/charges")));
    }

    @Test
    void charge_onConsistentTimeout_activatesCircuitBreaker() {
        wireMockServer.stubFor(post(anyUrl())
            .willReturn(aResponse()
                .withFixedDelay(3000)  // 3 second delay to trigger client timeout
                .withStatus(200)));

        // Client has 500ms timeout + circuit breaker that opens after 3 consecutive timeouts
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) client.charge(
                new ChargeRequest("tok_slow", new BigDecimal("1.00")));
        }).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreakerOpenException.class);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Fault simulation tests are slow by nature — `withFixedDelay(3000)` blocks for 3 seconds per invocation. Keep fault tests in a dedicated `@Tag("resilience")` group excluded from the default test run and included in a nightly or pre-release pipeline. WireMock scenarios are stateful within the server instance — always call `wireMockServer.resetAll()` in `@BeforeEach` to prevent scenario state from bleeding across tests. `Fault.RANDOM_DATA_THEN_CLOSE` is particularly useful for testing HTTP client robustness against malformed chunked encoding, which many production HTTP clients handle poorly.

---

### Pattern 179 — `@TestBean` — Replacing Spring Beans with Static Factory Methods in Boot 3.4+ [official]

`@TestBean` (Spring Boot 3.4+) is the successor to `@MockBean` / `@MockitoBean` for replacing a bean in the application context with a fully custom implementation (not a Mockito mock). It requires a static factory method in the test class (or a referenced class) and does not break context caching the way `@MockitoBean` can — the replacement is encoded in the context configuration, allowing contexts with the same replacement to be shared.

```java
@SpringBootTest
class FeatureFlagServiceTest {

    // Replaces the real EmailService bean with a no-op stub that records calls
    @TestBean(methodName = "stubEmailService")
    EmailService emailService;

    // Static factory — @TestBean discovers this by the methodName reference
    static EmailService stubEmailService() {
        return new EmailService() {
            final List<String> sent = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

            @Override
            public void send(String to, String subject, String body) {
                sent.add(to + ":" + subject);
            }

            @Override
            public List<String> sentEmails() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(sent); }
        };
    }

    @Autowired RegistrationService registrationService;

    @Test
    void register_sendsWelcomeEmail() {
        registrationService.register(new RegistrationRequest("bob@example.com", "Bob"));

        assertThat(emailService.sentEmails())
            .containsExactly("bob@example.com:Welcome to the platform!");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `@TestBean` produces a real replacement object, not a Mockito mock, so Mockito's `verify()`, `when()`, and `ArgumentCaptor` APIs are not available on it. This is by design — for mock-style interaction testing, `@MockitoBean` is still the right tool. `@TestBean` shines for replacing beans with test doubles that carry state (email recorders, in-memory repositories, deterministic clocks) because those objects cannot be trivially set up via `when(...).thenReturn(...)`. The static factory method must be accessible by name — use `methodName = "..."` to avoid name collision errors when the test class has multiple `@TestBean` declarations.

---

### Pattern 180 — `RestClient` + `MockRestServiceServer` — Testing Declarative HTTP Clients in Spring 6.1+ [official]

Spring Framework 6.1+ `RestClient` is the successor to `RestTemplate` for synchronous HTTP. Its builder-based API supports interceptors, which `MockRestServiceServer` uses to intercept and assert on outbound requests without a real network connection. Use `MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(restClient)` to wire the mock server to a `RestClient` instance.

```java
@SpringBootTest
class InventoryApiClientTest {

    @Autowired InventoryApiClient inventoryClient;  // uses RestClient internally
    @Autowired RestClient.Builder restClientBuilder;

    MockRestServiceServer mockServer;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUpMockServer() {
        mockServer = MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(restClientBuilder).build();
    }

    @AfterEach
    void verifyMockServer() {
        mockServer.verify();  // fails if any expected requests were not made
    }

    @Test
    void getInventory_parsesResponseAndReturnsStockLevel() {
        mockServer.expect(once(),
                requestTo("https://inventory.internal/api/v2/stock/SKU-A"))
            .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
            .andExpect(header("Accept", "application/json"))
            .andRespond(withSuccess(
                """
                {"sku":"SKU-A","quantity":42,"warehouse":"EAST-1"}
                """,
                MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        StockLevel level = inventoryClient.getStock("SKU-A");

        assertThat(level.sku()).isEqualTo("SKU-A");
        assertThat(level.quantity()).isEqualTo(42);
        assertThat(level.warehouse()).isEqualTo("EAST-1");
    }

    @Test
    void getInventory_on503_throwsServiceUnavailable() {
        mockServer.expect(once(), requestTo(containsString("/stock/SKU-OFFLINE")))
            .andRespond(withServiceUnavailable());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> inventoryClient.getStock("SKU-OFFLINE"))
            .isInstanceOf(InventoryServiceException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("503");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockRestServiceServer` operates at the interceptor level — it intercepts `ClientHttpRequest` objects before they leave the application, so it tests the full `RestClient` configuration (URL construction, headers, serialization) but not the network stack. It is not suitable for testing connection timeouts, SSL configuration, or proxy behaviour — use WireMock or Testcontainers HTTP mocks for those. `mockServer.verify()` in `@AfterEach` catches cases where the test passed without making the expected request — a subtle failure mode when the code under test short-circuits (e.g., returning a cached value) without actually calling the HTTP client.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

**Mockito `@Spy` on a Spring-managed bean proxied by `@Transactional` fails silently — the spy wraps the raw object, but the application context injects the CGLIB proxy, so the spy is unreachable and verification calls like `verify(spy).someMethod()` never match actual invocations** — WHY: Spring's `@Transactional` wraps beans in a CGLIB subclass proxy at context creation time. When you declare `@Spy MyService myService = new MyService()` and try to wire it via `@InjectMocks`, Spring injects the proxy, not the spy, because the spy exists outside the Spring container. Calls go through the proxy to the real object, bypassing the spy entirely. Fix: use `@MockitoSpyBean` (Spring Boot 3.4+, replacing the deprecated `@SpyBean`) to register the spy inside the Spring context where it wraps the proxy correctly, or restructure to test the service without Spring context involvement.

**`AssertJ` `usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(expected)` treats `null` fields in `expected` as "must be null" — if `expected.someField` is `null`, the assertion requires `actual.someField` to also be `null`, even if you intended `null` to mean "don't care"** — WHY: Recursive comparison semantics differ from `isEqualToIgnoringNullFields()` (which is lenient about nulls in `expected`). The recursive comparison API intentionally treats every field in `expected` as a required value, including `null`. Fix: use `.ignoringFields("id", "createdAt")` to explicitly exclude fields you do not want to assert, rather than setting them to `null` in the expected object. Alternatively, chain `.ignoringExpectedNullFields()` to skip null fields in `expected` — but be explicit about which direction you mean.

**`MockedStatic` opened in a `@BeforeEach` method without being stored in an instance field and closed in `@AfterEach` leaks across test methods on the same thread — subsequent tests receive the stubbed static behaviour without knowing it, causing intermittent failures that are nearly impossible to diagnose from the test output alone** — WHY: `MockedStatic` is backed by a thread-local Mockito mock scope. Forgetting to close it (via `try-with-resources` or explicit `mockedStatic.close()`) leaves the scope active. Because JUnit 5 reuses threads for test methods (especially with `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`), a leaked `MockedStatic` from test method A affects test method B, which may not stub the static at all and therefore receives an empty or default value. Fix: always use `try-with-resources` inside the test method itself, or store `MockedStatic<?>` in an instance field, open it in `@BeforeEach`, and close it in `@AfterEach`. Add a `@AfterEach void closeStaticMocks()` as a safety net.

**`@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` tests that share state via instance fields silently reset between methods when `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_METHOD)` (the default) is used — a new test instance is created for every method, so the `createdCustomerId` field set in `@Order(1)` is `null` in `@Order(2)`, causing a NullPointerException or a lookup for a missing record** — WHY: JUnit 5's default lifecycle is `PER_METHOD` — a fresh test class instance is constructed before each test method. `@TestMethodOrder` controls execution order but not instance lifecycle. The ordered execution pattern for stateful workflows requires `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` to share a single instance across all ordered methods. Fix: always combine `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` with `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` for stateful ordered tests. Add a comment explaining the shared-state dependency so future maintainers do not inadvertently change the lifecycle annotation.

**WireMock scenario state persists across `@Test` methods within the same `@SpringBootTest` context when `wireMockServer.resetAll()` is not called in `@BeforeEach` — the second test starts in the scenario state left by the first test (e.g., `"SECOND_FAILURE"` instead of `Scenario.STARTED`), causing the wrong stub to match and the test to observe unexpected behaviour without any clear error message** — WHY: WireMock's `WireMockServer` instance is a Spring singleton bean when using `@AutoConfigureWireMock` — it is shared across all tests in the same application context. Scenario state (`setState`, `willSetStateTo`) is mutable server-side state that is not automatically reset between test methods, unlike Mockito stubs which are method-scoped. Fix: call `wireMockServer.resetAll()` (or the more granular `wireMockServer.resetScenarios()`) in `@BeforeEach` for every test class that uses stateful scenarios. Add this as a team-wide coding standard enforced by a shared `@BeforeEach` in a base test class.

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### 181. `@WebMvcTest` with `MockMvcTester` — AssertJ-Fluent Controller Testing Without Raw `ResultActions` [official]

`MockMvcTester` (Spring Boot 4.0+) wraps `MockMvc` with an AssertJ-style fluent interface, eliminating the need for `andExpect(status().isOk())` chains and enabling readable, composable controller tests. It is auto-configured in `@WebMvcTest` classes and supports `bodyJson()`, `convertTo()`, and standard AssertJ matchers directly on the response.

```java
@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvcTester mvc;

    @MockitoBean
    private ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void getProduct_returnsProductJson() {
        given(productService.findById(42L))
            .willReturn(new Product(42L, "Widget", BigDecimal.valueOf(9.99)));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/products/{id}", 42L)
                .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .hasContentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.name").isEqualTo("Widget");
    }

    @Test
    void getProduct_whenNotFound_returns404() {
        given(productService.findById(99L))
            .willThrow(new ProductNotFoundException(99L));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/products/{id}", 99L))
            .hasStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockMvcTester` IDE auto-complete and assertion failure messages are dramatically better than raw `ResultActions` because AssertJ integrates with the IDE's "copy failing assertion" workflow. The drawback is that `MockMvcTester` is only available in Spring Boot 4.0+ (it does not exist in Boot 3.x), so codebases on Boot 3.x must continue using `MockMvc` + `andExpect()` chains or opt in via `spring-boot-test-autoconfigure` snapshot builds. JSON path assertions via `.bodyJson().extractingPath()` return `AbstractStringAssert` for string nodes and `AbstractIntegerAssert` for numeric nodes — calling the wrong assertion type produces a confusing ClassCastException rather than a descriptive failure message. [official]

---

### 182. Awaitility `fibonacci()` Poll Interval — Backoff-Friendly Async Condition Polling [official]

Awaitility supports pluggable `PollInterval` strategies. The built-in `fibonacci()` strategy generates polling intervals in the Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 ms…), providing rapid initial checks followed by natural exponential backoff — ideal for event-driven systems where the condition may be satisfied almost immediately or may take seconds. Use `iterative(d -> d.multipliedBy(2))` for exact doubling backoff.

```java
import static org.awaitility.Awaitility.await;
import static org.awaitility.pollinterval.FibonacciPollInterval.fibonacci;
import static java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.SECONDS;
import static java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS;

class OrderProcessingIT {

    @Test
    void orderEventPublished_eventuallyUpdatesInventory() {
        orderService.placeOrder(new Order("SKU-9", 2));

        await()
            .pollDelay(10, MILLISECONDS)           // skip first 10 ms
            .pollInterval(fibonacci())              // 1,1,2,3,5,8,13... ms
            .atMost(10, SECONDS)
            .ignoreException(OptimisticLockException.class) // transient
            .untilAsserted(() ->
                assertThat(inventoryRepository.findBySku("SKU-9").getQuantity())
                    .isEqualTo(98)
            );
    }

    @Test
    void orderStatus_remainsProcessingForFullWindow() {
        String orderId = orderService.placeOrder(new Order("SKU-1", 1)).getId();

        await()
            .during(500, MILLISECONDS)
            .atMost(1500, MILLISECONDS)
            .until(() -> orderRepository.findById(orderId)
                .map(o -> o.getStatus() == OrderStatus.PROCESSING)
                .orElse(false));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `fibonacci()` and `iterative(...)` poll intervals are more CPU-friendly than fixed short intervals for long-running async operations (e.g., 30-second Kafka consumer lag), but they add complexity. For simple 1–2 second waits, a fixed `pollInterval(100, MILLISECONDS)` is more predictable and easier to reason about during flaky-test diagnosis. `ignoreException` swallows exceptions as false conditions — if the ignored exception type is thrown permanently (infrastructure down), the test will time out rather than failing fast. Always pair with a realistic `atMost` timeout and add `failFast` for conditions that indicate permanent failure. [official]
