## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 301** — JUnit 5 `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` returning `Stream<Arguments>` for multi-field domain object cases
When a parameterized test requires multiple correlated fields (e.g., input, expected output, and a description), use `Arguments.of(...)` inside a `Stream<Arguments>` factory. The factory method can live in the same class or in a shared `TestData` utility, enabling reuse across test classes without duplicating data.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class PricingEngineTest {

    static Stream<Arguments> discountCases() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of("GOLD",   500.0,  0.20, 400.0,  "gold tier 20% off"),
            Arguments.of("SILVER", 200.0,  0.10, 180.0,  "silver tier 10% off"),
            Arguments.of("NONE",   100.0,  0.00, 100.0,  "no discount"),
            Arguments.of("GOLD",   50.0,   0.20, 40.0,   "gold on small order")
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "[{index}] {4}")
    @MethodSource("discountCases")
    void appliesCorrectDiscount(String tier, double base, double rate,
                                double expected, String label) {
        PricingEngine engine = new PricingEngine();
        double actual = engine.applyDiscount(tier, base);
        assertThat(actual).isEqualByComparingTo(expected);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: The `@MethodSource` name must match the static method name exactly — a typo silently skips all cases with a `PreconditionViolationException` at suite startup rather than at test runtime, which can be mistaken for a test-not-found problem in some CI dashboards. Prefer naming factory methods with the suffix `Cases` to make them easy to grep. [official]

---

**Pattern 302** — Mockito `InOrder` verification for interaction sequence correctness on collaborators
When the SUT calls two or more collaborators in a specific order (e.g., first `validator.validate()` then `repository.save()`), use `InOrder` to assert the sequence. Without `InOrder`, individual `verify()` calls pass even if the order is reversed, silently accepting incorrect behaviour.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InOrder;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.Mockito;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock Validator<Order>  validator;
    @Mock OrderRepository   repository;
    @Mock AuditLogger       auditLogger;

    @Test
    void savesOnlyAfterValidationAndLogsAfterSave() {
        Order order = new Order("item-1", 3);
        when(validator.validate(order)).thenReturn(ValidationResult.ok());
        when(repository.save(order)).thenReturn(order.withId(42L));

        OrderService sut = new OrderService(validator, repository, auditLogger);
        sut.process(order);

        InOrder seq = inOrder(validator, repository, auditLogger);
        seq.verify(validator).validate(order);
        seq.verify(repository).save(order);
        seq.verify(auditLogger).log(eq(42L), anyString());
        seq.verifyNoMoreInteractions();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `InOrder.verifyNoMoreInteractions()` is scoped only to the collaborators passed to `inOrder(...)`, not all mocks. Calling the global `verifyNoMoreInteractions(validator, repository, auditLogger)` after `InOrder` assertions double-counts already-verified interactions unless `ignoreStubs()` is applied, leading to false positives. Use one style per test. [official]

---

**Pattern 303** — AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison()` with `ignoringFields()` for deep equality ignoring generated fields
When asserting that a returned domain object equals an expected object except for server-generated fields (id, createdAt, version), `usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields(...)` avoids writing boilerplate field-by-field assertions and catches new fields added to the class automatically.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import java.time.Instant;

class UserServiceTest {

    UserService sut = new UserService(new InMemoryUserRepository());

    @Test
    void createdUserMatchesInputIgnoringServerFields() {
        CreateUserRequest req = new CreateUserRequest("alice", "alice@example.com");
        User actual = sut.createUser(req);

        User expected = User.builder()
            .username("alice")
            .email("alice@example.com")
            .active(true)
            .build();

        assertThat(actual)
            .usingRecursiveComparison()
            .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt", "version")
            .isEqualTo(expected);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `usingRecursiveComparison()` by default compares collections by order; if the SUT returns a `Set` or an unordered `List`, unexpected order differences cause spurious failures. Use `.withEqualsForType(Comparator, Collection.class)` or `.ignoringCollectionOrder()` when comparing collections that carry no ordering guarantee. [official]

---

**Pattern 304** — JUnit 5 `@ExtendWith` custom `ParameterResolver` for injecting shared heavyweight test fixtures
When multiple test classes need the same expensive resource (e.g., a parsed schema file, a compiled regex set, a deterministic RNG seed), write a `ParameterResolver` extension that creates the resource once per JVM and injects it as a constructor or method parameter. This avoids `static` fields on test classes and keeps resource lifecycle explicit.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class CompiledPatternsExtension implements ParameterResolver {

    private static final CompiledPatterns INSTANCE =
        CompiledPatterns.loadFromClasspath("/test-patterns.json");

    @Override
    public boolean supportsParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        return pc.getParameter().getType() == CompiledPatterns.class;
    }

    @Override
    public Object resolveParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        return INSTANCE;
    }
}

// Usage
@ExtendWith(CompiledPatternsExtension.class)
class PatternMatchingTest {

    @Test
    void emailPatternMatchesRFC5321(CompiledPatterns patterns) {
        Pattern email = patterns.get("email");
        assertThat(email.matcher("user@example.com").matches()).isTrue();
        assertThat(email.matcher("not-an-email").matches()).isFalse();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Because the singleton is created at JVM startup (class initialiser), any exception thrown during `loadFromClasspath` surfaces as a cryptic `ExceptionInInitializerError` rather than a test failure with context. Wrap the static initialiser in a try-catch that rethrows as `IllegalStateException` with a descriptive message pointing to the classpath resource. [community]

---

**Pattern 305** — Testcontainers `Network` with aliased containers for multi-service integration tests
When an integration test spans multiple containers that must communicate (e.g., an app container calling a DB container by hostname), create a shared `Network` and assign each container a `networkAlias`. This mirrors a real Docker Compose environment and avoids hard-coding container IP addresses.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.testcontainers.containers.*;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class MultiServiceIntegrationTest {

    static Network net = Network.newNetwork();

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16")
        .withNetwork(net)
        .withNetworkAliases("db");

    @Container
    static GenericContainer<?> app = new GenericContainer<>("myapp:test")
        .withNetwork(net)
        .withEnv("DB_HOST", "db")
        .withEnv("DB_PORT", "5432")
        .waitingFor(Wait.forHttp("/actuator/health").forStatusCode(200))
        .dependsOn(postgres);

    @Test
    void appReachesDatabase() {
        String url = "http://" + app.getHost() + ":" + app.getFirstMappedPort();
        assertThat(HttpClient.get(url + "/health").status()).isEqualTo(200);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Network.newNetwork()` creates an anonymous Docker network that is cleaned up after the test JVM exits, but only if Ryuk (the Testcontainers resource reaper) is enabled. If Ryuk is disabled (`TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true`) in a restricted CI environment, orphaned networks accumulate. Always call `net.close()` in an `@AfterAll` or register the network with `@RegisterExtension` so it implements `Closeable`. [official]

---

**Pattern 306** — AssertJ `SoftAssertions` with `assertSoftly` lambda for accumulating multiple failures per test
`assertSoftly` collects all assertion failures within the lambda and reports them together at the end, rather than stopping at the first failure. This is especially useful for validating API response DTOs or form validation results where all field errors matter.
```java
import org.assertj.core.api.SoftAssertions;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class OrderResponseDtoTest {

    OrderService sut = new OrderService(new FakePaymentGateway());

    @Test
    void successResponseContainsAllExpectedFields() {
        OrderResponseDto response = sut.placeOrder(validRequest());

        SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(soft -> {
            soft.assertThat(response.orderId()).as("orderId").isNotNull();
            soft.assertThat(response.status()).as("status").isEqualTo("CONFIRMED");
            soft.assertThat(response.total()).as("total")
                .isEqualByComparingTo(new BigDecimal("129.99"));
            soft.assertThat(response.estimatedDelivery())
                .as("estimatedDelivery").isAfter(LocalDate.now());
            soft.assertThat(response.lineItems())
                .as("lineItems").hasSize(2).doesNotContainNull();
        });
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `assertSoftly` uses a thread-local to collect errors; if the lambda spawns virtual threads or other `CompletableFuture` chains that call assertion methods off the calling thread, those failures are not captured by the same `SoftAssertions` collector and silently pass. Keep all assertion calls synchronous within the lambda. [official]

---

**Pattern 307** — Mockito `thenAnswer` with `AtomicInteger` counter to simulate retry-then-succeed behaviour
Use `thenAnswer` with a shared `AtomicInteger` to make a mock fail a configurable number of times then succeed. This enables testing retry logic in isolation without depending on timing or real external systems.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class RetryingPaymentClientTest {

    @Mock PaymentGateway gateway;

    @Test
    void retriesUpToThreeTimesAndSucceeds() {
        AtomicInteger callCount = new AtomicInteger(0);
        when(gateway.charge(any())).thenAnswer(inv -> {
            int n = callCount.incrementAndGet();
            if (n < 3) throw new TransientPaymentException("temporary failure #" + n);
            return ChargeResult.success("tx-" + n);
        });

        RetryingPaymentClient client =
            new RetryingPaymentClient(gateway, /* maxRetries= */ 3);
        ChargeResult result = client.charge(new ChargeRequest("tok_123", 5000L));

        assertThat(result.isSuccess()).isTrue();
        assertThat(result.transactionId()).startsWith("tx-");
        verify(gateway, times(3)).charge(any());
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `thenAnswer` answers are not type-checked at stub definition time — a wrong return type from the lambda throws a `WrongTypeOfReturnValue` at invocation time, not at stub setup. For complex return types, extract the answer lambda into a named `Answer<T>` implementation and add a unit test for the answer itself to keep test logic testable. [community]

---

**Pattern 308** — JUnit 5 `@Tag` + build-tool filtering for separating unit, integration, and E2E test suites
Annotate tests with `@Tag("unit")`, `@Tag("integration")`, or `@Tag("e2e")` and configure Gradle/Maven surefire to include or exclude by tag. This lets a developer run only fast unit tests during development without modifying test classes.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Tag;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Tag("unit")
class PriceCalculatorTest {

    @Test
    void computesVatCorrectly() {
        assertThat(new PriceCalculator().addVat(100.0, 0.19))
            .isEqualByComparingTo(119.0);
    }
}

@Tag("integration")
@SpringBootTest
class OrderControllerIT {

    @Test
    void createsOrderEndToEnd() { /* ... */ }
}
```
```groovy
// build.gradle — run only unit tests in default check task
test {
    useJUnitPlatform {
        includeTags "unit"
    }
}
task integrationTest(type: Test) {
    useJUnitPlatform { includeTags "integration" }
    mustRunAfter test
}
```
Tradeoff: `@Tag` values are plain strings with no compile-time safety — a typo like `@Tag("integartion")` causes that test to be silently excluded from both suites. Centralise tag constants in a `TestTags` interface (`String UNIT = "unit";`) and reference them as `@Tag(TestTags.UNIT)`, or enforce valid tag names with an ArchUnit rule that whitelists permitted tag strings. [community]

---

**Pattern 309** — Spring Boot `@WebMvcTest` with `MockMvcTester` for fluent controller slice tests
`MockMvcTester` (introduced in Spring Boot 3.4) wraps `MockMvc` with an AssertJ-compatible fluent API. Combined with `@WebMvcTest`, it gives fast, focused controller tests that load only the MVC layer (no `@Service` or `@Repository` beans), with expressive failure messages.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;
    @MockitoBean ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void getProductReturns200WithBody() {
        when(productService.findById(42L))
            .thenReturn(new Product(42L, "Widget", new BigDecimal("9.99")));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/products/42"))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.name").asString()
            .isEqualTo("Widget");
    }

    @Test
    void getProductReturns404WhenNotFound() {
        when(productService.findById(99L))
            .thenThrow(new ProductNotFoundException(99L));

        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/products/99"))
            .hasStatus(404);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@WebMvcTest` loads `@ControllerAdvice` beans in the same package, but beans in sibling packages (e.g., a global exception handler in `com.example.api.error` when the controller is in `com.example.api.product`) are silently excluded unless explicitly listed in `@WebMvcTest(controllers = ..., includeFilters = ...)`. Always verify that exception handlers under test are actually loaded by checking the response body format in a dedicated test. [official]

---

**Pattern 310** — jqwik `@Property` with `@ForAll @IntRange` for boundary-value arithmetic invariants
Property-based testing with jqwik verifies invariants across hundreds of generated inputs. Using `@IntRange` constrains the generator to a meaningful domain, preventing wasted cycles on values the SUT explicitly rejects and focusing shrinking on the interesting boundary range.
```java
import net.jqwik.api.*;
import net.jqwik.api.constraints.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DiscountCalculatorProperties {

    DiscountCalculator sut = new DiscountCalculator();

    @Property(tries = 500)
    void discountNeverExceedsOriginalPrice(
        @ForAll @DoubleRange(min = 0.01, max = 10_000.0) double price,
        @ForAll @IntRange(min = 0, max = 100) int discountPct
    ) {
        double result = sut.apply(price, discountPct);
        assertThat(result)
            .isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0.0)
            .isLessThanOrEqualTo(price);
    }

    @Property
    void zeroDiscountIsIdentity(
        @ForAll @DoubleRange(min = 0.01, max = 10_000.0) double price
    ) {
        assertThat(sut.apply(price, 0)).isEqualByComparingTo(price);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: jqwik shrinks falsifying examples by default (finding the minimal failing input), but shrinking doubles with `@DoubleRange` can take many iterations when the failure is at a precision boundary. Set `shrinkingMode = ShrinkingMode.BOUNDED` for tests where shrinking exceeds 30 seconds, accepting a larger counterexample in exchange for a bounded test runtime. [official]

---

**Pattern 311** — WireMock `stubFor` with `matchingJsonPath` for request-body content-based routing
WireMock's `matchingJsonPath` matcher lets a stub respond differently based on the JSON body of the incoming request — useful for testing downstream client code that sends different payloads and expects different responses without spinning up real services.
```java
import com.github.tomakehurst.wiremock.junit5.WireMockExtension;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.RegisterExtension;
import static com.github.tomakehurst.wiremock.client.WireMock.*;
import static com.github.tomakehurst.wiremock.core.WireMockConfiguration.wireMockConfig;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class PaymentClientWireMockTest {

    @RegisterExtension
    static WireMockExtension wm = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
        .options(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort())
        .build();

    @Test
    void returnsApprovedForSmallAmount() {
        wm.stubFor(post(urlEqualTo("/charge"))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.amount", lessThan("100")))
            .willReturn(okJson("{\"status\":\"APPROVED\",\"transactionId\":\"tx-1\"}")));

        PaymentClient client =
            new PaymentClient("http://localhost:" + wm.getPort());
        ChargeResult result = client.charge(new ChargeRequest("tok_abc", 50L));
        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo("APPROVED");
    }

    @Test
    void returnsDeclinedForLargeAmount() {
        wm.stubFor(post(urlEqualTo("/charge"))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.amount", greaterThanOrEqualTo("100")))
            .willReturn(okJson("{\"status\":\"DECLINED\"}")));

        PaymentClient client =
            new PaymentClient("http://localhost:" + wm.getPort());
        ChargeResult result = client.charge(new ChargeRequest("tok_abc", 500L));
        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo("DECLINED");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `matchingJsonPath` comparisons on numeric values compare the string representation of numbers, not numeric magnitude — `lessThan("100")` compares lexicographically, so `"99"` matches but `"9"` also matches while `"100.0"` does not because `"1" < "9"`. Always use integer string representations when using numeric comparison matchers, or use `equalTo` on specific known values rather than range matchers on strings. [community]

---

**Pattern 312** — JUnit 5 `@RegisterExtension` for a `FrozenClockExtension` injecting a deterministic `java.time.Clock`
Deterministic time is essential for tests involving deadlines, expiry logic, and TTL. A `ParameterResolver` extension that injects a `Clock.fixed(...)` instance removes the need for `Clock` to be passed through every constructor or stored as a mutable static.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.time.*;

@Target(ElementType.PARAMETER)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@interface FrozenAt { String value(); } // e.g. "2026-01-15T10:00:00Z"

public class FrozenClockExtension implements ParameterResolver {

    @Override
    public boolean supportsParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        return pc.getParameter().getType() == Clock.class
            && pc.isAnnotated(FrozenAt.class);
    }

    @Override
    public Object resolveParameter(ParameterContext pc, ExtensionContext ec) {
        String iso = pc.findAnnotation(FrozenAt.class).get().value();
        return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse(iso), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    }
}

// Test
@ExtendWith(FrozenClockExtension.class)
class TokenExpiryTest {

    @Test
    void expiredTokenIsRejected(@FrozenAt("2026-06-01T00:00:00Z") Clock clock) {
        Token token = Token.expiring(clock.instant().minusSeconds(1), clock);
        assertThat(token.isExpired()).isTrue();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: The `@FrozenAt` annotation stores the instant as a string parsed at test runtime, so an invalid ISO-8601 literal throws a `DateTimeParseException` during parameter resolution (not at compile time). A custom Checkstyle or ArchUnit rule that validates `@FrozenAt` values at build time is warranted in large codebases where many tests use this pattern. [community]

---

**Pattern 313** — ArchUnit layered architecture enforcement with `@AnalyzeClasses` and `layeredArchitecture()`
ArchUnit's `layeredArchitecture()` rule codifies the allowed dependency direction between architectural layers (controllers → services → repositories) and fails the build when a layer violation is introduced. This replaces manual code reviews for architectural drift.
```java
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.*;
import com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures.layeredArchitecture;

@AnalyzeClasses(
    packages = "com.example.shop",
    importOptions = ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class
)
class LayerArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule layerRule = layeredArchitecture()
        .consideringAllDependencies()
        .layer("Controller").definedBy("..controller..")
        .layer("Service").definedBy("..service..")
        .layer("Repository").definedBy("..repository..")
        .layer("Domain").definedBy("..domain..")
        .whereLayer("Controller").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
        .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Controller")
        .whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")
        .whereLayer("Domain").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Controller", "Service", "Repository");
}
```
Tradeoff: `layeredArchitecture().consideringAllDependencies()` checks transitive as well as direct dependencies and flags violations in third-party library classes that happen to match the package patterns (e.g., a library class in `..service..`). Use `ignoreDependency(Class, Class)` sparingly for known false positives, and prefer tighter package naming conventions (e.g., `com.example.shop.service` not `..service..`) to avoid unintended pattern matches. [official]

---

**Pattern 314** — Awaitility `await().untilAsserted()` with virtual-thread-spawning SUT for async event processing
When testing a system that processes events on virtual threads (e.g., an inbox processor), use `Awaitility.await()` with `untilAsserted()` to poll an assertion until it passes within a timeout, rather than inserting `Thread.sleep()` which makes tests timing-sensitive and slow.
```java
import org.awaitility.Awaitility;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.time.Duration;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class InboxProcessorTest {

    @Test
    void processesPendingMessageWithinOneSecond() throws Exception {
        InMemoryInbox inbox = new InMemoryInbox();
        InboxProcessor processor = new InboxProcessor(inbox,
            Thread.ofVirtual().factory());

        inbox.enqueue(new Message("hello", Priority.HIGH));
        processor.start();

        Awaitility.await()
            .atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
            .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(50))
            .untilAsserted(() ->
                assertThat(inbox.processedCount()).isEqualTo(1));

        processor.stop();
        assertThat(inbox.pendingCount()).isZero();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `untilAsserted()` swallows `AssertionError` on each poll attempt and rethrows only the last one on timeout. If the assertion throws an unexpected checked exception (e.g., an `IOException` from a test double), Awaitility wraps it in a `ConditionTimeoutException` with the original cause buried. Use `ThrowingRunnable` or convert to `RuntimeException` inside the assertion lambda to preserve the original message. [official]

---

**Pattern 315** — `@DataJpaTest` with `@Sql` and `SqlMergeMode.MERGE` for layered fixture data management
`@DataJpaTest` tests benefit from a declarative data setup via `@Sql`. Using `@SqlMergeMode(MERGE)` allows a class-level `@Sql` to load shared reference data (e.g., countries, currencies) while method-level `@Sql` loads test-specific records without overriding the class-level setup.
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.*;
import org.springframework.test.context.jdbc.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@DataJpaTest
@SqlMergeMode(SqlMergeMode.MergeMode.MERGE)
@Sql("/sql/ref-data.sql")                 // loaded before every test in this class
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;

    @Test
    @Sql("/sql/orders-three-pending.sql")  // merged with ref-data.sql
    void findsPendingOrders() {
        assertThat(repo.findByStatus("PENDING")).hasSize(3);
    }

    @Test
    @Sql("/sql/orders-one-shipped.sql")    // merged with ref-data.sql
    @Sql(scripts = "/sql/cleanup.sql",
         executionPhase = Sql.ExecutionPhase.AFTER_TEST_METHOD)
    void findsShippedOrders() {
        assertThat(repo.findByStatus("SHIPPED")).hasSize(1);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@DataJpaTest` runs each test in a transaction that is rolled back by default, which means `AFTER_TEST_METHOD` cleanup scripts run inside that transaction and the cleanup is also rolled back — the cleanup script is effectively a no-op. If cleanup is genuinely required (e.g., to reset a sequence or delete data inserted outside the transactional boundary), annotate the test with `@Commit` or `@Rollback(false)` and manage cleanup explicitly; otherwise rely on the implicit rollback. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas

**G16** — Mockito `verify(mock, never()).method()` passes even when the method is called with a *different* argument than expected
Why this matters: `verify(mock, never()).save(specificOrder)` only verifies that `save` was never called with `specificOrder` as the argument. If the SUT calls `save(someOtherOrder)`, the `never()` verification passes silently, giving a false green. The developer intended to assert that `save` was never called at all, but the argument matcher scoped the check to a single value.
Fix: Use `verify(mock, never()).save(any())` (or `verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock)` after accounting for expected interactions) when the intent is to assert that the method was never invoked regardless of argument. Reserve `verify(mock, never()).save(specificOrder)` only when the constraint is genuinely argument-scoped. [community]

**G17** — AssertJ `assertThat(list).contains(element)` passes when `element.equals()` is structurally correct but `hashCode()` is broken — the assertion uses `equals()` not hash-lookup, so the test passes while production `HashMap`/`HashSet` code silently drops the element
Why this matters: `assertThat(list).contains(item)` iterates the list calling `equals()` on each element. If `item.equals()` is correctly implemented but `hashCode()` violates the contract (e.g., always returns 0 or is inconsistent with `equals`), the list assertion passes. Any production code that puts the item into a `HashMap` or `HashSet` will silently fail to retrieve it. The test gives false confidence about a broken object contract.
Fix: For domain objects participating in collections, add an ArchUnit rule or checkstyle rule enforcing that any class that overrides `equals()` also overrides `hashCode()`. Add a companion property-based test (jqwik) asserting `a.equals(b) → a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` for the domain object in question. [community]

**G18** — `@SpringBootTest` `@MockitoBean` on a `@Scope("prototype")` bean causes the mock to be injected into the first prototype instance, but subsequent prototype instantiations get a fresh (non-mocked) instance, so stub configurations are lost mid-test
Why this matters: `@MockitoBean` registers a singleton mock in the Spring context. When the SUT requests a new prototype bean via `ApplicationContext.getBean()` or through an `ObjectFactory`, Spring creates a new instance using the real class, not the singleton mock. The first injection point (e.g., a constructor parameter) gets the mock, but any dynamic look-up gets the real bean, causing `NullPointerException` or unexpected behaviour that is difficult to diagnose because the test setup looks correct.
Fix: Replace the prototype-scoped dependency with a `Supplier<T>` or `ObjectFactory<T>` that can be stubbed to always return the same mock instance: `when(factory.getObject()).thenReturn(mock)`. Alternatively, refactor the SUT to avoid prototype scope for mockable dependencies, using constructor injection of a stateless service singleton instead. [community]

**G19** — JUnit 5 `@TempDir` fields in `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` tests receive the same path for all test methods rather than a fresh directory per method, because the directory is created once at field injection time
Why this matters: With `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`, JUnit creates the test class instance once. `@TempDir` fields are injected at instantiation, so all test methods share the same temporary directory path. If one test writes a file and a later test asserts the directory is empty, the assertion fails. This behaviour differs from the default `PER_METHOD` lifecycle where a fresh temp directory is injected before each test.
Fix: Declare `@TempDir` as a parameter on each `@Test` method (not as a field) when using `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`. JUnit injects a new temporary directory per method invocation regardless of the class lifecycle, making each test's filesystem state independent. [official]

**G20** — Testcontainers `withReuse(true)` combined with `@DynamicPropertySource` causes stale property values to be read from a previously cached Spring context when the container port changes between test JVM runs
Why this matters: `withReuse(true)` reuses a running container from a previous JVM run (identified by a hash of the container configuration). If the reused container has a different mapped port from the one that was stored in the Spring context cache (e.g., the cache was populated in the same JVM process with a different port assignment), the `@DynamicPropertySource` registered the old port, and the new test is communicating with a non-existent port. This is particularly subtle because the container appears healthy in Docker but the application cannot connect.
Fix: Avoid combining `withReuse(true)` with `@DynamicPropertySource` for the same container. Instead, use `@ServiceConnection` (Spring Boot 3.1+) which reads the connection details directly from the running container at Spring context creation time, bypassing the `@DynamicPropertySource` caching issue entirely. [official]

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 316** — `@JsonTest` with `JacksonTester` round-trip assertion for polymorphic subtypes via `@JsonTypeInfo`
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.json.JsonTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.json.JacksonTester;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@JsonTest
class ShapeJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    private JacksonTester<Shape> json;

    @Test
    void serializesCircle() throws Exception {
        var circle = new Circle(3.0);
        var written = this.json.write(circle);
        assertThat(written).hasJsonPathStringValue("$.type", "CIRCLE");
        assertThat(written).hasJsonPathNumberValue("$.radius", 3.0);
    }

    @Test
    void roundTripsCircle() throws Exception {
        var circle = new Circle(3.0);
        var content = this.json.write(circle).getJson();
        assertThat(this.json.parse(content)).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(circle);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@JsonTest` loads only Jackson-related beans, so any `@JsonComponent` converters registered via `@Component` scanning in the main context are not automatically available — you must import them explicitly with `@Import(MyJsonComponent.class)` or they silently fall back to default serialization, producing subtly wrong JSON without a test failure that points to the missing converter. [official]

---

**Pattern 317** — `ApplicationContextRunner` with `withPropertyValues` and conditional `@ConditionalOnProperty` auto-configuration testing
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfigurations;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.runner.ApplicationContextRunner;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class AuditAutoConfigurationTest {

    private final ApplicationContextRunner runner = new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(AuditAutoConfiguration.class));

    @Test
    void beanPresentWhenEnabled() {
        runner.withPropertyValues("audit.enabled=true")
              .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).hasSingleBean(AuditService.class));
    }

    @Test
    void beanAbsentWhenDisabled() {
        runner.withPropertyValues("audit.enabled=false")
              .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean(AuditService.class));
    }

    @Test
    void beanAbsentByDefault() {
        runner.run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean(AuditService.class));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ApplicationContextRunner` does not start a full servlet container, so any `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` conditions that depend on the presence of a `WebApplicationContext` evaluate to false; use `WebApplicationContextRunner` when testing beans that are conditional on the web tier, and reserve `ApplicationContextRunner` for non-web auto-configurations. [official]

---

**Pattern 318** — `@WebMvcTest` `MockMvcTester` with `bodyJson().convertTo(TypeRef)` for strongly-typed response extraction
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.servlet.MockMvcTester;
import org.springframework.core.ParameterizedTypeReference;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvcTester mvc;

    @Test
    void returnsProductList() {
        var typeRef = new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<ProductDto>>() {};
        var products = mvc.get().uri("/products")
                         .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                         .exchange()
                         .assertThat()
                         .hasStatusOk()
                         .bodyJson()
                         .convertTo(typeRef);
        assertThat(products).hasSize(3)
                            .extracting(ProductDto::name)
                            .containsExactly("Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `convertTo(TypeRef)` deserializes the response body using the `ObjectMapper` wired into `MockMvcTester`; if the test `ObjectMapper` has different module registrations than the production one (e.g., a `JavaTimeModule` added only in `@SpringBootTest` but absent in the `@WebMvcTest` slice), deserialization fails with a confusing `InvalidDefinitionException` — register shared modules via a `@TestConfiguration` imported into the slice test to keep them aligned. [official]

---

**Pattern 319** — `@RestClientTest` with `MockRestServiceServer` for testing `RestClient`-based HTTP client components
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.client.RestClientTest;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.test.web.client.MockRestServiceServer;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.match.MockRestRequestMatchers.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.response.MockRestResponseCreators.*;

@RestClientTest(WeatherClient.class)
class WeatherClientTest {

    @Autowired
    private WeatherClient client;

    @Autowired
    private MockRestServiceServer server;

    @Test
    void fetchesCurrentTemperature() {
        server.expect(requestTo("/api/weather?city=Berlin"))
              .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
              .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                      {"city":"Berlin","tempC":18.5}
                      """, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        WeatherResponse resp = client.getCurrentWeather("Berlin");

        assertThat(resp.city()).isEqualTo("Berlin");
        assertThat(resp.tempC()).isEqualTo(18.5);
        server.verify();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `MockRestServiceServer` records expectations in declaration order and verifies them sequentially by default; if the client issues requests in a non-deterministic order (e.g., driven by a parallel stream), use `server.expect(manyTimes(), anything())` with individual `andExpect` matchers rather than ordered expectations, otherwise the server reports spurious failures when requests arrive out of order. [official]

---

**Pattern 320** — JUnit 5 `TestWatcher` extension for capturing and reporting test outcome metadata in CI
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.*;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class OutcomeRecorderExtension
        implements TestWatcher, BeforeAllCallback {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> outcomes =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    @Override
    public void beforeAll(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        ctx.getStore(ExtensionContext.Namespace.GLOBAL)
           .put("outcomes-" + ctx.getUniqueId(), outcomes);
    }

    @Override
    public void testSuccessful(ExtensionContext ctx) {
        outcomes.put(ctx.getDisplayName(), "PASSED");
    }

    @Override
    public void testFailed(ExtensionContext ctx, Throwable cause) {
        outcomes.put(ctx.getDisplayName(), "FAILED: " + cause.getMessage());
    }

    @Override
    public void testDisabled(ExtensionContext ctx, Optional<String> reason) {
        outcomes.put(ctx.getDisplayName(), "DISABLED: " + reason.orElse("no reason"));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `TestWatcher` callbacks are invoked by JUnit's engine after the test method completes but before `@AfterEach` has run on its own annotation-driven logic; this means `testFailed` fires while the test's `@AfterEach` cleanup is still pending — do not rely on `testFailed` to observe post-cleanup state, and avoid throwing from `TestWatcher` callbacks since exceptions in callbacks are swallowed by JUnit and not surfaced as test failures. [official]

---

**Pattern 321** — JUnit 5 `@TestFactory` generating `DynamicTest` streams from external data at runtime
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.DynamicTest;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.DynamicTest.dynamicTest;

class CurrencyConverterDynamicTest {

    private final CurrencyConverter converter = new CurrencyConverter();

    @TestFactory
    Stream<DynamicTest> convertsAllSupportedCurrencies() {
        return Stream.of(
            new Object[]{"USD", "EUR", 100.0, 91.5},
            new Object[]{"EUR", "GBP", 100.0, 85.0},
            new Object[]{"GBP", "JPY", 100.0, 19_050.0}
        ).map(row -> dynamicTest(
            row[0] + " -> " + row[1],
            () -> {
                double result = converter.convert(
                    (String) row[0], (String) row[1], (double) row[2]);
                assertThat(result).isCloseTo((double) row[3], within(1.0));
            }
        ));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Unlike `@ParameterizedTest`, `@TestFactory` dynamic tests do not support lifecycle callbacks (`@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`) — JUnit does not run these annotations around each `DynamicTest`; the entire factory method has a single `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach` pair wrapping all generated tests. If each test case requires fresh state, initialise it inside the `DynamicTest` executable lambda rather than relying on lifecycle annotations. [official]

---

**Pattern 322** — `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` combined with `@Order` for stateful integration tests that depend on execution sequence
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
class UserRegistrationFlowIT {

    private String registeredUserId;

    @Test
    @Order(1)
    void registersNewUser() {
        registeredUserId = userService.register("alice@example.com");
        assertThat(registeredUserId).isNotNull();
    }

    @Test
    @Order(2)
    void activatesRegisteredUser() {
        userService.activate(registeredUserId);
        assertThat(userService.isActive(registeredUserId)).isTrue();
    }

    @Test
    @Order(3)
    void deactivatesUser() {
        userService.deactivate(registeredUserId);
        assertThat(userService.isActive(registeredUserId)).isFalse();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Ordered tests create an implicit dependency chain — a failure in `@Order(1)` propagates `null` or stale state to `@Order(2)` and `@Order(3)`, which then fail with misleading errors rather than a meaningful assertion message. Restrict this pattern to end-to-end workflow tests where the sequence reflects a real business flow, and add a `@BeforeAll` guard assertion that verifies preconditions so that downstream tests fail with a clear `AssumptionViolatedException` rather than a `NullPointerException`. [community]

---

**Pattern 323** — `AssertJ` `satisfies()` chained with lambda for multi-field assertion on a single object without soft assertions
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class OrderAssertionTest {

    @Test
    void orderHasExpectedProperties() {
        Order order = orderService.placeOrder("customer-42", List.of("item-1", "item-2"));

        assertThat(order)
            .isNotNull()
            .satisfies(o -> {
                assertThat(o.getCustomerId()).isEqualTo("customer-42");
                assertThat(o.getItems()).hasSize(2)
                                       .containsExactly("item-1", "item-2");
                assertThat(o.getStatus()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.PENDING);
                assertThat(o.getCreatedAt()).isBeforeOrEqualTo(Instant.now());
                assertThat(o.getTotalPrice()).isGreaterThan(BigDecimal.ZERO);
            });
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Unlike `SoftAssertions`, `satisfies()` stops at the first failing assertion inside the lambda — subsequent assertions within the same `satisfies()` block are not evaluated. This makes it better for read-through correctness checks where the first failure is meaningful on its own, but worse than `SoftAssertions` when you want a complete picture of all field failures in a single test run. [official]

---

**Pattern 324** — AssertJ `usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringCollectionOrder()` for asserting unordered collection equality on complex object graphs
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class TeamAssertionTest {

    @Test
    void teamMembersMatchRegardlessOfOrder() {
        Team actual = teamService.buildTeam("dev-squad");

        Team expected = new Team("dev-squad",
            List.of(
                new Member("Bob",  "DEVELOPER"),
                new Member("Alice", "LEAD"),
                new Member("Carol", "QA")
            ));

        assertThat(actual)
            .usingRecursiveComparison()
            .ignoringCollectionOrder()
            .ignoringFields("createdAt", "updatedAt")
            .isEqualTo(expected);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ignoringCollectionOrder()` applies recursively to all nested collections in the object graph, which can hide genuine ordering bugs in properties that should be ordered (e.g., a prioritised task list that must return tasks sorted by priority). When order is semantically significant for some collections but not others, combine `usingRecursiveComparison()` with a selective `withComparatorForFields()` that asserts ordering only on the fields where it matters. [official]

---

**Pattern 325** — Mockito `ArgumentCaptor` with `getAllValues()` for verifying multiple calls to the same method across a loop
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.mockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

class NotificationServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private EmailGateway emailGateway;

    @InjectMocks
    private NotificationService service;

    @Test
    void sendsOneEmailPerRecipient() {
        service.notifyAll(List.of("alice@example.com", "bob@example.com", "carol@example.com"));

        ArgumentCaptor<EmailMessage> captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(EmailMessage.class);
        verify(emailGateway, times(3)).send(captor.capture());

        assertThat(captor.getAllValues())
            .extracting(EmailMessage::to)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(
                "alice@example.com", "bob@example.com", "carol@example.com");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ArgumentCaptor.getAllValues()` returns a `List` whose elements reference the same mutable object if the SUT reuses a single object and mutates it on each call (e.g., a single `EmailMessage` whose `to` field is updated in a loop); all captured entries then reflect the final state, producing misleading assertion failures. Create a new object instance per call in the SUT, or assert on the mock interaction via `ArgumentCaptor.getValue()` for the last call only and verify count separately. [community]

---

**Pattern 326** — Mockito `MockSettings.withSettings().name()` and `MockSettings.verboseLogging()` for diagnosing stub configuration errors in complex test setups
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.mockito.*;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

class PaymentProcessorTest {

    @Test
    void diagnosesUnstubbedInteraction() {
        PaymentGateway gateway = mock(PaymentGateway.class,
            withSettings()
                .name("payment-gateway")
                .verboseLogging()
                .defaultAnswer(Answers.RETURNS_SMART_NULLS));

        PaymentProcessor processor = new PaymentProcessor(gateway);

        when(gateway.charge("tok_visa", 9999L)).thenReturn(ChargeResult.SUCCESS);

        ChargeResult result = processor.processPayment("tok_visa", 9999L);

        assertThat(result).isEqualTo(ChargeResult.SUCCESS);
        verify(gateway, times(1)).charge("tok_visa", 9999L);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `verboseLogging()` logs every stubbing and invocation to standard output, which is useful during investigation but must be removed before merging to avoid polluting CI build logs. `RETURNS_SMART_NULLS` returns typed empty values instead of `null` (empty collections, `Optional.empty()`, `0` for primitives), delaying `NullPointerException` to the actual usage site and printing a diagnostic message; this is valuable during development but can hide bugs where `null` from an unstubbed method should cause a fast failure. [official]

**Pattern 327** — Testcontainers `@ServiceConnection` with `PostgreSQLContainer` and Spring Boot 3.1+ for zero-`@DynamicPropertySource` integration tests
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@DataJpaTest(replace = DataJpaTest.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class ProductRepositoryIT {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
            new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository repository;

    @Test
    void savesAndRetrievesProduct() {
        repository.save(new Product("widget", 4.99));
        assertThat(repository.findByName("widget"))
            .isPresent()
            .get()
            .extracting(Product::price)
            .isEqualTo(4.99);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@ServiceConnection` with `@DataJpaTest(replace = Replace.NONE)` disables the embedded H2 datasource replacement, meaning the test uses a real PostgreSQL dialect; this catches SQL incompatibilities early but makes the test require Docker and increases startup time by 10–30 seconds per container cold-start. Use `@Container static` (class-level) rather than instance-level to share the container across all test methods in the class and amortise the startup cost. [official]

---

**Pattern 328** — Testcontainers `GenericContainer` with `withLogConsumer(new Slf4jLogConsumer(log))` and `WaitStrategy.forLogMessage` for custom non-standard containers
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.output.Slf4jLogConsumer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.wait.strategy.Wait;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class CustomCacheIT {

    private static final org.slf4j.Logger LOG =
        org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(CustomCacheIT.class);

    @Container
    static GenericContainer<?> cache =
        new GenericContainer<>("my-registry/fast-cache:2.3")
            .withExposedPorts(7379)
            .withLogConsumer(new Slf4jLogConsumer(LOG))
            .waitingFor(Wait.forLogMessage(".*Ready to accept connections.*\\n", 1));

    @Test
    void containerIsAccessible() {
        assertThat(cache.getMappedPort(7379)).isGreaterThan(0);
        assertThat(cache.isRunning()).isTrue();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Wait.forLogMessage()` uses a regex match on the container's stdout, which breaks silently if the upstream image changes its startup log message wording in a minor version update — the container times out after the `withStartupTimeout` deadline (default 60 s) with a `ContainerLaunchException` that shows the timeout but not the missed log message. Pin the image tag precisely, add a `withStartupTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(120))` buffer for slow CI agents, and prefer `Wait.forHttp("/health")` or `Wait.forHealthcheck()` when the container exposes a health endpoint. [community]

**Pattern 329** — Spring Boot `@AutoConfigureObservability` with `TestObservationRegistry` to assert Micrometer spans and metrics in slice tests
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.actuate.observability.AutoConfigureObservability;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.servlet.MockMvcTester;
import io.micrometer.observation.tck.TestObservationRegistry;
import io.micrometer.observation.tck.TestObservationRegistryAssert;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@AutoConfigureObservability
class OrderControllerObservabilityTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvcTester mvc;

    @Autowired
    private TestObservationRegistry observationRegistry;

    @Test
    void recordsObservationForPlaceOrder() {
        mvc.post().uri("/orders").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
           .content("{\"item\":\"widget\"}").exchange()
           .assertThat().hasStatusOk();

        TestObservationRegistryAssert.assertThat(observationRegistry)
            .hasObservationWithNameEqualTo("order.placed")
            .that()
            .hasLowCardinalityKeyValue("status", "SUCCESS");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `TestObservationRegistry` accumulates all observations across test methods when the Spring context is shared; a prior test's observations remain visible in later tests, causing `hasObservationWithNameEqualTo` to match stale entries and produce false positives. Call `observationRegistry.clear()` in a `@BeforeEach` method to ensure each test starts with a clean observation slate. [official]

**Pattern 330** — WireMock `response-template` with Handlebars `jsonPath` extraction for dynamic echo responses in contract tests
```java
import com.github.tomakehurst.wiremock.junit5.WireMockTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static com.github.tomakehurst.wiremock.client.WireMock.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@WireMockTest(httpPort = 9090)
class PaymentEchoContractTest {

    @Test
    void echoesTransactionIdFromRequestBody() {
        stubFor(post(urlEqualTo("/payments"))
            .willReturn(okJson("""
                {"transactionId":"{{jsonPath request.body '$.transactionId'}}",
                 "status":"ACCEPTED"}
                """)
            .withTransformers("response-template")));

        var response = httpClient.post("http://localhost:9090/payments",
            """{"transactionId":"txn-abc-123","amount":50.00}""");

        assertThat(response.body())
            .contains("\"transactionId\":\"txn-abc-123\"");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Response templating evaluates Handlebars expressions at request time using WireMock's built-in Handlebars engine; the `jsonPath` helper resolves JSON body paths, but it requires the `wiremock-standalone` jar or the `response-template` transformer to be on the classpath and registered. If WireMock is started programmatically (not via `@WireMockTest`), you must call `options().extensions(new ResponseTemplateTransformer(true))` — omitting it causes the template literals to be returned verbatim without expansion, which is difficult to distinguish from a correct response in a test assertion. [community]

---

### Community Gotchas

**G21** — JUnit 5 `@TestFactory` with `@BeforeEach` does not reset state before each dynamically generated test
Why this matters: `@BeforeEach` runs once before the entire `@TestFactory` method, not once per `DynamicTest` produced by the factory. If the test class has mutable shared state (e.g., a list that accumulates results, or a mock whose invocation count matters), all dynamic tests see the same pre-factory state, and any state mutated by test N is visible to test N+1. This produces order-dependent failures that only manifest when the factory produces more than one test case.
Fix: Initialise all per-test state inside the `DynamicTest` executable lambda (a `ThrowingRunnable` or `Executable`). For Mockito mocks, inject them as method parameters using `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` and capture them in the lambda's closure; alternatively, call `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` at the start of each lambda to reinitialise the annotated fields before each dynamic test body runs. [official]

**G22** — `@MockitoBean` invalidates the Spring test context cache when placed on different fields with the same type across test classes, causing unnecessary full context re-loads
Why this matters: Spring caches application contexts keyed by their configuration fingerprint. Each unique combination of `@MockitoBean` declarations (type + qualifier) is part of that fingerprint. If `ClassA` declares `@MockitoBean UserService userService` and `ClassB` declares `@MockitoBean UserService sut`, Spring treats them as different contexts and spins up a new application context for each class, even though the underlying bean type is identical. In large test suites this doubles or triples total test execution time.
Fix: Standardise `@MockitoBean` field names across test classes in the same suite, or extract a shared `@TestConfiguration` base class/interface that declares all mocks consistently. Alternatively, use `@MockitoBean(name = "userService")` with an explicit bean name to make the fingerprint deterministic regardless of field naming. [community]

**G23** — AssertJ `assertThat(optional).isPresent()` followed by `.get()` throws an unchecked `AssertionError` if the `Optional` is empty, but the error message says "Expected optional to contain a value" rather than pointing to the field that was null in the SUT
Why this matters: When a domain method returns `Optional.empty()` because of a null field deep in the object graph, the top-level `isPresent()` failure message does not indicate which field was null. Developers spend time in the debugger tracing back to the empty `Optional` source instead of getting a direct path to the root cause from the assertion message.
Fix: Use `assertThat(optional).hasValueSatisfying(value -> assertThat(value).isNotNull())` to get a two-level failure message that names both the optional and the inner value. For repository lookups, prefer `assertThat(repository.findById(id)).as("Product with id %s should exist", id).isPresent()` — the `as()` label is prepended to the failure message and immediately identifies the missing entity without opening a debugger. [community]

**G24** — Mockito `@Spy` on a Spring `@Service` that uses constructor injection causes `NullPointerException` during spy construction because Mockito calls the no-arg constructor, bypassing Spring's dependency injection
Why this matters: `@Spy` requires a no-arg constructor (or an explicit instance to wrap). When `@Spy` is applied to a class that only has a constructor with parameters and relies on `@Autowired` constructor injection, Mockito attempts to call the no-arg constructor via reflection; if none exists, it either fails to create the spy or creates an instance with all fields `null`. Subsequent method calls on the spy that delegate to `callRealMethod()` then throw `NullPointerException` on the first field access.
Fix: Supply the fully constructed object explicitly: `@Spy MyService myService = new MyService(realDependencyA, mockDependencyB)`. Alternatively, use `@MockitoSpyBean` in Spring integration tests to let Spring construct the bean and then wrap it in a Mockito spy, preserving all injected dependencies while still allowing stubbing of specific methods. [official]

**G25** — WireMock `resetScenarios()` called in `@AfterEach` clears scenario state but not recorded stubs, leaving previously registered stubs active across test methods
Why this matters: `WireMockServer.resetScenarios()` resets all scenarios to their initial state, but does not remove stub mappings. If test method A registers a stub via `stubFor(...)` and test method B relies on WireMock having no stubs for the same URL, test B receives the response from A's stub rather than a 404, producing a false green. This is especially subtle when tests are run in a different order in CI than locally.
Fix: Call `WireMockServer.resetAll()` (or `WireMock.reset()` for the static API) in `@AfterEach` to remove both stub mappings and scenario state. When using `@WireMockTest`, stubs are automatically reset between tests — reserve `@WireMockTest` for simple scenarios and only manage a `WireMockServer` instance manually when you need fine-grained lifecycle control. [community]

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 331** — JUnit 5 `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` returning a `Stream<Arguments>` for multi-argument table-driven tests
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DiscountCalculatorTest {

    static Stream<Arguments> discountScenarios() {
        return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of("GOLD",   1000.0, 150.0),
            Arguments.of("SILVER", 1000.0,  80.0),
            Arguments.of("BRONZE", 1000.0,  20.0),
            Arguments.of("NONE",   1000.0,   0.0)
        );
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "tier={0} price={1} => discount={2}")
    @MethodSource("discountScenarios")
    void calculatesCorrectDiscount(String tier, double price, double expectedDiscount) {
        var calculator = new DiscountCalculator();
        assertThat(calculator.calculate(tier, price)).isEqualTo(expectedDiscount);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@MethodSource` keeps test data co-located with the test class and supports complex object arguments, but the factory method must be `static` (or the test class must use `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`); forgetting this causes a `JUnitException: Cannot invoke method` at runtime rather than a compile error, which is disorienting when the method is clearly visible in the class. [official]

---

**Pattern 332** — JUnit 5 `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` with `@InjectMocks` and `@Mock` for zero-boilerplate service unit tests
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InjectMocks;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock OrderRepository orderRepository;
    @Mock PaymentGateway paymentGateway;
    @InjectMocks OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void placesOrderAndChargesPayment() {
        var order = new Order("item-1", 2, 49.99);
        when(orderRepository.save(any(Order.class))).thenReturn(order.withId(42L));
        when(paymentGateway.charge(42L, 99.98)).thenReturn(PaymentResult.SUCCESS);

        var result = orderService.place(order);

        assertThat(result.orderId()).isEqualTo(42L);
        assertThat(result.paymentStatus()).isEqualTo("SUCCESS");
        verify(paymentGateway).charge(42L, 99.98);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `MockitoExtension` enables strict stubbing by default — any stub set up with `when(...)` that is never called causes an `UnnecessaryStubbingException`, which keeps tests lean but breaks if a test conditionally triggers a code path that does not call every stub. Use `@MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT)` on a per-test or per-class basis to relax this only where truly needed rather than disabling it globally. [official]

---

**Pattern 333** — AssertJ `SoftAssertions.assertSoftly()` for collecting all field-level failures in a single assertion pass
```java
import org.assertj.core.api.SoftAssertions;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class InvoiceValidationTest {

    @Test
    void invoiceHasCorrectFields() {
        Invoice invoice = invoiceService.generate("order-99");

        SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(soft -> {
            soft.assertThat(invoice.id()).isNotNull();
            soft.assertThat(invoice.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("149.97");
            soft.assertThat(invoice.currency()).isEqualTo("USD");
            soft.assertThat(invoice.lineItems()).hasSize(3);
            soft.assertThat(invoice.issueDate()).isNotNull();
            soft.assertThat(invoice.dueDate()).isAfter(invoice.issueDate());
            soft.assertThat(invoice.status()).isEqualTo("PENDING");
        });
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `assertSoftly` collects every failing assertion and reports them all together at the end of the lambda, eliminating the first-failure-stops-all problem of hard assertions; however the lambda receives a `SoftAssertions` instance rather than `Assertions`, so IDE auto-import completion suggests different method names and developers occasionally mix `soft.assertThat` with a top-level `assertThat` import, causing a single hard failure that breaks early and loses the remaining soft results. [official]

---

**Pattern 334** — Mockito `doAnswer()` with `InvocationOnMock` for async callback stubbing
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class NotificationDispatcherTest {

    @Mock NotificationSender sender;

    @Test
    void invokesCallbackOnSuccessfulSend() {
        doAnswer(invocation -> {
            Notification n  = invocation.getArgument(0);
            SendCallback cb = invocation.getArgument(1);
            cb.onSuccess(n.id());
            return null;
        }).when(sender).sendAsync(any(Notification.class), any(SendCallback.class));

        var capturedId = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference<String>();
        var dispatcher = new NotificationDispatcher(sender);
        dispatcher.dispatch(new Notification("notif-1", "Hello"), id -> capturedId.set(id));

        assertThat(capturedId.get()).isEqualTo("notif-1");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `doAnswer()` is the only safe way to exercise callback-style async APIs without starting real threads, but `invocation.getArgument(n)` uses an unchecked cast; if the argument index is wrong the test throws `ClassCastException` at the cast site inside the lambda rather than at the `doAnswer(...)` call, making the stack trace point to Mockito internals. Always document the argument indices with inline comments for maintenance clarity. [community]

---

**Pattern 335** — Testcontainers `@Container` with `@DynamicPropertySource` for injecting container ports into Spring `@SpringBootTest`
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertyRegistry;
import org.springframework.test.context.DynamicPropertySource;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
@SpringBootTest
class ProductRepositoryIT {

    @Container
    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void postgresProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url",      postgres::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
    }

    @Autowired ProductRepository repository;

    @Test
    void savesAndRetrievesProduct() {
        var saved = repository.save(new Product("SKU-001", "Widget", 9.99));
        assertThat(repository.findById(saved.id())).isPresent()
            .hasValueSatisfying(p -> assertThat(p.sku()).isEqualTo("SKU-001"));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@DynamicPropertySource` registers properties as `Supplier` lambdas evaluated lazily after the container starts, which correctly races container startup against Spring context creation; using `postgres.getJdbcUrl()` eagerly (without a method reference) instead captures the URL before the container has assigned its mapped port, producing a connection URL with `0` as the port that silently passes container readiness checks but fails at JDBC connect time. [official]

---

**Pattern 336** — AssertJ `assertThat(list).extracting()` with multiple field names for collection field projection
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.groups.Tuple.tuple;

class UserSearchTest {

    @Test
    void returnsMatchingUsersWithCorrectFields() {
        List<User> users = userService.searchByDepartment("Engineering");

        assertThat(users)
            .hasSize(3)
            .extracting(User::name, User::role, User::active)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(
                tuple("Alice", "LEAD",   true),
                tuple("Bob",   "SENIOR", true),
                tuple("Carol", "JUNIOR", true)
            );
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `extracting()` with multiple method references projects each element into a `Tuple`, enabling concise table-like assertions on collections without writing per-element `satisfies()` blocks; however `containsExactlyInAnyOrder` compares `Tuple` instances by value equality, so if any projected field returns `null` (e.g., `active` is not yet populated by a lazy JPA relationship), the tuple comparison fails with a message that shows `null` but does not identify which entity had the missing field — add `.as("user list")` before `extracting` to label the containing assertion for clearer failure output. [official]

---

**Pattern 337** — JUnit 5 `@Nested` classes for grouping tests by SUT state or precondition
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Nested;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;

class ShoppingCartTest {

    ShoppingCart cart;

    @BeforeEach void newCart() { cart = new ShoppingCart(); }

    @Nested
    class WhenEmpty {
        @Test void totalIsZero()    { assertThat(cart.total()).isZero(); }
        @Test void checkoutThrows() { assertThatThrownBy(cart::checkout)
            .isInstanceOf(EmptyCartException.class); }
    }

    @Nested
    class WithItems {
        @BeforeEach void addItem() { cart.add(new Item("A", 10.00)); }

        @Test void totalReflectsItem()  { assertThat(cart.total()).isEqualTo(10.00); }
        @Test void checkoutSucceeds()   { assertThatCode(cart::checkout).doesNotThrowAnyException(); }

        @Nested
        class AfterDiscount {
            @BeforeEach void applyDiscount() { cart.applyDiscount(0.10); }
            @Test void totalIsReduced()  { assertThat(cart.total()).isEqualTo(9.00); }
        }
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@Nested` classes share the outer class's `@BeforeEach` lifecycle, so each outer `@BeforeEach` runs before each inner test — this is by design for incremental state layering, but it becomes a maintenance trap when someone adds an expensive outer `@BeforeEach` that now runs for every leaf test even if those inner tests do not use the outer state. Profile test execution time after adding outer setup methods to detect unexpected inflation. [official]

---

**Pattern 338** — Mockito `verify()` with `InOrder` for sequence-sensitive multi-collaborator orchestration tests
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InOrder;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class CheckoutOrchestratorTest {

    @Mock InventoryService   inventory;
    @Mock PaymentService     payment;
    @Mock FulfillmentService fulfillment;
    @Mock AuditLogger        audit;

    @Test
    void executesStepsInCorrectOrder() {
        var orchestrator = new CheckoutOrchestrator(inventory, payment, fulfillment, audit);
        orchestrator.checkout(new Order("order-77"));

        InOrder inOrder = inOrder(inventory, payment, fulfillment, audit);
        inOrder.verify(inventory).reserve(any());
        inOrder.verify(payment).charge(any());
        inOrder.verify(fulfillment).schedule(any());
        inOrder.verify(audit).log("CHECKOUT_COMPLETE", "order-77");
        inOrder.verifyNoMoreInteractions();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `InOrder` verifies that the specified interactions occurred in the stated sequence relative to each other, but it does not prevent additional unordered interactions between collaborators. If the orchestrator calls `audit.log()` twice (once before and once after `fulfillment.schedule()`), `inOrder.verify(audit)` only matches the first matching call, silently ignoring the second unless `verifyNoMoreInteractions()` is called on the `InOrder` object — call it on the `InOrder` instance, not on the mocks directly, to catch extra ordered calls. [official]

**Pattern 339** — AssertJ `assertThatThrownBy()` with chained `havingCause()` for wrapped exception root-cause assertions
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class DataImportServiceTest {

    @Test
    void wrapsParseExceptionInDomainException() {
        var service = new DataImportService(new StrictCsvParser());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.importFile("malformed.csv"))
            .isInstanceOf(DataImportException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("Failed to import")
            .havingCause()
                .isInstanceOf(CsvParseException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("line 3")
            .and()
                .hasFieldOrPropertyWithValue("lineNumber", 3);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `havingCause()` navigates to `Throwable.getCause()` and returns a new `AbstractThrowableAssert` scoped to that cause, enabling precise assertions on the wrapped exception without manually unwrapping; using `getCause()` in a lambda passed to `satisfies()` achieves the same result but loses the fluent chain and introduces a null risk if the cause is absent — `havingCause()` fails immediately with "Expected cause to be present" when the cause is null, giving a cleaner failure message. [official]

**Pattern 340** — Testcontainers `Network.newNetwork()` for multi-container integration tests with inter-container DNS resolution
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterAll;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.containers.Network;
import org.testcontainers.containers.wait.strategy.Wait;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@Testcontainers
class CacheIntegrationTest {

    static final Network NET = Network.newNetwork();

    @Container
    static final GenericContainer<?> redis =
        new GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine")
            .withNetwork(NET)
            .withNetworkAliases("cache");

    @Container
    static final GenericContainer<?> app =
        new GenericContainer<>("my-app:latest")
            .withNetwork(NET)
            .withEnv("REDIS_HOST", "cache")
            .withEnv("REDIS_PORT", "6379")
            .waitingFor(Wait.forHttp("/health").forPort(8080));

    @AfterAll
    static void closeNetwork() { NET.close(); }

    @Test
    void appConnectsToCacheOverDockerNetwork() throws Exception {
        var client = java.net.http.HttpClient.newHttpClient();
        var response = client.send(
            java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI.create(
                "http://localhost:" + app.getMappedPort(8080) + "/cache-status"))
                .build(),
            java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        assertThat(response.body()).contains("\"connected\":true");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Using a shared `Network` instance as a `static final` field lets all containers communicate over an isolated Docker bridge network via container aliases; however the `Network` object itself is not annotated with `@Container` and is not automatically closed by the Testcontainers JUnit 5 extension — always call `NET.close()` in `@AfterAll` to avoid Docker network leaks that accumulate across test suite runs and eventually exhaust the Docker daemon's network limit. [official]

**Pattern 341** — JUnit 5 `@EnabledIfSystemProperty` and `@DisabledIfEnvironmentVariable` for environment-conditional test execution
```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.EnabledIfSystemProperty;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.DisabledIfEnvironmentVariable;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SlowIntegrationTest {

    @Test
    @EnabledIfSystemProperty(named = "run.slow.tests", matches = "true")
    void fullEndToEndPaymentFlow() {
        // runs only when -Drun.slow.tests=true is passed to the JVM
        var result = paymentIntegrationClient.processRealTransaction("test-card");
        assertThat(result.status()).isEqualTo("SETTLED");
    }

    @Test
    @DisabledIfEnvironmentVariable(named = "CI", matches = "true")
    void requiresLocalDockerDaemon() {
        // skipped in CI pipelines where CI=true is set
        try (var container = new org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")) {
            container.start();
            assertThat(container.isRunning()).isTrue();
        }
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Conditional annotations allow tests to be selectively skipped without test runner profiles, but they silently skip rather than fail when conditions are unmet, creating a risk that critical integration tests are never run if the activation property or environment variable is absent from a pipeline. Document the activation condition in `@DisplayName` and add a CI job-level assertion that verifies the expected tests were not skipped in each run. [official]
