**Pattern 454** — Mockito `mockConstruction` with `MockInitializer` for Testing Collaborators Constructed Inside Methods
```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class PaymentProcessorTest {

    @Test
    void processPayment_delegatesToGatewayAndRecordsAttempt() {
        AtomicReference<PaymentGateway> capturedGateway = new AtomicReference<>();

        try (MockedConstruction<PaymentGateway> gatewayMock =
                mockConstruction(PaymentGateway.class, (mock, ctx) -> {
                    capturedGateway.set(mock);
                    // ctx.arguments() gives constructor args: assert gateway gets correct merchant ID
                    assertThat(ctx.arguments()).containsExactly("MERCHANT-42");
                    given(mock.charge(any(), any())).willReturn(PaymentResult.SUCCESS);
                })) {

            PaymentProcessor processor = new PaymentProcessor("MERCHANT-42");
            PaymentResult result = processor.process(new Payment("100.00", Currency.EUR));

            assertThat(result).isEqualTo(PaymentResult.SUCCESS);
            assertThat(gatewayMock.constructed()).hasSize(1);
            verify(capturedGateway.get()).charge(eq(new Money("100.00", Currency.EUR)), any());
        }
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `mockConstruction(PaymentGateway.class, MockInitializer)` intercepts every `new PaymentGateway(...)` call within the try block, giving full control over what the mock returns and allowing assertion on constructor arguments via `ctx.arguments()` — this covers the pattern where the class under test creates its own collaborators internally (service locator pattern, factory method that uses `new`), which standard `@MockitoBean` injection cannot handle; the thread-locality of `MockedConstruction` means it only intercepts `new` calls on the thread that created the mock, so `new PaymentGateway(...)` on a different thread (e.g., inside a `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()`) will not be intercepted and will invoke the real constructor instead — always synchronise the construction point to the test thread or use `@TestBean` production-config replacement for async scenarios. [official]

**Pattern 455** — Spring Boot `@DataJpaTest` with `@Sql(executionPhase = AFTER_TEST_METHOD)` for Precise Data Cleanup
```java
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class ProductRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17");

    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;

    @Test
    @Sql("/sql/products-seed.sql")
    @Sql(scripts = "/sql/products-teardown.sql",
         executionPhase = Sql.ExecutionPhase.AFTER_TEST_METHOD)
    void findByCategory_returnsOnlyMatchingProducts() {
        List<Product> electronics = productRepository.findByCategory("ELECTRONICS");

        assertThat(electronics)
            .hasSize(3)
            .extracting(Product::getName)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("Laptop", "Phone", "Tablet");
    }

    @Test
    @Sql("/sql/featured-products-seed.sql")
    @Sql(scripts = "/sql/featured-products-teardown.sql",
         executionPhase = Sql.ExecutionPhase.AFTER_TEST_METHOD)
    void findFeatured_returnsFeaturedOnlyProducts() {
        List<Product> featured = productRepository.findByFeaturedTrue();

        assertThat(featured)
            .isNotEmpty()
            .allSatisfy(p -> assertThat(p.isFeatured()).isTrue());
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@Sql(executionPhase = AFTER_TEST_METHOD)` runs cleanup SQL after the test method body completes — including after any `@AfterEach` methods — making it suitable for cleaning up data that must persist through the test execution (e.g., data that an async event listener must read before the test can assert on it); unlike `@Transactional` test rollback, `AFTER_TEST_METHOD` cleanup commits and then deletes, which means `AFTER_COMMIT` transaction event listeners fire correctly and see the committed data before it is cleaned. The tradeoff is that cleanup SQL runs in a separate transaction from the test, so if the teardown script fails (e.g., a foreign key constraint violation because a test inserted related rows the teardown script does not delete), the database is left in a dirty state that affects subsequent tests — always use `TRUNCATE ... CASCADE` or `DELETE FROM ... WHERE ...` with explicit join order in teardown scripts rather than `DELETE FROM table` without constraint-safe ordering. [official]

**Pattern 456** — Java 25 `StableValue` — Lazy One-Shot Initialization Without Double-Checked Locking
```java
import java.lang.invoke.StableValue;  // JEP 502, Java 25 preview

// Production configuration holder — computed exactly once, then stable forever
public final class AppConfig {

    // StableValue<T> is a holder that can be set at most once, then read cheaply
    private final StableValue<String> resolvedBaseUrl = StableValue.of();
    private final StableValue<HttpClient> httpClient   = StableValue.of();

    public String getBaseUrl() {
        return resolvedBaseUrl.orElseCompute(() -> {
            // This lambda runs at most once, even under concurrent access
            String raw = System.getenv("APP_BASE_URL");
            return raw != null ? raw.stripTrailing() : "https://api.example.com";
        });
    }

    public HttpClient getHttpClient() {
        return httpClient.orElseCompute(() ->
            HttpClient.newBuilder()
                .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL)
                .build()
        );
    }

    // StableValue.of(supplier) — factory variant for constructor injection
    public static AppConfig forEnvironment(String envPrefix) {
        // Computed immediately but held stably
        StableValue<String> env = StableValue.of(() ->
            Optional.ofNullable(System.getenv(envPrefix + "_ENV"))
                    .orElse("production")
        );
        return new AppConfig();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `StableValue<T>` (JEP 502, Java 25 preview) provides lazy, thread-safe, guaranteed-once initialization without `synchronized`, `volatile`, or `AtomicReference` boilerplate — the JVM treats the value as stable after the first write, enabling JIT constant-folding and devirtualization optimizations that `volatile` fields prevent; `orElseCompute` guarantees the supplier is called at most once and throws `IllegalStateException` if called recursively (circular dependency detection). The limitation is that `StableValue` is a preview API in Java 25 and requires `--enable-preview` at compile time and runtime — do not use in library code targeting Java < 25 compatibility, and always guard usage behind a runtime feature flag or module requirement check until the API graduates to standard. [community]

**Pattern 457** — `StructuredTaskScope.Joiner` Custom Fan-Out with Partial Results (Java 25 — JEP 505)
```java
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope;
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner;

// Collect all successful results; log and discard failures; never fail-fast
public class ProductEnrichmentService {

    private final PricingService    pricingService;
    private final InventoryService  inventoryService;
    private final ReviewService     reviewService;

    public EnrichedProduct enrich(String productId) throws InterruptedException {
        // Custom Joiner: collect successes, tolerate failures
        try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(
                Joiner.<EnrichmentResult>allSuccessfulOrThrow())) {

            var priceTask     = scope.fork(() -> pricingService.getPrice(productId));
            var inventoryTask = scope.fork(() -> inventoryService.getStock(productId));
            var reviewTask    = scope.fork(() -> reviewService.getSummary(productId));

            scope.join();  // wait for all forks to complete

            return EnrichedProduct.builder()
                .productId(productId)
                .price(priceTask.get())        // throws if fork threw
                .stockLevel(inventoryTask.get())
                .reviewSummary(reviewTask.get())
                .build();
        }
    }

    // Partial-success variant using ShutdownOnFailure replaced by custom Joiner
    public Optional<BigDecimal> getPriceWithFallback(String productId) throws InterruptedException {
        try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(
                Joiner.<BigDecimal>anySuccessful())) {
            scope.fork(() -> pricingService.getPrimaryPrice(productId));
            scope.fork(() -> pricingService.getFallbackPrice(productId));
            return scope.join();  // returns Optional<BigDecimal> — first success wins
        }
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow())` (JEP 505, Java 25) replaces the older `ShutdownOnSuccess`/`ShutdownOnFailure` factory methods with a composable `Joiner` interface, enabling custom fan-out policies without extending `StructuredTaskScope` — the `Joiner.anySuccessful()` built-in implements a race pattern that returns the first successful result and cancels remaining forks immediately, which is ideal for pricing fallback or multi-region health checks; the structured nature of `StructuredTaskScope` guarantees that no forked task outlives the enclosing `try` block's scope, preventing leaked virtual threads even when `join()` is interrupted. The compatibility note: the `ShutdownOnSuccess` and `ShutdownOnFailure` inner classes from earlier preview versions were removed in the JEP 505 finalization — migrate to `Joiner.anySuccessful()` and `Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow()` respectively. [community]

**Pattern 458** — `jqwik` `@StatefulTest` with `@Action` for State-Machine Property Testing
```java
import net.jqwik.api.*;
import net.jqwik.api.stateful.*;

class ShoppingCartStateMachineTest {

    @Property
    void cart_operations_maintain_invariants(@ForAll("cartActions") ActionSequence<ShoppingCart> actions) {
        actions.run(new ShoppingCart());
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<ActionSequence<ShoppingCart>> cartActions() {
        return Arbitraries.sequences(
            Arbitraries.oneOf(
                addItemAction(),
                removeItemAction(),
                clearCartAction()
            )
        );
    }

    private Arbitrary<Action<ShoppingCart>> addItemAction() {
        return Combinators.combine(
            Arbitraries.strings().alpha().ofMinLength(3).ofMaxLength(20),
            Arbitraries.bigDecimals().between(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.01), BigDecimal.valueOf(999.99))
        ).as((sku, price) -> new Action.JustMutate<>(cart -> {
            int sizeBefore = cart.size();
            cart.addItem(new CartItem(sku, price));
            assert cart.size() == sizeBefore + 1 : "addItem must increase size by exactly 1";
            assert cart.getTotalPrice().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) >= 0 : "total must remain non-negative";
        }));
    }

    private Arbitrary<Action<ShoppingCart>> removeItemAction() {
        return Arbitraries.just(new Action.JustMutate<>(cart -> {
            if (cart.isEmpty()) return;  // pre-condition: only remove if not empty
            CartItem first = cart.getItems().get(0);
            cart.removeItem(first.getSku());
            assert !cart.getItems().contains(first) : "removed item must not remain in cart";
        }));
    }

    private Arbitrary<Action<ShoppingCart>> clearCartAction() {
        return Arbitraries.just(new Action.JustMutate<>(cart -> {
            cart.clear();
            assert cart.isEmpty() : "cleared cart must be empty";
            assert cart.getTotalPrice().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) == 0 : "cleared cart total must be zero";
        }));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ActionSequence`-based stateful testing in jqwik generates random sequences of operations and verifies that class invariants hold after every operation — this catches state-transition bugs (e.g., removing the last item from a cart sets the total to `null` instead of `BigDecimal.ZERO`) that example-based tests miss because they only cover specific sequences; when a failing sequence is found, jqwik shrinks it to the minimal sequence of operations that reproduces the failure, making root-cause diagnosis fast even for complex state machines. The limitation is that `Action.JustMutate` uses Java `assert` statements for postcondition checking, which are disabled unless the JVM is started with `-ea` — always enable assertions in test JVM forks via `<argLine>-ea</argLine>` in Maven Surefire or `jvmArgs('-ea')` in Gradle test configuration, otherwise invariant violations will silently pass. [community]

---

**Pattern 459** — AssertJ 4.x `assertThat(record).isRecord().hasRecordComponent()` for Structural Record Assertions
```java
// AssertJ 4.0+ — native record introspection assertions
@Test
void order_record_has_expected_structure_and_values() {
    record Order(String id, BigDecimal amount, OrderStatus status) {}

    Order order = new Order("ORD-001", new BigDecimal("49.99"), OrderStatus.PENDING);

    // AssertJ 4.0 adds first-class record support
    assertThat(Order.class)
        .isRecord()
        .hasRecordComponents("id", "amount", "status");

    assertThat(order)
        .isInstanceOf(Order.class)
        .extracting(Order::id, Order::amount, Order::status)
        .containsExactly("ORD-001", new BigDecimal("49.99"), OrderStatus.PENDING);

    // Verify record canonical constructor preserves equality contract
    Order duplicate = new Order("ORD-001", new BigDecimal("49.99"), OrderStatus.PENDING);
    assertThat(order)
        .isEqualTo(duplicate)
        .hasSameHashCodeAs(duplicate);

    // isSealed check (AssertJ 4.0 native support)
    assertThat(OrderStatus.class).isSealed();
}
```
Tradeoff: AssertJ 4.0's `isRecord()` and `hasRecordComponents(String...)` assertions verify at the reflection level that a type is a Java record and that its component names match expectations — this catches refactorings where a record component is renamed or reordered (which changes the serialization contract) without updating downstream code that depends on component names for JSON mapping or persistence column mapping; `isSealed()` verifies sealed class declarations, which is useful in architecture tests that enforce that all domain event types are sealed. AssertJ 4.0 requires Java 17+ as a minimum JVM version — projects still supporting Java 11 must stay on AssertJ 3.x, where these specific record and sealed-class assertions are not available natively and must be approximated with `isInstanceOf(Record.class)` and reflection-based component enumeration. [community]

---

**Pattern 460** — Spring Boot 4.0 `RestTestClient` for Reactive and Servlet Integration Testing
```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureRestTestClient  // new in Spring Boot 4.0 — replaces TestRestTemplate for modern stacks
class OrderIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private RestTestClient restTestClient;  // fluent, type-safe, works with both servlet and reactive

    @Test
    void createOrder_returnsCreatedStatusAndOrderId() {
        CreateOrderRequest request = new CreateOrderRequest("CUST-001", BigDecimal.valueOf(99.99));

        restTestClient
            .post().uri("/api/v1/orders")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .bodyValue(request)
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isCreated()
            .expectHeader().exists("Location")
            .expectBody(OrderResponse.class)
            .value(response -> {
                assertThat(response.orderId()).startsWith("ORD-");
                assertThat(response.status()).isEqualTo("PENDING");
                assertThat(response.totalAmount()).isEqualByComparingTo(BigDecimal.valueOf(99.99));
            });
    }

    @Test
    void getOrder_whenNotFound_returns404WithProblemDetail() {
        restTestClient
            .get().uri("/api/v1/orders/{id}", "ORD-NONEXISTENT")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound()
            .expectBody()
            .jsonPath("$.type").isEqualTo("https://example.com/problems/order-not-found")
            .jsonPath("$.title").isEqualTo("Order Not Found")
            .jsonPath("$.status").isEqualTo(404);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `RestTestClient` (Spring Boot 4.0, module `spring-boot-resttestclient`) provides a unified, fluent HTTP client for integration tests that works identically against both servlet-based (`spring-boot-starter-web`) and reactive (`spring-boot-starter-webflux`) stacks, replacing the older `TestRestTemplate` (which was removed in Spring Boot 4.0) and supplementing `WebTestClient` (which required a reactive stack to auto-configure); `RestTestClient` supports `RFC 7807 ProblemDetail` response assertions natively via `.expectProblemDetail()`. The migration note: if upgrading from Spring Boot 3.x, replace all `@Autowired TestRestTemplate` injections with `@Autowired RestTestClient` and convert blocking `getForEntity` calls to the fluent `get().uri(...).exchange()` chain — Spring Boot 4.0 removes `TestRestTemplate` from auto-configuration entirely, so compilation will fail without this migration. [official]

---

**Pattern 461** — ArchUnit `MethodCallRule` for Forbidden API Enforcement Across Packages
```java
@AnalyzeClasses(
    packages = "com.example",
    importOptions = ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS
)
class ForbiddenApiRulesTest {

    // Enforce: production code must not call System.exit()
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_system_exit_in_production_code =
        noClasses()
            .should().callMethod(System.class, "exit", int.class)
            .because("System.exit() kills the JVM without triggering shutdown hooks or Spring lifecycle events; use ApplicationContext.close() or throw an exception instead");

    // Enforce: repositories must not call Thread.sleep() — causes connection pool starvation
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_thread_sleep_in_repositories =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..repository..")
            .should().callMethod(Thread.class, "sleep", long.class)
            .because("Thread.sleep() in a repository method holds the JDBC connection for the sleep duration; use Awaitility or database-level retry instead");

    // Enforce: domain classes must not import Spring annotations
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_must_not_depend_on_spring =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("com.example.domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage(
                "org.springframework..",
                "jakarta.inject.."
            )
            .because("Domain model must remain framework-agnostic to be testable without Spring context");

    // Enforce: deprecated APIs must not be called in new code
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_deprecated_api_calls =
        noClasses()
            .should().callCodeUnitWhere(modifier -> modifier.isAnnotatedWith(Deprecated.class))
            .because("Deprecated API usage creates upgrade risk; use the recommended replacement documented in the @deprecated Javadoc");
}
```
Tradeoff: `callMethod(Class, String, Class<?>...)` matches method invocations by exact class, method name, and parameter types — this is more precise than `dependOnClassesThat().haveFullyQualifiedName()` because it identifies the specific call site rather than any dependency on the class; however, if the forbidden method is called via an interface (e.g., `ExecutorService.submit()` delegates to `ThreadPoolExecutor.execute()` internally), ArchUnit only sees the call to the declared interface method, not the implementation — use `callMethodWhere(HasName.AndFullName.Predicates.nameContaining("sleep"))` to catch method name patterns across multiple classes when the exact declaring class may vary. [official]

---

**Pattern 462** — JUnit 6 `CancellationToken` for Cooperative Test Cancellation
```java
// JUnit 6.0+ — cooperative cancellation for long-running tests
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.CancellationToken;

@ExtendWith(CancellationTokenExtension.class)
class DataMigrationTest {

    @Test
    void migrateRecords_completesOrCancelsCoopertaively(CancellationToken cancellationToken) {
        DataMigrationJob job = new DataMigrationJob(sourceDb, targetDb);
        job.setCancellationToken(cancellationToken);

        MigrationResult result = job.run(10_000);  // migrate up to 10k records

        // If test was cancelled (e.g., by JUnit timeout or IDE stop), check result
        if (cancellationToken.isCancellationRequested()) {
            // Partial result is acceptable — verify consistency of what was migrated
            assertThat(result.getMigratedCount())
                .as("partial migration must not corrupt data")
                .isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0);
            assertThat(result.getLastMigratedId())
                .as("last migrated ID must be consistent with migrated count")
                .satisfies(id -> {
                    if (result.getMigratedCount() > 0) {
                        assertThat(id).isNotNull();
                    }
                });
        } else {
            // Full completion — verify all records migrated
            assertThat(result.getMigratedCount()).isEqualTo(10_000);
            assertThat(result.getFailedCount()).isZero();
        }
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `CancellationToken` (JUnit 6.0+) is injected by JUnit's `CancellationTokenExtension` and signals cooperative cancellation when a test is aborted by a `@Timeout`, by the IDE's stop button, or by JUnit's `LauncherExecutionRequest` cancellation API — the test method receives the token as a parameter and can poll `isCancellationRequested()` to terminate early and still assert on partial state, rather than being forcibly interrupted by `Thread.interrupt()` which leaves shared resources in an unknown state. The limitation is that cooperative cancellation requires the system under test to poll the token — it cannot interrupt blocking I/O or `Thread.sleep()` calls; for tests that must interrupt blocking operations, combine `CancellationToken` with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` in a `CancellationTokenExtension` `afterEach` callback, or use virtual threads where `interrupt()` wakes up blocking I/O via the `InterruptibleChannel` mechanism. [official]

---

**Pattern 463** — `Mockito.verify` with `inOrder` and `timeout()` for Async Interaction Ordering
```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class NotificationDispatcherTest {

    @Mock
    private EmailService emailService;

    @Mock
    private AuditLogger auditLogger;

    @InjectMocks
    private NotificationDispatcher dispatcher;

    @Test
    void dispatchWelcomeNotification_sendsEmailThenLogsAudit() throws Exception {
        UserRegisteredEvent event = new UserRegisteredEvent("user@example.com", "Alice");

        dispatcher.handleAsync(event);  // fires on a background thread

        // Verify order: email must be sent before audit is logged
        InOrder inOrder = inOrder(emailService, auditLogger);
        inOrder.verify(emailService, timeout(2_000)).send(
            argThat(email -> email.getTo().equals("user@example.com")
                         && email.getSubject().contains("Welcome")));
        inOrder.verify(auditLogger, timeout(2_000)).log(
            eq("USER_WELCOME_SENT"),
            argThat(ctx -> ctx.containsKey("userId")));

        // Verify no further interactions on either mock
        verifyNoMoreInteractions(emailService, auditLogger);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `inOrder.verify(mock, timeout(millis))` combines ordering verification with async waiting — the `timeout()` mode polls until the interaction occurs or the timeout expires, then checks ordering against interactions that have already occurred on the `inOrder` verifier; this catches race conditions where the email and audit log calls happen correctly but in the wrong order (audit before email), which would indicate a logic bug in the notification pipeline. The known limitation is that `timeout()` uses wall-clock polling and does not integrate with Awaitility's condition model — for complex multi-step async assertions, prefer `Awaitility.await().untilAsserted()` for the condition check and use `inOrder.verify()` without `timeout()` after `untilAsserted()` completes, because mixing `timeout()` with `InOrder` can produce non-deterministic failures when the background thread has slightly different timing between CI environments. [community]

---

**Pattern 464** — WireMock `JsonBodyPattern` with `matchingJsonPath` for Deep Request Body Assertions
```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.NONE)
@ExtendWith(WireMockExtension.class)
class PaymentGatewayClientTest {

    @RegisterExtension
    static WireMockExtension wireMock = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
        .options(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort())
        .build();

    @Test
    void chargeCard_sendsCorrectlyStructuredPayload() {
        wireMock.stubFor(post(urlEqualTo("/v1/charges"))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.amount",
                equalTo("4999")))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.currency",
                equalTo("EUR")))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.card.last4",
                matching("[0-9]{4}")))
            .withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath("$.metadata.orderId",
                present()))
            .willReturn(aResponse()
                .withStatus(200)
                .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .withBody("{\"id\":\"ch_test_001\",\"status\":\"succeeded\"}")));

        PaymentGatewayClient client = new PaymentGatewayClient(wireMock.baseUrl());
        ChargeResult result = client.charge(
            new ChargeRequest(Money.of(49.99, "EUR"), "4242", "ORD-001"));

        assertThat(result.getChargeId()).isEqualTo("ch_test_001");
        assertThat(result.getStatus()).isEqualTo("succeeded");

        // Verify the stub was hit exactly once
        wireMock.verify(1, postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/v1/charges")));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `matchingJsonPath("$.field", valuePattern)` asserts on individual JSON fields within the request body using JSONPath expressions, enabling fine-grained contract verification without deserializing the full payload — multiple `withRequestBody(matchingJsonPath(...))` calls are ANDed together, so all must match for the stub to activate; if any condition fails, WireMock returns its default 404 "not matched" response, and `wireMock.findUnmatchedRequests()` shows which JSONPath expression did not match, making debugging mismatch failures efficient. The performance note: `matchingJsonPath` with `WireMock.equalTo` performs exact string comparison on the JSON-encoded value — for numeric JSON fields, `"4999"` is the string representation of the number `4999`, not the integer; always test what the client sends (integer vs string) and align the matcher type accordingly to avoid stub misses that produce confusing 404 responses during the first test run. [official]

---

**Pattern 465** — Java `SequencedCollection` Reverse Iteration with `reversed()` for Ordered Processing
```java
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.SequencedCollection;

public class AuditTrailProcessor {

    // SequencedCollection (Java 21) provides first/last access + reversed() view on any ordered collection
    public List<AuditEvent> getMostRecentFirst(SequencedCollection<AuditEvent> events) {
        // reversed() returns a reversed-order view without copying — O(1) overhead
        return events.reversed().stream()
            .filter(e -> !e.isSystemEvent())
            .limit(50)
            .toList();
    }

    public Optional<AuditEvent> getLatestFailure(Deque<AuditEvent> eventDeque) {
        // getFirst()/getLast() on SequencedCollection — uniform API across List, Deque, SortedSet
        return eventDeque.reversed().stream()
            .filter(e -> e.getSeverity() == Severity.ERROR)
            .findFirst();
    }

    public void processChronologically(LinkedList<AuditEvent> events) {
        // addFirst / addLast / removeFirst / removeLast — unified across all sequenced collections
        events.addFirst(AuditEvent.systemMarker("BATCH_START"));
        events.addLast(AuditEvent.systemMarker("BATCH_END"));

        // Iterate in encounter order (insertion order for LinkedList)
        for (AuditEvent event : events) {
            processEvent(event);
        }

        events.removeFirst();  // remove BATCH_START marker
        events.removeLast();   // remove BATCH_END marker
    }

    private void processEvent(AuditEvent event) { /* ... */ }
}
```
Tradeoff: `SequencedCollection.reversed()` returns a reversed-order *view* backed by the original collection — mutations to the original are reflected in the view and vice versa — making it safe for read-only streaming but dangerous if code concurrently modifies the original while iterating the reversed view; use `List.copyOf(collection.reversed())` to materialize a snapshot if the original may be mutated during iteration. The unified API (`getFirst()`, `getLast()`, `addFirst()`, `addLast()`, `removeFirst()`, `removeLast()`, `reversed()`) is available on `List`, `Deque`, and `SortedSet` via the `SequencedCollection` and `SequencedSet` interfaces, replacing the inconsistent legacy access patterns (`list.get(0)` vs `deque.peekFirst()` vs `sortedSet.first()`). [official]

### Community Gotchas

**G66** — Spring Boot `@SpringBootTest` with `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` and `RestTestClient` Base URL Defaults to `localhost:80` Without `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient`
Why this matters: `RestTestClient` injected via `@Autowired` in a `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` test will default to `http://localhost:80` as its base URL if `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` is not present on the test class, because the auto-configuration that wires the random port into the `RestTestClient` base URL only applies when `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` triggers the `RestTestClientAutoConfiguration`. Tests that omit this annotation will silently send all requests to port 80 (likely not running), receive `Connection refused` errors, and fail with confusing `WebClientRequestException` messages rather than `AssertionError` messages that indicate what the test was actually checking.
Fix: Always pair `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `@AutoConfigureRestTestClient` when using `RestTestClient` injection. Alternatively, inject `@LocalServerPort int port` and construct `RestTestClient.bindToServer().baseUrl("http://localhost:" + port).build()` explicitly, which makes the port binding visible and removes the dependency on auto-configuration ordering. [official]

**G67** — `jqwik` `@Property` Shrinking Finds a Minimal Counter-Example That Passes After Code Fix but `@Seed` Replay Fails
Why this matters: When jqwik finds a failing property and shrinks the counter-example to a minimal reproducer, it reports the seed that was used to generate the original failing case. If a developer fixes the bug and re-runs the test with `@Property(seed = "<reported-seed>")` to verify, the seed replay generates the same *original* random sequence — but the shrunk minimal counter-example is a different value that was derived from the shrinking process, not from the seed directly. The seed replay test passes because the original unshrunken input no longer triggers the bug, giving false confidence that the shrunk minimal case is also fixed. The actual minimal case may still fail if the fix was too narrow.
Fix: Always test the shrunk minimal counter-example explicitly as an `@Example` (a fixed, named example test) rather than relying on seed replay: copy the shrunk value from the failure message into a dedicated `@Example` method with an `@Tag("regression")` annotation. This creates a permanent regression test for the exact minimal case that was found, and the seed replay is only used for debugging, not for verifying the fix. [community]

**G68** — ArchUnit `noClasses().should().callMethod()` Does Not Detect Calls Made Via Reflection or Method Handles
Why this matters: `noClasses().should().callMethod(System.class, "exit", int.class)` correctly prevents bytecode-level `System.exit(0)` calls in production classes. However, code that calls `System.exit` via `Method.invoke(null, 0)` (reflection) or `MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(System.class, "exit", ...)` (method handles) is not detected by ArchUnit's static bytecode analysis — ArchUnit analyzes `INVOKESTATIC` and `INVOKEVIRTUAL` bytecode instructions, not `Method.invoke` calls which appear as regular method calls to `java.lang.reflect.Method`. This creates a false-safe architecture rule that passes while the forbidden pattern is used via indirection.
Fix: For reflection-based forbidden API calls, add a complementary `noClasses().should().callMethod(Method.class, "invoke", Object.class, Object[].class).because(...)` rule scoped to the packages most likely to call `Method.invoke` on forbidden targets, and supplement with static analysis tools (SonarQube or SpotBugs) that can track taint flow from `Class.getMethod("exit")` to `Method.invoke()`. Accept that bytecode-level architecture rules cannot cover all reflection patterns and document this limitation in the rule's `because()` clause. [community]

**G69** — Testcontainers `DockerComposeContainer` `waitingFor(service, Wait.forHttp(...))` Hangs When the Service Exposes Multiple Ports and the Wrong Port Is Inferred
Why this matters: `DockerComposeContainer.waitingFor("backend", Wait.forHttp("/health").forPort(8080))` appears to wait for the `/health` endpoint on port 8080 of the `backend` service. However, when the compose file maps multiple ports for a service (e.g., `ports: ["8080:8080", "9090:9090"]`), Testcontainers' port-mapping resolution can infer the wrong mapped host port if `forPort()` is not called, and silently waits for the unmapped port — which never responds — causing the test to hang until the Startup timeout (default: 60s) and fail with a generic `ContainerLaunchException` rather than a port-resolution error. This is particularly common when migrating from single-port to multi-port service definitions.
Fix: Always call `.forPort(containerPort)` explicitly on `Wait.forHttp()` strategies when the service exposes multiple ports, and validate the actual host-port mapping with `container.getServicePort("backend", 8080)` at test startup. Add a `@BeforeAll` assertion that `container.getServicePort("backend", 8080) > 0` to fail fast with a clear error message if the port mapping is missing from the compose file, rather than discovering the misconfiguration as a 60-second timeout. [official]

**G70** — Mockito `@InjectMocks` Fails Silently When a Constructor Has a Type-Incompatible Dependency and Falls Back to Property Injection
Why this matters: `@InjectMocks` tries three injection strategies in order: constructor injection → setter injection → field injection. If constructor injection fails because a `@Mock` field has a type that does not match any constructor parameter (e.g., the mock is `List<String>` but the constructor expects `List<User>`), Mockito silently falls back to property injection and injects `null` for the unmatched parameter, or injects via a setter that may not initialize the field correctly. The test then compiles and runs but the `@InjectMocks` class has a `null` field, causing a `NullPointerException` deep inside the tested method rather than at injection time — making the error message completely unrelated to the actual injection failure.
Fix: Avoid relying on `@InjectMocks` for classes with complex generics or multiple same-type dependencies. Instead, use explicit constructor instantiation in a `@BeforeEach` setup method: `service = new OrderService(mockRepo, mockEmailSender, mockAuditLog)`. This makes the wiring visible, fails fast with a compile error if the constructor signature changes, and prevents the silent null-injection that `@InjectMocks` produces on type mismatches. For large classes where explicit construction is verbose, add an `assertThat(service).hasNoNullFieldsOrProperties()` assertion after `@InjectMocks` injection to catch silent injection failures before they produce confusing NPEs. [community]

## Extension — Iteration 44: Gap-Fill on Builder, Optional, Streams, Records, var, Generics

### Staged (Step) Builder Pattern — Compile-Time Required Field Enforcement

The standard `Builder` pattern (see the earlier `HttpRequest.Builder` example) silently accepts an incomplete build call: `new EmailMessage.Builder().build()` compiles and throws only at runtime when `Objects.requireNonNull` fires. The **Staged Builder** (also called Step Builder) uses a chain of single-method interfaces to enforce that every mandatory field is supplied before `build()` becomes accessible — turning a runtime error into a compile error.

```java
// Staged Builder: each interface exposes exactly one method, returning the next stage
// The caller CANNOT skip a mandatory field; the compiler prevents it.

public final class EmailMessage {
    private final String to;
    private final String subject;
    private final String body;
    private final String from;          // optional
    private final boolean html;         // optional

    private EmailMessage(Builder b) {
        this.to      = b.to;
        this.subject = b.subject;
        this.body    = b.body;
        this.from    = b.from;
        this.html    = b.html;
    }

    // === Staged interfaces — one per mandatory field, in order ===

    public interface ToStage    { SubjectStage to(String recipient); }
    public interface SubjectStage { BodyStage subject(String subject); }
    public interface BodyStage  { OptionalStage body(String body); }

    // All optional fields and build() live on the final stage
    public interface OptionalStage {
        OptionalStage from(String sender);
        OptionalStage html(boolean html);
        EmailMessage build();
    }

    // Concrete builder implements all stages
    public static final class Builder
            implements ToStage, SubjectStage, BodyStage, OptionalStage {

        private String to, subject, body;
        private String from  = "noreply@example.com";
        private boolean html = false;

        private Builder() {}

        @Override public SubjectStage  to(String r)       { this.to      = r; return this; }
        @Override public BodyStage     subject(String s)  { this.subject = s; return this; }
        @Override public OptionalStage body(String b)     { this.body    = b; return this; }
        @Override public OptionalStage from(String f)     { this.from    = f; return this; }
        @Override public OptionalStage html(boolean h)    { this.html    = h; return this; }
        @Override public EmailMessage  build()            { return new EmailMessage(this); }
    }

    // Entry point: returns the first stage, NOT the Builder itself
    public static ToStage builder() { return new Builder(); }
}

// Usage — the type system guides the call order; skipping a mandatory step = compile error
EmailMessage msg = EmailMessage.builder()
    .to("alice@example.com")           // returns SubjectStage — only subject() available
    .subject("Hello!")                 // returns BodyStage — only body() available
    .body("Please see the attachment.") // returns OptionalStage
    .html(true)                        // optional — may be omitted
    .build();

// COMPILE ERROR — cannot call build() before all mandatory stages:
// EmailMessage broken = EmailMessage.builder().to("x").build(); // no build() on SubjectStage
```

**When to use:** Choose Staged Builder when (a) 2+ mandatory fields have the same type (positional confusion would be possible without staged guidance), or (b) the domain enforces a logical ordering for field initialization (e.g., start → end dates). For simple objects with distinct-type mandatory fields, the standard `Builder` with `requireNonNull` in `build()` is less verbose and equally clear.

**Trade-off:** Staged Builder requires N interface declarations for N mandatory fields. For objects with 5+ mandatory fields, this creates significant interface boilerplate. A pragmatic hybrid: use Staged Builder only for the first one or two truly critical fields (e.g., the primary key or invariant-defining dimensions), and expose the rest as optional on the final stage.

### `Optional<T>` — Advanced Chaining: `or()`, `stream()`, and `flatMap()` with Nested Optionals

The introductory `Optional` section covers `map`, `filter`, `orElse`, and `ifPresentOrElse`. Three additional methods fill important gaps in real-world API design: `or()` (Java 9+), `stream()` (Java 9+), and `flatMap()` with nested Optionals.

```java
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

// =========================================================
// Optional.or() — Java 9+ — return an alternative Optional
// =========================================================
// Use when the fallback itself may be absent (the fallback is another Optional,
// not a plain value). Unlike orElse(T), or() does not unwrap.

public Optional<User> findUserByIdOrEmail(String id, String email) {
    return userRepo.findById(id)
        .or(() -> userRepo.findByEmail(email));  // only called if findById returns empty
    // The result is still Optional<User> — caller controls unwrapping
}

// Chain multiple fallback sources without nested ifs:
Optional<Config> effectiveConfig = localConfig()
    .or(this::remoteConfig)      // only fetched if local is absent
    .or(this::defaultConfig);    // last resort

// =========================================================
// Optional.stream() — Java 9+ — bridge to Stream API
// =========================================================
// Converts Optional<T> to a Stream<T> of 0 or 1 elements.
// The key idiom: use in flatMap to filter out empties from a Stream<Optional<T>>

List<String> ids = List.of("u1", "INVALID", "u3", "INVALID");

// BAD — filter + get requires presence check; verbose
List<User> users = ids.stream()
    .map(userRepo::findById)          // Stream<Optional<User>>
    .filter(Optional::isPresent)       // keep non-empty
    .map(Optional::get)                // unwrap — safe after filter but ugly
    .toList();

// GOOD — flatMap(Optional::stream) collapses empties in one operation
List<User> users2 = ids.stream()
    .map(userRepo::findById)           // Stream<Optional<User>>
    .flatMap(Optional::stream)         // Optional::stream = empty → zero elements
    .toList();                         // Stream<User> with holes removed

// =========================================================
// Optional.flatMap() — avoid double-wrapping
// =========================================================
// Use flatMap (not map) when the mapping function itself returns Optional.
// map() produces Optional<Optional<T>>; flatMap() flattens to Optional<T>.

public record Address(String street, Optional<String> apt) {}
public record User(String name, Optional<Address> address) {}

// WRONG — map produces Optional<Optional<Optional<String>>>
Optional<Optional<Optional<String>>> wrong = user.map(User::address)
    .map(optAddr -> optAddr.map(Address::apt));

// CORRECT — flatMap flattens each level to Optional<String>
Optional<String> apt = Optional.of(user)
    .flatMap(User::address)         // Optional<User> → Optional<Address>
    .flatMap(Address::apt);         // Optional<Address> → Optional<String>

// Full example: navigate a nullable chain safely
String aptDisplay = Optional.ofNullable(getUser())
    .flatMap(u -> Optional.ofNullable(u.address()))
    .flatMap(a -> Optional.ofNullable(a.apt()))
    .orElse("No apt");
```

**Decision rule for `map` vs `flatMap` on `Optional`:** If the function returns a plain value `T`, use `map`. If the function returns `Optional<T>`, use `flatMap` — otherwise you get `Optional<Optional<T>>`.

**Decision rule for `orElse` vs `or`:** If the fallback is a plain value (always computed), use `orElse(value)`. If the fallback is itself an `Optional` that might be empty, use `or(() -> computeFallbackOptional())`. If the fallback is a plain value that is expensive to compute, use `orElseGet(() -> expensiveDefault())` — the supplier is only called when the Optional is empty.

### Generic Records — Parameterized Value Carriers

Records can declare type parameters, making them reusable as generic containers. The compact canonical constructor validation applies to the typed component just as it does to concrete records. Generic records are particularly useful as return types that carry both a value and metadata.

```java
// Generic pair — similar to Map.Entry but with named semantics
public record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {
    // Compact canonical constructor: null-check both components
    public Pair {
        Objects.requireNonNull(first,  "first");
        Objects.requireNonNull(second, "second");
    }

    // Static factory — type inference keeps call sites clean
    public static <A, B> Pair<A, B> of(A first, B second) {
        return new Pair<>(first, second);
    }

    // Map over the first component; second is unchanged
    public <C> Pair<C, B> mapFirst(java.util.function.Function<A, C> fn) {
        return new Pair<>(fn.apply(first), second);
    }
}

// Usage
Pair<String, Integer> score = Pair.of("Alice", 95);
Pair<Integer, Integer> lengths = score.mapFirst(String::length);  // (5, 95)

// Generic result type — carries either a value or an error, never both
public sealed interface Result<T> permits Result.Ok, Result.Err {

    record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {
        public Ok { Objects.requireNonNull(value, "value"); }
    }

    record Err<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {
        public Err { Objects.requireNonNull(message, "message"); }

        public Err(String message) { this(message, null); }
    }

    // Factory methods
    static <T> Result<T> ok(T value)                          { return new Ok<>(value); }
    static <T> Result<T> err(String msg)                      { return new Err<>(msg); }
    static <T> Result<T> err(String msg, Throwable cause)     { return new Err<>(msg, cause); }

    // Exhaustive pattern match on result
    default <R> R fold(
            java.util.function.Function<T, R> onOk,
            java.util.function.Function<String, R> onErr) {
        return switch (this) {
            case Ok<T>  ok  -> onOk.apply(ok.value());
            case Err<T> err -> onErr.apply(err.message());
        };
    }
}

// Caller — no try/catch needed; errors are values
Result<User> result = userRepo.findById(id);
String display = result.fold(
    user  -> "Found: " + user.name(),
    error -> "Error: " + error
);

// Generic page — wraps a slice of results with pagination metadata
public record Page<T>(List<T> content, long total, int page, int size) {
    public Page {
        content = List.copyOf(Objects.requireNonNull(content));  // defensive copy
    }

    public boolean hasNext()     { return (long) (page + 1) * size < total; }
    public boolean hasPrevious() { return page > 0; }

    public <R> Page<R> map(java.util.function.Function<T, R> fn) {
        return new Page<>(content.stream().map(fn).toList(), total, page, size);
    }
}
```

**Limitations of generic records:**
- You cannot use a type parameter as a bound in the compact canonical constructor (`T extends Comparable<T>` is fine as a declaration, but you cannot call `first.compareTo(second)` inside the constructor without the bound on the record itself).
- Type erasure applies: `new Pair<String, Integer>(...) instanceof Pair<String, Integer>` is a compile error — use `instanceof Pair<?, ?>` with ungrouped wildcards for runtime instanceof checks.
- Records cannot extend classes (they implicitly extend `java.lang.Record`), so generic records cannot be used in an inheritance hierarchy — sealed interfaces with record permits are the idiomatic alternative.

### `var` Type Inference — Advanced Patterns and Pitfalls

The introductory `var` section covers the happy path. Here are the subtle edges that trip up developers in production code.

```java
// === PITFALL 1: var with diamond operator loses type information ===
// The diamond infers the type from the declared variable type.
// With var, there is no declared type — the compiler infers Object for the element type.
var list = new ArrayList<>();          // compiles; list is ArrayList<Object>
var list2 = new ArrayList<String>();   // GOOD — element type preserved in RHS

// GOOD — always supply the type parameter when using var with constructors
var users   = new ArrayList<User>();
var headers = new HashMap<String, List<String>>();

// === PITFALL 2: var with anonymous types and intersection types ===
// var CAN capture anonymous class types that have no name — use this power carefully.
// The inferred type is more specific than any expressible type.
var handler = new Object() {
    void handle(String s) { System.out.println("Handling: " + s); }
};
handler.handle("event");  // works — handle() is visible on the inferred anonymous type
// BUT: cannot assign handler to any named type; cannot pass it to a method with a typed parameter

// === PITFALL 3: var changes the inferred type of literals ===
var x = 1;         // int (not Integer — no auto-boxing at declaration)
var d = 1.0;       // double
var f = 1.0f;      // float  — suffix required; without f, inferred as double
var l = 1L;        // long

// === PITFALL 4: var with null — does not compile ===
// var n = null;    // COMPILE ERROR: cannot infer type for local variable initialised to null

// === PITFALL 5: var in enhanced-for is safe but limits readability for complex types ===
// Use var to improve readability when the RHS makes the type obvious.
for (var entry : userMap.entrySet()) {            // GOOD: Map.Entry<K,V> inferred from map type
    System.out.println(entry.getKey());
}
for (var item : complexMethod()) {                // BAD: type of item unclear without inspecting method
    process(item);                                // prefer explicit type if return type is non-obvious
}

// === PITFALL 6: var with conditional expressions narrows to widest compatible type ===
var result = condition ? 1 : 2L;    // inferred as long (int promoted to long in ternary)
var obj    = condition ? "hi" : 42; // inferred as Object | Serializable — not String or Integer

// === PITFALL 7: var in try-with-resources is fully supported ===
try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    // reader is BufferedReader; close() called automatically
    return reader.lines().collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
}

// === CORRECT USAGE SUMMARY ===
// USE var when:
//   - RHS is a constructor call: var x = new Foo()  → type obvious
//   - RHS is a factory method with a descriptive name: var path = Path.of(...)
//   - Loop variable over entrySet() or similarly typed collections
//   - try-with-resources to reduce visual noise on long resource types

// AVOID var when:
//   - RHS is a method call whose return type is not obvious from the method name
//   - Diamond inference would produce ArrayList<Object> instead of ArrayList<T>
//   - The type carries important domain information (e.g., Optional<User> vs Object)
//   - Public API: var is only for local variables; it cannot appear in method signatures
```

---

### Streams API — `Collectors.toMap()` with Merge Function and Downstream Collector

The introductory Streams section covers `groupingBy`, `joining`, and `toList()`. Two frequently missed `Collectors.toMap()` behaviors create runtime exceptions in production code when they could be caught at design time.

```java
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.List;

record Product(String sku, String name, double price) {}

// =========================================================
// Problem 1: toMap() throws on duplicate keys
// =========================================================
List<Product> catalog = List.of(
    new Product("A1", "Widget",   9.99),
    new Product("A1", "Widget v2", 10.99),  // duplicate SKU!
    new Product("B2", "Gadget",   24.99)
);

// BAD — throws IllegalStateException: "Duplicate key A1"
Map<String, Product> bad = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Product::sku, p -> p));

// GOOD — merge function: keep the latest (higher-priced) version on conflict
Map<String, Product> bySkuKeepLast = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Product::sku,
        p -> p,
        (existing, incoming) -> incoming  // merge: keep the newer entry
    ));

// GOOD — merge function: accumulate into a list when duplicates are expected
Map<String, List<Product>> bySku = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Product::sku,
        p -> new java.util.ArrayList<>(List.of(p)),   // start list with this product
        (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; }          // merge lists on collision
    ));

// =========================================================
// Problem 2: toMap() returns HashMap (unordered) by default
// =========================================================
// The 4-argument overload lets you supply the map factory.

// GOOD — preserve insertion order with LinkedHashMap
Map<String, Double> orderedPriceMap = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Product::sku,
        Product::price,
        (a, b) -> a,            // keep first on duplicate
        java.util.LinkedHashMap::new    // map factory — preserves insertion order
    ));

// GOOD — groupingBy with a downstream collector (sum prices per category)
record OrderLine(String category, double amount) {}

Map<String, Double> revenueByCategory = List.of(
    new OrderLine("Electronics", 199.99),
    new OrderLine("Books",        24.99),
    new OrderLine("Electronics",  49.99)
).stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        OrderLine::category,
        Collectors.summingDouble(OrderLine::amount)   // downstream: sum amounts
    ));
// {Electronics=249.98, Books=24.99}

// GOOD — groupingBy with counting downstream
Map<String, Long> countByCategory = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        p -> p.name().substring(0, 1),   // group by first letter of name
        Collectors.counting()
    ));
```

### Streams API — Building a Custom `Collector`

`Collector.of()` lets you build reusable, composable terminal operations for cases that `toList()`, `toMap()`, and `groupingBy()` cannot express. A `Collector` has four components: a `Supplier` (creates the mutable result container), an `Accumulator` (folds one element into the container), a `Combiner` (merges two containers for parallel streams), and a `Finisher` (produces the final result from the container).

```java
import java.util.stream.Collector;
import java.util.StringJoiner;

// Custom collector: join a stream of strings into an Oxford-comma list
// "Alice", "Alice, Bob", "Alice, Bob, and Carol"
public static Collector<String, ?, String> oxfordJoin() {
    return Collector.of(
        () -> new java.util.ArrayList<String>(),                  // supplier: empty list
        java.util.List::add,                                       // accumulator: add element
        (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; },                     // combiner: merge lists
        list -> switch (list.size()) {                             // finisher: format the list
            case 0 -> "";
            case 1 -> list.get(0);
            case 2 -> list.get(0) + " and " + list.get(1);
            default -> {
                String allButLast = String.join(", ", list.subList(0, list.size() - 1));
                yield allButLast + ", and " + list.get(list.size() - 1);
            }
        }
    );
}

// Usage
String result = Stream.of("Alice", "Bob", "Carol")
    .collect(oxfordJoin());
// → "Alice, Bob, and Carol"

// Custom collector: batch elements into fixed-size sublists
public static <T> Collector<T, ?, List<List<T>>> batching(int batchSize) {
    return Collector.<T, List<List<T>>, List<List<T>>>of(
        ArrayList::new,
        (batches, element) -> {
            if (batches.isEmpty() || batches.get(batches.size() - 1).size() == batchSize) {
                batches.add(new ArrayList<>());
            }
            batches.get(batches.size() - 1).add(element);
        },
        (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; },  // NOTE: combining may break batch boundaries
        java.util.Collections::unmodifiableList,
        Collector.Characteristics.IDENTITY_FINISH // omit finisher overhead if not needed
    );
}

// Usage — process items in batches of 100 for bulk-insert
List<List<Product>> batches = catalog.stream()
    .collect(batching(100));
batches.forEach(batch -> db.bulkInsert(batch));
```

**When to write a custom Collector vs. using `gather()` (Java 22+ Gatherers):** Custom `Collector` is the right choice when the result is a final value (a list, map, or aggregated object) — it is the terminal operation. `Stream.gather(Gatherer)` is the right choice when you need a stateful *intermediate* operation (e.g., sliding windows, running totals) that feeds further stream operations. For Java 21 and below, custom `Collector` covers both roles, but a `Gatherer` expresses intent more clearly for intermediate stateful transformations in Java 22+.

### Generics — Recursive Bounds and Intersection Types

Beyond PECS, two advanced generics patterns appear in library design and domain modeling: **recursive (self-referential) bounds** and **intersection type bounds**.

```java
// =========================================================
// Recursive (self-referential) bound: <T extends Comparable<T>>
// =========================================================
// Used when a method needs the elements to be comparable to each other.
// The bound says "T must be comparable to instances of T itself".

public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T min(List<T> list) {
    if (list.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("Empty list");
    T result = list.get(0);
    for (T t : list) {
        if (t.compareTo(result) < 0) result = t;
    }
    return result;
}

// More idiomatic: use Comparable<? super T> to allow subtype comparisons
// (Effective Java Item 31: use Comparable<? super T> not Comparable<T>)
public static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T minPermissive(List<T> list) {
    return list.stream().min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow();
}

// Recursive bound for fluent builders (the F-bounded polymorphism pattern):
// Allows a base builder's methods to return the concrete subclass type, not the base type.
public abstract static class AbstractBuilder<T, B extends AbstractBuilder<T, B>> {
    protected String name;
    protected String description;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public B name(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        return (B) this;    // cast is safe: B is always the concrete subclass
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public B description(String desc) {
        this.description = desc;
        return (B) this;
    }

    public abstract T build();
}

public static final class ProductBuilder
        extends AbstractBuilder<Product, ProductBuilder> {
    private double price;

    public ProductBuilder price(double price) {
        this.price = price;
        return this;  // returns ProductBuilder, not AbstractBuilder
    }

    @Override public Product build() {
        return new Product(name, description, price);
    }
}

// Usage: fluent chain returns the concrete builder type — no casting needed
Product p = new ProductBuilder()
    .name("Widget")           // inherited from AbstractBuilder; returns ProductBuilder
    .description("A widget")  // same
    .price(9.99)              // ProductBuilder-specific; would be inaccessible if base returned AbstractBuilder
    .build();

// =========================================================
// Intersection type bounds: <T extends Runnable & AutoCloseable>
// =========================================================
// Use when a method needs the argument to satisfy multiple interfaces simultaneously.
// Wildcards cannot express intersection bounds; named type parameters can.

public static <T extends Serializable & Comparable<T>> void sortAndSerialize(
        List<T> items, java.io.OutputStream out) throws Exception {
    List<T> sorted = items.stream().sorted().toList();
    try (var oos = new java.io.ObjectOutputStream(out)) {
        oos.writeObject(sorted);
    }
}

// Intersection type in variable declaration (using cast — only at assignment)
// Cast to intersection type: captures that the value satisfies both interfaces
<T extends Runnable & AutoCloseable> void runAndClose(T task) throws Exception {
    task.run();
    task.close();
}

// Practical: a method that accepts any collection that is both Iterable and Closeable
// (e.g., a ResultSet wrapper)
public static <T extends Iterable<String> & AutoCloseable> List<String> drainToList(T source)
        throws Exception {
    try (source) {
        List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
        source.forEach(result::add);
        return List.copyOf(result);
    }
}
```

**Rules for intersection bounds:**
- Classes must come first: `<T extends MyClass & Runnable>` is valid; `<T extends Runnable & MyClass>` is a compile error (a class cannot appear after an interface in an intersection).
- You can intersect at most one class and any number of interfaces: `<T extends Base & Readable & Closeable>` is legal.
- Intersection bounds cannot be expressed with wildcards — they require a named type parameter, which is why they appear in generic method signatures rather than in field or variable declarations.

**Pattern 466** — Staged Builder enforcing mandatory-field order at compile time
```java
// Demonstrates compile-time prevention of incomplete object construction.
// Each stage interface exposes exactly one method returning the next stage.
// build() is only accessible after ALL mandatory stages have been completed.

// The core insight: callers interact with stage interfaces, not Builder.
// Stage interfaces form a typestate chain: ToStage → SubjectStage → BodyStage → OptionalStage.
// Missing a stage means the next stage's methods are not available — compile error, not runtime NPE.
EmailMessage msg = EmailMessage.builder()
    .to("bob@example.com")
    .subject("Q4 Update")
    .body("Please review the attached figures.")
    .from("finance@example.com")  // optional
    .build();
```
Tradeoff: The Staged Builder trades interface boilerplate (N interfaces for N mandatory fields) for compile-time safety. The boilerplate pays off when multiple mandatory fields share the same type (e.g., two `String` parameters — without stages a caller could transpose them and the compiler would not complain). For objects with heterogeneous mandatory field types, `Objects.requireNonNull` inside a standard `build()` catches the same mistake at runtime with less interface ceremony. The F-bounded variant of `AbstractBuilder<T, B extends AbstractBuilder<T, B>>` is the complementary technique for inheritance hierarchies where the base builder's methods must return the concrete subclass type to preserve fluency. [community]

---

**Pattern 467** — `Optional.or()` and `Optional.stream()` for multi-source fallback and Stream integration
```java
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.List;

// Multi-source Optional fallback: .or() chains without unwrapping
Optional<Config> config = localConfig()
    .or(this::remoteConfig)
    .or(this::defaultConfig);

// Stream integration: flatMap(Optional::stream) removes absent elements from Stream<Optional<T>>
List<User> resolvedUsers = userIds.stream()
    .map(userCache::findById)      // Stream<Optional<User>>
    .flatMap(Optional::stream)     // drop absent entries; flatten to Stream<User>
    .toList();
```
Tradeoff: `Optional.or(Supplier<Optional<T>>)` is strictly lazier than `orElseGet(Supplier<T>)` when the fallback source is itself optional — `or()` keeps the value wrapped and only invokes the supplier when the preceding Optional is empty, making it composable without breaking out of the monadic chain. `Optional.stream()` enables idiomatic bridge from Optional-returning repository methods to Stream pipelines without verbose `filter(Optional::isPresent).map(Optional::get)` — the `flatMap(Optional::stream)` idiom appears frequently in repositories that convert `Optional<T>` lookups over a list of IDs into a compact `Stream<T>` of resolved entities. [official]

**Pattern 468** — Generic records as type-safe result and pagination containers
```java
// Result<T>: sealed + records eliminate checked-exception threading through call stacks
public sealed interface Result<T> permits Result.Ok, Result.Err {
    record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {}
    record Err<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {}

    static <T> Result<T> ok(T v)                     { return new Ok<>(v); }
    static <T> Result<T> err(String msg, Throwable t) { return new Err<>(msg, t); }

    default <R> R fold(
            java.util.function.Function<T, R> onOk,
            java.util.function.Function<String, R> onErr) {
        return switch (this) {
            case Ok<T>  ok  -> onOk.apply(ok.value());
            case Err<T> err -> onErr.apply(err.message());
        };
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Generic records inherit all record constraints: no mutable state, no extension (they implicitly extend `java.lang.Record`), and type erasure at runtime. The sealed + record pattern for `Result<T>` is a compile-safe alternative to checked exceptions — the compiler enforces handling of both `Ok` and `Err` cases in a switch expression with no default branch, exactly like checked-exception handling but without polluting method signatures. The limitation is that `Result<T>` does not interoperate with Java's existing exception hierarchy, so bridging back to checked-exception APIs requires an explicit `fold()` call or a `.orElseThrow()` equivalent. Generic `Page<T>` records are widely used in Spring Data–style pagination; the `map()` method on `Page<T>` enables transforming the content type (e.g., `Page<User>` → `Page<UserDto>`) without changing pagination metadata, a pattern that becomes idiomatic once the record is established. [official]

**Pattern 469** — `Collectors.toMap()` with merge function to handle duplicate keys safely
```java
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;

// Merge function keeps the first entry when duplicate keys are encountered
Map<String, Product> catalog = products.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Product::sku,
        p -> p,
        (existing, incoming) -> existing,   // keep first on collision
        LinkedHashMap::new                  // preserve insertion order
    ));

// Merge function to accumulate into a list (when duplicates are intentional)
Map<String, List<Order>> ordersByCustomer = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Order::customerId,
        o -> new ArrayList<>(List.of(o)),
        (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; }
    ));
```
Tradeoff: The 2-argument `Collectors.toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)` throws `IllegalStateException` on the first duplicate key — this is intentional: when uniqueness is a domain invariant, the exception surfaces bad data early. The 3-argument form with a merge function is appropriate when the domain explicitly allows duplicates (e.g., order lines per customer, skus with version history). The 4-argument form adds a map factory; use `LinkedHashMap::new` when insertion order matters (e.g., producing JSON output that preserves field order) or `TreeMap::new` for natural-key sorted output. Never use `(a, b) -> b` (keep-last merge) without a comment explaining why the later entry should win — reviewers will interpret it as a mistake rather than an intentional deduplication strategy. [official]

---

**Pattern 470** — Generics recursive bounds and intersection type constraints
```java
// F-bounded polymorphism for fluent builder hierarchies:
// B extends AbstractBuilder<T, B> ensures methods return the concrete subclass type.
public abstract static class AbstractBuilder<T, B extends AbstractBuilder<T, B>> {
    protected String name;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public B name(String n) { this.name = n; return (B) this; }

    public abstract T build();
}

// Intersection bound: T must satisfy multiple interfaces simultaneously
public static <T extends Serializable & Comparable<T>> List<T> sortedSnapshot(
        Collection<T> source) {
    return source.stream().sorted().collect(Collectors.toList());
}

// Practical: drain an AutoCloseable Iterable in one method
public static <T extends Iterable<String> & AutoCloseable> List<String> drainToList(
        T source) throws Exception {
    try (source) {
        var result = new ArrayList<String>();
        source.forEach(result::add);
        return List.copyOf(result);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: F-bounded polymorphism (`<B extends AbstractBuilder<T, B>>`) is the only Java pattern that enables inherited builder methods to return the concrete subclass type without requiring callers to cast — it is widely used in Lombok-generated builders, Jackson's `ObjectMapper.copy()` pattern, and AssertJ's `AbstractAssert<SELF, ACTUAL>`. The limitation is that the `(B) this` cast inside the base class is unchecked — if a subclass fails to bind `B` to its own type (e.g., `class FooBuilder extends AbstractBuilder<Foo, BarBuilder>`), the cast produces a `ClassCastException` at the call site rather than a compile error; document the self-referential constraint clearly. Intersection bounds (`<T extends A & B>`) are less common but essential for methods that need both serialization and ordering (e.g., serializing a sorted result set), or for resource-handling utilities that combine `Iterable` with `AutoCloseable`. The constraint that a class bound must appear first (`<T extends BaseClass & Interface>`, never `<T extends Interface & BaseClass>`) is enforced by the compiler. [community]
